Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 20:08:07 GMT

UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days.

As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at the Event Complex on the outskirts of Aberdeen, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has been in Paisley and Edinburgh and the prime minister has been in Motherwell.

The SNP is buoyant, its activists gathering for the first time since it won, in May, a fifth consecutive Scottish Parliament election, albeit with fewer seats than they won in 2021.

Next year will mark the moment the party has been in devolved power at Holyrood for 20 years.

It is quite the contrast with where the SNP found itself just two years ago, pulverised by the landslide at the general election in 2024 where Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP.

As I wrote a year ago, the SNP's critics point to what they see as a dismal domestic record, on the NHS and the number of deaths among drug addicts, for instance.

The SNP counter Scotland has more police officers per person than England and Wales and the highest spend per school pupil in the UK.

No matter the arguments, the result in May was clear - the SNP leader and First Minister John Swinney has his own mandate. Little wonder, given the state of the party when he took the job, that the conference brochure has a front page photo of a smiling Swinney cradling a glass of whisky.

And remember it wasn't just an electoral pummelling the SNP was dealing with, but the jaw dropping details which culminated in the jailing of Peter Murrell, the party's former chief executive - and estranged husband of the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon - for embezzling more than £400,000 from the party.

Swinney now looks ahead to a parliamentary term with all that behind them and a new prime minister to deal with in Downing Street.

Burnham and Swinney share a diagnosis that Westminster has failed to deliver and political power is better administered closer to people than it ever has been.

But, crucially, the prime minister sees the "drama" of the constant questions around Scottish independence as a distraction.

For Swinney, independence has been and remains his lifelong political goal.

We have had a glimpse this week as to how that dynamic between the two men may play out.

Burnham's critics, including the SNP, have seen this former Mancunian mayor's devolutionary instincts as having a distinctly English flavour. The prime minister, on his trip to New College Lanarkshire, sought to counter that.

"I do want a good growth in every postcode here, and in the rest of the UK, and I want to work with the first minister to deliver it. We won't agree on everything, but we can agree on something," he said.

"I want us to design a new model together of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, one that puts control in the hands of local people."

Burnham has offered to devolve powers on localised employment support, currently held by the Department of Work and Pensions.

Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland, Douglas Alexander, said Scotland was "one of the most centralised nations in Europe", an assertion flatly rejected by Swinney.

Scotland's first minister has said he wants "much more opportunity for a regional dimension to take forward skills, economic opportunity and planning" and his team acknowledge this vision includes overlaps with the regional combined authorities seen in parts of England, albeit without mayors.

It will be intriguing to observe, given the rivalry and grit that exists between Labour and the SNP, how things develop beyond the prime minister's speech.

Here in Aberdeen, activists have seized upon the prime minister's reflections on Brexit to argue that if he can revisit the outcome of the referendum in 2016 on the European Union, Scots should be able to revisit the one in 2014 on independence.

There have been plenty of mentions too of an exchange in the Commons last month between SNP MP Chris Law and Andy Burnham, when Burnham suggested another Scottish independence referendum could be held, if public opinion showed demand for one.

SNP folk think - perhaps hope - this represents the prime minister's authentic view.

He and Downing Street have seen sought to squash this idea and he said he wanted to "move on" from a debate about Scottish independence.

Privately, senior SNP figures accept the authority to sanction another referendum lies with Westminster and the UK government says no. So, their focus is seeking to steadily build the case for independence in how they choose to govern.

Within the party, a new group called, you guessed it, "Independence" has been set up.

Speaking at its launch event, the SNP's former Policy Convener Toni Giugliano argued that "countries don't become independent by waiting for permission. They do so when support becomes unstoppable and when a national consensus for change is built".

Furthermore, he argued, fundamental questions about what an independent Scotland would look and feel like must be answered now - such as the currency that would be used and how the state pension would work.

These are the long term questions.

For now, the tussle is more short term, as the SNP ponders when the prime minister might call a general election.

Buoyed by its recent victory at Holyrood, the party senses Labour vulnerability in the swathe of seats Labour took from them two years ago.

Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:58:05 GMT

Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office.

Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment.

On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action.

"It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required."

Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post.

The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking".

"Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said.

However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery."

He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian".

Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent.

Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics".

Earlier this year, four of the group's activists were jailed after causing £1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.

In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk.

The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group.

Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month.

Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland.

In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister.

'Well-known' man asks court to stop publication of sexual offence allegation

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:46:14 GMT

An individual described as "well-known" has asked London's High Court to prevent two media organisations from publishing "serious allegations", including of a sexual nature, against him.

The court heard he had submitted medical evidence saying that if the allegations were made public this would "almost certainly" lead to him "attempting to take his own life", and that the prospect of publication had already led to two suicide attempts.

The court was told that Independent Television News and Guardian News & Media had carried out an investigation into the individual's "conduct over a period of years".

The individual, who has been granted anonymity in the court proceedings, denies the allegations.

The court was told that following an investigation that ITN, which produces news for ITV and Channel 4, and Guardian News & Media, which publishes the Guardian, sent two letters to the the well-known individual in the spring of 2026.

As well as denying the allegations, the individual responded with medical reports stating that there was a risk to his life if the information was published.

At an injunction hearing at London's High Court, lawyers representing ITN and Guardian News & Media said that "it would be wrong" for the court to "restrain publication" when the "law provides for a detailed and well-established scheme by which the interests of those at risk of suicide is specially protected by NHS mental health professionals".

The court has also granted anonymity to other individuals in the case.

Two individuals who have agreed to be identified in any ITN and Guardian News & Media report concerning the allegations were given anonymity in the current proceedings by High Court judge Mr Justice Nicklin. The nature of the allegations or how these two journalistic sources relate to them is not known.

A third journalistic source for the ITN and Guardian News & Media investigation has also been granted anonymity in the current proceedings. She has alleged that she was the victim of a sexual offence by the well-known individual.

The court will decide whether the ITN and Guardian News & Media will be permanently prevented from naming the well-known individual and publishing the allegations against him at a trial due to be held later this month.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Dubois and Wardley at career-heaviest for rematch

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:42:22 GMT

This video can not be played

'Life on the line' for Dubois & Wardley in rematch

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley both weighed in at their career-heaviest and promised another explosive encounter in Saturday's heavyweight world-title rematch in London.

WBO champion Dubois tipped the scales at 18st 2lb (115kg) while Wardley came in at 17st 10lb (112kg) before their meeting at the O2 Arena.

The British rivals produced a fight-of-the-year contender in Manchester in May, with Wardley flooring Dubois twice before the Londoner rallied to stop his bloodied and battered opponent in the 11th round.

"I draw confidence from the successes I had in the first fight - getting knockdowns in the first and third," Wardley, 31, said.

"I need to capitalise on those moments better. I'm ready to put on a cleaner performance."

Dubois, 29, is more than 2lb heavier for the rematch, while Wardley has added more than 6lb.

Asked for his prediction, Wardley added: "Revenge, Fabio Wardley, knockout win."

This video can not be played

Wardley and Dubois face-off

Dubois v Wardley 2 - blood, bravery & a heavyweight gamble

Dubois v Wardley 2 - all you need to know

Daniel Dubois (left) has won 23 of his 26 professional fights, with 22 knockouts, while Fabio Wardley has 20 wins, 19 by knockout, one defeat and one draw.

The final pre-fight formalities took place at Old Spitalfields Market in east London, with the two heavyweights taking to the scales amid the bustle of street-food stalls and shoppers.

A couple of hundred fans gathered beneath the market's Victorian roof, some having made the trip specifically for the event while others stopped to see what the fuss was about.

It was a rather subdued affair, with a smaller turnout than when Moses Itauma and Filip Hrgovic weighed in at the same venue in August.

Wardley arrived more than an hour before the event, appearing as relaxed as he has throughout fight week and even stopping for selfies with supporters afterwards.

Dubois arrived much later and has appeared in little mood for conversation this week. Once again, he was typically economical with his words.

"I know him now and know what to expect. I'm ready to go and do my job," the Londoner said. "I'm ready for a tear up. Let's go."

There was no drama at the obligatory face-off, despite the fierce rivalry that has developed between them, and two-time world champion Dubois was quick to leave the stage afterwards.

With 41 knockouts between them from 43 victories, few expect the contest to go the distance.

Wardley, sporting Ipswich Town's newly-launched third kit with his name printed on the sleeve, was still bearing the scars of his punishing defeat in Manchester five months ago.

A cut across the bridge of his nose, first sustained during his 2024 draw with Frazer Clarke, reopened against Dubois and left his face badly swollen and bloodied.

The punishment he absorbed has raised questions over whether his decision to take an immediate rematch has come too soon but Wardley remains confident he can reverse the result.

"It's simply seek and destroy now," he said.

Promoter Frank Warren is predicting a "blockbuster" 2027 for the heavyweight division, with lucrative fights awaiting Saturday's winner.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in Cardiff on 11 December, while British prospect Itauma is set to return in January following his world-title defeat by Hrgovic.

Warren confirmed there is no clause for a third fight between Dubois and Wardley but the Queensberry Promotions boss refused to rule out a trilogy if the Ipswich fighter avenges the only defeat on his record.

"If that happens it's a natural fight," Warren said. "That's what's so intriguing about this. Who will they fight next year? We want to find out who is the best."

Police feared Andrew would delay search by saying King owned his home, documents show

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:37:26 GMT

Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might have tried to stop officers entering his home in Sandringham by saying it belonged to the King, according to legal documents.

Senior officers were concerned the King's brother could argue it was not his property, and that separate legal permission would have to be sought before officers could enter it.

Delaying access would have risked the loss of evidence, the force said.

The background to Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February has emerged in legal documents, when police asked a judge for warrants to raid the former prince's homes.

Lawyers for Mountbatten-Windsor successfully argued those warrants were unlawful in court last week.

Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest came after the US Department of Justice published material which showed his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The BBC has approached Mountbatten-Windsor's representatives for comment and he has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The arrest of the former prince, on 19 February, was on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

On 18 February, Thames Valley Police asked for permission from the Central Criminal Court for warrants to search Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.

The request included the police outlining the scenarios in which they believed they would need search warrants to ensure access to the properties.

They feared that Mountbatten-Windsor or his legal team would want to see "judicial authority" before allowing the police to enter, the documents show.

The police were concerned that Mountbatten-Windsor or his representatives could argue that the Sandringham Estate was the property of King Charles - and that it would be a slow process getting a separate right of access.

Such a delay would "frustrate the nature and purpose of the search," said the police, in their application for search warrants.

There was also a concern that no one would be present at the property and that media attention could be drawn to the police presence outside while not being able to enter.

Any of those delays could have meant the police would have been unable to gather the evidence they wanted, they argued - and "given the gravity of this investigation", the police asked for search warrants.

In separate documents filed as part of Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge against the warrants, he said: "These assertions were no more than speculation."

The documents also detail the type of information the police were seeking inside the properties.

They say: "Paper-work, diaries, business records or other documentary evidence of AMW's [Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's] time as Special Representative for Trade and Investment.

"Further evidence as to any action, communication, comment or in relation to matters following the release of material by the FBI concerning the late Jeffrey Epstein as AMW will be aware that Thames Valley Police is conducting an assessment.

"Specifically mobile phone(s) and computer(s) [to include electronic notebooks, surfaces, iPads and any older electronic devices," which could have held information about links to Epstein at the time when Mountbatten-Windsor had been the UK's trade envoy."

The documents show the search of Royal Lodge, Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor, continued until 24 February.

They also reveal his police interview at Aylesham Police Station began at 15:00 GMT and he was released under investigation at 18:36.

The legal documents give details of why the police wanted to talk to Mountbatten-Windsor, including the claim that when he was a UK trade envoy he had forwarded Jeffrey Epstein official reports from official visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong.

There was also a claim, arising from emails in the Epstein files released in the US, that Mountbatten-Windsor had briefed Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan.

Also mentioned is the suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor held meetings with a private investment firm and then suggesting to Epstein that he might invest in the company.

The legal documents have emerged after a High Court hearing earlier this month in which Thames Valley Police accepted the warrants it used to search Mountbatten-Windsor's homes were unlawful.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers used a judicial review to successfully challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.

Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.

That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.

But items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.

Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.

Thames Valley Police force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.

At the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.

However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."

Rahm sacrifices £75m to secure exit from LIV Golf

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 17:52:10 GMT

Jon Rahm joined LIV Golf after leaving the PGA Tour in December 2023

Jon Rahm will give up a reported £75m owed to him by LIV Golf after reaching a separation agreement that will secure his exit from the league.

The league filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its multibillion-dollar backing.

Spaniard Rahm was listed as the organisation's top unsecured creditor when LIV filed for bankruptcy, with $7.4m (£5.5m) owed to him for the rest of the 2026 season alone.

ESPN reported he is owed about $100m (£75m), external from the remainder of the $300m, (£222m) contract he signed when he left the PGA Tour for LIV Golf in December 2023.

Despite LIV securing a possible $300m in financing from BC Partners Credit to try and move forward with 'LIV 2.0', Rahm has deemed the proposed terms are "unacceptable".

Instead, he has waived his entire claim in order to have a "complete economic walk-away".

However, he will take the rights to 'Legion XIII' - the name of the LIV team Rahm captained - although he will not be allowed to use it to make a team in TGL - the indoor high-tech golf league launched by Tiger Woods and Rory McIlroy.

Rahm was the most high-profile name to join LIV when he left the PGA Tour.

Some players, including Brooks Koepka, have since returned to the PGA Tour, which rewrote its rules in December to allow the five-time major winner to come back, subject to certain sanctions.

Rahm did not follow suit and remained under long-term contract with LIV, but in May reached a deal with the DP World Tour - formerly the European Tour - to retain his membership and remain eligible for next year's Ryder Cup.

LIV golfers are automatically banned for a year by the PGA Tour. The DP World Tour offers a pathway because the leading 10 players on the European circuit currently gain access to PGA Tour membership.

In August, former world number one Rahm won his third straight LIV season title.

He previously said he had no regrets over joining LIV and backed organisers to make it sustainable.

Off Campus star collaboration 'gave me chills', says Babydoll singer

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:57:00 GMT

The singer behind the TikTok viral hit Babydoll says collaborating with an Off Campus star was "mind-boggling".

Jamie Miller, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, was close to calling it quits on his music career at the start of 2026, deciding it was his "last chance", financially and emotionally.

But over the summer everything changed when Babydoll caught the attention of people on social media, leading to a viral dance, his first UK top 10 single, and reaching number one in the US iTunes pop chart.

When Miller saw a comment from actor Antonio Cipriano, saying he "needed this song", he sent him a message suggesting he feature on a recording – then "panicked" and added "haha, joking".

"I'm a fan of Antonio's voice, and I have been a fan for a long time," he said.

"He messaged back and was like, 'If you're actually not joking, I'd be honoured'."

Cipriano headed to Los Angeles, where Miller now lives, and they recorded Babydoll on the day they first met.

"It was the best time ever," said Miller.

"We're coming up at the same time, he has an amazing career in acting and I feel like the stars aligned even for us to do this and the world is rallying around us as a duo too. The opportunities that we're having right now are incredible."

Amazon Prime Video's ice hockey romance series Off Campus – based on a book series by Elle Kennedy - has similarly taken the world by storm this year, ranking as the third most-watched series launch in the platform's history.

It has raised the profile of numerous artists, with a soundtrack merging old favourites with new music.

Asked if he would like to be involved with the series in future, Miller said: "I'm such a fan of the show. I think it's absolutely incredible what they're doing, what Antonio is doing. In any capacity, I would love to. We'll see."

On Friday, the original version of Babydoll moved from number three to number two in the official UK charts - beaten only by Taylor Swift's Patient Zero.

Miller also recently supported The Jonas Brothers on the US leg of their tour, and said bringing Cipriano out as a guest star at some of the shows was "mind-boggling".

"I think the easiest thing about it was we're doing it together, for the first time. It was his first arena, it was my first arena, and I think that's the most amazing situation to be in, because we can lean on each other.

"Backstage we would say to each other, 'we're so lucky, our lives are not normal, we're going out to play for 20,000 people, what are we doing bro?'.

"Introducing him gave me chills because, as well as my dreams coming true right now, his dreams are too.

"It's so nice and needed, to have a friend who can guide you through."

At 19, Miller competed in The Voice UK, coming third place with coach Jennifer Hudson.

But his love for music first began accidentally, when he took part in a primary school show.

"If you auditioned for the play, then you got to skip out math class," he recalled.

"Just to see the reaction from the teachers after they asked me to sing a song, was just absolutely like 'I want to do this, this is actually incredible.'

"All my mates were rugby players and football players, whereas I just wanted to do music. After that one audition, I was hooked."

Now 29, Miller admits the past couple of years have been "really tough", adding changes in the music industry and in his personal life had left him feeling quite lost.

"Going into this year was my last chance to try and cut through. This industry is really hard, it's really expensive as well," he said.

"I think the thing with success, people think you have a lot of money... I didn't really see that side of that. So financially, this year, I couldn't really make it work anymore. I was on my last legs."

He continued: "Going into this year, I'd built my career off sad music, and I'm not sad anymore, I'm happy.

"I think Babydoll maybe brought a bit of light to a world that needed it. I know that sounds really cliché to say, but I do feel that is true, we needed some joy."

Miller said the whirlwind nature of Babydoll's success had led to accusations he was an "industry plant" - someone who appears to be self-made, while actually having backing from significant investors or supporters.

"I wish I was an industry plant, I've done this for nine years," he said with a laugh.

"At first, I was getting told this was coming across as a gimmick. But that's the thing, I'm not trying to be cool, I'm trying to just have fun.

"Literally, my mentality was 'if I'm going out, and this is my last chance at music, I'm going out my way.'"

Miller said he "never had any social media campaign" planned and it "happened the most organic way possible".

As the Babydoll dance took hold of social media, Miller collaborated with an array of stars including actors Jennifer Love Hewitt, Lucy Hale and Julianne Hough, as well as popstar Meghan Trainor.

"All these incredible people I've been able to do it with, they've said it themselves, they've said 'we needed this song'.

"From all sides of the world, it's kind of unified people in a way, and it's just a beautiful thing to be a part of something that made someone smile."

Miller said he was "proud" of his new music and was excited to share his latest album with the world and to tour it – in particular, he said, to bring it to Wales.

But he added the non-stop nature of the past couple of months had been "really hard to process".

"It feels like so many life changes are happening around me, but I'm still the same person. It's dystopian, in a way.

"Especially being from Wales, you don't really see stuff like this happening to people all the time. Tom Jones is absolutely incredible, but I feel like he's really been the one that's flown the flag, and rightfully so.

"I'm very appreciative for everything that's going on right now, and thank my lucky stars. I just hope I'm doing Wales proud, to be honest."

NHS staff may have breached tiger attack victim's medical records

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:53:07 GMT

Medical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, a spokesperson has said.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday.

In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case.

It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".

Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives.

They said: "We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so.

"We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits.

"The trust has commenced an investigation to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches and the actions of these individuals.

"We have also reported this matter to the Information Commissioner's Office and we will continue to keep William's family informed as our investigation progresses."

An inquest at Doncaster Coroner's Court on Thursday heard that Chapman had died of "multiple traumatic injuries".

Chapman had attended the park at about 13:30 BST on Saturday, climbed over two fences and entered the tiger enclosure.

After the attack, park staff secured the tiger and paramedics attended, who confirmed Chapman's death at the scene, the inquest was told.

Senior coroner Nicola Mundy said Chapman had a history of mental illness, a diagnosis of schizophrenia and had suffered previous bouts of psychosis.

The inquest heard that the 24-year-old was under adult mental health services in Doncaster, but was "highly functioning and independent with no care requirements".

The self-employed online trader was born in Chichester, West Sussex, and lived in Doncaster at the time of his death.

Ex-top official Robbins reaches settlement with government over sacking

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:38:18 GMT

Sir Olly Robbins has reached an out-of-court settlement with the government, after he was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson to be US ambassador.

Sir Olly was fired by then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer earlier this year, after it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The FDA union, which represented him in the legal action, said Sir Olly had been made a "scapegoat" to "mask the misjudgement" of Sir Keir.

How much Sir Olly received in the settlement has not been made public.

It came after he requested a judicial review over the decision to dismiss him.

A government spokesperson said Sir Olly "had a distinguished public service career over three decades".

A statement added: "The government has reached a settlement with Sir Oliver following his dismissal. We will not be commenting further on HR matters."

Lord Mandelson was announced as the UK's ambassador to the US in December 2024, before in-depth vetting had been carried out, and formally took up the role in February 2025 after being granted security clearance.

Just seven months later, he was sacked after further information emerged about his previous friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Sir Olly was sacked in April, in the wake of a Guardian story that revealed the peer's security clearance had been granted despite vetting officials raising concerns, with the prime minister later saying he was "furious" he had not been informed at the time.

Sir Keir has previously said he sacked Sir Olly after not accepting his explanation for why clearance was granted, telling MPs in April: "I did ask him, and I did not accept his explanation. That is why I sacked him."

Sir Olly has since defended his role in the process, saying that the government's vetting processes must "remain absolutely confidential".

He previously told MPs that he had not seen the documentation from UK Security Vetting, the government's in-house vetting unit, containing their vetting assessment of Lord Mandelson.

He said that instead, he was given an oral briefing, during which he was told the vetting agency considered Mandelson to be a "borderline case", but that the Foreign Office may wish to grant clearance with "appropriate risk management".

Dave Penman, head of the FDA union, said: "This settlement may bring an end to the Judicial Review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.

"The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgement of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations - which is quite the feat.

"We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process."

Sir Olly said: "I am grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time.

"I want to thank the FDA for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life".

Sir Olly, who was appointed to the Foreign Office job in early 2025, has held a number of senior civil service roles and was previously the government's lead official during Brexit negotiations with the EU.

Do Manchester City have any grounds to win their appeal?

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:17:01 GMT

This video can not be played

BBC Sport's Dale Johnson, Dan Roan, Laura Scott and Sami Mokbel assess Manchester City's position

Manchester City face "substantial hurdles" if they are to have any chance of winning their appeal after being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, a leading lawyer has told BBC Sport.

City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating "sham contracts" to inflate sponsorship deals by £830m.

The club have said they are "innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League" and they have "irrefutable evidence" the ruling "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

In their appeal, City will argue the payments were made by the United Arab Emirates government as a shareholder of the sponsors, while there are inconsistencies in the Commission's judgement.

Therefore, City say the sponsorship amounts were legitimate and not topped up by the owners.

James Severn, Member of the London Solicitor Litigation Association (LSLA) and Partner at Penningtons Manches Cooper, told BBC Sport the appeal is "not simply an opportunity to invite a new panel" to get the verdict overturned.

"City will need to identify a material error of law, principle or fact, or serious procedural unfairness, which materially affected the Commission's decision," Severn said.

"The Appeal Board nevertheless has broad powers to allow or dismiss the appeal, vary the decision or make any other order it considers appropriate."

Manchester City have been sponsored by Etihad since May 2009

Etihad Airways, one of City's principle sponsors at the centre of the case, had previously stated that the Abu Dhabi government had not paid for its sponsorship of Manchester City.

That came in court documents as part of a US investigation in New York in 2015.

City will argue this does not have the full context of the situation and is not proof they have been inconsistent with evidence.

The club are adamant government documents fully support their case - but, Severn said, if these were already available to the Commission they may not be much use in an appeal.

"The bank statements, government records and contemporaneous payment documents could be powerful evidence if they establish a clear audit trail showing the disputed funds came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the owners," Severn added.

"However, if that evidence was already before the Commission, which nevertheless concluded that the arrangements were a sham, City will face an uphill struggle to demonstrate the finding was materially wrong."

Shortly before City's appeal was confirmed, Etihad Airways issued a statement saying it had never been "given the opportunity by the Premier League to be represented, to provide relevant information, or to ensure the accuracy and fairness of information relied upon".

Severn said Etihad Airways' complaint "does not, of itself, establish procedural unfairness".

"Etihad was not the respondent and is unlikely to have had an independent right to participate in the proceedings," Severn said. "It is likely to have been open to either party to obtain and present such evidence to the Commission.

"If the Appeal Board is prepared to consider new evidence from Etihad, it is likely to carry greater weight if supported by contemporaneous documents."

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City’s inflatable banana craze

A key part of City's defence will be that the Independent Commission relied too heavily on the emails obtained through the Football Leaks files.

"If City can demonstrate the Commission fundamentally misunderstood the emails, failed to consider their proper context or reached conclusions inconsistent with other contemporaneous documents, that could amount to a material factual error," Severn added.

"City's difficulty is that the Commission heard extensive witness and documentary evidence but nevertheless made serious findings of sham arrangements and disguised owner funding."

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport the commission found "the documents were retrofitted to fit the crime".

"The Commission must have concluded that the evidence and the credibility of the witnesses put up by Manchester City were poor," Maguire said.

"However, from a legal point of view, this is an area they could attack if Manchester City's team can prove that the commission itself was a flawed construct in the sense that the members were Premier League picks rather than Manchester City's, and therefore the deck was stacked against the club to begin with.

"But that seems remote."

Severn added that the retired senior judges and leading barristers, who sat on the Commission, have "spent their careers interpreting complicated facts, dealing with witnesses and applying relevant weight to evidence".

While adding that it would be "impossible to assess reliably" the chances of City winning their appeal, Severn added that "doing so will not be easy".

But Maguire believes that while it will be difficult for City to be successful, "there is a route".

City have brought in Mark Howard KC to advise the club in their appeal, while Etihad Airways has enlisted the services of respected law firm Quinn Emanuel.

Maguire said: "Given the lawyers that have been recruited by Manchester City, they may go down what's been described to me as a mess and noise approach.

"That means trying to discredit everything to do with the process of the Commission rather than necessarily the evidence that was presented.

"I've seen the documents that Abu Dhabi presented to the New York case. I'm not a lawyer, but from an accounting point of view, they can be seen in more than one way."

Even though Premier League regulations state an appeal must be heard within 12 weeks, or by Christmas Eve, Severn added that "given the scale and complexity of the proceedings, a final outcome may not be known for some time".

Nurse stole £750k from 99-year-old woman for cosmetic surgery and home improvements

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:07:37 GMT

A nurse who stole £750,000 from a vulnerable 99-year-old and spent the money on cosmetic surgery and home improvements has been struck off.

Rebecca Louise Burwood exploited the resident who was living at Bryn Yr Haul Care Home in Mold, Flintshire, where she was deputy manager, for her own personal and financial gain.

She coerced the pensioner from 2017 to 2023 and also bought a car and campervan with the stolen money, as well as obtaining ownership of the woman's home.

A Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) hearing found Burwood's fitness to practise was impaired by reason of misconduct and imposed a striking-off order, meaning she will be removed from the nursing register.

The NMC hearing was told Burwood had a longstanding relationship with the woman before she moved into the home in 2018.

The panel heard the resident had no family members and was vulnerable after a fall. She was dependent on Burwood for friendship and social contact.

It found that, between 2017 and 2023, Burwood abused a position of trust and power, becoming the resident's lasting power of attorney, while also overseeing her care.

Burwood withdrew money from the woman's bank account, accepted ownership of her house and received thousand of pounds, which was used for her own benefit, including for building work and the purchase of vehicles.

Evidence presented showed more than £370,000 had left the resident's account over five years, with £160,000 of that from making large cash withdrawals at ATMs.

She also took the resident to the solicitors and got her to transfer the ownership of her £400,000 house.

The hearing was told there was "evidence to show Mrs Burwood used the funds for house improvements, utility bills and council tax", and there were "allegations that Mrs Burwood used some of the funds for personal cosmetic surgery".

She convinced the resident to pay £20,000 for a car and £9,000 for a campervan, which she said was purchased so the pair could go on days outs.

Burwood claimed the work on her home had been so the elderly woman could live with her in the event of another outbreak of Covid - however it had been paid for before any Covid lockdown in the UK.

Burwood told the tribunal the woman asked her to withdraw cash from her bank account and make donations to charities each week.

She claimed the donations, which were between £250 and £500 each time, would usually go towards charities that supported the blind or those with heart issues.

Burwood said she would either put the cash in charity pots while she was out and about, or hand donations directly to staff in local charity shops.

Her legal representative Victoria Rees said the resident had told her "she didn't want anything to be left by the time she died, as she didn't want the government to have her money", adding Burwood "didn't keep any records of the amount of money she withdrew or the amount of money she donated".

The pensioner's bank referred the matter to North Wales Police and the force launched an investigation.

The resident's bank account was frozen following concerns about spending, but Burwood attempted to have restrictions lifted and took the resident to a bank branch.

Bank staff claimed Burwood was "almost blackmailing" the woman, and told her to ask for the accounts to be unlocked.

The panel found Burwood told the woman she would not be able to take her on outings if she could not access her money.

The hearing was told the resident later told safeguarding staff she was shocked by the amount of money that had been spent from her account.

Another nurse also said they overheard Burwood tell the woman, "I will give you the money back" and "sign here".

She reported the conversation as evidence of financial abuse and it was decided Burwood would only make supervised visits to the woman.

Burwood claimed she had only been asking the pensioner to "sign a condolence card" and it was "not in relation to signing a document".

She claimed the resident's eyesight was "very poor" so she had held the card for her, showed her where she should sign and stopped her from signing over the printed words in the card.

Police investigated, but the woman did not want to take further action as she described Burwood as a friend, and believed she had "learned from her mistakes".

The panel concluded there had been a significant imbalance of power in the relationship.

In its ruling, the panel said Burwood had engaged in a "sustained, calculated course of conduct" and had manipulated the resident for personal gain.

It added Burwood had taken advantage of the trust the woman had placed in her and "weaponised" it against her.

The panel also found Burwood acted dishonestly by failing to tell her employer she held financial lasting power of attorney for a resident at the care home where she worked.

It said her actions amounted to serious misconduct, breached fundamental nursing standards and caused both financial and emotional harm.

In its decision, the committee said Burwood's actions were "deplorable" and she was "morally culpable", adding that public confidence in the profession would be undermined if a finding of impairment was not made.

The panel determined Burwood's conduct was "morally reprehensible, showed premeditated behaviour and indicated a deep-seated attitudinal problem".

It determined her behaviour fell far below the standards expected of a registered nurse.

Burwood said she "deeply regretted her actions" adding she "saw the resident as her nanna" as an explanation for why she crossed professional boundaries.

The victim has since died, but had only been left with enough money to pay for 23 months of care before the council would have had to step in.

James Bradford, operations director at Bryn Yr Haul nursing home, said the team there was "deeply saddened by this incident" and "extend our sincere apologies to everyone affected".

"The welfare and safeguarding of our residents remain our absolute priority," he said.

"We fully support the NMC's decision and, since these events, there have been changes in management, and our safeguarding policies and procedures have been reviewed to ensure the continued safety and wellbeing of everyone in our care."

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:00:30 GMT

A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.

Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.

This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.

While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".

Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.

He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.

This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.

Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.

Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.

Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.

Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.

Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.

The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.

An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."

He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.

Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".

"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."

Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.

In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.

"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."

"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".

That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.

"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.

"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."

All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.

Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.

But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.

The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.

I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."

Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

Does Scott's Disney+ exit unmask wider issue in coverage of women's game?

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:49:55 GMT

Alex Scott regularly presents the BBC's live coverage of the Women's Super League

On Thursday, former England footballer Alex Scott stepped away from Disney+'s coverage of the Women's Champions League after two rounds of matches.

The streaming giant is in the second season of a five-year deal to cover European football's flagship competition and this year introduced new formats, including a watchalong show with Scott alternating presenting duties with Shebahn Aherne.

However, it has had some technical issues and been criticised for a difficult opening night that included an unscheduled advert break during Arsenal's game against HB Koge.

Scott has not said why she left this role but told BBC Sport she was "grateful" for the opportunities she had at Disney+ and hoped to "continue working together" in the future.

But does her sudden departure highlight the challenges broadcasters face covering the women's game in an ever-changing media landscape?

Ad break in Women's Champions League was unscheduled

The explosion in interest in women's football during the past five years has been spearheaded by two of the biggest broadcasters in the UK – Sky Sports and the BBC.

In snapping up the Champions League before the 2025-26 season, Disney added its heft into the game, recognising its potential for capturing new audiences.

Indeed, Scott herself has launched her own YouTube show this season, One More Word WSL, which she presents on a Sunday night alongside ex-England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams.

Broadcasters have ramped up experiments with format, style and tone - Disney+ even had a dog on set during their coverage - but perhaps unsurprisingly, not every idea proves to be successful.

Journalist Carrie Dunn, who has covered women's sport for more than two decades, says opinions about coverage reflect a tension at the heart of the game.

"The challenge broadcasters are finding is that they are not sure who the audience is," she says. "A lot of it is targeted at a new generation and it's clearly not for people who have watched women's football for longer.

"Often it's a resourcing issue. Budgets are being cut and you're finding the same presenters and the same pundits trying to be all things to all people. It just doesn't work."

Alex Scott, Fara Williams, Ellen White and Steph Houghton are among the former England internationals that front coverage of women's football in the UK

In the summer, the BBC announced its Women's Super League highlights show would not return for the 2026-27 season, but insisted it remained "fully committed to women's football".

To illustrate, it cited a bespoke new YouTube channel, the introduction of a debate show entitled The Women's Football Fallout, exclusively on BBC iPlayer, and the availability of clips and analysis on the BBC Sport website as evidence.

The decisions are part of a move away from linear television that the BBC says reflects changing audience habits.

It is a shift in emphasis that comes with difficulties.

"It's a tough balance where you've got to explain some context to the new fans without patronising your older fans," Dunn adds. "That's something the major broadcasters have not found a solution to yet.

"If people are willing to take risks on different kinds of women's sports coverage, that's fantastic.

"But start by choosing one thing and doing it really well – and that's got to be decent match coverage."

Watch The Women's Football Fallout on BBC iPlayer

Follow BBC Sport's Women's Football channel on YouTube

Bigger and more ambitious than ever - women's football on the BBC

Aston Villa interim boss Brian Sorensen started as a coach in Denmark in 2009 and believes the innovations in women's football coverage are a good thing, even if some do not always work.

"A lot of positive things are happening, but there are a lot of new areas that we haven't tried before," he said. "Sometimes it's trial and error and finding the right way for us.

"From when I started - with the worst live stream you've ever seen - to where we are now, is a very big improvement."

Andree Jeglertz, manager of champions Manchester City, agrees, acknowledging that the fact women's football has a much bigger audience now is a huge positive.

"I think the most important thing is that it is available and that people can see the best players on TV or live," he said. "The more, the better, no matter what."

Tottenham counterpart Martin Ho says the onus is on clubs and players to ensure the product on the field is worth watching.

"Whatever a broadcast partner decides to do, they have their reasons for it," he said. "All we can control is that we put on a good advert for women's football."

Finally, Chelsea's Sonia Bompastor suggested she was open to new expressions in covering the game provided they were properly analysed.

"Anytime you try to do something new, you will please some people and upset others," she told BBC Sport. "Sometimes you need to be patient and analyse as it is too soon to say if something is right or not."

Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:36:39 GMT

Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.

Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.

On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.

His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".

The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.

"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.

Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.

The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

Former Sale Sharks lock Andrews dies at team hotel in La Rochelle

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:33:04 GMT

Andrews joined Sale in February 2024 and made 45 appearances for the club before heading back to his native South Africa at the end of last season

Former Sale second row Hyron Andrews has died at his Johannesburg Lions' team hotel before their Champions Cup match at La Rochelle on Saturday.

A statement from SA Rugby stated that his death had been an "accident" and that the 31-year-old had "died after a fall".

The public prosecutor in La Rochelle is investigating, with local reports claiming Andrews suffered a heart attack while in the shower.

"We are heartbroken by the passing of Hyron," said Lions chief executive Rudolf Straeuli.

"He was not only a gifted rugby player, but also a cherished member of our Lions family having recently joined us this season.

"On behalf of our chairman, Mr Altmann Allers, the board and everyone at the Lions, I extend our deepest sympathies to [Andrews' wife] Maighlin, their young sons Hendrix and Emerson and the entire Andrews family.

"We stand with them in their sorrow and will remember Hyron with great affection and respect."

The Lions will fulfil their fixture against La Rochelle, which kicks off at 17:30 BST, in Andrews' honour.

A moment's silence will be observed at all the opening round's fixtures with organisers EPCR extending their sympathies to Andrews' family.

"This is terrible and distressing news; our hearts go out to Hyron's family and the whole Lions rugby community," said Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union.

"There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maighlin, and for his extended family, friends, team-mates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow.

"His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him."

Andrews began his career at the Sharks in Durban, where he played alongside a clutch of Springbok Rugby World Cup winners including Siya Kolisi, Eben Etzebeth and Lukhanyo Am

Andrews left Sale in the summer to return to his native South Africa. He made 45 appearances for the club after arriving in February 2024 from the Durban-based Sharks as injury cover for England international lock Jonny Hill.

"Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant team-mate," said Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson.

"He was so skilled on the field but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with.

"He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him.

"It was a big move for Hyron and his wife Maighlin to come to England, but he truly made a second home in Manchester. It was incredible to see how he and his family embraced the club and area.

"Most importantly, he was a loving husband to Maighlin and a doting father to his two gorgeous boys. It was an absolute privilege to get to know him and it's just absolutely devastating for everyone."

While he was yet to earn senior international honours, Andrews had represented the Junior Springboks in 2015.

Andrews' death comes 10 years on from the sudden death of Munster coach Anthony Foley in Paris before a Champions Cup fixture.

Foley, 42, died in his sleep on the eve of a match against Racing 92 after a heart condition caused fluid to build up in his lungs.

Munster's present-day players will wear commemorative tops, featuring the Munster club crest and Foley's shirt number eight as part of their pre-match routine at their match against Racing on Saturday.

The Lions, who play their home matches at Ellis Park, are making their first appearance in Europe's premier club competition, with South African sides introduced into the continental competition in the 2022-23 season.

They have won two of their first three matches in the United Rugby Championship so far this season, including beating defending champions Leinster in their first game of their campaign.

Andrews had played in all three games, making his first start for his new club in Saturday's 57-15 defeat by the Bulls.

In an interview with the Mapantsula a Rugby Show,, external published earlier this week, Andrews talked about the various Johannesburg attractions he has visited since arriving in the city.

"We work hard here, it's good to decompress, get away and spend some time with the family," he said.

"When the family is happy, you are happy and it shows when you go to work."

The Lions will fulfil their fixture against La Rochelle, which kicks off at 17:30 BST, in Andrews' honour.

A moment's silence will be observed at all the opening round's fixtures with organisers EPCR extending their sympathies to Andrews' family.

"This is terrible and distressing news; our hearts go out to Hyron's family and the whole Lions rugby community," said Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union.

"There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maighlin, and for his extended family, friends, team-mates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow.

"His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him."

Andrews began his career at the Sharks in Durban, where he played alongside a clutch of Springbok Rugby World Cup winners including Siya Kolisi, Eben Etzebeth and Lukhanyo Am

Andrews left Sale in the summer to return to his native South Africa. He made 45 appearances for the club after arriving in February 2024 from the Durban-based Sharks as injury cover for England international lock Jonny Hill.

"Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant team-mate," said Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson.

"He was so skilled on the field but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with.

"He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him.

"It was a big move for Hyron and his wife Maighlin to come to England, but he truly made a second home in Manchester. It was incredible to see how he and his family embraced the club and area.

"Most importantly, he was a loving husband to Maighlin and a doting father to his two gorgeous boys. It was an absolute privilege to get to know him and it's just absolutely devastating for everyone."

While he was yet to earn senior international honours, Andrews had represented the Junior Springboks in 2015.

Andrews' death comes 10 years on from the sudden death of Munster coach Anthony Foley in Paris before a Champions Cup fixture.

Foley, 42, died in his sleep on the eve of a match against Racing 92 after a heart condition caused fluid to build up in his lungs.

Munster's present-day players will wear commemorative tops, featuring the Munster club crest and Foley's shirt number eight as part of their pre-match routine at their match against Racing on Saturday.

The Lions, who play their home matches at Ellis Park, are making their first appearance in Europe's premier club competition, with South African sides introduced into the continental competition in the 2022-23 season.

They have won two of their first three matches in the United Rugby Championship so far this season, including beating defending champions Leinster in their first game of their campaign.

Andrews had played in all three games, making his first start for his new club in Saturday's 57-15 defeat by the Bulls.

In an interview with the Mapantsula a Rugby Show,, external published earlier this week, Andrews talked about the various Johannesburg attractions he has visited since arriving in the city.

"We work hard here, it's good to decompress, get away and spend some time with the family," he said.

"When the family is happy, you are happy and it shows when you go to work."

Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:31:04 GMT

Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.

The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.

"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.

Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.

"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.

Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.

The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.

Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.

All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."

But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.

There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.

American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."

In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

Despite the video evidence and testimony, the Israeli prime minister's office said the facts remained unclear and were under investigation.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.

As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.

Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.

The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.

Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.

What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:21:32 GMT

A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.

Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.

The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.

Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.

He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."

Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end.

"Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."

Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.

They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.

Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.

The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.

"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.

His failure to establish that the window was not closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.

"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences," he said.

The judge added there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.

She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".

In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".

While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said there was no testimony he was drunk.

After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".

He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.

"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.

He described his client as an "incredible father".

"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."
