Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:06:59 GMT

A woman who alleges she was indecently assaulted by Russell Brand has told his trial she was left feeling "bewildered and confused".

The woman, who worked at MTV at the time, said the entertainer went from "jovial" to a "wild-eyed maniac" as he attempted, she alleged, to pull her into a toilet.

Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

The woman gave evidence on Friday from behind a screen at Southwark Crown Court in London, on the third day of Brand's trial.

She told the jury the alleged incident at MTV lasted for about 20 seconds, adding: "It was a very short exchange."

Asked how she felt after the alleged attack by Brand, the woman said: "Bewildered, confused, 'what the hell happened there?'"

She said Brand went from someone who was "affable" to a "wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet".

"I was confused that that actually just happened - anyone would be," she said.

The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.

After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it.

"He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."

Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.

The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.

She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door.

"He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".

Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."

She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.

The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away.

"I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.

The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.

She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".

Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."

But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said.

Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand.

"I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.

Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary.

"You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said.

"It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."

The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."

The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."

Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."

The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."

The woman was speaking after a former flatmate of Brand's, Andrew Dobson, earlier told the jury that "sex was a huge preoccupation" for the entertainer.

Dobson gave evidence after another woman told the court on Thursday that Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room in Bournemouth in 1999.

She said she had met Brand, before he was famous, while she was attending the Labour Party conference.

Dobson told the court on Friday he attended the Bournemouth conference and had written music for a fringe event that Brand was part of.

Karmy-Jones asked Dobson how he would describe Brand's character as he got to know him before he was famous.

Dobson told the court Brand was a "very vibrant character, very egotistical".

"I would say lively," he continued. "Sort of quite demanding and persuasive. I think erratic would be maybe a slightly better term."

Dobson also told the court that "sex was a huge preoccupation for him", referring to Brand.

He said he recalled a couple of nights when "clearly the pursuit of getting somebody in bed would be a preoccupation" for Brand.

The jury heard that Dobson was staying in the same guesthouse with Brand and other cast members.

The morning after Brand is alleged to have raped a woman, he returned to the place where some of the cast had been staying, the jury heard.

Asked by the prosecutor to describe the "circumstances of how he came home", Dobson replied: "My primary recollection is very hurried and rushed... I recall Russell coming in and suddenly an urgency we had to leave, things being really hurried".

The prosecutor asked the witness: "Where did urgency come from?"

Dobson replied: "I can't recall anything specific that was said. I only remember the atmosphere and panicked, urgent. Feeling tense and confusing."

He went on to tell the jury there had been an "abrupt change of atmosphere" from what had been a "fun week" to an "abrupt change of tone".

Under cross-examination by Brand's barrister, it was put to Dobson that in his witness statement he said that Brand was one of few men he knew that women would swoon over.

Dobson replied: "He was certainly charismatic".

Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues.

Norwegian teen 'hitman' jailed over UK murder plot

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 13:43:21 GMT

A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.

Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard.

During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday.

The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."

The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes.

"You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."

Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about £21,000, to carry out the killing.

He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.

Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.

There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.

Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country.

"You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."

He was told: "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."

Natland was at the Briar Court Hotel with two handguns hidden under his bed when he was arrested by police.

When he saw officers at the door, he mimed shooting one of them with his hands before he was pushed against the wall and handcuffed.

"There was pressure because he'd come into the country, and we knew his intention was to carry out a murder on UK soil," said Flanagan.

"We had to move at pace and we intervened really quickly, and just before he sort of moved towards committing that murder."

Natland grew up in the oil city of Stavanger in south-west Norway.

Despite being a promising young footballer, he started taking drugs aged 13 and later dropped out of school.

He previously told the Old Bailey that by last year he was taking drugs "pretty much every day".

He became paranoid his parents were trying to kill him and he ended up in a psychiatric unit with drug-induced psychosis.

Natland's barrister, Paul Hynes KC, said the "mental illness was exacerbated, if not created, by the self-induced consumption of drugs", which had "affected his ability to make rational, good decisions".

The defendant said he spent a short period in a "home for problem children" where he met one of those who later recruited him to the Foxtrot Network, a teenager with the username UnknownHustler.

Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself."

Within two days of being recruited, Natland flew from Stavanger to Manchester, using the emergency passport as his normal one had expired.

He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester and was told to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.

Instead, he took a taxi to the hotel in Huddersfield before taking another taxi to a wooded area.

He picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, and was directed to a stolen Nissan with false plates to be used in the killing.

The judge added at sentencing: "You returned to the hotel with two guns and 19 bullets.

"You were sent directions to where a stolen car bearing false number plates was parked with its key, after which you bought rubber gloves, took photos and made videos of what you had acquired, including with the money spread out on the hotel bed."

From his hotel room, Natland bragged to his girlfriend he had the "bangs in the bag" and took selfies in his room.

At his trial, one of Natland's footballer friends recalled him talking about the "Swedish Foxes" and telling him: "I'm going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die."

Natland also confided in his girlfriend before leaving for the UK, saying in a message: "I'm going on crazy mission."

According to her, he said: "Now I can finally kill someone and it's perfect as I get money to do it.

"I can kill someone and life will be wonderful."

Giving evidence, Natland said he wanted to look "cool" to his peers but it was just "bravado" and inside he was "terrified".

He told jurors: "I wasn't an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn't."

Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he would have shot himself in the foot to get out of the "pickle" he was in.

Flanagan said: "Natland was clearly being tasked by someone in the Foxtrot Network, an organised criminal group sanctioned by the UK and the US due to its involvement in orchestrating violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime.

"The intended target of this specific assassination has never been identified, and we found no evidence of any direct link to Iran in this case.

"However, as recent events have shown, Counter Terrorism Policing will seek to proactively disrupt any attempts by hostile states to carry out criminal acts in the UK."

Natland was told he will have to serve at least two thirds of the 20-year sentence behind bars.

The Norwegian lawyers acting for the 19-year-old said they would work to have him transferred to Norway to serve his sentence.

"Twenty years is a very severe sentence for a boy who was 18 when he was arrested," they said in a statement.

"The other young people convicted in the related proceedings in Norway mainly received youth sentences or community sentences.

"We will take the time to consider the sentence carefully, together with him, his family and his British legal team."

Counter Terrorism Policing said it continued to investigate those suspected of helping Natland obtain firearms and a stolen car.

In September 2025, a 27-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and was later released under investigation.

Two men, aged 30 and 27, were arrested in Bradford on 20 May on suspicion of handling stolen goods, specifically a car.

They were taken into custody before being released on bail.

Catherine says nature can help children's emotional growth

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 12:06:22 GMT

The Princess of Wales has launched a project promoting the use of nature to help develop young children's social and emotional development.

"Nature is such an extraordinary environment for us all and, in this tech-driven, digital age, spending quality time outdoors has never been more important," says Catherine, in a social media post.

This is the latest stage in Catherine's campaign to improve the status of early years education and to find ways to improve children's wellbeing.

She says that research has shown "just how important nature is for our psychological and physiological wellbeing".

In her own recovery from cancer, the princess has spoken about the importance of spending time in nature, which she described as her "sanctuary".

She has hailed the holistic benefits of nature, which she described in almost spiritual terms, in a series of videos showing the changing seasons.

This faith in nature is now being applied to her early years project - the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood.

She wants to encourage ways of using the natural world to improve children's sense of creativity and to help their emotional development - and sites for such educational visits could be provided by the Duchy of Cornwall.

A new photograph of Catherine taken on Thursday in Cornwall by Josh Shinner has been released to accompany the project.

"This project is about exploring how nature, creativity and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children," says the princess.

"We believe that taking a whole-child approach is important, and nature becomes a wonderful place to explore how we can successfully nurture the social and emotional skills that underpin lifelong health and wellbeing.

"My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children and their families across the UK."

Dr Nicola Kemp of the Froebel Trust, which supports early years education research, said: "A growing body of evidence shows that regular contact with nature can support children's development in many ways, helping to foster curiosity, creativity, emotional wellbeing and social connection."

The Princess of Wales has looked for ideas for improving early years education, including her trip earlier this year to Reggio Emilia in Italy, which had developed a system that prioritised relationships and learning through play.

There is no funding announced so far for the project, but Catherine is using her profile to promote a cause that she once described as her "life's work".

The emphasis on families enjoying the natural world is also an antidote to an overload of screens and mobile phones, with Catherine having warned of an "epidemic of disconnection" from too much tech disrupting family life.

Street Fighter movie is 'made by fans for fans' - but can it KO the critics?

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 12:06:04 GMT

Video game fans have been treated to a two-hit combo of big screen adaptations recently.

First came Resident Evil, director Zach Cregger's movie version of the long-running horror game series.

The next contender is Street Fighter, the arcade classic fighting game that's been separating fans from their loose change since 1987.

Both have been turned into disappointing live-action films before.

But Cregger's attempt at Resident Evil, which impressed both critics and fans, seemed to break the curse.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to Street Fighter cast members Noah Centineo, Callina Liang and Andrew Koji to find out why they think the action movie can do the same.

The film, directed by Kitao Sakurai, follows Ken Masters, played by Centineo, and Ryu, played by Koji.

The two characters - long-standing icons of the games - are martial artists who trained under the same teacher before their relationship went sour.

Chun-Li, played by Liang, recruits the pair to compete with other elite fighters in the World Warrior tournament, organised by crime boss M. Bison.

The large ensemble cast includes about 15 characters from different instalments of the video game series, and is packed with references and Easter eggs.

"It's absurd, it's wild, it doesn't take itself too seriously," Centineo tells Newsbeat.

"And everyone who made it loves the world of Street Fighter. Grew up playing the game, loves the game."

He says it was "extremely important" for the film to stay faithful to the series, describing it as "a movie made by fans for fans", who can expect "meticulous" attention to detail.

Centineo says the film's stunt team closely studied each character's video game movements to ensure their signature moves were accurately depicted on film.

His co-star Liang says her intense training regime was designed to help her replicate character Chun-Li's famous moves and distinctive, muscular look.

"I was eating 12 eggs a day, like, 4,000 calories, training a lot," she says.

"My motto the whole time was just 'give it your best and some more'".

Liang says she wanted to put work in "for the fans" but does stress she was careful not to take things too far.

Her fellow actor Koji thinks it's a winning formula.

"I think we've got the right approach, got the right cast, right energy," he says.

"I think we could feel it when we first read the script."

Critics, though, haven't been convinced.

The Guardian called it a "garish and incoherent mess", but praised Liang as "formidable" and complimented her "genuinely impressive" fight scenes.

Gaming website IGN described the film as getting off to a "stylish start", but said it "increasingly feels disconnected from any sense of reality, even its own" along the way.

There was almost universal criticism of the "confusing" and "chaotic" plot, but some reviewers did praise the fight choreography and visuals of the film.

It's a contrast to Resident Evil, released last month, which was almost universally praised by critics and hit $300m at the global box office four weeks after release.

But will fans show up for Street Fighter?

Tayyib Mahmood, who uploads film and video game reviews to his tsreeltalk accounts, says he enjoyed Street Fighter.

"I think that it was true to what the games are," he says.

"It's taking these characters and putting them into these costumes which are unrealistic, it embraces how ridiculous these games are.

"You've got the different fighting styles, you've got these larger-than-life characters and I think the movie commits to all of that and I think there is a lot of personality to this film."

Mahmood says he has criticisms of the film, such as a weak story, but thinks the attention to the "visual identity" of Street Fighter is impressive.

He also points out that fandoms of specific video games don't always agree on what would make a good adaptation.

"I don't think that every movie needs to be loved universally," he says.

"I think that sometimes a film knows exactly who it's for and I think it does need to commit to audiences and accept that other people might hate it."

Your child didn't get a party invite - here’s what to do

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 11:17:28 GMT

It's around this time of year when children start coming home with party invitations in their school bag. It's exciting and a sign they're making friends as they embark on school life. But what do you do when your child doesn't get an invitation?

If your little one has been left off the list, here are some ways to help them cope.

Educational and child psychologist Dr Sasha Hall, who's mum to a three-year-old boy and five-year-old girl, says the first thing to understand is that this scenario is "completely normal".

"Unfortunately it's going to happen to all our children at some point in our parenting journey," she tells CBeebies Parenting Download.

Dr Hall says while it may be tempting to get involved, it is not helpful in the long term.

"We can't remove all the obstacles, but we can give them the skills to manage," she says. "It's about building their resilience... what skills can we teach rather than change their outcomes?"

Comedian, author and mum-of-two Cariad Lloyd says it is a "rough" position for a child to find themselves in.

"When they're little, it feels like first love... everything feels so heightened, especially with the party thing. Everyone gets not invited to somebody's party."

Dr Hall suggests planning an alternative activity for your child to focus on instead of the party.

"Yes, that child said you can't come, but let's find another friend you can do something else with," she says.

Lloyd adds that the more the party situation crops up throughout their primary school years, the more you can explain the different outcomes to them.

"They will be invited to lots of parties and not invited to loads and you'll stop counting them," she says.

"They will come back and be like 'so-and-so was upset because they're not invited'. And you'll be like, 'oh, do you remember when you were not invited to that one's party?' They all kind of take it in turns so it becomes less dramatic."

Dr Hall says it's important to explain to your child that the decision to leave them off the list is not about them.

"There are so many factors at play, especially with five to seven-year-olds, they're too little to have built up any kind of idea that they're naughty, it most likely has nothing to do with your child," she says.

Lloyd agrees it's worth explaining possible reasons: "They can't afford to have 20 kids at a party so they're doing six instead and you didn't make the cut."

Dr Hall says there could be a myriad of reasons why your child hasn't been invited.

"It's about the parents' own childhood experience - if they only had a couple of friends at that age they may be happy and comfortable with a smaller party - or they might want a big party in the hope of bringing their child out of their shyness."

Dr Hall says parents should remember it is not until children are slightly older that friendships take on a deeper meaning, so what may seem like a big deal now is likely to blow over.

"Around the age of two is when we start seeing them show an interest in others, but it's still kind of parallel play," she says.

"And then it's around three to five where they're actually socially motivated to choose preferences. So they might say 'I played with this child today', but it's around about five to seven where those friendships become more stable and that they're really meaningful to the child."

She says parents should give children plenty of time and opportunities to form friendships.

"There's a piece of research that looked at how do adults go from acquaintances to friends and it says it takes 40 to 60 hours - acquaintance to good friend is 200.

"We then can't assume that because you've gone to soft play and your child has seen that kid twice that therefore you can say that's your friend."

For more advice on all aspects of parenting including friendship and shyness go to the CBeebies Parenting YouTube channel.

The Olympic sprinter now bedbound for 22 hours a day

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:31:22 GMT

This video can not be played

'It feels like you're days away from death' - Beth Dobbin

Beth Dobbin is so determined to raise awareness of the illness that has decimated her life that she is speaking out, despite knowing it could trigger a brutal deterioration in her health.

Five years ago, she ran for Great Britain at the Tokyo Olympics. Now, at 32, she spends more than 22 hours a day in bed.

"I've done little things like attend a blood test at the doctors and been in bed for months after. So doing this interview, chatting away for 30 minutes, that could have an impact on me in 2027," she says.

"But I felt like it was really important to do that to get the message out."

She now only gets out of bed to eat and use the bathroom.

Dobbin has been diagnosed with ME, or myalgic encephalomyelitis - a chronic, fluctuating disease, causing symptoms such as sleep problems, problems with thinking and memory, pain and severe, persistent fatigue that does not improve with rest, and more.

A conversation, or even something so simple as a light too bright or a sound too loud, can cause a "crash" that lasts 24, 48 hours, or in the worst cases, months on end.

This year, Dobbin has left the house on just five occasions.

"It's life-decimating like I can't even put into words," she says. "I feel like I've lost everything.

"I have still got my family, but I've lost my independence, my health, the ability to work, the ability to exercise."

For Dobbin it all started with back-to-back Covid and glandular fever infections in the winter of 2021-22. She had not been unwell with either, only discovering she had contracted both through retrospective tests.

She had been sleeping a bit more and her running times were slightly down, but nothing that raised alarm. As time went on, she noticed soreness in the glands of her neck and armpits and a general sense of not quite feeling herself.

British Athletics doctors ran tests that gave no answers, so she carried on, assuming it was lingering glandular fever that would eventually pass.

She qualified for that year's World Championships, Commonwealth Games and European Championships in what was an unusually condensed season owing to the backlog from the pandemic.

Her health progressively deteriorated. At the Worlds, she struggled with a painful throat and was waking at unusual times in the night. At the Commonwealths, she was dizzy while running and her body was more sore than normal.

At the Europeans, she false-started after losing all feeling in her legs while in the blocks. She spoke of her "year of hell" in an emotional interview with BBC Sport after that race.

This video can not be played

'It's been a year from hell' - Dobbin emotional after false start

"When the Europeans had finished, I had this huge rest and the symptoms were just piling on. Things were getting worse and worse," Dobbin says. "I was struggling to stand up, I was sleeping loads, in bed all the time.

"After six weeks, I went back to training. I managed three weeks.

"[Doctors] were just really shocked that I still wasn't doing well and I'd had these viruses months ago.

"I think I saw four or five different specialists because the symptoms that I was having, they were across multiple [body] systems. All the specialists said 'this is ME' and we don't want it to be that because there's nothing out there for it."

ME has no known cure or specific treatment, with patients often relying on off-label medication to manage a condition that can cause more than 200 symptoms, including nausea, headaches, poor cognitive function and brain fog.

The condition is also known as chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), a label Dobbin strongly rejects. As a former athlete who balanced working eight-hour shifts with training before turning professional, she says she has "known fatigue my whole life" and believes the term fails to capture the severity of the illness.

"I wish it was just fatigue, that would be a walk in the park," she says. "It's so much more than that. If I thought of fatigue in my top 20 symptoms it might just make the cut."

Instead, she says, it feels like her entire body "is shutting down; it feels like you are a few days from death".

More than 400,000 people in the UK are thought to have ME, although the true figure could exceed one million, with severity ranging from people able to work or study to those requiring round-the-clock care and tube feeding.

Despite the length of time she spends in bed, Dobbin often feels too unwell to sleep and requires medication to help her do so.

"Even things like sitting up for a prolonged period of time can take it out of me so I prefer to be just propped up in bed, and that doesn't mean I feel fine. It doesn't get rid of my symptoms, but it makes them less hellish."

This video can not be played

The Olympic sprinter who can't leave her bed

For Dobbin's parents and sister Faye, who sit close by to her in support during the interview at the family home in Doncaster, the impact is clear.

"I'm just so desperate to help her but I can't because there is nothing. I'd take her anywhere, I'd take her to America if I had to, but there's nothing," says her father Jim, a former footballer who played for Barnsley, Grimsby and Doncaster Rovers.

Mum Jean adds: "You wake up every day and just feel sad. She should be building her life, living her best life.

"Every day you worry about how she's going to be that day. It's a worry about what our future life's going to be like, who's going look after her if we can't look after her.

"There is nothing out there. There is nowhere to go. You go to the GP and there's nowhere for them to send you to. It's really at the back of the queue as far as research, knowledge, expertise, funding."

There are limited specialist services for ME within the NHS and Dobbin says she has found herself educating the GPs she spoke to about the condition.

She had to wait 22 months before she got a face-to-face appointment with a private specialist she sourced herself after her British Athletics funding ended.

On Sunday, Dobbin's younger sister Faye will run the Yorkshire Marathon to raise money for ME Research UK.

"You just feel so helpless and we've been saying this for years now, what can we do?" Faye says.

"It feels like [the marathon] is all I can do other than supporting her emotionally.

"It does feel quite like grief in a way. I'm always worried about Beth. She's always on my mind. I'm worried about what kind of day she is having. What if she never improves? What if she gets worse? What if she gets another virus?"

Beth Dobbin competes for Scotland at the 2022 Commonwealth Games during a summer in which she was suffering debilitating early symptoms of ME

Asked about her future, Dobbin is straight to the point: "It's very bleak, unfortunately.

"The only positive thing really to say is that Covid happened six years ago now and it's like the whole medical community has woken up."

Since the Covid pandemic and the emergence of long Covid, for which there is a significant overlap in symptoms with ME, there has been a surge in attention and increase in research funding for the condition.

She added: "There will be something, I hope, in the future.

"I said I wanted to speak about it. It's not necessarily that I want to discuss it [but] it's raising that awareness. And unfortunately, athletes are believed a lot more than the average person.

"A lot of people that have this illness that I've spoken to have said to me 'I don't get believed, people think I'm lazy'. I've never experienced one person that doesn't believe me and that's because, why would an athlete just suddenly stop after 20 years?

"I've got a slight platform. If this happened to most people they wouldn't be able to speak about it, so I do feel like I've got a bit of a duty to do that."

'People call them pervert glasses': Blind users fear backlash over smart tech

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:23:00 GMT

Fraser Fleming approaches the corner of a busy Glasgow city centre street and asks his smart glasses to describe the road ahead.

A voice coming from tiny speakers in the arms of the specs tells him there are several parked cars and a person walking in his direction.

For 44-year-old Fraser, who is registered blind, this is "game changing" information.

"I know how to approach the street and what sort of care to take," he says.

"If I need to maybe take my time or if I can just walk at normal pace."

Fraser, who began losing his sight in his early twenties, says his AI-powered Meta smart glasses have become part of his everyday life during the past two years.

They help him to navigate public transport, read street signs and order from menus – but he's started to think twice about wearing them in public.

"People are calling them pervert glasses," he says, referring to multiple reports of them being used to secretly film and harass people, particularly women and girls, with the footage being shared online.

Fraser says this is having a negative effect on anyone wearing them, including visually-impaired people.

"We are definitely not using them to record people in dodgy situations," he says.

"We're using them to lead an independent life."

Fraser, from Motherwell, told the BBC's Your Voice he would often take his glasses off if he thought there was a chance of a confrontation.

"I've got enough to worry about getting from A to B," he says.

"I'll just put the glasses away and have to rely on my other senses in order to navigate around, which is going to make life a lot more difficult for me."

Tracey Rogerson, who uses the technology to help with her sight loss, shares Fraser's concerns.

"I was shocked to hear that they were being called pervert glasses because for me, they're such a big part of my life to help me maintain my independence," she says.

Meta, the company that owns WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, started selling smart glasses in 2021, and has sold about two million pairs since February last year.

It says there is a light on the frames which makes it clear the smart glasses are recording, but it also warns users not to engage in harmful activities.

As a result of the backlash against the glasses, some venues and events have banned or at least restricted their use over fears about covert filming, including ComicCon Scotland, which takes place in Edinburgh later this month.

This means Gordon Brown, who is severely sight-impaired and has attended the event with his family for the past three years, won't be going this year.

He says the impact of the ban on people with disabilities has been overlooked.

"Even if I was to put my glasses on quickly, just to read a sign or something, I wouldn't feel comfortable," says Gordon, from Inverkip.

"I think it's a matter of principle now, the fact that they're not willing to engage, and they're not willing to listen to a minority group.

"You know, we're not talking about thousands of people all of a sudden turning up wearing smart glasses."

Monopoly Events, which runs some of the biggest comic and entertainment conventions in the UK, announced in July that it had banned Meta glasses to "stop secret filming" of guests and attendees.

The ban applies to Meta glasses and other "wearable recording devices."

The company was contacted by the BBC about Gordon's comments.

Cosplay artist Spill The Tea was at a comic convention in Birmingham earlier this year when she was secretly filmed.

She later discovered the footage was posted online.

The performer, who has 1.9 million followers on TikTok, says she felt "violated".

"He was purposefully trying to provoke me or purposefully trying to make strange comments to get a reaction out of me so that he could get that perfect clip that he could post on social media and capitalise off it," says the London-based artist.

She says her experience demonstrates why restrictions are needed, but she thinks there should be exceptions for people with disabilities.

"For people who need the glasses and who really have to use them, I think they should be able to use them," she says.

"They shouldn't have to deal with the fact there's been a certain group of people who have spoiled it for them."

In a statement, Meta said: "We are proud that our AI glasses give blind, low-vision and hearing-impaired people greater independence in daily life.

"They were built to be noticed, which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video.

"It cannot be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it."

The hero dinner lady who died saving five children in the Aberfan disaster

BBC News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:11:56 GMT

On 21 October 1966, as a primary school and surrounding homes in Aberfan were engulfed by slurry from a collapsed coal tip, a dinner lady was collecting money from pupils.

Within moments, 144 people were dead, including 116 children, on what was the last day of class at Pantglas Junior School before the half-term holiday.

But five children were saved that day by the heroic actions of Nansi Williams, who died shielding the group.

"Apparently she was holding as much of us as she could, and trying to get us under a table," said Aberfan survivor Paul Harries, who has spoken to the media for the first time.

Harries, who was aged six at the time, was one of the five who was found alive under Williams' body.

"She gave everything to give us a future, and she lost everything," he said.

"Nansi Williams was a hero. A true hero. My hero."

He continued: "If it hadn't been for Nansi Williams, then instead of 116 children dying that morning it would have been 121.

"It would have been us, 100%."

As the 60th anniversary of the disaster approaches, Williams will be honoured with a purple plaque to commemorate her courage.

The King, Queen and Prince of Wales will visit Aberfan, in Merthyr Tydfil county, next week to mark the anniversary, following on from the late Queen Elizabeth who visited Aberfan eight times.

"The only reason I'm speaking about it now is because Nansi's story needs to be told and recognised for what she has done," Paul, now 66, said.

He recalled how an avalanche of slurry swept through the school just minutes after lessons began.

He had walked from the infant school to the junior school hall to pay a shilling for his school dinner.

It was there Williams was collecting the money from him and four other children.

"The infant school was totally missed by the tips," he added.

"So it was only by chance that we were not in the infant school, which was safe. We were in the junior school which caught the brunt of it."

Harries cannot remember the moment the building collapsed, but said: "I can remember being dug out.

"I was rushed straight to hospital with the other four children that were buried with me."

It was only later that he learnt of Nansi's heroics.

"My mother and father told me the story," he said. "They said 'your dinner lady died protecting you five children'."

When rescuers found them, Williams was still shielding the group.

Williams, who was 44, was a familiar figure to that generation of Aberfan children.

Another pupil, Janett Bickley, remembers her as a kind and popular presence.

"Oh, Nansi was lovely," she said.

"My mother and Nansi were friends.

"If you were lucky you could hold her hand in the yard at break time."

She recalled proudly walking around the playground thinking "I'm holding Nansi's hand today".

Like many pupils, Bickley remembered Williams collecting dinner money and leading children to lunch.

"She was trying to protect children," she said.

"She died, and they lived."

Bickley believes there are many people who should be recognised for their courage on that day, but agreed Williams was a hero.

"I think Nansi went way, way beyond what she needed to do," she said.

"She could have saved her own life. She cared more for the children."

Nansi's godson, Dai Powell, campaigned for greater recognition and said stories of what happened were passed down through his family for decades.

"My ultimate hero. No-one will ever touch her," he said.

"We'd all like to think we'd do the same thing, but until it happens we don't really know.

"Her heroism is just unbelievable."

The purple plaque scheme celebrates women who have made important contributions to their communities in Wales or shown exceptional courage.

"She didn't think of herself at all, she just thought of the children," said Rhian Connick, secretary of the Purple Plaque Committee.

For Harries, the plaque will ensure her story survives long after those who remember her are gone.

"Every year I go straight to Nansi's grave and put flowers there," he said.

"My family know the story of Nansi because if it hadn't been for her, they wouldn't be here today.

"There would be no son, no grandchildren.

"It's something permanent now.

"People can look at it and read it, and find out about her story."

Antarctica’s ‘doomsday’ glacier will keep melting even if oceans cool

New Scientist October 15, 2026

The world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is already collapsing at an alarming rate due to ocean warming, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise. Now, a new study shows that it will continue to lose ice for at least the next 150 years, even under the impossible scenario of extremely cool oceans.

This means that future ice loss from the glacier is unavoidable, even under the most optimistic climate mitigation scenarios.

Dubbed the “doomsday glacier”, this vast mass of ice is roughly the size of Great Britain. Together with the neighbouring Pine Island glacier, it’s the area of Antarctica losing the most ice, mainly due to melting by the warmer ocean waters.

Advertisement

The race to understand how and when Thwaites glacier will collapse

“The Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers are the biggest contributors to sea-level rise in Antarctica at the moment, and they’re losing ice at an increasing rate,” says Rosie Williams at the British Antarctic Survey.

If Thwaites glacier collapses completely, it is expected to trigger a more widespread loss of the ice sheet covering West Antarctica, causing a calamitous sea-level rise of 5 metres. So determining how it behaves in future is crucial.

To explore this, Williams and her colleagues “did something quite wild”, she says. In three different computer models of the ice sheet, they turned off all ocean-driven melting – an impossible condition in reality, even under the most extreme ocean cooling scenarios – and watched what would happen over the next 150 years. The aim was to see the future trajectory of Thwaites glacier and Pine Island glacier, even without warming oceans.

Free newsletter

Surprisingly, the glaciers followed opposite paths. Pine Island glacier re-advanced and became more stable. “But with Thwaites glacier, we found something really different,” says Williams. Over the entire 150 years of the simulations, the glacier continued to lose ice, even though the rate of loss slowed over time. “Our general expectation was… if you turned off that ocean melting, the ice would be able to thicken and re-advance. It’s somewhat of a surprise that Thwaites glacier can’t do that.”

The researchers think that Thwaites is still being affected by extreme El Niño conditions in the 1940s which destabilised Antarctica’s glaciers and kick-started their retreat. “We’re still seeing some effect of that playing out today with Thwaites. [Glaciers] are really slow-moving. They have a long memory,” she says.

On top of this, human-induced climate change has probably accelerated the melt, says Ted Scambos at the University of Colorado Boulder. “Ocean heat delivered to the base of the ice … over the past four decades or so, as a result of anthropogenic warming, has pushed the Thwaites system into an inherently unstable configuration,” he says.

Warmer ocean is driving the Antarctic sea ice ‘regime shift’

But despite future ice loss being locked in, this doesn’t mean that strategies to reduce climate change and ocean warming are futile. “Almost the opposite,” says Williams. “Under the zero-melt scenario, [Thwaites glacier] still loses ice, but the more warming you have in the ocean, the faster that ice is lost, so it’s still really essential to bring down our emissions and control that rate of ice loss.”

“Every fraction of a degree really matters for trying to preserve these glaciers into the future, which matters for all of us, in terms of sea-level rise globally,” says Williams.

The temperature of the ocean adjacent to Thwaites glacier is projected to rise at triple the historical rate throughout the 21st century, leading to increased ice melting. The big worry is that this may trigger a doomsday scenario of run-away collapse of Thwaites glacier that, in turn, would trigger the collapse of the whole of the West Antarctic ice sheet in a process called marine ice sheet instability.

The floating ice shelf of world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is detaching, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise

Here, the study by Williams and her colleagues offers slight hope. “We haven’t crossed the point of no return,” says Mathieu Morlighem at Dartmouth College, New Hampshire. “In the best-case scenario…if melt from the ocean stops, Thwaites doesn’t… lead to a collapse of the West Antarctic ice sheet.”

The big question for the future is what happens with realistic ocean temperatures, says Williams, who is now working on this.

Meanwhile, another study published this week revealed other worrying news about Thwaites glacier. A more precise model of how the glacier interacts with the ocean indicates that it might retreat more rapidly than previously thought, potentially contributing to double the sea-level rise previously projected.

Geophysical Research Letters DOI: 10.1029/2026GL122843

Why a high school in Virginia is getting a quantum computer

New Scientist October 15, 2026

In January, Skyview High School in Virginia will become the first high school in the US to have a quantum computer on its premises. Made by the quantum computing and sensing firm XeedQ, it will be a teaching device aimed at inspiring the next generation of quantum innovators.

The quantum computing industry is in a period of expansion and both governments and private investors are increasing their focus on the field. Yet, many of the industry’s leaders agree that, in addition to investing in quantum technology, there ought to be a concerted effort to grow the quantum workforce as well. Fairfax County Public Schools (FCPS) in Virginia aims to meet this challenge by providing its high school students with hands-on access to a working quantum computer. FCPS Superintendent Michelle Reid says that this is a bet on a career pathway that is “globally exploding” and could set students up for pursuing one of the 800,000 quantum-related jobs projected to be created within the next decade.

You can now buy a DIY quantum computer

The quantum computer, called XQ1, will contain four qubits, or basic building blocks of quantum computation, each of which will be based on a diamond imprinted with specifically designed defects. These types of qubits can operate at room temperature. Gopalakrishnan Balasubramanian at XeedQ says the firm designed XQ1 – which is about the size of a small refrigerator – to be robust enough to withstand the conditions of a classroom and run continuously for several years. He says that XQ1 will cost about $900,000. Reid says that this will still work out cheaper for FCPS than, for instance, a new programme to teach students welding skills.

Advertisement

The computational power of a quantum computer is related to its number of qubits, so XQ1 won’t enable students to run sophisticated programs. Instead, it will allow them to develop intuition for, for example, the probabilistic nature of qubits. Students will be able to test how repeatedly preparing a qubit in one quantum state, equivalent to giving the quantum computer the same inputs over and over, doesn’t necessarily always lead to the same result, or the same output, when the qubit is read out later, says Balasubramanian.

The world’s first fully 3D-printed microscope went big in 2025

In this way, some of the most fundamental ways in which quantum computers behave differently from conventional computers will become intuitive to students way before they enroll in college and undergo a rigorous formal education in quantum physics, he says. Additionally, students will be able to change electromagnetic pulses that control qubits as well as study the impacts of environmental noise on their functioning. They will work in teams of two or three and learn the coding language Python in the process.

“We anticipate students will work directly with the system and observe the physics in action,” says Reid. She says that XQ1 will initially be part of mathematics and physics classes for students in their last or second to last year of high school, but that the curriculum might expand in future years. Students from other schools in Fairfax county will also have a chance to interact with the machine through weekend programmes, she says. “Our young people are so excited about it,” says Reid.

Google showcases way to fix quantum computer errors more efficiently

New Scientist October 15, 2026

Making quantum computers error-proof is one of the biggest challenges currently facing the technology. Researchers at Google Quantum AI have now demonstrated one way to do so more efficiently. Their work suggests the smaller quantum computers that will be available in the next few years could be more impactful than expected.

Quantum computers can run mathematical operations, analogous to addition or multiplication, that conventional computers cannot. This makes them suitable for solving some problems that had previously been considered unsolvable, such as those that underpin cryptography.

Most important among the quantum operations the computers run are “non-Clifford gates”, which are the key ingredients for algorithms that transcend conventional computation.

Advertisement

We may finally have a way to rate a quantum computer’s usefulness

But there is a problem. Quantum computers are very error-prone, and their building blocks, called qubits, must be encoded into special groups, or “logical qubits”, before they can execute operations reliably. Executing non-Clifford gates in an error-corrected way requires large numbers of qubits, which means having to build very large quantum computers – a formidable engineering challenge.

Now, Emma Rosenfeld at Google Quantum AI and her colleagues have used the firm’s Willow quantum computer to show that the error-correction process can be made more efficient. Their new technique ultimately reduced Willow’s errors 40 times.

At the centre of their advance is the idea of a “magic state”, which is a special quantum state that qubits must assume before the quantum computer can run error-corrected non-Clifford operations. Creating these states had, so far, been a real bottleneck for quantum computing, says Rosenfeld. “It eats up a lot of qubits and a lot of time,” she says.

Free newsletter

In 2024, her colleagues at Google Quantum AI proposed a more efficient method for creating magic states called “magic state cultivation”. Here, instead of many imperfect qubits being repeatedly combined and manipulated into a magic state that is then put towards running an error-corrected operation, the magic state is “grown” within a smaller patch of qubits.

The Google researchers showed that magic state cultivation could, in theory, enable quantum computers to run consequential programs with just one-tenth the number of qubits we had expected they would need. The new experiment by Rosenfeld and her colleagues proves that magic state cultivation works in practice.

This is not the first time that new methods for making magic states have lowered a quantum computer’s error rates. Advances in creating magic states and error-correcting non-Clifford gates have also been achieved in experiments with quantum computers that have qubits based on ions. Willow’s qubits, which are based on tiny superconducting circuits, achieved error rates similar to those past experiments, but Rosenfeld says that they work more quickly, potentially reducing the quantum computer’s overall runtime.

A quantum computer made from extremely cold atoms can correct its own errors during long computations, an important prerequisite for becoming truly useful

“This is an impressive demonstration of a promising recent idea pioneered by Google,” says Isaac Kim at the University of California, Davis. “It’s an approach that can make fault-tolerant quantum computing substantially cheaper.” The new work demonstrates one of the building blocks necessary for universal quantum computing and could be a “gamechanger” in terms of building intermediately sized quantum computers with hundreds of logical qubits, says Dominik Hangleiter at ETH Zurich in Switzerland.

Zhenyu Cai at Imperial College London says that while this experiment is a significant step forward, Willow’s errors will need to be reduced further before it can tackle truly useful problems. Additionally, Kim says that in the experiment, Willow generated good magic states only for a fraction of its computational runs: only 8 per cent of Willow’s computations produced high-quality magic states that could then be put into further use.

Rosenfeld says that this percentage ought to increase as she and her colleagues refine the technique and improve Willow’s hardware. It is, in this case, also affected by a very careful benchmarking technique that the team used, which may not be used in future applications, she says. “This is the first demonstration that the concepts work. We’re not done.”

Science DOI: 10.1126/science. aee7961

Towering glacial ice cliffs may collapse in fits and starts

New Scientist October 15, 2026

The world’s thickest glaciers may “calve” icebergs up to three times faster than previously predicted. However, such rapid retreat may not be sustained over long periods.

Instead, the large bodies of ice – which include Antarctica’s Thwaites glacier – may collapse in bursts, with intervening periods of stability.

The behaviour of tall ice cliffs is one of the biggest sources of uncertainty in predicting future sea level rise. Several of the world’s largest glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica extend out to sea, with their bases resting on the sea floor. Their coastal edges can form ice cliffs looming as high as 100 metres above the ocean’s surface.

Advertisement

The race to understand how and when Thwaites glacier will collapse

For years, researchers have feared that such marine-based glaciers might be vulnerable to runaway cliff collapse. The idea here is that each time an ice cliff collapses, it exposes a new, taller – and so potentially even less stable – ice cliff further towards the glacier’s interior. The loss of ice due to runaway collapse of these ever-taller cliffs could potentially double the amount of sea level rise expected over the next 100 years, according to an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report. But we don’t yet have enough empirical data to know how likely it is that runaway cliff collapse will occur, so previous studies have relied on ideal mathematical models to envision the process instead.

Caroline Needell at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology-Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute Joint Program and her colleagues used satellite data to provide the first direct, large-scale observations of how the tallest ice cliffs actually behave, offering a firmer basis for estimating the danger of runaway collapse – and the rapid sea level rise that could result.

According to the study, the risk of runaway collapse depends on two main factors: how steeply the sea floor beneath the glacial ice deepens, and how quickly the ice flows seawards. Imagine an up-ended jar of thick honey spilling onto a plate: it won’t remain in a tall, stable shape, but will thin outwards at the edges. In a similar way, if the viscous flow of ice is fast enough, it will thin out the edge of a glacier, reducing cliff height. Even if the glacier is thicker further towards its interior, sufficiently rapid ice flow appears able to compensate, lowering those ice cliffs and preventing a runaway effect.

This idea has been suggested by idealised mathematical models, but had never been systematically measured in real glaciers. “None of the glaciers we observed underwent unstable retreat, even though they did retreat much faster than our current models predict,” says Needell.

Free newsletter

That retreat could speed up even further in the future. Needell notes that most glaciers in the study are “buttressed” by sea-floor features. For instance, a series of underwater ridges currently help stabilise Thwaites from beneath.

“Over the next decades, it’s going to jump from one pinning ridge to another,” almost like “tripping” downhill, says Douglas Benn at the University of St Andrews in the UK. Eventually, Thwaites will reach a point where those ridges disappear. “The bed then begins to get real deep,” says Benn. At that point, which the glacier may reach within the current century, “the whole structural integrity of the ice becomes unviable”.

The floating ice shelf of world’s widest glacier – Thwaites glacier in Antarctica – is detaching, with worrying implications for global sea-level rise

That is when runaway collapse becomes a real possibility. However, those conditions may also speed up the flow of ice, thus thinning out any looming cliffs. The key question, says Needell, is whether thinning can outcompete rapid ice loss, restabilising the glacier. Her study suggests that it might – but the question remains open.

Robert Larter at the British Antarctic Survey points out that we haven’t yet seen this kind of runaway cliff collapse. One study suggests that it may have happened in the vicinity of Thwaites around 12,000 years ago. “The problem is, nobody was around to take observations at the time,” he says. “It’s a possibility we have to keep our eye on.”

Science DOI: 10.1126/science. aee0658

Adding a probiotic supplement to formula milk slashed rates of respiratory infections in babies who weren’t breastfed. “It’s phenomenally exciting,” says Daniel Davis at Imperial College London, who wasn’t involved in the research. A high burden of early-life infections has been linked to more moderate to severe infections in later life and an increased risk of allergies. “Modifying formula milk to help set up good immune health for babies is a really powerful concept,” says Davis.

Can prebiotics, probiotics or postbiotics help your ageing microbiome?

However, such interventions could have unintended consequences, including actually increasing the risk of allergies. “If you increase the power of someone’s immune response against infections, that might make them more likely to be susceptible to allergies or autoimmunity,” says Davis, who learned about the supplement at the Immunology of the Exposome conference at the Royal Society in London on 12 October. “These interventions are likely to have both pros and cons; we don’t know what those all are yet.”

Prior trials suggest that supplements containing sugars from breast milk, called human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), cut rates of respiratory infections in such infants. These sugars are fermented by gut bacteria, including Bifidobacterium longum infantis, to produce short-chain fatty acids, molecules that seem to enhance immune responses against pathogens like viruses and bacteria.

But some babies, especially those in Western nations, lack B. longum infantis in their guts, which may be related to their mother’s diet. Previously, Petter Brodin at Imperial College London and his colleagues found that supplements that boost levels of this bacterium seemed to improve immune health in breast-fed babies.

Now, Brodin’s team has developed a supplement containing both HMOs and B. longum infantis and tested it on formula-fed babies, who are more likely to lack B. longum infantis.

With funding from Nestlé, which develops formula milk, the researchers recruited 223 infants – aged between 2 and 5 weeks – who were exclusively formula fed in Manila, the Philippines. About half of the infants were randomly assigned to drink formula milk made from a powder containing the probiotic supplement, while the remaining infants consumed the same milk without the supplement.

The parents – who were blinded as to which group their baby was in – logged whenever they showed symptoms of respiratory infections, such as sneezing, coughing or a runny nose, until they were 6 months old.

Babies born too soon seem to have stronger connections in one of the major brain areas that supports language processing if they regularly heard their mother read them a story while in intensive care

During this time, 23 per cent of the infants in the supplement group were recorded as developing an infection, compared with 40 per cent in the formula-only group. The researchers need to carry out large trials that track the supplement’s effects in different countries over time, says Davis. Brodin says the team is planning to explore how it affects the risk of allergies and asthma.

Japan is launching a mission to Mars’s largest moon Phobos

New Scientist October 16, 2026

We may be on the verge of solving the mystery of the Martian moons. On 20 October, the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launches towards the larger of the two moons, Phobos, with the goal of bringing back a sample that may finally explain how Phobos and its sibling, Deimos, formed.

MMX will launch from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan. If all goes to plan, it should arrive at Mars in August 2027, entering an orbit that keeps it alongside Phobos so it can build a detailed map of the surface. Along the way, it will also observe the surface of Deimos.

Once the map is complete enough, the spacecraft’s operators at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) will use it to pick out a spot on Phobos for MMX to land. During one or two brief landings, it will take on two tasks: to drop off a small rover called IDEFIX and to pick up samples. The rover is the first anyone has ever placed on such a small cosmic body, so part of its purpose aside from scientific observations is to confirm that a wheeled rover even works on an object with such low gravity.

Advertisement

Possible signs of ancient life on Mars are rich in complex carbon

The samples, though, are the most important part of the mission. MMX has two different sampling devices: one that shoots a puff of gas onto the surface, blowing dust and pebbles back up into a sampling container, and another that blasts a hollow cylinder into the ground to take a sample a several centimetres deep. After the samples are taken, they will be stowed away inside the spacecraft, which will then head back towards Earth. It is expected to arrive home in 2031.

Once these samples get back to Earth and are analysed by scientists on the ground, they should finally solve the mystery of how Phobos and Deimos formed. For more than a century, researchers have debated whether the two are captured asteroids or formed from an impact on Mars, similar to how Earth’s moon formed. On first look, their shapes and surfaces resemble asteroids, but their circular orbits around Mars’s equator are more consistent with the impact hypothesis. Figuring out what they are made of should settle it once and for all.

Free newsletter

This will also help illuminate what the solar system was like billions of years ago when these strange moons formed. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds,” said Tom Statler, part of the NASA team that is collaborating on the MMX mission, in a statement.

If we are very lucky, the samples from Phobos may even contain bonus bits of dust and debris from Mars itself. Impacts on the planet could have launched material into space, which would have collected on the moon’s surface and been preserved there for billions of years. That means that these samples could illuminate not just the history of Phobos and Deimos, but also of Mars.

El Niño has killed hundreds of children in Sudan

New Scientist October 16, 2026

Hundreds of children have died of starvation and disease in a drought in Sudan caused by the record-breaking El Niño. The risk of this leading to a full-blown famine is growing.

Almost half the country is experiencing drought, which in some areas is the worst in decades, according to a warning from the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a partnership of the United Nations and charity organisations. As a result, crops are failing and people are dying in a “humanitarian catastrophe, already of historic proportions”, it said.

This El Niño will bring predictable disasters, so why aren’t we ready?

Hunger has reached famine levels in two refugee camps in Darfur, a region in western Sudan. While that’s not enough for the IPC to declare a famine across the region, the partnership said it has resulted in hundreds of deaths. Most of these are children, who are particularly vulnerable to malnutrition, as well as outbreaks of cholera and measles. At least 1800 people have died of malnutrition in three areas of Darfur controlled by a rebel faction led by Abdel Wahid al-Nur, according to the group.

Advertisement

Almost 29 million people, 62 per cent of the country’s population, are already being forced to eat less or go hungry. As the spotty harvest comes in, they won’t be able to store food or make money to buy it before the next rainy season in June, dramatically increasing the risk of widespread famine, says Manon Radosta at the non-governmental organisation CARE, a member of the IPC.

“Families are skipping meals. They’re not eating or they’re eating just porridge,” she says. “It would not take much to tip it. We cannot predict it, but we’re extremely worried that the situation will be so severe that people will be massively starving.”

Droughts and flooding brought by El Niño threaten crops around the world, raising the risk of increased prices and famines

In 2003, ethnic minorities in Darfur rebelled against Sudan’s largely Arab government, and government-backed Arab paramilitaries began killing civilians in a conflict that led to about 300,000 deaths. Twenty years later, the paramilitaries launched a civil war against Sudan’s new military government and killed thousands of non-Arab civilians in Darfur. Some of these massacres bore the “hallmarks of genocide”, the UN found.

The war has displaced 14 million people and disrupted farming and livestock herding. Prices of food and fuel have also shot up as the US-Iran conflict interrupts shipping on the Strait of Hormuz. Now, El Niño has reduced rainfall to crops including the main staple, sorghum, and withered vegetation for grazing. Ninety per cent of Sudan’s agriculture relies on rain rather than irrigation.

During this natural climate phase, weakened easterly trade winds allow warm water to slosh back eastwards across the tropical Pacific. A centre of rising, moist air that is heated by this water moves eastward as well, shifting atmospheric circulation.

A 2025 review paper suggested the rising air in the central-eastern Pacific transports heat to the east and west through atmospheric waves, encouraging air to descend rather than rise over the Sahel region across the continent, including in Sudan.

Free newsletter

“That descent warms and dries the air, inhibiting upward motion of the air masses that produces summer monsoon rainfall,” says Emily Black at the University of Reading, UK. The atmospheric waves promote easterly winds that blow against the movement of warm, moist air from the Atlantic Ocean into the heart of Africa, the paper added.

The El Niño is also forecast to bring potentially devastating drought to vulnerable countries in southern Africa, as well as heavy rainfall and flooding to the Horn of Africa. Nations including the US and the UK have cut foreign aid funding that could help prevent these extreme weather events from turning into humanitarian disasters.

High-income donor countries have given only $1.25 billion of the $2.87 billion in aid the UN has said is needed this year in Sudan. “The gap means right now we are unable to keep people alive,” says Radosta.

A monster El Niño is brewing in the Pacific Ocean – but there may be ways we can stop the worst impacts from occurring

Besides providing funds, other countries should pressure Sudan’s warring parties to stop targeting markets and water sources with drone strikes, she adds. The United Arab Emirates has been accused of arming the paramilitaries, while Turkey, Russia, Egypt and Iran are backing the armed forces.

The El Niño is still heating up and could exceed the previous sea-surface temperature record by 60 per cent. That will warm the atmosphere, and probably make 2027 the hottest year ever. It could also bring heatwaves across the tropics next March, April and May, say Liz Stephens, also at the University of Reading.

During the last El Niño in 2024, Sudan experienced prolonged temperatures above 40°C (104°F). “We’re loading the dice for some really extreme heat next year across the Sahel,” says Stephens. “We might expect to see increased mortality due to that as well.”

Scientists have just voted to abolish leap seconds

New Scientist October 16, 2026

Leap seconds, previously used to keep the world’s clocks in sync with Earth’s rotation, are to be abolished. Instead, universal time will be allowed to drift up to an hour from astronomical time before it is corrected. Representatives from 69 countries voted for the change on 15 October at a meeting of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in Versailles, France.

As the gap between clock time and astronomical time slowly grows, the effect will eventually be “like living on daylight saving time”, but permanently, says Emily Akkermans, curator of time at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London.

For most of history, our clocks have been set by the apparent position of the sun in the sky. But in 1967, after the development of super-accurate atomic clocks, physicists defined an international time standard called coordinated universal time (UTC), based instead on the speed of a particular vibration of the caesium-133 atom.

Advertisement

The epic quest to redefine the second using the world’s best clocks

Natural fluctuations in Earth’s rate of rotation meant periodic corrections were needed to keep universal time in sync with the sky. As the rotation slowed, physicists added extra leap seconds. Twenty-seven have been added to UTC since they were introduced in 1972.

Now, that strategy is to be abandoned. This is partly because technological systems, from stock markets to telecommunications to GPS, have become much more reliant on precise timekeeping. That means introducing leap seconds is more complex, potentially risking the failure of mobile phone networks or electricity grids. Previous leap seconds have caused websites to crash and disrupted airlines’ booking systems, says Setnam Shemar at the National Physical Laboratory (NPL) in Teddington, UK.

“Time is now so much more important and integrated into these systems,” says Akkermans. “What once worked has become more problematic.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

What’s more, Earth’s rotation has recently begun to accelerate slightly, raising the daunting possibility of needing “a first-ever negative leap second”, said Noël Dimarcq, who heads the BIPM’s committee on time and frequency, in a statement. The practical consequences of such a jump backwards in time are hard to predict.

Physicists have been debating what to replace the leap second with for the past 30 years. At the BIPM meeting, they finally voted for a “leap hour”, which means that UTC will be allowed to diverge from astronomical time for up to an hour before being corrected. That should ensure an uninterrupted flow of time for “several centuries”, said Dimarcq. The change will take effect from 20 May 2027.

Once considered an oddity of quantum physics, time crystals could be a good building block for accurate clocks and sensors, according to new calculations

Shemar emphasises that the effects involved are very small: “It’ll be many hundreds or even thousands of years before a leap hour is needed.” He adds that physicists will still be accurately tracking Earth’s rotation to provide information for astronomy and celestial navigation.

The leap hour isn’t the only temporal innovation being planned, though. The BIPM meeting also asked for proposals on a new definition of the second – needed because optical clocks are now much more accurate than the caesium clock that time is currently based on – and called on international agencies to start considering how to define a universal time standard for the moon. Overall, the changes “will have a profound impact on future timekeeping both on Earth and other planets”, said Dimarcq.
