Can a positive mindset protect us from the sniffles?

New Scientist October 16, 2026

The threat seems to be everywhere. On the tube, on the bus, as I the queue for coffee, I find that I am surrounded by coughs and sneezes, spreading diseases.

I eat healthily, exercise and try to get 8 hours of sleep to fend off the dreaded lurgy. It is only recently, however, that I started wondering whether our mental life might also play a part in our body’s defences. And the more I dug into the available literature, the more convinced I have become that it is critical.

Too busy to meditate? Microdosing mindfulness has big health benefits

Our attitudes, I have discovered, can subtly shape our immune system’s activity, which directly influences how likely we are to develop symptoms. If we want to fend off infection, we would do well to look after our minds as well as our bodies.

Advertisement

One of the first studies to explore this possibility arrived in the early 2000s, when Sheldon Cohen at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and his colleagues recruited 334 plucky volunteers who were willing to be infected with the common cold. In the month before the trial, they took regular questionnaires about their feelings throughout the day, noting emotions both positive (cheerful, at ease, energetic) and negative (sad, on edge, hostile).

On infection day, the scientists gave each participant a nasal drop containing one of two rhinoviruses known to cause sniffles, then held them in quarantine for five more days to observe whether any symptoms developed – quantified through objective measures. The team estimated the participants’ mucus production, for example, by collecting and weighing the snotty tissues they had used.

Cohen’s results were unequivocal. People with a sunnier emotional style were about a third less likely to develop symptoms than those who were less positive. Quite amazingly, the influence of the positive feelings was independent of the negative feelings – meaning that people who managed to feel both cheerful and anxious, for instance, were still less likely to develop symptoms than those who were neither cheerful nor anxious. This may sound counterintuitive, but it is perfectly possible to feel multiple emotions at the same time, and Cohen’s results seemed to suggest that positive feelings play the greatest role in our health.

I might have been sceptical if this were the only evidence, but multiple other studies have since confirmed and extended these findings. Cohen and his colleagues have shown that a so-called positive emotional style (PES) could also protect participants from influenza, for example – even after they controlled for a host of factors including age, sex, education, race and body mass.

While the exact mechanisms are unclear, it almost certainly comes down to stress, which is known to throw our defences into disarray. Someone under a lot of pressure may struggle to summon the resources to identify the virus when it first takes hold, leading to a suppressed immune response. Alternatively, the immune system may leap into action too quickly and too eagerly, bombarding the body with the inflammation that lies behind many of our symptoms.

How important is thinking about your breath for calming yourself down? We now know that slow breathing is effective even without conscious involvement

In the case of the common cold, it seems that the second potential mechanism is the most relevant. Someone with a more positive frame of mind may find it easier to cope with life’s stresses, meaning that the body becomes less inflamed when they face a pathogen. Along these lines, Cohen has found that people’s symptoms, such as a runny nose, are directly correlated with their levels of IL-6, a pro-inflammatory signalling protein called a cytokine, after infection. This was much lower among those with a PES. A group of researchers led by Sara Puig Pérez at Valencian National University, Spain, meanwhile, found that optimists have lower levels of another pro-inflammatory cytokine, TNFα, which has been linked to the fatigue and lethargy that often accompanies our sniffles, and this seemed to be reflected in fewer overall symptoms. It seems that the optimist’s body is simply better able to fine tune its response to the threat at hand.

As fascinating as this is, I’m mostly interested in the ways that I might use this information to protect myself, so I was delighted to find a trial of an eight-week mindfulness course by Bruce Barrett at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and his colleagues. Like Cohen, Barrett looked for objective evidence of infection, with blood tests, cheek swabs and nasal washes, rather than relying solely on reported symptoms.

The mindfulness course had previously been shown to cultivate a more positive mindset – and this had the desired effect on the participants’ health. The participants were generally less likely to develop a respiratory illness after practicing mindfulness. And for those who did develop signs of an infection, the symptoms were less severe. The benefits were comparable to those of exercise, which is also known to increase the efficiency of the immune system. The meditators were also less likely to take time off work due to illness than the control group, who had been put on a waiting list for the course.

Mindfulness may not be your thing. As I’ve written previously, I’ve personally struggled with it in the past, although I’m now finding new ways to incorporate it into my life. Given the very general link to good feelings, I’m sure that plenty of other kinds of self-care would bring similar protection. Social connection also seems to boost the immune response, so you might try to reach out to the people who matter most to you, for instance.

With the nights drawing in over the northern hemisphere, it is very easy to succumb to the winter blues, so now could be the perfect time to focus on the things that bring you comfort. A sneeze-free sniffle season may just be one of many benefits.

Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?

New Scientist October 16, 2026

AI has grown so adept at solving mathematical puzzles that critics fear the flood of new proofs it creates will overwhelm academics and actually set the field back. Until now, AI has had limited impact on other areas of science, but there are signs that physics may be about to experience a similar upset.

John Sous at Yale University says AI models may have an unfairly bad reputation when it comes to physics because of the way they are tested. Cutting-edge models have previously scored as low as 30 per cent on six different tests designed specifically to assess AI’s ability on tough physics problems, but this doesn’t square with the successes Sous and his colleagues have seen when using them, he says.

Checking the problems in the benchmark revealed a litany of errors and ambiguous definitions. Once corrected, scores soared to as high as 94 per cent. The problem didn’t lay with AI, but in the tests not providing the necessary information.

Advertisement

“I think anything that’s well defined, even if it’s very hard, I suspect that AI will be very good at it – arguably better than the best experts,” says Sous. “This is backed up by our data.”

But while some parts of physics can be very well defined – physicist Vladimir Arnold once said that mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap – many aren’t. And it is in the new, uncharted, fuzzy and cutting-edge parts of physics where AI may struggle.

arXiv might not survive AI slop onslaught, warn mathematicians

Sous says that interesting physics comes when we find something confusing, some phenomenon we observe in nature, a material or the cosmos that we don’t understand. It is then a physicist’s job to create a model, an approximation or a simulation that captures and predicts that phenomenon.

“That’s a very artistic, a very creative process,” says Sous. “Can AI really take the next step and do the full job of a theoretical physicist? Do end-to-end research: define, create, explore, test? The picture is not clear yet.”

One reason mathematics has been at the tip of the spear of AI progress is formalisation. This technique turns a mathematical idea into computer code that can be methodically checked; the process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, it is considered correct beyond all reasonable doubt. It allows AI to process a problem and know when it has arrived at a correct solution.

Subscriber-only newsletter

While some advances have been made in using formalisation to test physics, it is early days in comparison to mathematics. And physics problems can often be messier and harder to pin down.

What is clear is that AI is already being used by physicists, not only to write computer code and do maths, but even to design and run experiments. Logan Wright, also at Yale University, is now teaching a course on using AI in physics research, and says that the syllabus is constantly changing to catch up with developments.

The key, says Wright, is to create experiments where the inputs and outputs can be computer controlled. Then that control can be handed over to an AI that is able to pull the appropriate levers to explore the problem space and arrive at meaningful results.

“It doesn’t have hands, it doesn’t have eyes, it just interacts with the world through language and code,” says Wright. “So if we can set up an experiment in which all the observations are reduced to code, and all the actions are reduced to code… then AI can actually be very helpful.”

Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

One such experiment currently underway in Wright’s laboratory involves analysing how different shapes of laser pulses affect a rubidium atom. The researchers use Anthropic’s AI Claude to control the laser pulses and gather data on their effects.

“Claude can now basically say ‘I think this laser pulse is gonna produce this output’, right,” says Wright. “And it can test that.”

Wright says that such experiments can run overnight and complete as much work as a human would in a week – and human physicists can even use an app on their phone to suggest ideas that come to them while they are away from the lab, and get the results when they return.

“It’s not going to be [the case that] all of the universe can be explored in that way. It’ll be like very constrained domains,” says Wright. “I think part of the next frontier of physics will be to make as much progress as we can in those domains.”

Wright says that it is already entirely possible that AI will soon design an experiment that humans don’t understand, ask humans to build it and generate exciting new results. “But just to be clear, just like in math, there’s a debate about does it count as science if we get a result that we don’t understand anything about,” says Wright.

Election 2026: Small town struggles – Raetihi battles Winstone mill closures aftermath

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

Raetihi has suffered some tough times between elections with mill closures and a cost of living crisis. Photo / Mike Scott

Two years on from the mill closures, Raetihi is holding on but jobs in the small central North Island town are scarce, rents are high and shops are empty. With an election looming, locals tell Mike Scott they don’t expect miracles – they just want the basics to work again.

When Turuhia Edmonds went to work, his day began with a 100m walk to the pick-up spot outside Ruapehu Farm Supplies on Raetihi’s main street.

As a shift worker at the Karioi pulp mill, Edmonds’ pick-up time was either 5.15am or 5.15pm.

The freezing winter mornings were most memorable, with deep frosts or snow on the ground and sleepy homes puffing smoke.

Even if it was early, it was busy. Shearing vans collected crews; forestry workers headed off in utes and trucks.

The evening pick-ups were livelier, with kids on bikes or kicking rugby balls and friendly waves from passing cars.

“Just the normal sort of things you’d see in a small town,” Edmonds says.

The pick-ups, run by Dempsey’s, the local transport company, were part of the deal for shift workers at Karioi pulp mill, toiling two days on, two nights on, then four days off.

The vans collected workers from towns like Raetihi, where about a quarter of the mill’s workforce lived.

Edmonds, born and bred in the town of about 1100, was a relative newcomer to the mill.

Previously, he was a shearer who had chased work around the world. A back injury, first suffered in his late 20s, ended that gig.

Family told him to try the mill, so he did, taking a pay cut to get in the door, from the high $90,000s to about $68,000.

But the mill represented opportunity. Training and graft saw him quickly go from general hand to trainee and then a fully fledged operator working shifts, and by 2024 he was on close to $120,000.

Everyone there knew it was “life-changing money”, he says. It even meant he could start house hunting.

“I had just got pre-approval from the bank ... only three weeks before they announced it.”

Edmonds’ house plans halted when Winstone Pulp International first declared it would close the Karioi pulp mill and the Tangiwai sawmill, blaming sustained increases in electricity costs.

The closures were confirmed on September 10, 2024, and about 230 jobs, including Edmonds’, disappeared – a serious blow for nearby towns including Ōhakune, Waiōuru, Taihape and Raetihi.

The impact didn’t end with the Winstone employees but rippled through other workforces, Edmonds says.

Truck deliveries of logs to the sawmill ceased, as did work for contractors who hauled chip and slash between the mills.

“There’s the cleaners and our service people who used to come in and clean all of our control rooms and the entire mill.”

The closures immediately tested the resilience of the small towns and especially Raetihi, which in Edmonds’ view was already in decline.

On his 100m walk to the pick-up, he would pass old and worn homes unlikely to be insulated, he says.

On the main street where he waited, there were already shuttered shops, with more now.

When Edmonds went to the primary school, the roll was about 300. It is now 89.

Even before the closures, the 2023 Census shows the median personal income in Raetihi was $33,200, $8300 short of the national figure.

It’s tough to swallow for Edmonds, who came back to town in 2018 to stay – a big reason was that he loved his childhood in Raetihi. He still goes fishing, eeling and hunting with his whānau.

“I watch a few stories about Tokoroa and Murupara and all this. We’re very similar in those problems with drugs and alcohol and high unemployment and poverty.

“I think the longer it has to go on where they struggle through that, I think it becomes something that becomes just a normal part of life.”

After the closures, numerous reports claimed redundant mill workers and their families would up sticks and leave.

The Ngā Waihua o Paerangi Trust, formerly Ngāti Rangi Trust, has monitored 186 of the 213 former workers on its list.

Nineteen, about 10%, are working in Australia. Almost half, 92, are living or working outside the Ruapehu district, chief executive Helen Leahy says.

Some found work outside the district and kept their families at home, but the travel costs and time apart became unsustainable. High petrol prices have only added to the strain.

“Culturally, economically, socially this has been an enormous loss for our local community,” Leahy says.

“We have heard of grandmothers crying at the fact that their children have had to leave the area; taking precious mokopuna with them.

“Former WPI workers were not only employees. They were also parents, coaches, volunteers, trustees and people who contributed to local organisations and the wider community.”

Of those monitored, 105, or 56.5%, are in work. A further 30 are in seasonal or casual jobs, and 30 are looking.

Nearly all have taken a substantial drop in pay, and with a large skilled workforce suddenly job hunting, competition for even minimum-wage roles has increased across Ruapehu communities.

Leahy cautions that the raw numbers don’t tell the whole story.

“The employment figures should not be taken to mean the effects of the closures have been resolved simply because someone has returned to some form of work.”

Set out like cutlery for giants, long-bladed chainsaws sit on the tables in the front room of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua’s offices.

A class teaching forestry skills to people seeking work has finished for the day, the gear left ready for the morning session.

The iwi collective represents the descendants of Uenuku, Tamahaki and Tamakana, and in 2025 its Treaty settlement with the Crown became law.

Chief executive Te Moananui Rameka, 10 months into the job, says the loss of people, piled on top of living in one of the most disadvantaged regions, breeds misery and desperation.

“What follows is chaos,” he says.

“When jobs disappear, what do you do? ... You have to go somewhere else if you can. Households lose income, businesses lose customers, the whole region starts to degrade.

“You can see it in people’s faces ... you see people struggling, deciding what to buy, what’s a priority on their shopping list today, because they have less and less money.”

Chair Aiden Gilbert says decisions made long ago still shape the present.

“A hundred years ago, 50 years ago, even 30 years ago, and 25 years ago, they are still taking effect on us, how we behave today.”

New decisions still confound him, he says, such as the Government’s refusal to help with rising electricity costs and keep the two mills open.

He points to Rio Tinto’s Tiwai smelter, which he says enjoys subsidised power, “but we can’t even get the subsidy to keep this mill open”.

Gilbert fears the Government’s next decisions will make things worse in a place where many rely on welfare.

“I believe the Crown is now thinking about, well, how much [welfare] can we actually do away with?”

Instead of growing “the crumbs that we call a quantum” – the $21.7 million that was part of the recent Treaty settlement meant to lift the iwi’s future – there will be an expectation or demand to plug gaps left by lost benefits, he believes.

Rameka backs up Gilbert – the iwi will be expected to “step into that void”, he says.

“And fundamentally, we will anyway, because that is our responsibility ... but, at the same time, you’ve got to help us.

“Just because [a settlement’s] been signed doesn’t mean our job has been done.”

Raetihi has been a movie set more than once, and you can see why.

Wide streets, old historic frontages. The snow and glaciers on Mt Ruapehu shine under the spring sun. There are native forests to trek, rivers to fish and bike paths to cycle.

What’s not to like?

Craig Hughes and his wife chose it from Auckland 12 years ago, buying a small farm and planting it up with fruit trees and berries.

“I’m in full support of this little community. It’s great living here.”

He was winding down towards retirement when his go-getter wife came home at the start of the year and told him she had bought him a restaurant.

“I said, ‘You did what?’”

The previous owners were selling. The cafe had stopped paying its way after the mills closed, Hughes says.

So in January the couple took over the old Coach Cafe, renamed it Robin’s Nest Bistro, and got down to business.

The town had no sit-down restaurant, he says.

“They were all takeaways. I wanted somewhere comfortable to eat, not expensive. You can sit down, relax, and then go. I’m not here to make millions of dollars ... this is my retirement plan.”

Across the street from Robin’s Nest sits a row of six closed shops and buildings. Hughes reckons a lack of trade isn’t the only reason.

“They’ve been shut for a long time because they’re owned by someone else. Not living here.”

Given the chance, he’d fix that himself.

“If I won money, that’s what I’d do. I’d buy them, do them up.”

Winter was quiet, he admits. One recent move to lift trade was opening earlier for lunch, but even that proved frustrating and expensive.

Extending his liquor licence to cover the afternoon cost about $5000 and plenty of time.

Hughes has been a long-time Greens voter yet found himself eyeing a split vote, drawn to Act and the promise of less red tape for people like him.

“The only good thing I’ve heard [Act leader David] Seymour say is, he was going to help the small businesses.”

Ruapehu Mayor Weston Kirton would love to help the workers who lost their jobs.

But that’s central Government’s job, he says.

The Ruapehu District Council does help with the Mayor’s Taskforce for Jobs in getting young people into work. It also encourages new industry into the area when it can, like the growing pet food factory on the edge of Taumarunui.

Running the district is hard enough. The council has been going through all its services, asking ratepayers what matters to them and where it could cut, such as “does Taumarunui really need one hall, or two?”, Kirton says.

If the council stripped back to core services, rates would fall to 2.7%, he says.

“But we can’t match the affordability with the expectation of central Government.

“When you add back in everything that the Government’s told us we need to do, it [the rates] gets up to plus 10%.”

In August, Local Government Minister Simon Watts announced plans to cap council rate rises at 4% a year.

The district can’t seem to catch a break either.

The Chateau Tongariro remains closed, meaning fewer bed nights and people spending time in the region.

There have been some poor snow years on the commercial ski fields, and Covid hammered tourism.

And then industry like Karioi and Tangiwai mills exits the room.

Housing is squeezed. Ōhakune is a ski town, and holiday homes keep prices up there. The pressure spills down the road to Raetihi.

Between 30% and 40% of the district’s homes are owned by out-of-district ratepayers, Kirton says.

At the 2023 Census, nearly a quarter of Raetihi’s homes sat unoccupied, a figure that includes holiday homes and is more than double the national rate.

“You get outside investors coming in, and they grab those cheap houses in front of those who are wanting a first home.”

The Census put the town’s median rent at $250 a week, but people the Herald spoke to quoted more than $400.

If it weren’t for the higher meat and wool prices being earned from farming, and the farmers paying rates, the area would be in dire straits, Kirton says.

“If you’ve got an old car and it’s bloody breaking down every five minutes, there’s been more money on the bloody repairing ... you just put it down a big hole,” he says.

“If you were to get a decent car, functional car, then the maintenance of that is actually far less.”

Asked what the area needs from any incoming Government in November’s election, Kirton says “a bit of capital injection”.

If they can fix the car, then the district can get on with the journey, he reckons.

So what’s in it for politicians to help this way? That’s part of the problem, Kirton admits.

“There’s not as many votes here as ... in Auckland. They can spend two days in Auckland and get 10 times the votes than they would if they come here.”

On Raetihi’s main street, wrapped in white plastic, is the Waimarino Health Centre, a Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora facility getting a $4.4m upgrade.

When work finishes in the second half of 2027, the GP clinic, district nurses and mental health team will work together under one roof.

Disconnected services have been one of locals’ biggest frustrations, Whanganui Regional Health Network (WRHN) chief executive Judith Macdonald says.

The network owns Ruapehu Health, the town’s general practice, which will run from the new building.

“We would really like to say that people get a seamless service and that it’s more connected.”

For now, there is no permanent doctor in Raetihi. Nurse practitioners and nurses work alongside rostered locums and online doctors.

WRHN is advertising for a permanent doctor, but Macdonald doesn’t expect to find one who will live in Raetihi.

“The reality is in remote rural communities, the days of old are gone now. We’re never going to be in a position to probably sustain someone permanently up there.”

The current clinic is also shut at weekends.

The Herald was told that if you get hurt at the weekend, call an ambulance – you’ll get a bed far sooner than if you make the 90-minute drive to Whanganui Hospital yourself.

Macdonald says such advice is unnecessary because there is an on-call service and online doctors can assess patients.

The upgrade won’t deliver everything locals wanted. The original concept envisaged an integrated wellness centre that went beyond treatment to having programmes for wider community wellbeing.

“The dollars didn’t quite go as far as we would have liked,” Macdonald says.

For Edmonds, health services hassles are a bugbear. Waiting three weeks for a GP appointment and the delays in receiving a script are painful.

Like Kirton, he wants the basics working.

“I don’t want too many new things because I’d rather have what we have sort of fixed up and made fit for purpose again, and, you know, working properly.”

Edmonds wants investment that’s worthwhile, “not like a token bunch of money that’s been chucked at us”.

But he suspects Raetihi gets put in “the too hard basket”.

The best outcome for Raetihi and the district – “it all comes down to people having jobs”, he says.

At Te Korowai o Wainuiārua, where the chainsaws sit ready for the next class of keen learners, they are over empty promises.

Gilbert has learned to read every word the Crown puts in front of him.

“‘We may consider it’, ‘we will consider it’, it’s a totally different meaning,” he says.

“‘You will do it’, and that’s how you hold your honour.”

Rameka wants the country to see the people of the region and not just the poverty.

“We’re a proud people, we’re a beautiful people with a deep whakapapa knowledge ... the economic hardship doesn’t define who we are.

“Hope is a whānau member getting reliable work, bringing more money home. Hope is the ability to go out and buy food, enough food to put on the table. Hope is a roof that doesn’t leak.

“And a power bill that’s not going to run you dry.”

Mike Scott is a senior journalist at the Herald. His work spans writing, photography and video and he has won numerous journalism awards, including Videographer of the Year and Best Documentary. He has worked in media for more than 25 years, producing stories across New Zealand and internationally.

Cervical cancer: The women left in painful positions from failed prevention

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

Lizzie Boekhorst at home in Wellington with her beloved dog. Photo / Mark Mitchell

Women have been left in painful positions by a history of flawed prevention against cervical cancer in New Zealand. Both parties are now pledging to make changes, but for many the words feel empty, Eva de Jong writes.

Mother-of-two Lizzie Boekhorst had to choose between having another child or removing her uterus after being diagnosed with cervical cancer.

From inside her family home in Churton Park, Wellington, Boekhorst remembers what it felt like sitting in a doctor’s room, with her baby daughter on her lap, and being told she must choose between a total hysterectomy or further procedures to attempt to remove the cancer cells.

“It was really hard,” she says.

“My husband and I decided we would rather protect our current family unit and have the surgery, than risk any cancer being left. There were no guarantees they could get it all so it felt like the right decision to reduce the risk and anxiety about the cancer remaining and getting worse.

“It still left its mark, even though I was one of the lucky ones.”

She felt lucky to already have two beautiful kids and wanted to safeguard her family unit, but in recent years, she has wondered what it would have been like to have another child.

A hysterectomy involves the total removal of the uterus and cervix, with the ovaries remaining.

After the surgery, Boekhorst wasn’t able to lift anything heavier than a kettle for six weeks and her baby daughter was just 9 months old at the time.

She had to rely on her wider family for extra support, as even at night, to breastfeed her baby she would have to hobble into the next room and wait for her husband to place her on to her lap.

“The children want to climb all over you, but since you have to be so careful, that was a really hard part of it.”

Navigating other decisions such as when it was safe to push a pram was tricky.

At age 39, Boekhorst is someone who went to school before the HPV vaccine started being offered to students.

It frustrates her to see myths being spread about the vaccine.

Infection with the HPV virus is common, with an estimated 70-80% of sexually active individuals becoming infected at some stage during their life.

The Weekend Herald recently reported on how the uptake of the HPV vaccine was stalled by damaging myths about the virus being linked to sexual promiscuity with many schools declining to offer the vaccine.

The failure to deliver vaccination and screening prevention equitably has been reflected in the higher rates of endometrial and cervical cancer among Māori and Pacific women.

Health New Zealand prevention screening national director, Alana Ewe-Snow, says cervical screening participation has increased significantly for Māori and Pacific women with the impact of self-testing and dedicated efforts by health providers.

Boekhorst is concerned about the huge portion of people missing out on the opportunity to protect themselves through the HPV vaccine, who might think that living a conservative sexual life, with one partner, is a form of protection.

She would like to see increased accessibility, funding and education about the HPV vaccine as well as the empowering of wāhine to be able to access cervical screening services later in life.

Immunisation Advisory Centre senior Māori medical adviser and Onehunga GP Mamaeroa David has witnessed first-hand the way in which barriers to cervical screening and the HPV vaccine prevents women from accessing treatment they desperately need.

She urges any woman who is experiencing abnormal bleeding, heavy bleeding or bleeding outside their period to book an appointment with their GP and not to take the risk of normalising these symptoms.

“One of my saddest cases was a woman who’d been my patient for a very, very long time,” David says.

“And then she never really shared how heavy her periods had been, but that’s also because women can normalise the worst things.”

It wasn’t until years later when the woman was experiencing non-stop bleeding that she phoned David to tell her, but because she had missed consecutive smear tests she was too worried to come in to the practice.

David urged her to go to the hospital or be seen by a GP, but she refused.

“I wrote a letter so that it was in writing and sent it to her, I said you need to go to the hospital, I cannot rule out cancer. And she still wouldn’t go to the hospital.”

The woman did end up being diagnosed with cervical cancer, and it was heartbreaking for David to witness, especially as there was continuing resistance from her daughters to getting the HPV vaccine.

“Any woman who’s had to have gynaecological stuff, it’s so, demeaning or it just feels terribly invasive. And when it’s a cancer where you have no choice and it’s repeatedly people constantly having to examine you vaginally, you know, it’s painful,” David says.

“You’re bleeding from your vagina or you’re being examined vaginally, and it’s such a sacred space for our Māori and Pacific women.”

It is clear to Boekhorst that it often falls on women to follow up with their clinic about getting cervical smear tests, and it can easily be pushed to one side because of the cost.

In September, the Government released its Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan with a target of 2040 and announced it would make screening for cervical cancer free from March next year.

Australia is on track to become the first country in the world to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035, but New Zealand is lagging far behind this goal: the HPV vaccination national coverage among 15-year-olds is about 60%.

The World Health Organisation’s goal is 90% vaccination coverage and the elimination of cervical cancer, which would mean reducing the incidence rate to fewer than four cases per 100,000 women.

Each year about 175 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer and 55 people die from it.

The recent introduction of self-testing for cervical smears has hugely improved access, and David says previously she regularly saw women who would not participate in traditional speculum smears.

“As much as that early HPV screening could have saved her life, actually getting the HPV vaccine could have stopped her from having any issue at all,” she says.

As a GP, she has seen many examples of women who ignore symptoms of bleeding or pain because they are busy caring for their family and often put their own health last when it comes to seeking out treatment.

But the system has also let them down.

Recently, a major review found nearly one million cervical cancer screening notifications were missed or unsent by Health New Zealand’s national register.

University of Otago Associate Professor Dr Peter Sykes, who works in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, says the Government’s cervical cancer elimination plan 2026-2040 has been described as “very much a top-down Wellington document”.

Many community providers have complained about a lack of consultation, he says.

“The principles in the new strategy are fair and non-controversial, but it’s about how it’s implemented and making sure that Māori benefit,” he says.

Sykes says community providers felt they could achieve the goal better if priority groups like Māori were considered and offered earlier input at the beginning of the process.

David says the “Smear Your Mea” campaign that was launched by kapa haka star Talei Morrison in 2017 was an incredible example of ways to reach Māori wāhine effectively through public health messaging.

Morrison, who died of cervical cancer, worked tirelessly through a grassroots campaign to encourage other women to get a smear test.

“The majority of people who I’ve seen with HPV cancers are mums, who have kids that are still young,” David says.

“I think it should be about having a whole wellbeing focus and looking after our mothers, rather than just being about vaginal examination, it’s about bringing that honour back.”

Screening coverage for Māori women has increased and Pacific women have exceeded that national screening target, according to Health New Zealand, but there is still work to be done to lift national results.

In the past, there have been horrific consequences for women in New Zealand who were let down by the health system.

A study carried out by Dr Herbert Green at National Women’s Hospital in Auckland that began in 1966 was labelled “The Unfortunate Experiment”, as women involved who had abnormal cervical smear results were left untreated.

The experiment resulted in the Cartwright Inquiry into patients’ rights being carried out by the Government and led to significant reforms.

Cancer Society head of advocacy and public affairs Rachael Neumann has worked in public health and chronic disease prevention for more than 20 years and says those recent missed cervical screening notifications highlight a need for significant commitment to redesign the system.

“We need to think about when contacting hard-to-reach communities if a letter is enough,” she says.

“You know about 175 people develop cervical cancer each year and about 55 will die. We have to make sure things like this don’t happen in the future.

“You can have a nice plan, but you need funding and commitment from politicians and our health sector to bring the results to fruition.”

David would like to see a shift among parents to speaking openly with their children about the importance of the HPV vaccine for protection.

“There’s so much shame around that kind of cancer that people just have no idea how common [it] is,” she says.

Boekhorst’s daughter was just 6 months old, and she was still coming out of the haze of having a newborn baby, when she realised she was overdue for a cervical smear – a check-up that was the last thing on her mind.

She was always good at keeping up with her cervical smears and this ultimately saved her life.

A tough part of having cervical cancer that surprised her was how difficult and awkward it felt to talk openly about the cancer, and she found there weren’t a lot of support groups for people following a hysterectomy.

“Where it’s located is in a very private part of your body and drawing attention to that in any form is very uncomfortable, and there’s negative perceptions around risk factors and things.

“But the more I’ve talked about my experience, the more I’ve heard from others.”

She joined an online support group based in the US and now continues doing advocacy for the Cancer Society to support cervical cancer prevention.

“It was detected really early for me so the system worked in that regard, but the recovery process was really long mentally, physically and emotionally.

“If we can reduce the risk, then other women won’t have to go through this at all,” she says.

Letters: Muldoon and Black Power are a political precedent for affinity

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

Former Prime Minister Robert Muldoon had regular meetings with Black Power. Photo / Getty Images

Letter of the week: Muldoon and Black Power

There has been negative feedback about the recent meeting of Green Party and Te Pāti Māori members with the Mongrel Mob. It seems history has been forgotten. There is a precedent set by former National Prime Minister, Rob Muldoon, who had an affinity with Black Power.

When he died in 1992, 100 Black Power members did a haka of respect as the hearse left his funeral service at the Auckland Town Hall. This is all documented in various publications, including Barry Gustafson’s biography titled His Way, published in 2000.

Vivienne Hill, Henderson.

Eden Park trains

Several years ago, we took three small boys to Eden Park to watch the All Blacks play England. The grounds were packed, the All Blacks won, to the delight of the boys. We had parked our car at Sylvia Park and used trains to get to the stadium. So easy. The return trip was just as smooth, one train in to Britomart, another out to Sylvia Park.

The key to the mass exit of the stadium was the efficiency of the Māori Wardens. They marshalled the crowd into carriage-size groups and monitored the movement, no pushing, no shouting, no anger.

Our only problem was three starving boys, which necessitated a very late stop at McDonald’s.

Linley Jones, Half Moon Bay.

Parties need to quantify promises and hyperbole

As the election campaigns draw closer to the day that will determine who will lead our country, and we are bombarded with sometimes fatuous promises, one constant that I (and I am sure others) find empty and irritating is the hyperbole that is a part of the election debate.

We hear with monotonous regularity, terms such as: “rip-off”, “price gouging” and “excess profit”.

It seems that these emotive terms are never quantified, nor examples given.

Cost-of-living pressures are a given and the empty promises about how all parties are going to address this issue include attacking the grocery sector.

Let the “excess profits” supposedly generated by this sector be quantified, so voters can make a measured decision about the veracity of this supposition. Then compare the facts with those from other sectors.

Is the hyperbole perhaps the reason no potential overseas competitor is interested in entering the New Zealand market with its skinny margins?

Let informed electors decide.

Mike Donovan, Remuera.

Eventuate the positive

The common feature of this general election is negativity.

National has a campaign slogan “No New Taxes”. Many parties have stated categorically who they could not form a coalition with. Many are now saying they would not have certain coalition partners in specific ministerial posts.

Is it any wonder polls show no single party will get more than 30% of the party vote, but seven parties will get above the 5% threshold to enter Parliament.

Have we become a nation that knows what it doesn’t want but cannot agree on anything that might benefit everybody?

Peter D. Graham, Helensville.

Public service cuts

When will the nonsense stop? The Greens pledge to cancel National’s $2.4 billion public service cuts. Where is this money going to come from – borrow more, raise taxes or cut something else? The public service had increased by more than 30% under Labour – it basically expanded faster than the economy.

So, when the Greens say “restore funding”, they’re effectively saying keep paying for a structure already proven as not delivering better outcomes.

New Zealand’s public‑service workforce is not small by international standards. It sits above Australia’s, and well above the UK’s, when measured as a share of the total workforce. This is why many economists argue the sector is “bloated” relative to comparable countries.

Ian MacGregor, Greenhithe.

State of charter schools

The country supports the following secondary school systems: state schools, state integrated schools, private schools, Māori medium state schools and now newly established charter schools.

I have been a board member and sometime chairman of two young single-sex secondary schools for 18 years that have established themselves to become two of the premier state schools in New Zealand.

I am also familiar with California charter schools and magnet schools.

In looking at charter schools, the new style of schools, I see little to commend them when compared to traditional schools.

I am also familiar with US charter schools and magnet schools.

Here they receive bigger contributions from Government, have fewer curriculum restrictions and other forms of relaxation and oversight.

In looking at the various measurements of achievement and success of secondary schools, they have extensive criteria to be measured against.

One can measure a school’s success in many forms and the need to enlarge the choice to include a Charter school in the mix is entirely unnecessary and adds further to the cost of education.

It is essential to have in place universal standards and expectations that are measurable.

These are obtained by strong, effective leadership and support.

If the school leadership is strong, there is no need for so-called charter schools in New Zealand.

Peter Burn, Gulf Harbour.

Capping nurses scandalous

It is scandalous that the Luxon administration is capping the numbers of nurses to be trained at a time when the Starship children’s hospital is suspending some cancer treatment because of nursing staff shortages, and while Health New Zealand is preventing recruitment into nursing vacancies. Is this how Luxon is growing the economy? How unfortunate that this was not revealed before Wednesday’s NZ Herald/3Now Leaders’ Debate.

Hugh Webb, Hamilton.

A quick word

The Greens promise to fund $247-plus billion should they get into Parliament – it is laughable. It’s high time all parties forget frivolous spending and concentrate on the real issues.

Ian Doube, Rotorua.

I have been a primary teacher for over 40 years. The expectation has always been to have maths, reading and writing. I’ve never encountered a teacher that has not timetabled and delivered the required hours into their daily programme.

Suzanne Corlett, Ramarama.

The Green Party says it’s open to funding the Mongrel Mob to address drug addiction. It might be argued there exists a rough parallel to Joe Kennedy sucking up to American organised crime in order to score votes for Jack.

Peter Culpan, Te Atatū Peninsula.

Mauao Māori wardens spat at and pelted with bottles while guarding closed maunga

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Māori Wardens protecting Mauao say they have been spat at, had bottles and food thrown at them and dealt with repeated cordon breaches.

Since the fatal Mauao landslide on January 22, Ngā Wātene Māori o Mauao wardens have worked in shifts to guard the cordon around the closed maunga.

Wardens say the job has brought verbal and physical abuse, dangerous breaches and difficult working conditions, including having to build their own makeshift shelter against the weather.

Sophie Te Moni is chairwoman of Ngā Wātene Māori o Mauao Charitable Trust, which is contracted by Tauranga City Council to provide security at the cordon.

She also works as a warden at the base of Mauao.

Te Moni said wardens had been at Mauao since 8am on January 22 and initially had 12 volunteers around the base.

“From that day forward, we’ve been working 24/7.”

Currently, two wardens are based at the Mount Main Beach end of the cordon.

It has not been easy for the group as they try to protect the slip-scarred maunga they regard as whānau.

“We look after him to make sure that he’s not being disrespected.”

The wardens’ co-ordinator Katrina Hoko said they had seen several breaches, usually from “hyped up” young people.

Te Moni recalled three boys breaching the cordon and going to the top of the main landslide.

“It was so scary because we could see them and the police refused to go in because it was a dangerous area.”

Police said the trio were later arrested and charged.

Hoko said while many people the wardens met had been supportive, including locals offering support and food, wardens had also been verbally and physically abused.

“We’ve been spat at,” she said. Bottles and food had also been thrown at them.

Te Moni said wardens were told to remain polite despite the hostility, which had usually come from locals.

“I say, just be polite and they won’t come back.”

She said the wardens write daily reports to track what happens, including any negative encounters.

She said the Māori Wardens based at Mauao receive funding from the council in the form of a koha (donation). This covered costs including fuel, meals, uniforms and wet weather gear.

Local Facebook users recently raised concerns about the wardens’ working conditions at the cordons, with photos of their makeshift shelter shared.

The shelter, made using tarps, metal framing, timber posts, rope and cords, was described as looking like “a homeless shelter”.

Te Moni said they initially used their limited funding to hire a caravan to provide shelter on the Pilot Bay side and later bought some gazebos, which had since “blown away” in the harsh winds.

“Since then my crew constructed that thing that’s out there.

“It’s quite ugly, but it’s the only kind of shelter they could put up themselves that stayed there.”

She said they were in the process of removing it, as the council had said it would create a shelter.

Tauranga City Council recovery manager Charlie Rahiri said it contracted the trust to provide security from the start of the emergency response.

Its contract required the trust to provide welfare items, including temporary shelter.

Rahiri acknowledged the wardens’ current facilities were “not ideal”.

“The council is working with Ngā Watene Māori o Mauao to repair and/or replace this structure that has been damaged.”

He said some “unacceptable and disrespectful behaviour such as throwing bottles and food at wardens” happened in January, right after the slip, but quickly stopped.

Wardens’ daily reports to supervisors were not passed to the council unless there were cordon breaches or health and safety issues of concern.

Security would remain necessary because Mauao was still a “high-risk” area and active recovery site, and breaches continued, Rahiri said.

He said the recent reduction from seven to two wardens was a trial because there had been fewer breaches of the “more robust” Pilot Bay fencing.

More people were also around after the boat ramp and surf club reopened on Adams Ave.

The council has previously said it hopes to repair and partially reopen the tracks on Mauao this summer, if that can happen safely.

A September 1 progress report on recovery efforts said it spent $192,919 on security in the initial response to the Mauao weather event, and $645,723 on security for the ongoing Mauao recovery.

Total expenses related to the response and recovery exceeded $5.1 million.

Western Bay of Plenty Police area commander Inspector Clifford Paxton said three young men who breached the Mauao cordon on February 11 were charged under the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act and pleaded guilty.

Two were fined $800, while the third was due in court in January.

He said the cordons on Mauao were clearly signposted and monitored by CCTV.

“They are in place to protect public safety, and there is no excuse for breaching them.”

Ayla Yeoman is a Local Democracy Reporting journalist based in Tauranga. She holds a Bachelor of Arts majoring in communications, politics and international relations from the University of Auckland, and has been a journalist since 2023.

Waikato development: 301-home project in doubt over Cambridge fill plan

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

ResourceCo’s Cambridge site, viewed from across the Waikato River, where a major managed fill operation is proposed.

Developers are considering abandoning a consented and approved 301-home project in Cambridge because of a proposed managed fill expansion nearby.

The consented housing project, called Arikirua, was approved in February last year.

It is being developed jointly by St Peter’s School, 3MS Development and Te Awa Lifecare on land owned by the school.

Meanwhile, waste disposal company ResourceCo lodged a resource consent application with Waipā District Council in October last year to extend its nearby recycling facility.

The application is still being considered.

St Peter’s School Trust board chairman John Macaskill-Smith said ResourceCo’s proposal at 3831 Cambridge Rd conflicted with the town’s long-term residential growth plans.

“Many local people may be unaware this consent application is even being considered.”

ResourceCo proposes filling an existing sand quarry with more than 1.36 million cubic metres of approved soil, including material containing low levels of contaminants.

Managed fill sites may contain soil including heavy metals, hydrocarbons, and pesticide residues, within acceptance limits.

Waipā District Council said it had not yet decided whether to grant the consent.

It classified the proposal as a non-complying activity and decided to “limited-notify”, rather than publicly notify, the application.

Its assessment identified 22 properties potentially affected by minor amounts of dust and another four potentially affected by dust and noise.

The council’s report also acknowledged strong community interest and previous complaints about ResourceCo’s existing recycling facility.

However, the council said those factors did not constitute “special circumstances” requiring public notification.

It said case law made clear that community interest alone was insufficient.

Macaskill-Smith said St Peter’s and 3MS already had consent for their 301-lot development across the Waikato River from the ResourceCo site.

“We’re sitting on a consented and approved development; it’s not like we’re waiting for anything. It’s all ready to go.”

3MS was also behind Bridleways Estate, a Cambridge West residential development with more than 250 sections, parks, walking and cycling routes, and a proposed primary school, Macaskill-Smith said.

Between Arikirua and Bridleways Estate, more than 500 residential lots are consented in the area.

Macaskill-Smith said the school, 3MS and Te Awa Lifecare believed extending the fill operation would conflict with Cambridge’s planned residential growth.

“There’s a really clear and well-articulated long-term plan for the growth of the Cambridge community, and it’s residential by nature.”

If the managed fill went ahead, Macaskill-Smith said the three parties would reconsider proceeding with Arikirua.

“If council grants the new consents for the managed fill site, we will need to seriously consider abandoning this development altogether.

“Who’s going to want to buy a section opposite that?”

Truck movements, dust, smells and the site’s proximity to the Waikato River were among the groups’ concerns.

Waipā District Council had already invested about $20 million in infrastructure to support Cambridge’s residential growth, he said.

However, the council said the $20m figure referred to the development contribution assessed against Arikirua, not money already spent on infrastructure.

If the Arikirua subdivision did not proceed, the council would reassess the development contributions model, with any shortfall not falling on existing ratepayers.

The council said it had invested significantly in roading, stormwater and other infrastructure supporting Cambridge’s growth, much of which served a wider area.

ResourceCo managing director Henry Fullerton-Smith said the proposal would rehabilitate the quarry while providing the managed fill capacity that Waipā needed.

Sand extraction had left a large quarry void that eventually needed to be filled, while the district was short of consented capacity for low-level soils generated by subdivisions, roads and infrastructure projects.

Without local capacity, material would have to be trucked further away, increasing truck movements, costs and emissions, or be sent unnecessarily to landfill.

Fullerton-Smith said the proposed volume reflected the quarry’s size and the material required to create a stable, free-draining landform.

The maximum 21m fill depth applied only to the deepest part of the quarry.

“The site will not be filled above its original landform.”

Dust and noise were among the effects the council considered during its notification assessment.

Fullerton-Smith said dust controls would include water carts and sprinklers, wheel washing, limiting active tipping areas, monitoring and progressively capping and grassing completed areas.

An acoustic assessment predicted 55 decibels (dB) at the southern boundary, above the 50dB daytime limit.

The council said that exceedance was part of the reason the boundary property was notified.

It said it would next consider the final decision and any conditions that could apply if it granted consent.

Fullerton-Smith said the noise prediction represented a worst-case scenario with all plant operating simultaneously at the closest point to the boundary.

He said ResourceCo respected the council’s notification process and affected parties had the opportunity to participate.

A joint Waipā District Council and Waikato Regional Council hearing is being organised, with a decision to follow.

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Former schoolteacher Damian Patrick Young still maintains his innocence more than two years after he was jailed for indecently assaulting three students.

The 59-year-old, who was imprisoned for two years and seven months in June 2024, will be released on November 2 after a parole hearing yesterday.

Young worked at two Christchurch schools during the offending.

Neither of the schools can be named.

Under the pretence of viewing films and dimming the lights in his classes, he approached girls and inappropriately touched them.

They were aged 6 to 8.

Two of the 10 indecent assault accusations against him were representative.

He elected a trial, during which the jury heard statements from the girls.

The parents who complained about him also testified.

In his defence, educators, former educators and co-workers told jurors Young had little opportunity to offend.

But the jury found him guilty of six charges, including the representative ones.

Young appealed the convictions in 2025, claiming Judge Jane Farish failed to maintain balance or neutrality during the trial.

The Court of Appeal disagreed, saying Judge Farish was not biased towards the Crown or Young, and dismissed the appeal.

Young yesterday told Parole Board members Judge Gus Andree Wiltens, Matire Kupenga-Wanoa and Materoa Dodd that while he maintained his innocence, he would do nothing to jeopardise reintegration into the community.

Speaking from Rolleston Prison, Young said he was looking to rebuild relationships with family and friends and believed he could live in the community with their support.

Judge Andree Wiltens asked Young what needed to happen to ensure he was safe.

Young said isolation, physical and mental health were things he needed to monitor.

“If I keep an eye on these things, things should go well for me.”

He planned to take up landscaping.

“It is important that I do work; I need to be active and have a purpose.”

Judge Andree Wiltens asked Young if he had thought about study.

Young said he might look at distance learning around psychology.

Young said he had been called on by other prisoners to help with their studies.

A Corrections officer described him as a model prisoner.

The judge asked Young if he had looked at the report that outlined his release conditions.

Young said he understood them and would abide by the conditions.

A family member told the board they accepted he had been found guilty.

His family had been actively involved in his safety plan and would be monitoring him, she said.

The family would also provide financial support.

“We have stood united with Damian; we will hold him to account if we have any doubt, if he is in any way breaching his release conditions or the CSO [Child Sex Offender Register].”

Tauranga raw milk farm: Former chef builds an almost self-sufficient family life

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

Welcome Bay farmer Loren Gibbs in the eight ASHB dairy shed. Photo / Catherine Fry

Move aside, Tom and Barbara. The Good Life in Tauranga has stepped up its game.

Loren and Michaela Gibbs are living the good life with their four children and are almost self-sufficient in seasonal food while also supplying locals with produce through their farm shop in Welcome Bay.

The couple had been living in Melbourne, where Michaela worked in event management, and Loren worked as a trained chef for 12 years.

“It got to a stage where we both really wanted to come home and be near family,” Loren Gibbs said.

“Michaela’s parents, Daryl and Larisa, were retired dairy farmers, had owned TVMG in Matamata and were now living on a lifestyle block in Welcome Bay.”

After moving in with Michaela’s parents, Gibbs did a stint as a stay-at-home dad while Michaela worked.

“Then the veggie and raw milk set-up where Michaela’s parents got their raw milk from came on the market,” he said.

Daryl and Larisa proposed that, if they bought the land, Loren and Michaela could run it.

“It has a good symmetry to being a chef, but I had no experience in farming,” Gibbs said.

“We still said yes!”

While the contract and funding for the land were being sorted out, Gibbs worked alongside the old owners for six months, learning how to grow produce from seed, animal care and milking in the eight ASHB shed.

“Because the farm was already set up, any capital could be put straight into the business,” he said.

The first task was to get the raw milk supply consistent, achievable by having cows calving throughout the year.

“With 30 cows, we aim to have two calves a month to keep the milk supply constant,” Gibbs said.

“We run a Hereford bull, so all our calves can be sold as beefies.

“There are no bobby calves in our set-up.”

Gibbs runs half the number of cows that could be run on the 7.5ha set aside for grazing.

“It means the pasture has time to recover and there’s plenty of grass available,” he said.

“We have healthy, well-fed cows.”

The soil and pasture are slowly being improved using natural fertilisers through Eco Farms.

Cleanliness and hygiene were essential around raw milk, and Gibbs said he spent more time cleaning, sanitising and stripping the teats than actually milking.

“The milk goes through a paper filter and cooling system before entering the cooled vat for dispensing.

“The kids often sit at the cowshed with their bowl of dry cereal and choose a cow for me to hand milk until their cereal is covered with creamy, fresh milk.”

The farm produces around 150 to 180 litres of milk a day, about 1000 litres a week, with raw milk forming the backbone of the business.

The team wants to keep the 1000sq m market garden manageable and not too intense.

They don’t claim to be organic growers but avoid synthetic pesticides, herbicides and fertilisers.

“We use ‘no dig’ gardening principles,” Gibbs said.

“By not disturbing the soil, but layering the garden with the nutrients it needs to feed the soil and thus the plants, you have a healthier nervous system within the soil.”

In winter, they slow the garden down, letting areas rest and restore.

During summer, the garden is pumping, and it’s all hands on deck with harvesting produce for the farm shop.

They only grow outdoors and in season.

“I’m also fascinated by edible weeds and flowers, and I add them to our salad mix,” he said.

“It’s probably the chef in me coming out; I want people to have healthy and attractive food!”

As well as learning how to care for the animals, Gibbs has taught himself how to butcher the pigs, sheep and chickens they raise for homekill.

He finds it fascinating to butcher the cuts of meat he used as a chef.

Each family has their own home on the property, and it works well for all of them.

Daryl works on the farm two days a week doing anything from relief milking to building all their ideas for developing the property.

Larisa does the accounts, fills in on the farm and helps look after her four grandchildren so Michaela can get out on the farm, as well as doing the marketing and socials for the business.

Gibbs said he got to spend so much time with his family, a far cry from his cheffing days, and eight years on, he wouldn’t change their good life for anything.

Peter Reynolds: The Pukekohe grower who helped shape modern horticulture

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

Pukekohe grower Peter Reynolds is easing into retirement after “70 years farming and the two years before that thinking about it”.

When Peter Reynolds arrived at his table at the 2026 New Zealand Horticulture Conference gala dinner, he was surprised to find himself seated with government and industry leaders who were unusually quiet.

He soon found out why when he was announced as the recipient of the Horticulture Bledisloe Cup.

“They were worried they’d give the game away,” Reynolds laughed.

The sector’s highest honour, the cup recognises outstanding and meritorious contributions to the horticulture industry.

Reynolds’ long career in farming and growing has spanned potato, onion and pumpkin production, as well as cattle and sheep farming, and kiwifruit production.

He has been a staunch advocate for growers, technical innovation and best practice, supporting numerous research projects across the 15 blocks around Pukekohe and Tuakau that made up the multigenerational family business.

He has also championed environmental stewardship, showing how shelter belts, riparian planting systems, advanced soil control mechanisms, along with cropping and grazing land rotation systems go hand in hand with commercial success.

Reynolds has also had a role in uniting diverse grower groups, leading to the establishment of Potatoes New Zealand and Onions New Zealand.

At 72 – after what he describes as “70 years farming and the two years before that thinking about it” – he is easing into retirement on a 20ha block where he is fencing off wetlands, undertaking extensive native planting and farming cattle.

“Blown away” to receive the cup, he said he saw it as an honour for his extended family and the wider Pukekohe community.

The Reynolds family has deep roots in the district, with his father’s forebears arriving from Ireland in 1865 and his mother’s in 1911.

Reynolds said his family leased and bought little plots of land, running small-scale dairy farms and growing potatoes and grain.

“In their pockets they bought barberry seeds for hedging,” he said.

“They grew plants and sold them all over the North Island.”

“This was very useful after the war, when there was no metal for fencing.”

He said farmers used barberry hedges for shelter, to control animals, and to keep them out of waterways.

“They also brought acorns with them to grow oak trees.

“A lot of the oak trees around the area were planted by my family, including at the Pukekohe Racetrack.”

Reynolds’ father, Tom, began farming with his father and uncle before five years overseas during World War II, returning in 1946 and marrying Maureen Flynn in 1949.

“During the war Dad was an armourer, repairing equipment, guns and cannons in makeshift workshops in the back of Army trucks,” Reynolds said.

“Following the war, he came back and got stuck into farming.”

Reynolds said there were no tractors in the area at the time, so they used horses instead.

“As tractors came along, Dad started modifying equipment to use behind the tractors along with other farmers and engineers.”

He said this type of collaboration could still be seen today.

“Through the years, very good engineering businesses have developed in Pukekohe building world-class field and packhouse equipment, and a lot of that grew out of people building what they needed for their own farms and sharing ideas.

“Whatever worked on your farm might work on another, and the next year there might be a good idea from another farm that would work on yours.”

“I’ve always found farmers share that way.

“You can walk on to any farm in the world, and you are mates right away, sharing ideas.”

Tom and Maureen had seven boys, then three girls.

Through the 1950s and 1960s, they farmed sheep and grew onions.

Tom developed an early-harvesting onion which the Reynolds still grow, ready for harvesting just as stocks of the Pukekohe Long Keeper variety run out.

All of the brothers wanted to farm and started while still at school, leasing some land and growing potatoes and onions.

In the 1970s, the business expanded by purchasing and leasing more land, moving into beef and growing potatoes, onions, pumpkins and kiwifruit.

The family business has undertaken much of the transport and packing of produce.

“Our produce has taken many honours at the Pukekohe Show,” Reynolds said.

“The show is very dear to our hearts. We have always been proud of the success of our potatoes and onions over several generations.

“Also, some of our ancestors used to have their fruit in the show; we still grow enough onions to enter.”

From the outset of his career, Reynolds attended research and field days and hosted trials, before stepping into sector leadership with grower groups.

“We’ve been very aligned with research,” he said.

“Researchers would come here and know we would look after their trials.”

Before becoming a regular at grower meetings, Reynolds was usually found on the rugby field.

“Our parents encouraged us to get involved with grower groups, but when we were younger, we were too busy playing rugby,” he said.

“In 1982, I started going to Pukekohe Vegetable Growers meetings and was soon being sent to conferences as a delegate.”

He said he’d attended many conferences and grower meetings over the years, where he enjoyed meeting other growers from around the country.

“This has led to lifelong friendships with other growers and industry personnel throughout New Zealand and overseas.”

With most of the Reynolds brothers now retired, the family have sold two farms and leased others, and are now selling their packhouse equipment and some farm equipment.

“All the next generation have worked in the business, with none of them deciding to make it a career,” Reynolds said.

“We’re happy with that. We were given that choice as young people.

“There was no compulsion to stay farming; we just all wanted to.

“People leasing our land really appreciate it because our farms have good, well-structured soils, and we have developed the farms to very high standards and installed modern, automated irrigation systems and other infrastructure.”

Looking ahead, Reynolds said promoting understanding of the cost of producing healthy food would be a major challenge for horticulture.

“Increasing compliance costs being imposed by councils and Government are a hindrance to business, and I’ve made many submissions to Government and councils over the years pushing back against unworkable regulations,” he said.

Reynolds said the industry also needed to support young people wanting to pursue careers in horticulture.

“I’ve done a fair bit of mentoring, and we give young fellas leasing our land a hand and lend them equipment – because that’s how we got going – our uncles used to lend us their tractors at weekends; those opportunities are so important.

“I see the opportunities for the sector in the technological developments coming over the next 10 years – particularly drones, not just for spraying, but for a whole range of other work too.”

When Reynolds returned to his table at the dinner, there was plenty of conversation with his fellow diners, including Agriculture Minister Todd McClay, Potatoes New Zealand chief executive Kate Trufitt, and Horticulture New Zealand chief executive Kate Scott and chairwoman Bernadine Guilleux.

The congratulations haven’t stopped since, with many people contacting him and sharing memories of the business.

He thanked Horticulture New Zealand for the recognition.

“It was totally unexpected, as was being made a life member of Potatoes New Zealand last year – I am blown away; it’s been a real highlight.”

He also thanked his parents.

“Another highlight of my life is being a child of Tom and Maureen.

“It’s been a very good life being one of the Reynolds.

“It’s in our DNA to enjoy what we do, look out for others, and that is how we have lived our lives.”

Rural general practice needs more than another working group - Dr Angus Chambers

New Zealand Herald October 16, 2026

Rural healthcare needs funding, not another working group. Photo / 123rf

Pahīatua’s healthcare struggles are not an isolated problem. They’re a symptom of a rural primary care system at breaking point, writes General Practice Owners Association chairman Dr Angus Chambers.

Rural New Zealand deserves the same access to quality, face-to-face healthcare as people living in our cities.

But that access is increasingly at risk.

Across the country, rural practices are struggling to recruit and retain doctors, nurses and other health professionals.

Six staff at the Pahīatua Medical Centre resigned on the same day last month, amid growing concern around extreme workloads and patient safety. Over the past two years, 81 staff have resigned from the Tararua Health Group.

In some communities, telehealth is becoming the only option because there simply are not enough clinicians available to provide face-to-face care.

Telehealth has an important role in modern healthcare. But it cannot become the default because we have failed to make rural face-to-face general practice sustainable.

Providing care in rural New Zealand is harder and more expensive. Practices serve smaller, dispersed populations.

Patients often travel further. Vacancies can remain open for months, and smaller teams have less capacity to absorb staff shortages or unexpected increases in demand.

Yet our funding model does not adequately recognise those realities.

In some cases, rural practices are effectively paid less for delivering a model of healthcare that costs more to provide.

It should be no surprise that we struggle to attract doctors and other health professionals to rural communities when the practices employing them are financially constrained and the work can involve greater professional, personal and practical costs.

The Government has recognised some of these pressures.

This year, following negotiation, rural practices received an additional $3.1 million and a 3.16% increase in rural funding.

That was welcome, but it does not address the fundamental problem.

The Government has also established a rural working group to examine workforce and other challenges.

We welcome genuine efforts to improve rural healthcare. But we should be realistic about what another working group can achieve.

Rural working groups have examined these challenges for years. Too often, they reach the same sticking point: funding.

We do not need another diagnosis of a problem that is already well understood. We need action.

The situation at Pahīatua Medical Centre shows what can happen when persistent workforce shortages and financial pressures converge.

Staff have publicly warned of significant delays in preventive screening programmes, months-long waits for appointments and growing concerns about patient safety.

Frontline clinicians have described a situation where demand continues to grow while staffing levels struggle to keep pace.

It is important not to pretend that every factor behind the situation is precisely understood, but what is clear is that Pahīatua is not simply a local issue.

It is a warning sign for rural healthcare across New Zealand.

What is happening there reflects challenges that many rural practices know all too well: difficulty recruiting clinicians, increasing pressure on remaining staff, and a constant struggle to provide the timely, face-to-face care that communities deserve.

Australia offers some useful lessons.

After facing significant rural general practice workforce challenges, it introduced financial incentives, including rural loadings and payments for doctors choosing rural pathways.

It has also used creative initiatives such as online “speed-dating” sessions and tours connecting trainees with regional communities.

The lesson is not that New Zealand should copy Australia. It is that incentives matter.

Attracting people is only part of the answer.

Retaining them requires sustainable practices, professional development, housing, childcare and career opportunities.

That starts with making rural general practice financially viable.

Pahīatua again illustrates why retention matters just as much as recruitment.

Rural practices cannot function when there is difficulty filling vacancies as quickly as they arise.

Every departure places further pressure on those who remain, increasing workload, burnout and the risk of a downward spiral that becomes increasingly difficult to reverse.

In the General Practice Owners Association’s (GenPro’s) Seven Steps to Restore General Practice election briefing, we called for a minimum 30% cumulative increase in general practice funding over three years, with funding that keeps pace with the cost of providing care.

For rural practices, there should also be a premium reflecting factors such as remoteness, population size, distance and workforce availability.

A properly designed rural premium would help make rural practices more attractive places to work, support investment in facilities and technology, and give doctors greater certainty when considering a rural career.

Rural general practice should be treated as essential health infrastructure.

When a practice loses capacity, patients may have to travel further, preventive care can be delayed, and hospitals face additional pressure.

Increasingly, patients may simply be offered telehealth because there is no clinician available to see them in person.

That is not a sustainable workforce strategy.

The rural working group may produce useful ideas. But we should not confuse activity with progress.

If the Government wants to address the rural workforce crisis, it must ensure the practices employing that workforce are financially viable.

Rural communities do not need another conversation about why their healthcare services are struggling.

Communities such as Pahīatua are already experiencing the consequences of workforce shortages and years of under-investment in primary care.

The warning signs are visible today. The question is whether policymakers are prepared to act before more rural practices reach breaking point.

New Zealand’s rural communities deserve better than a system that continually acknowledges the problem while failing to address its root causes.

They need a funding model that makes rural healthcare sustainable and a workforce strategy that gives health professionals a genuine reason to choose, and stay in, rural New Zealand.

Because where someone lives should never determine whether they can see a healthcare professional face-to-face.

Dr Angus Chambers is chair of the General Practice Owners Association.
