Is the Pope a Catholic? Yes, but that’s where the certainty ends

Sydney Morning Herald October 17, 2026

Popular culture has given us some wildly unlikely fictional pontiffs. The thing is, they keep coming true.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Article gifting is here

Give anyone free access to subscriber-only stories when you subscribe.

There are many unlikely papal moments in Paolo Sorrentino’s 2016 series The Young Pope: the Pope emerges from under a pile of babies, the Pope tames a kangaroo, the Pope spies on a couple having sex in their living room. Still, none is more unbelievable in these times than the Pope insisting that his face be hidden from the public.

“I do not have an image because I am no one,” says newly elected Pope Pius XIII (Jude Law). If he must appear it will be as “a dark shadow, [a] silhouette”.

Pius name-checks Banksy, JD Salinger and Daft Punk – “the most important figures in their respective fields” – none of whom let themselves be seen. “The Vatican survives on hyperbole,” he says, “So we will give them hyperbole. But this time in reverse.”

He has a point. The Pope is famous despite, not because of, his face. Take an ordinary man, dress him in a white pellegrina and zucchetto, add a chunky pectoral cross and you have the kind of instant recognition very few living people command. We’re talking Elvis Presley or Dolly Parton-level recognition from silhouette alone.

It’s this instant identification that makes the Pope such an effective vehicle for dramatic or comedic intervention. In Italian satirist Pierfrancesco Diliberto’s new film Holy Cannoli (Che Dio perdona a tutti) the protagonist, Arturo, eats so much sugar in one hit that he hallucinates the Pope (Carlos Hipólito) is in his living room. The absurdity, the wonder and the inclination to actually listen when the apparition speaks come almost entirely from the instantly identifiable costume, at least to begin with.

As the film goes on, it becomes clear that this is a fictionalised version of the late Pope Francis, but he could just as easily be an entirely invented character. His role in the film is to guide atheistic Arturo in his quest to be worthy of his devoutly Catholic girlfriend. For this, he does not need to be an actual Pope; he needs to be both a symbol of official Christianity and benign father-figure who will appeal to the audience regardless of religious belief.

The actual Pope also performs that role, of course, though his perceived benignity and appeal are far from universal. They also differ fairly dramatically depending on the specifics of the man in the costume. An Economist survey in June found the current Pope Leo XIV had the highest favorability rating among all the public figures polled, coming in a whopping 54 percentage points higher than the US president. The Public Religion Research Institute points out that his predecessor, Pope Francis, had even higher ratings at the same point in his papacy, and both have been consistently seen more favourably than Pope Benedict XVI.

So the Pope is a symbol, yes, but he’s also a person. The best papal fiction exploits this tension by testing what belongs to the former and what to the latter.

Returning to The Young Pope, for example, we have a pontiff whose (relatively) young age of 47 quickly becomes the least of it as we discover he is also a chain-smoking, American, hard-core reactionary who has no interest in making nice with the public, his own cardinals or Vatican bureaucrats. He also happens to look distractingly like Jude Law.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

0:36

The view from the Vatican

How popular fiction has depicted the Pope.

The conceit is that one or more of these things make him an extremely unlikely choice for pontiff but in fact, every one of these (except the Jude Law thing) has been true of at least one real pope. Pontiffs younger than Law’s Pius include medieval teen Popes Benedict IX and John XII; those said to have loved a ciggie include John XXII and Benedict XVI; and the ones who battled with their own curia are probably more common than those who didn’t. (An American pope didn’t exist until 2025, well after the show finished its run, but the joke is well and truly history now.)

So despite the show’s sumptuous surrealism, it, like others in the genre of pope fiction, provides a strangely realistic thought experiment in what the enormous multi-part engine of the Vatican can and cannot absorb when it comes to an individual pope’s quirks and personal qualities.

A clear answer can be found in the many retellings of the medieval legend of a female pope. The specific characteristics of the woman said to have disguised herself as a monk before rising all the way to the top job varies wildly across versions. But from Lawrence Durrell’s Pope Joan (1954) to Donna Woolfolk Cross’ 1996 version; from Caryl Churchill’s play Top Girls (1982) to my own 2024 novel Rapture, the Pope’s female body is an absolute dealbreaker for the institution. In legend, in history, and very much in real life right now, the Pope can be almost any kind of person, as long as that person is a man.

Really, almost any kind of person? Let’s consider the sub-genre of pope fiction that we might call Borgia-core (after the most obvious example, Showtime’s The Borgias), which revels in the juxtaposition of holiness and horniness, piety and perversion. The thing about these salacious stories of corrupt and hedonistic popes is that they’re taken right out of the history books. (Albeit from sometimes unreliable and agenda-driven sources.) The medieval era in particular was rife with men who took to the role with the spirit of Pope Leo X (another young Pope, at 37) who is said to have declared: “God has given us the papacy; now let us enjoy it”.

In contrast, the entirely fictional pontiff depicted by John Malkovich in The New Pope (the 2020 follow-up to The Young Pope) is decidedly unwilling to make the office his own. The conclave elected him because of his centrist views and he is unwilling to disappoint them. When the actor Sharon Stone (playing herself) asks him (having presented him with her stilettos as a gift) when “the pointless taboo” of gay marriage for Catholics will end, he answers: “When the church has a brave, revolutionary, resolute Pope. Qualities none of which I possess.”

A brave, resolute Pope is exactly what we find in 1968’s The Shoes of the Fisherman (adapted from Morris West’s 1963 novel) which features a Ukrainian pope who uses his knowledge of life behind the Iron Curtain to negotiate peace between the Soviet Union and the US, becoming a serious geopolitical actor who effectively stops World War III.

As with The Young Pope’s American pontiff, The Shoes of the Fisherman can appear to have manifested a real one not too far down the line. Ten years after the film, Polish-born John Paul II became, like the fictional Pope Kiril, the first non-Italian Pope in more than four centuries. Like Kiril, his experience of living in the Soviet bloc led him to intervene significantly — and successfully — in the diplomatic struggle to end the Cold War.

Walter F. Murphy’s The Vicar of Christ (1979) also features a politically interventionist (and American) Pope. The book’s Pope Francis (30 years before the real life one of that name) is a war hero and US Supreme Court justice before he becomes a man of the cloth. The fictional Francis is a resolutely progressive pope on questions of moral and social teaching. His opposition to war is equally uncompromising, and so effective that he is ultimately assassinated by those for whom war is an indispensable feature of the political order.

That a pope could be powerful enough to threaten a political regime is examined in Graham Greene’s story The Last Word (1988). Greene imagines a dystopian future in which “the last Pope” is an elderly man living alone in a bedsit with a contraband bible and broken crucifix. Organised religion has been eradicated in the name of one-world government and yet, still, as a general carries out the final act of executing the old man who was once its figurehead, he experiences the “strange and frightening” thought that “what this man believed may be true”.

The question of which kind of pope – centrist, progressive, reactionary or non-European – the church most needs is at the heart of 2024’s Conclave. The film is, in part, a study of how the people who know the role best disagree about who should fill it. The characters argue and grapple and pray, connive and conspire, and though for some it is a matter of personal ego and power-hunger, most are driven by a desire to find the right man for the job.

Conclave is indisputably fiction but in real life, as the Catholic Church’s cardinals gathered to choose a new Pope after the death of Pope Francis in May 2025, POLITICO reported that some of those eminent men were watching the film for pointers. It was, according to one cardinal, “a helpful research tool at a time when so many of the conclave participants have little experience of Vatican politics and protocol”.

Audiences outside the Vatican were apparently doing the same: streams of the film shot up 283 per cent in the lead-up to the real-world version and social media was flooded with memes about it.

As helpful as that film may have been for explaining the process of choosing a pope, it doesn’t necessarily help when it comes to understanding how becoming one might actually feel. What is it like to be a man one moment and a monumental, instantly recognisable symbol the next?

Nanni Moretti’s Habemus Papam (We Have a Pope, 2011) suggests it is a living nightmare. In the opening scenes, we are shown the prayers of the cardinals at the conclave: not me, not me, please not me, they each pray. The unlucky contender (Michel Piccoli) tries to rise to the call, but the moment before he is to address the crowd in St Peter’s Square, he screams and refuses. A psychiatrist is brought in to intervene, though given the session is conducted in the presence of the increasingly panicked cardinals, it is no surprise when the reluctant Pope bolts at the first opportunity.

One wonders if a similar impulse passed through Cardinal Ratzinger when he was elected Pope Benedict XVI in 2005. His reluctance was widely known within the Vatican: not only did he not want to be Pope, but he had asked twice in the preceding years to be released from his role as prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith only for Pope John Paul II to refuse. Benedict later said that his election “felt like a guillotine”.

A fictionalised version of Benedict features in 2019’s The Two Popes, but his unwillingness to serve is not explored. Indeed, the film portrays Ratzinger openly campaigning for the position, in contrast to his eventual predecessor who is shown as reluctant to take on the role. It’s a reminder that a real-life Pope who has been fictionalised is still, well, fiction.

In Habemus Papam, when the runaway newly elected Pope is asked by a psychiatrist what he does for a living, he answers simply: “I’m an actor”.

The answer reveals a lot about this particular fictional Pope who doesn’t know how to play this next role he’s been given. This is what papal fiction does: it lets us watch the role collide with the person playing it and try to figure out what the papacy actually is. What endures despite the changing person? Is it only the stunning backdrop, millennium-old ritual and fancy Swiss guards?

The Pope is supposed to be the ultimate symbol of continuity, the same white figure emerging onto the same balcony. Yet the person inside can change the meaning of the role entirely. A pope from behind the Iron Curtain once belonged to the realm of geopolitical fantasy; then a Polish cardinal walked onto the world stage. An American pope once seemed ridiculous; now a Chicagoan is on the papal balcony.

Perhaps that is why the Pope remains such a useful character. The costume supplies the instant recognition, ritual brings millennia of accumulated authority, but the bloke underneath it all introduces the possibility that something entirely new will happen. Fiction keeps putting someone new into the role to see what happens and, as in real life, believers and unbelievers alike keep watching.

Emily Maguire’s Rapture (Allen & Unwin) is the story of a female Pope in the 9th Century. Holy Cannoli opens in cinemas on October 22.

Damned if you work, damned if you retire: The Baby Boomers stuck in a catch-22

Sydney Morning Herald October 17, 2026

Baby Boomers are increasingly working well past retirement age, often filling critical skills gaps out of financial necessity or passion. Yet it’s a generation that has become a punching bag for a host of very 21st-century grievances.

Theo Newbegin cuts a wiry silhouette striding between towers of peaches and pears in the echoing vastness of the SPC canning factory in Victoria’s Shepparton. Newbegin’s weathered face and long, white beard may bear witness to his 67 years, but once he jumps behind the wheel of a forklift and whips around a labyrinth of palettes, readying them for loading onto a truck, the decades melt away. His right knee might bark at him occasionally, but his lightning-fast reflexes put younger workers to shame. “I don’t feel any different to how I was in my 40s,” he grins. “People ask if I go to the gym.”

Clocking in at 2.30pm for an eight-hour shift at the cannery is merely the second act of Newbegin’s working day. He’s already hammered out a full morning of roofing – a trade he’s been toiling at since age 17. Amid a tradie shortage, he’s in constant demand, particularly for his repair work on old-school hardwood rafters, which he says modern materials can’t match.

“Fixing an old hardwood roof gives you a real sense of satisfaction,” he beams. “These new radiata pine ones? You can bounce up and down on ’em.”

Between five kids, nine grandkids, and his wife, Jenny – who’s still powering through full-time work as a medical receptionist at 65 – Newbegin appears to be hardwired for perpetual motion (“my dad worked ’til he was 75,” he shrugs). Forget fine dining, Pacific cruises or the latest high-tech baubles; the four motorbikes he dotes on like prized thoroughbreds are his single indulgence.

Newbegin is part of a fast-growing club of older Australians delaying retirement well beyond the expected finishing line of 67. Today, more than 760,000 Australians over 65 are in the workforce, the highest level since Australian Bureau of Statistics’ tracking began in 1995. “Twenty years ago, one in 10 men were working at age 70; today it’s one in four,” says Terry Rawnsley, director of planning and infrastructure economics at KPMG.

Over the two decades from 2003 to 2023, retirement rates among 65- to 69-year-old Australians plunged significantly, with women’s numbers dropping from 86 per cent to 66 per cent and men’s falling from 73 per cent to 61 per cent, according to the University of Melbourne’s most recent Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey findings.

Why are Australians staying on the clock? Although many remain in the workforce seeking purpose and social connection, the underlying driver for most is just to pay the bills. Rawnsley reckons something bigger is brewing – a shift in how we actually see retirement.

For Marion Wales, a 78-year-old dental nurse in Moss Vale in NSW, it’s the fact her superannuation coffers are running low, and she has an 81-year-old husband with limited mobility to support. “I can’t retire now because the pension isn’t covering our bills, and we don’t have enough in the super kitty,” she says. “I also want to have a decent life.”

For Anne Drane, a property manager for a real estate agency in south-western Sydney’s Liverpool, working three days a week is necessary to cover soaring private health insurance premiums and medical costs for a lung condition. But she also loves her job, and completed a financial counselling certificate only four years ago. “I like to keep busy, and also want to be able to afford to travel,” the 78-year-old enthuses.

For Shane Scully, 67, renting in Sydney while raising two teenage daughters makes working a financial necessity. “I don’t have an option. I need to keep working,” he says flatly. Yet Scully, who designs outdoor classrooms and sensory gardens for public schools and special education units, finds his work deeply rewarding: “Turning a barren space into something that brings joy to the kids ... this makes it all worthwhile.”

For 75-year-old Brisbane-based educator Margaret Harrington, teaching has been a passion for more than 45 years – and something she continues out of a deep love for the calling rather than financial necessity. When she was made redundant from classroom teaching a decade ago, her students refused to let her go, telling her, “We know where you live and will come to you” – and she’s continuing to tutor privately from her home.

All of this has done nothing to dent the national sport of Boomer-bashing. It kicked off a few years back when Gen Z provocateurs leveraged the catchphrase “OK, Boomer” to slap down anything they pinned as peak smugness by their elders.

Boomer-bashing has turned into a minor publishing industry in recent years: from highbrow US takedowns like A Generation of Sociopaths by Bruce Cannon Gibney, and OK Boomer, Let’s Talk: How My Generation Got Left Behind, by Jill Filipovic, to Australian Fiona Wright’s satirical novel Kill Your Boomers, published this year. Comedians and influencers alike have joined the pile-on, from Tom Ballard trying to turn a comedy festival crowd into a choir of Boomer-haters back in 2019 with “When the f--- are Baby Boomers going to die?” to US YouTuber Caleb Hammer griping to podcaster Joe Rogan in June that this generation “had the best housing market, college, jobs – they were set up for everything”.

Boomers, so the resentment story goes, hit the historical jackpot: dirt-cheap houses, free uni degrees, careers so stable they’d bore – or bring – a young gig economy worker to tears, and plump super payouts. And to top it all off, these silver-haired fat cats retired early, slapped a “SKI” (spend the kids’ inheritance) sticker on their shiny new LandCruiser, and flipped the bird at the young ’uns as they hit the open road. What a bunch of self-serving parasites, right?

Except most of it is baloney.

The lucky generation? Sure, for the top tier of older Baby Boomers, the 20 per cent who control most of the overall wealth of their generation, but there is a vast and frequently overlooked gulf between the haves and have-nots. The Baby Boomers most at risk of financial stress are the “forever renters”, those locked out of home ownership and battling rental increases of nearly 40 per cent in real terms since the early 2000s, according to HILDA.

While at least 66 per cent of retirees own their homes outright, HILDA reports, an increasing number of younger ones – so-called “Generation Jones” (those born between 1954 and 1965) – are more likely to be still shackled to a mortgage. Vanguard’s 2026 How Australia Retires report found 24 per cent of Baby Boomers now expect to retire with a mortgage.

If you imagine most Boomers accumulated massive super payouts by the time they reached their 60s, think again. Super didn’t even exist until July 1992, when early Boomers were already in their 40s. Even then, it kicked off at just 3 per cent of earnings before taking more than a decade to crawl up to 9 per cent (it’s now 12 per cent). Without a place to call your own or a fat super nest egg to pay the rent, retirement in a pricey capital city with no income coming in apart from the government pension can be a fast track to poverty.

For University of Melbourne senior research fellow Dr Kyle Peyton, who is a fresh-faced 39, the most eye-opening statistic to emerge from the HILDA survey was a doubling between 2003 and 2023 in the number of retirees who are renting, now 12 per cent and rising. “The divide between Australians who own property and those who don’t is deeply concerning – not just for financial security, but for social cohesion,” he observes. “It’s a divide that exists within generations as well as between them.”

The new face of the housing crisis isn’t a struggling 20-something; it’s a single woman over 55 only one rental hike away from living in her car or couch-surfing. Having poured decades of sweat in and out of the workforce raising families and then caring for ageing parents, she can wind up with only a small super nest egg. “By the time they retire, Australian women typically have around one-third less superannuation than men,” notes Myra Hamilton, a sociologist at the University of Sydney. “While the super gap has narrowed in recent years, parity for women is still decades away at current rates. A quarter of grandparents – and it’s usually grandmothers – provide care for a child in a typical week, enabling their children to stay in the workforce.”

Much of the current wave of Boomer-bashing comes from young privileged commentators with no clue of what working-class life was really like in the 1960s, ’70s and ’80s. In 2023, Myra Hamilton, a Millennial, co-wrote a hard-hitting op-ed for this newspaper with her father Clive Hamilton, who recently retired from Charles Sturt University as professor of Public Ethics. “We now have a cohort of younger commentators furiously mining the data and cherry-picking the numbers to find new reasons to excoriate Baby Boomers,” the pair wrote.

Patricia Sparrow, CEO of COTA (Council on the Ageing), complains there are two deeply damaging media narratives on Boomers. “They’re either living on Easy Street or they’re frail and blocking up hospital beds. Both entirely ignore the huge social contribution Boomers are making.”

Don’t assume the Boomer-bashing doesn’t have a real-life impact. Myra Hamilton recalls that after delivering a talk in which she dismantled the myth that Boomers are universally comfortable and uncaring, an older woman approached her with tears welling in her eyes. ” ‘Thank you so much,” she said. “It hurts deeply to be branded selfish. I poured my life into raising my children, worked part-time, put everything on hold to care for my ageing parents, and I’m still pushing through work every day to cover my expenses. I love my children – yet society keeps accusing my generation of stealing their future.’ ”

While more older Australians are remaining in the workforce, participation rates are still below that of countries such as Sweden, Japan and New Zealand, according to the OECD. And it’s been estimated by KPMG that boosting labour-force participation among experienced older workers could increase GDP by $29 billion.

Growing up in the decades after World War II, Boomers lived at a time of far greater austerity than today: a more threadbare welfare net, sparse workplace protections, widespread discrimination based on gender and colour, and zero universal healthcare. Gough Whitlam’s original Medibank didn’t arrive until July 1975, only to be scaled back months later when Malcolm Fraser came to power – leaving the country to wait until 1984 for Bob Hawke to finally establish the Medicare system we now take for granted.

Whitlam abolished tuition fees at universities in 1974, but it was middle-class kids, not working-class youth, who took advantage of it, insists Clive Hamilton. “The idea that Baby Boomers universally benefited from free higher education is a myth; university participation rates at that time were under 15 per cent,” he tells Good Weekend.

But life was so much cheaper back then, and everything’s outrageous today, right? Think again. For a reality check, let’s rewind to 1975, a year when the first Baby Boomers were in their late 20s, when flared jeans were de rigueur, lava lamps set the mood for disco hits like Lady Bump, and when a household purchase at a retail stalwart like Waltons or Grace Bros meant a Seriously Big Buy.

The family car? A popular vehicle like a Holden Kingswood sedan automatic would set you back about $4070, or a premium Cortina XL E, $4000, nearly two-thirds the median annual salary of the time ($6448). Contrast that with today’s family-sized SUVs: an MG ZS Vibe starts at just $22,990 – a mere third of today’s median annual salary of $74,000-78,000 – with Chinese hybrids like the Chery Tiggo 4 Urban and the BYD Atto 2 DM-1 starting at under $25,000.

Home entertainment? When colour television was launched in Australia on March 1, 1975 (“C-Day”), a Baird set (remember when the Brits manufactured TVs?) cost about $1300 – a staggering $11,667 in today’s dollars. Even the cheapest portable AWA-Thorn carried a price tag of $400, or $3700 now. TVs were so punishingly expensive that for many families, like mine, owning a TV wasn’t an option – we rented one for several years. Fast-forward to 2026: you can pick up a 55-inch LED Kogan smart TV for $449: a weekend impulse buy.

Whitegoods? In 1975, buying a $400 fridge or a $250 fully automated washing machine meant many months of disciplined saving or a dreaded lay-by: the equivalent of forking out $3500 to $4000 today. Even a humble Victa lawnmower carried the modern equivalent of a $1200 price tag. Now, a 4-stroke model is a steal for $424 at Bunnings. (It’s easy to forget how much globalisation and supply chains shifting to Asia have brought down prices.)

Groceries? Staples such as milk, butter, eggs and bread cost way less now than in 1975 when adjusted for wages; chicken is much cheaper, red meat pricier, and while ice-cream and biscuits are cheaper, they’ve suffered shrinkflation (here’s looking at mini-you, Chocolate Montes and Cornettos). Some items, such as washing powder, are marginally more expensive, but the prices of all plastic consumer goods (Glad Bags, Tupperware) have plummeted. Economists today may sweat over an inflation rate of 4 per cent, but in 1975, it was galloping at a wallet-shredding 15 per cent. Grocery prices were moving faster than a disco beat.

Dining out? Until the 1980s, your options were milk bars, hotel dining rooms, department-store cafeterias, tearooms and a handful of cafes in Sydney’s Potts Point or Melbourne’s St Kilda. Try asking a 1975 waiter for an oat milk piccolo whatevs, or quizzing them about the “provenance” of the sirloin or whether the peas are “hyper local” or not, and they’d most likely assume you were on a bad acid trip.

Clothing? Just about every item of casual and formal wear was far more expensive in 1975, when many garments were still manufactured locally, made to last and, in many working-class families, were passed down to younger siblings. When I recall to Anne Drane that my mother, a seamstress in a shirt factory, insisted on making most of my teenage shirts, much to my annoyance, she warms to the theme (“yes, we relied on our auntie to make all our clothes”). Today we’ve traded durable, locally made craftsmanship for “fast fashion” – a relentless tsunami of ultra-cheap, synthetic junk that winds up in landfill at the end of each season.

International travel? In 1975, a standard return economy airfare from Sydney to London on a major carrier like Qantas cost about $2300 – about a third of the median annual wage. Today, a return economy airfare on Qantas for the same trip costs much the same – starting at about $2200, less than 3 per cent of the median annual wage. Once largely the preserve of the well-heeled, international travel has become as mundane as booking an interstate bus trip.

Margaret Betteridge, 73, who has worked as a curator at the City of Sydney for more than 30 years, recalls her first flight overseas to London in September 1975 to do a course in museum studies. “My salary was around $3000 per annum and the airfare to London cost a bit more than that,” she recalls. “Because it was so expensive, people who flew to Europe either saved up a long time, if they were young, or if they were old, tended to be very comfortable financially.”

Today’s acquisitive lifestyle, hypercharged by the internet’s endless digital bazaar, makes 1975 look positively spartan by comparison. We’re drowning in smartphones, iPads, Fitbits, Sonos, noise-cancelling headphones, flatpack furniture, disposable threads and – ugh! – plastic plants as decor. Consumerism didn’t truly hit its stride in Australia until the ’80s and ’90s, when tariff walls were brought down, ushering in the so-called “affluenza” era of cheap imports – and a mountain of landfill.

While financial strain is very real today, and risks getting much worse because of deteriorating international conditions, decades of lifestyle creep have turned what were once luxuries into non-negotiables. We might be skint, but do we really have to ditch our cafe breakfasts or streaming subscriptions?

Today’s great expectations were noted by many of the Boomers interviewed for this story. “This need for instant gratification – ‘We’re entitled to this now’ – didn’t exist a few decades ago,” muses Drane, who recounts a childhood in south-western Sydney’s Revesby in the 1950s marked by poverty and missed meals while her mother toiled at part-time jobs and her father struggled with post-war trauma and alcoholism.

There’s no denying, though, that Boomers were blessed with a big stroke of historical luck with housing. In 1975, a Sydney home cost about $28,000 – manageable at four times the average annual income. Today, that same dream requires $1.53 million, a suffocating 16 to 18 times the median annual salary. And yes, history has been generous to Boomers in terms of building equity in bricks-and-mortar over the decades. But this doesn’t mean they gamed the system: all they did was stay in their homes while market forces over time drove values through their roof.

Today’s housing market is brutally unfair for young people, but it’s pure piffle to imagine that getting a home loan or paying a mortgage were pieces of cake in decades past. Home loan interest rates didn’t just climb in the 1970s and ’80s – they throttled the household budget, rising from 10 per cent in 1975 to a punishing 17.5 per cent by 1990.

For my own working-class parents, both of whom worked in factories from the 1950s to the 1980s, home ownership was but a distant mirage for the entire time I was growing up. When I finally managed to help them buy a home, my monthly mortgage repayments became a high-wire act across a chasm of soaring interest rates that drove me to getting a second job until they began to fall after a year or so.

Lucky for them, they had a son: back in the 1950s, ‘60s, and ’70s, a single woman applying for a housing loan might as well have asked a bank manager for the keys to the vault. Banks routinely demanded a male “financial chaperone” – a father, brother, or partner – to sign off as guarantor, assuming the little lady would eventually resign to pop out babies anyway. Just ask Drane. When she sought to buy her first home as a 25-year-old single woman in the early 1970s, she had to jump through hoops, even though she was beginning her career in the Commonwealth Bank at the time. “To be considered, I got a second job and worked seven days a week for a year to meet their strict criteria,” she says.

It wasn’t much easier 10 years later for teacher Margaret Harrington, who applied for a loan in 1983. Even with tens of thousands of dollars in the bank from her divorce settlement, her request for a modest top-up to buy an apartment fell on deaf ears. The then 30-something had to go to five different banks before finally finding a lender willing to treat her as an independent borrower. “It was a terrible experience, made worse by bank managers making sexist remarks,” she recalls.

Back then, sexism was baked into the entire workplace. Drane recalls with absolute clarity being passed over for promotion after promotion for less-qualified males during her banking career in the 1970s. It wasn’t until the banks were deregulated in the 1980s and social attitudes began to change that those roadblocks started crashing down. By 1993, Drane didn’t just walk into a bank, hat in hand for a housing loan – she was manager of a suburban branch of the St George bank.

Younger Boomers and Gen Xers undoubtedly profited nicely off the Howard government’s 1999 tax perks, including capital gains cuts and boosts to negative gearing, which many economists believe unintentionally drained capital away from start-ups and innovation, a regrettable shift expertly exposed in Amy Remeikis’s recent book Where it All Went Wrong.

“Howard turned housing from a place to live to a source of wealth,” she writes. But if you imagine Boomers monopolise the rentals and are to blame for your latest rent hike, sneak a peek at your landlord’s ID. ATO figures show that more than 73 per cent of landlords are Gen Xers or Millennials, with Boomers holding under 27 per cent (a number that COTA insists is now much lower, and set to crater, as older people offload investment properties and pass away).

If Gen Zers imagine they’re the first generation to face a raw deal, they may draw some comfort from the fact high home-ownership rates in Australia have been the historical exception, not the rule: from Federation until World War II, barely half the nation owned the roof over their heads. And home-ownership levels have remained pretty steady over the past 50 years (68 per cent in 1975 compared with 66 per cent today), although that may be under threat in the years to come.

And don’t fall for the line – often pushed by pro-development YIMBY cheerleaders – that senior Australians are selfish for wanting to stay in the family home, where they built their lives. Look around our suburbs, and you’ll see that all too often, Granny’s big, leafy backyard is bulldozed, not for a duplex or low-rise apartments, but for a brick-veneer mansion with a small paved courtyard. Forget the modest family cottage of 1975 – a sensible 130 to 150 square metres. Today’s typical Aussie house has bloated into a monstrous brick-veneer box of between 214 to 235 square metres, bursting with cinema rooms, multiple bathrooms, and empty bedrooms galore – all built to house tiny families that are half the size of those in the 1970s.

In our rapidly ageing nation, keeping senior Australians in the workforce, particularly in critical sectors like aged care, education and health, is no longer an option but an economic necessity. “Australia is shooting itself in the foot by treating willing and capable older workers like a financial liability rather than an economic lifeline,” argues Chris Grice, CEO of National Seniors Australia.

Championing the peak body’s “Let Pensioners Work” campaign, Grice believes the system actively discourages people over retirement age from staying in the workforce. For every dollar earned above $226 a fortnight for singles, the pension is slashed by 50 cents; for couples earning above $396 a fortnight, it reduces by 25¢ in the dollar. (Centrelink’s Work Bonus helps you keep more of your pension if you meet eligibility requirements, however.) Slapping seniors with fortnightly income reporting can also be a disincentive because of all the red tape, notes Grice.

Even finding a job when aged over 55 can be a marathon. ABS data shows it takes older jobseekers an average of 20 months to land a new role after losing one – more than double the nine months for younger applicants (15 to 54). COTA’s State of the Older Nation 2025 report reveals that 38 per cent of people over 50 have experienced some form of age discrimination and one in two recruiters show little or no openness to hiring workers 65 and over. “Ageism can be a significant deterrent for seniors trying to re-enter the workforce,” says COTA’s Sparrow.

Chris Grice says that institutional ageism remains rampant in recruitment and promotion, particularly in financial services, media and some areas of hospitality and sales. AI may be a double-edged sword, he says, enabling instant screening-out of older applicants, yet also simplifying software processes and helping seniors bridge technical skill gaps.

In a basic sense, Boomers are caught in a damned-if-you-work, damned-if-you-don’t catch-22. Stick around in the office and you’re a job-hoarder robbing eager young things of a career ladder; retire and you’re a freeloading burden bleeding taxpayers dry. For many manual labourers and tradies, there isn’t even a choice: decades of hard physical toil make working past their 60s virtually impossible.

Painting Australia’s 3 million Baby Boomers as a uniform group of comfortable, home-owning Anglo-Saxons ignores a far more diverse and complex reality. It erases the waves of European migrants – 2 million in total between 1945 and 1965 – who spent decades breaking their backs in low-paid factory jobs, and the Indigenous Australians who have battled racism and job discrimination for their entire lives. “Boomers aren’t a single, homogeneous group,” says Sparrow. “The rich diversity of our broader community exists across every age bracket.”

Beneath all the anti-Boomer noise lies a fundamental truth that now seems long forgotten: these old-school trailblazers forged the very social freedoms we take for granted today. This was, after all, the generation of the counter-culture, one which transformed the rights for women, gay people and, to a degree, Indigenous Australians, as well as launching the environmental movement, says Clive Hamilton, whose 2016 book, What Do We Want? The Story of Protest in Australia, traces the grassroots history of these movements – and the high price some then-young people paid for their principles (arrests, fines, legal consequences). “Let’s be clear: only between 10 and 20 per cent of Baby Boomers were active participants, but the majority of young people supported their broader aims,” he says.

To this day, surveys consistently show Boomers outperforming Millennials and Gen Z when it comes to sustainable habits like recycling and curbing waste. The bitter irony? Many of the hard-won environmental protections and equal rights agendas that Boomers fought for are now under assault from populist demagogues – US President Donald Trump, the UK’s Reform leader Nigel Farage, One Nation’s Pauline Hanson – whose reactionary rhetoric is supercharged by social media algorithms.

A landmark University of Melbourne study recently exposed a dark rise in misogynistic attitudes in Australian classrooms: nearly a third of teenage boys believe gender equality has gone too far, with one in four agreeing violence is a fair response to feminism. It’s a sad spectre: impressionable young blokes taking life lessons from manosphere hucksters like brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate, now languishing on remand in a Miami, Florida prison, fighting extradition to the UK for charges of rape and human trafficking. (At his Miami bust, Andrew Tate looked less like a badass and more like a dancer at a Barry Manilow tribute, sporting an unbuttoned purple silk shirt, skin-tight Capri pants and pointed loafers, for which social media roasted him into oblivion.)

“If the Tate brothers had arrived in the 1960s and 1970s, they’d have been laughed off the stage,” chuckles Clive Hamilton. “The crowd would have been shouting, ‘Get off, you fools.’ The Tates are a reactionary backlash to the rights that Boomer women – and men – fought so hard to build.”

The young blokes pining for the good ol’ days of strict gender roles and “trad” wives remain amusingly blind to the crushing financial pressures placed on men of that era as sole breadwinners – and the battle-hardened grit of the women, forged by survival instincts in a man’s world (a theme vividly captured in Dorothy Hewett’s 1959 novel Bobbin Up). Had they been transplanted back to the factory floor of the 1950s and ’60s, these young keyboard warriors typing outrage from their family bedrooms would have been chewed up and spat out before smoko.

Besides, younger people can’t take much of the high ground with Boomers, when they’re about to become beneficiaries of their largesse. The country’s much-heralded, mega financial handover from Boomers to Gen Xers and Millennials is rapidly accelerating, notes KPMG’s Terry Rawnsley, as Boomers sell off larger homes, bankroll their offspring’s property ambitions and prepare to pass over a mammoth $3.5 trillion in the coming years.

Some weeks after our interview, Shane Scully messages me. He’d just been admitted to hospital for an angiogram, where doctors discovered an artery that was 95 per cent blocked. Surgeons inserted a large stent in the nick of time – dodging what cardiologists ominously call the “widowmaker”.

After the near-fatal scare, Scully was back at work within just over a week. He’s been prescribed meds and advised to walk more and adhere to a stricter diet, but the new regimen has inconveniently coincided with one of the most frantic times in his business.

For many working Boomers, the real daily grind isn’t the job itself but rather, looking after your health. “It’s a bitch getting old, I tell you,” reflects Scully.

‘I feel like I’m going to be sick’: Witnesses and victims are often traumatised in court. Enter an army of volunteers

Sydney Morning Herald October 17, 2026

The courtroom can be a confronting place for witnesses as well as victims. But court volunteers offer a reassuring presence that ensures they’re not navigating the legal system on their own.

It’s just before 9am on a spring morning in downtown Newcastle, when a sheriff unlocks the revolving door to the courthouse complex. A woman with short, chestnut hair is first to enter. Passing through the security scanner, she gives the officers a friendly hello before heading to her office. After reviewing her schedule for the day, the woman – whom I’ll call Jennifer – takes the lift to the upper levels of the courthouse, the largest of its kind in regional NSW, to begin her rounds.

Jennifer introduces herself to a young woman sitting outside one of the courtrooms, and quietly asks if she is a victim or a witness. The young woman confirms she is a prosecution witness, here to give evidence in a sexual assault trial. Her best friend is the alleged victim, and she’s clearly anxious.

Jennifer tells her she’s a court support officer who helps prosecution witnesses and victims. As she begins explaining court formalities, the young woman suddenly becomes agitated. She’s spotted the defendant. When he takes a seat nearby, Jennifer clocks the young woman’s rising distress. “Would you like to move away?” she asks.

Immediately, the young woman is on her feet. Jennifer leads her to the furthest corner of the waiting area, asking if she’s OK. “I feel like I’m going to be sick,” the young woman says. She’s afraid of having to testify in front of the defendant, and worried about her friend, who will give evidence first via video link. “We’ve never been to court,” the young woman says. “We don’t do bad things.”

Jennifer assures her a social worker will be with her friend. She shows her a diagram of the courtroom, pointing out the witness box and where the judge, the lawyers and the defendant will sit. She shows her where to bow to the judge – “just a little bow, no curtsy” – and explains she’ll be asked to swear an oath or an affirmation to tell the truth.

Listening intently, the young woman doesn’t notice that you can catch glimpses of the city’s sparkling harbour through the floor-to-ceiling windows. Nor does she pay any attention to the cooking show playing on the television mounted to a nearby wall.

“I’m worried I’ll cry,” she says. “I just don’t want him to see me get upset.” “You don’t worry if you cry,” Jennifer tells her. “You’re not a robot.”

A detective and police prosecutor arrive to speak with the young woman, so Jennifer tells her she’ll be back before it’s her turn in the witness box. “You’ll get through it,” she promises. “You will.”

From homicide and domestic violence, to manslaughter and armed robbery, Jennifer has sat through dozens of trials and hours of harrowing testimony. She’s heard graphic descriptions of sexual assault, and borne witness to the grief that plagues families whose loved ones have fallen victim to senseless crimes. She knows the secret location of the safe room, where victims can wait to avoid coming face-to-face with their alleged perpetrators. She’s had hours of training in court procedures and attends several professional development courses every year. But she’s never been paid a cent for her work.

She’s a 72-year-old retired speech therapist and grandmother who spends a couple of days a week supporting strangers as they relive what is often the most traumatic event of their lives.

Jennifer works for Victims and Witnesses of Crime Court Support (VWCCS), an independent organisation staffed almost entirely by volunteers. First established in Sydney 20 years ago, the VWCCS now has more than 120 volunteers who work at the Downing Centre courts in Sydney’s CBD, and at Parramatta, Waverley and Newcastle courts. A similar organisation, Court Network, operates in Victoria, where about 250 volunteers support 78,000 court users (including the accused) annually across all court jurisdictions.

The VWCCS agreed to allow Good Weekend to follow Jennifer, as long as we didn’t reveal her real name. “We’re not counsellors, not lawyers,” Jennifer says. “We’re decent people who like to help.”

Walking through the Newcastle courthouse in her burnt-orange jumper, trousers and black flats, Jennifer presents as a softer antidote to the imposing black silhouettes of the barristers’ gowns that sweep past. “Morning Harry, busy day?” she cheerily asks a tall, lanky guy in a grey suit. He’s a police prosecutor, she whispers. Jennifer’s on a first-name basis with many of the prosecutors and court staff. She’s been working here longer than many of them, she says.

Eight years ago, after she’d retired from her job as a speech therapist and her three children had all left home, she read a newspaper article that said volunteers were needed to start the court support program in Newcastle.

“I thought it … could make a difference in people’s lives,” she says. “I wondered if I could do that.”

Back then, Jennifer had never been inside a courtroom. But she would soon see for herself just how confronting the court process could be, particularly for those involved in sexual assault and domestic violence trials. These make up the majority of the cases Jennifer attends to, and sometimes her role extends to sitting beside complainants in the witness box while they give evidence.

Jennifer says it’s not uncommon for witnesses to vomit while testifying. “They’re so traumatised, you’ve got to relive what happened to you,” she says. “You have to know when to grab the bin.”

During sentencing hearings, volunteers are also allowed to read victim impact statements on behalf of victims. Jennifer recalls sitting with a 15-year-old sexual assault victim as she began reading her statement. When the girl faltered after the first sentence, Jennifer asked whether she’d like her to read on her behalf. Reading the girl’s written words, Jennifer detailed the devastating impact of the assault, pausing towards the end to ask whether the victim wanted to read her final lines.

“We just waited until she could do it,” Jennifer recalls. “She said she would not be defined by that crime, she was going forward to make a life for herself. It was such a positive statement for her to make in the courtroom. It was important she be given every chance to do it, and she did.”

While the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions operates its own Witness Assistance Service, staffed by social workers, psychologists and counsellors, it may refer some adult witnesses to the volunteer service if they don’t have the capacity to support all victims and witnesses of crime.

The organisation also assists families of victims. “The government isn’t able to provide dedicated witness support in every matter, which is why organisations like Victims and Witnesses of Crime Court Support play such an important role,” Hannah Damkar, NSW Victims of Crime commissioner, said. “No one can take away the trauma of a crime or the stress that can come with court proceedings; however, supportive people can make the experience feel less overwhelming … What strikes me about these volunteers is their generosity – they choose to give their time to support complete strangers. That compassion and kindness can have an enormous impact on someone’s experience of the justice system.”

The criminal justice system is often fiercely criticised for how victims are treated. The NSW government recently introduced reforms intended to reduce the trauma experienced by sexual assault complainants when giving evidence, including allowing them to pre-record testimony. Jennifer believes there is now a greater awareness among judges and lawyers about how the court process can amplify a victim’s trauma, compared to when she began volunteering for the VWCCS.

She cites the introduction of specialist support services for domestic violence victims as a major improvement, and she’s seen how seemingly minor adjustments can make a difference, such as judges telling alleged perpetrators to remain in the courtroom while the alleged victim leaves first. “There’s recognition, but women still live in fear,” Jennifer says. What hasn’t changed, she adds, is the level of distress she sees, particularly among sexual assault victims. “No two cases are exactly the same, but the trauma is shared by the victims.”

Protecting volunteers from suffering vicarious trauma from what they hear in criminal trials is paramount, according to Maggie Weiley, the organisation’s vice-president. They have access to a counsellor anytime they feel they need support. The volunteers are mostly retired women “with a big heart”, and come from a range of professional backgrounds, says Weiley, a former advertising executive, who began volunteering in Sydney in 2007.

The volunteers undergo a rigorous selection process, which includes three interviews. People who have been victims or witnesses of crime are not accepted. “We think it’s best practice not to run the risk of retraumatising,” says Weiley.

Volunteers also attend training sessions with police prosecutors, detectives, legal academics, and victims of crime. They complete 40 hours of court observation, and write a paper about their experience, before embarking on a three-month probation period, under the supervision of experienced court support officers. They are not allowed to give legal advice to clients or discuss details of cases.

The organisation has helped more than 28,000 victims and witnesses since it was established in 2006 by Pieta Thornton, a former corporate executive.

Weiley says Thornton’s vision was to develop a team of highly trained volunteers who could support victims and witnesses of crime. “When you think about the adversarial nature of the court, that you have to recall – with crystal-clear clarity – something that happened years ago … it’s a very difficult day for people, possibly among the worst days of their lives,” says Weiley. “It’s very unnerving for people. They feel they’re on trial.”

The organisation recently recruited a new batch of volunteers to help expand the service next year. Weiley says they look for non-judgmental people with strong communication skills. She says it’s a challenging but rewarding role. “You can assess on that day the impact that it’s had on someone’s life,” she says. “I think, with many of us, it’s underpinned by a real sense of social justice and a strong desire to have a meaningful life.”

Jennifer says many of the volunteers remain with the organisation for years. “I think most people stay because it’s purposeful and they end up better people,” she says. “We learn not to judge. We learn life can be cruel.”

Jennifer attended training sessions about stress and trauma, but hasn’t felt the need to see a counsellor. “Most of the volunteers here and in Sydney feel that they cope well because we’re doing something positive. We work at leaving it here,” she says. “We start when we walk in, we finish when we walk out.”

Just before lunchtime on the day of the sexual assault trial in Newcastle, Jennifer heads back upstairs to check on the witness waiting to give evidence, taking a handful of chocolates with her. “It’s a tension-breaker,” she says.

Shortly after the witness accepts Jennifer’s chocolate, a court officer calls the witness’s name. Having waited for several hours, it’s now her turn to tell the jury what she knows. As she walks into the courtroom, Jennifer is close behind, silently indicating to the witness where she should stop and bow to the judge before she enters the witness box.

The prosecutor begins by asking for her name and how long she has known the alleged victim. She calmly answers questions about what her friend told her happened on the night of the alleged assault. From the other side of the courtroom, the defendant silently watches on. His lawyer’s cross-examination is brief, and when there are no more questions, the judge dismisses the witness. She bows and follows Jennifer out of the courtroom, embracing her as soon as they’re through the heavy courtroom doors. Volunteers are not allowed to have any contact with clients after their day in court, so for Jennifer, this is goodbye.

Later, the young woman tells me how anxious she’d felt coming to court that morning, and how Jennifer had helped to calm her nerves. “She was a familiar face that I could look for in the courtroom,” she says. “She’s a very comforting presence. I’m just really glad she was here.”

Neither the witness nor Jennifer are in court the next day when the jury returns a not guilty verdict.

It’s a day off for Jennifer, and she’s left behind the tension of the courtroom in exchange for the simple joy of watching her grandson on stage in his preschool concert. It’s a jarring contrast, but she’ll be back at the courthouse the following week, on the lookout for the next stranger who needs a compassionate ear, a quick guide to court etiquette or just the distraction of a sweet treat.

“We let the witnesses and victims know we’re there just to support them,” Jennifer says. “And that they’re not on their own.”

If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact Victims and Witnesses of Crime Court Support. You can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. You can reach Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

The winner is Cindy: The story behind Brisbane 2032’s emblem inspiration

Sydney Morning Herald October 17, 2026

A pink cockatoo from the Glass House Mountains became the unlikely muse for the Brisbane 2032 Games identity after a rainy-day shoot with photographer Joel Sartore.

Fifteen years after National Geographic photographer Joel Sartore walked into a Sunshine Coast parrot sanctuary with a camera, he laid his eyes on the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games emblem.

Little did Sartore know, as he aimed his lens at a pink cockatoo called Cindy, that his photograph would one day help launch a global brand.

The connection to the bird he snapped in the Glass House Mountains in 2011 was unmistakable from the moment he saw the Brisbane 2032 emblem last week.

“When I saw it, I thought ‘I get it, I get it’ – it looks like fire, it looks like something that’s organic and wild,” Sartore says.

“I just thought that it’s smart. I loved it – I just loved it. But, of course, I’m a little biased now.”

This masthead spoke to Sartore when he was in Washington DC, where his Photo Ark: Animals of Earth exhibit was showing at the National Geographic Museum of Exploration.

The following day, Sartore was due to head to the Mexican border to document even more species, but not before he reflected on the inadvertent role he played in inspiring a new global brand.

“It’s really incredible. First, the Animals of Earth exhibit here at the Geographic, which is wonderful, and now this. I’m very blessed and lucky, and I’m really curious how that came about,” he says.

“I wish my folks were alive to see this – they’d think I’d made good.”

Sartore was shown the Olympic emblem last week, after National Geographic was alerted of the role he played in its development.

“Somebody asked me what I thought it looked like and I said it looks like a cockatoo that’s cresting,” he says.

“I was ready to move on. But then they said ‘You know, that’s based on the cockatoo you shot in Australia years ago.’ I’m like, seriously, wow!” he says.

Sartore clearly remembers the photo shoot at Parrots in Paradise – a side quest when he was on assignment for a National Geographic feature on koalas.

While in Australia, Sartore took the opportunity to work on his Photo Ark project – a quest to document as many of Earth’s species as possible.

It was then he met Parrots in Paradise founder Dail Martins.

“I went there on a rainy day and she had nobody there,” Sartore says.

“She was just so generous with her time, and she brought her birds out. I photographed all the ones I needed in this thing set up in her backyard under a tent cover, under a canvas.”

Among those birds was Cindy – a gregarious pink cockatoo with a flair for modelling.

“The way she was leaning in, she really liked [Malins] – a lot of people that handle parrots like that, they can talk to their birds and trigger that cresting of those feathers,” Sartore says.

“Just a beautiful bird, everything about her.”

“She really was a sweetheart,” Malins says of Cindy.

Sadly, Cindy died last year. Malins guessed she was about 30 years old, but could not be certain.

What she did know was that Cindy entered their lives in 2000, as Parrots in Paradise evolved from an idea to reality.

“There was a guy selling two birds and I was after an Alexandrine,” Malins says.

“We arrived at his place, and there was two very small, pristine little cages: one perch, one food bowl and one water bowl at either end – nothing else, absolutely nothing.

“Nothing to amuse the birds. Nothing to make them interested.

“We bought the Alexandrine and as we drove away, I said to [husband] Mark, ‘We can’t leave it there – we’ve got to go and go back and get her’.

“So we did. That’s how Cindy came to us. She was a sweetie.”

A sociable bird too, Malins says.

“She loved my husband. She loved showing off to people every time somebody came in,” she says.

“She’d step up on their hands, flick out her wings and throw a crest out. She loved the people.”

Malins says everyone at Parrots in Paradise was “absolutely blown away” by Cindy’s involvement in the Olympic emblem design process.

“We get very excited when anything happens here,” she says.

“To realise our little lovely Cindy that we’ve known so long is the poster girl for 2032 is really special.

“She was lovely and everything about her was great.”

Cindy was photographed as part of Sartore’s 30-plus-year Photo Ark project—a global quest to document every species in human care using plain studio backgrounds.

“To date, we’ve photographed nearly 19,000 species this way using black and white backgrounds and studio lighting,” he says.

“By using this technique, we give all animals an equal voice because there’s no size comparison. A mouse and an elephant are the same size in these pictures.”

While hard to quantify Photo Ark’s success in raising awareness, Sartore says there have been some tangible, positive results for conservation – including here in Australia.

He pointed to the impact of his photography of the red handfish, a Tasmanian species that has a higher population at a breeding centre in a Hobart university than in the wild.

“When we named that our 18,000th species, the folks in Tasmania got a hold of us and said featuring that fish as a milestone species helped save their breeding efforts, because they didn’t know where their funding was going to come from next,” he said.

“They heard from people all around the world that wanted to help support them – that’s a big win for us because it doesn’t happen near nearly often enough.”

The project typically keeps Sartore away from his Nebraska home for half the year.

“In terms of captive species, there’s probably 30-to-40,000, because things change a lot, especially at aquariums and rehabbers,” he says.

“In terms of the numbers of animals in the wild, there’s about 1.5 million described now.

“I like to say we’re just getting started.”

Bystander who killed Oregon shooter identified as father of girls at elementary school

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 20:37:21 GMT

Kaylub Giamanco, who was reportedly driving home when he heard gunshots, ‘not seeking recognition’, family says

Details are beginning to emerge about Kaylub Giamanco, the man who brought the deadly shooting at elementary school in Bend, Oregon on Thursday, to an end by fatally shooting the 16-year-old suspect in the midst of a violent rampage.

Authorities have yet to officially release the man’s identity, but Kaylub Giamanco’s family issued a statement on Friday confirming that he shot and killed the suspect.

“The tragedy at Silver Rail elementary has devastated the Bend community,” the family wrote, asking for privacy and declining further media interviews. “He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support.”

Speaking briefly to reporters on Friday, his mother read the statement from her phone and said her son appreciated the support but wanted to remain private.

A lifelong resident of Bend with two daughters at Silver Rail elementary, where three children aged five, eight and 11, and a teacher were killed, and a seven-year-old child and another teacher critically injured, Giamanco was reportedly driving to his home near the school when he heard gunshots and decided to take action.

“Yes, my brother shot the shooter in yesterday’s events at the Bend elementary school,” Kameron Giamanco wrote in a public Facebook post on Friday that reiterated the family’s request for privacy in the aftermath of the traumatic event.

“He’s an absolute HERO. However, we are not speaking to media at this time. He’s not ready, nor is the family.”

Though she did not name him, Oregon’s governor, Tina Kotek, praised the man who followed the shooter into the school during a news conference on Thursday.

“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life,” she said, “your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well.”

The Bend police chief, Mike Krantz, said officers responded in minutes after multiple 911 calls came in from within and outside the school. Shortly after officers arrived on scene, he said, the attacker was shot by a bystander inside the school.

“An officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz said. Officers on scene located “five people who had succumbed to their injuries, including the suspect”.

The shooter has been identified by law enforcement officials as John J Griffin II, and authorities are still investigating what led to the deadly attack. He was using a pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother, according to reporting from the Associated Press.

“This is going to be a long investigation,” Krantz said, adding that the police would maintain a large presence at the school for the next few days.

Anna Betts and Abené Clayton contributed reporting

Katie Zacharia fired after five days as White House press secretary

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 19:29:43 GMT

Zacharia hosted widely panned first briefing on Tuesday and faced scrutiny after admitting she didn’t pass bar exam

Donald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was fired on Friday, just five days after she assumed the role, according to a White House official.

The person was not authorized to speak publicly about the personnel decision that had not yet been formally announced. Zacharia, a little-known conservative political commentator prior to her selection as Trump’s chief spokesperson, came under immediate scrutiny after a widely panned inaugural briefing on Tuesday. The 14-minute exchange was soon followed by a barrage of questions over her legal credentials after she admitted she did not pass the bar exam.

In an interview on Thursday, Zacharia detailed her whirlwind sprint to the podium to replace Karoline Leavitt as the White House press secretary, stepping into the role as the president faces multiple headwinds just weeks before the midterm elections next month.

On Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia’s tenure would be short-lived, telling reported that he had asked his embattled press secretary to “reconsider” the job.

“I said: ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need it,’” Trump said, speaking outside the White House. “I said to her: ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”

During her first – and apparently only – press briefing, Zacharia stumbled through prepared remarks highlighting Trump’s accomplishments in his presidency. She made a notable gaffe when she called her husband “the president”.

Members of the White House press corps were left puzzled when she departed the podium after only taking questions from three predominantly conservative media outlets.

She spent the next hours and days trying to clarify swirling questions about her résumé, after reports emerged revealing that Zacharia, whom Trump has referred to as an “attorney”, had never passed the bar exam. She later confirmed that she took the bar once and failed.

Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school in California, and repeatedly called herself a lawyer.

She defended using the term to describe herself professionally, claiming there was a difference between a “lawyer” and an “attorney”, a title reserved for those licensed to practice law.

She had previously shared social media posts identifying herself as an “attorney”. And when the White House officially announced her appointment, the statement described her as an “attorney”.

Over the last few days, Zacharia has spoken with members of the media in an effort to try to move past the criticism and make the case that she was ready to take on the role as the president’s chief spokesperson.

In an unexpectedly tough interview on Thursday evening, Fox host Sean Hannity grilled Zacharia about her first press briefing, asking bluntly: “What happened?”

Zacharia sought to explain that she had had little time to prep in the days between accepting the job and holding her first press briefing and argued that the conservative Daily Mail, one of only three outlets she took questions from, was “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity, a Trump ally, also pressed her on her decision to identify herself as a “lawyer”.

“Why get into this long, drawn-out definition of the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction,” he asked.

In a Friday appearance on Fox & Friends, host Lawrence Jones continued, telling Zacharia: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary, and you never want to be the story.”

She said she hoped to “build the trust and confidence of everyone around me” but could not say when her next press briefing would be.

Masterplan review – Stanley Tucci is wasted in Amazon’s smooth-brained heist caper

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 19:24:23 GMT

A ‘family’ of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thriller

In the last half-decade Stanley Tucci has been a source of near-inexhaustible on- screen delight, whether making friends with nonnas in his delightful cooking shows or smartly judged supporting turns in Conclave and The Devil Wears Prada 2. He is an actor well placed for a star vehicle of his own, and this one, Masterplan, sounds good on paper: an art heist fronted by the actor at his most debonair, flanked by a grandson of a French New Wave legend (Victor Belmondo, related to Breathless star Jean-Paul) and a buzzy breakout of The White Lotus (Simona Tabasco, winning in season two of Mike White’s comedy).

There’s a good bit of pulpy fun to have here, with double, triple and quadruple crossing, silly spy gadgetry which has been updated to include retina scan cloning and something called “VR intrusion”. As British criminal mastermind Roger, Tucci is game to send up aristo archetypes, even if his character often veers into parody. “I’m English,” his character says at one point. “‘Not bad’ is what I say when I orgasm.”

“Not bad” is what I say about Masterplan, a straight-to-streaming Amazon Prime offering that the studio is burying this weekend, seemingly choosing to focus on its just-released romantic drama Love of Your Life. Cybersecurity hacker Chiara (Tabasco) and explosives expert Jay (Belmondo) are Europe’s leading young criminals, working together remotely under aliases and using some kind of dark web app to sign up for new gigs. When they meet for the first time while breaking into a mansion on the shores of Italy’s Lake Geneva, sparks fly. “Sixty seconds, in and out,” promises Jay before Chiara snaps back playfully: “Don’t you use that name on Tinder?”

Just as you settle in for an evening of will-they-won’t-they hijinks, the film pulls a bait and switch. It turns out that the pair have been set up by Roger (Tucci), a veteran thief himself who has the “job of a lifetime” for them: a decade-in-the-making plan to make off with the Mona Lisa in a complicated scheme that involves drones, trickery, truffle-related espionage and a long-forgotten tunnel that conveniently exists under the Louvre. Also: they are in fact brother and sister, the result of an energetic mid-90s for Roger when he seduced their respective mothers.

You would think the fact that they are now siblings would put the kibosh on Jay and Chiara’s flirtation, but the film seems to feel otherwise. As the makeshift family relocate to Paris to put plans in motion for the heist, Chiara makes jokes about the size of her half-brother’s “hammer” and offers to settle squabbles through a round of strip poker, which strikes me as an unusual way for siblings to bond.

Despite the jokes that land with a thud, Masterplan is on safer ground when it sticks to the espionage. That is thanks to Thomas Vincent, the director, recapturing some of the juice he showed in the episodes of Bodyguard he directed, and I would rate Masterplan as a hair better than Role Play, the dull film he previously made for Amazon. When it isn’t trying to dazzle you with technology, Masterplan has a few twists on heist movie tropes (including a very clever use of a helium balloon) that avoids it feeling like a total retread of the Ocean’s 11 franchise, even if it doesn’t come close to matching the ingenuity of those films. And while the characters are too thinly drawn to make you care too much about them, I appreciated flourishes that nod to the female and gay male gaze, such as the diva moment where Tabasco’s character dons a platinum blond wig and the camera’s lustiness for Belmondo, who has a talent for losing his shirt.

Everything isn’t as it seems, and while the film should really end 30 minutes before it does, it has a few final tricks up its sleeve in the third act, as the characters begin to learn who they can really trust and Chiara’s hacking skills are put to the test once more. Even as the plot becomes increasingly ridiculous, ample bangs and explosions ensure that the nearly two-hour runtime doesn’t totally drag. The best you can offer Masterplan is faint praise: it could breeze by as company to your Sunday night takeout even if you will struggle to remember it a week later.

Masterplan is streaming on Amazon Prime Video now

‘It’s really not a drama’: Carrick sticks to the script after Martínez storm

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 19:00:09 GMT

Manchester United head coach produced a masterclass in dialling down emotion before a tricky trip to Leeds

Michael Carrick returned his most impressive performance precisely when required as he took questions in the midst of the first crisis engulfing him as Manchester United’s manager.

His team are bombing in the league after the club’s poorest start since 1986 and out of the Carabao Cup, and after Tuesday’s Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid Lisandro Martínez showed up ruptures at United by calling out the director of football, Jason Wilcox.

All of this two months into a first full campaign piloting United after last term ended so rosily for the former United midfielder.

On the final day of last season, United won 3-0 at Brighton and Carrick secured an impressive third-place finish, 48 hours after agreeing a two-year deal to continue as head coach.

By last Saturday, United had six points from the first six games after drawing 1-1 with Tottenham at Old Trafford, placing Carrick’s job in jeopardy as the walls closed in on him a fortnight before the clocks go back.

A game at Leeds in January proved to be Ruben Amorim’s last in charge at Manchester United after he greeted the 1-1 draw by demanding his colleagues in the recruitment department “do their job”. With an uncanny circularity Carrick heads to Elland Road on Sunday after Martínez made similar comments. Amorim’s team were sixth going into that game; Carrick’s start the weekend 13th.

On Friday, though, came a masterclass from Carrick in dialling down emotion as Martínez’s explosive comments about Wilcox – “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director” – were addressed and he repeatedly referred to the “really good feeling” at the club.

“It’s really not a drama for us as a group,” he said. “The boys have trained really well. This morning there was a really good feeling around the squad … so we’ve moved on pretty quickly.”

If this seems less than credible, and almost certainly a stance coached by United’s PR mandarins, what else would Carrick be expected to say? More obvious was how the zen-like performance required from the club’s leader was being delivered. Even when he broke from the script to interrupt an inquisitor this strengthened the sense of Carrick being in control – hardly easy given the heightened glare on United since Tuesday evening.

When the positive vibes trope was challenged by a questioner saying: “We’ll have to take you at face value”, Carrick’s interjection came with a smile. “I’m telling you the truth when I say that,” he said. “Do you not believe me, no? The players totally believe me. I’m telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen it for a while, actually, and that’s it, plain and simple, you know? We’re emotional, we’re passionate, we care a lot.”

When signing on to be the permanent United manager, Carrick had overseen only 21 games at elite level – in two caretaker spells at the club. United had 17 league games to play when he replaced Amorim, and Carrick has shown signs of faltering this season when having to compete on four fronts.

Elimination by Brighton at the earliest stage of the Carabao Cup was not a great calling card regarding an ability to juggle competitions, and there was a surprising reaction from him after the 2-0 opening-day loss at Hull. He bridled at the suggestion United had lacked “passion” during a first-half horror show. “Oh come,” Carrick said. “That’s ridiculous.”

A faulty United rearguard is hampering an attack that is functioning far better and has the most shots (125) and most touches in the opposition box (205) in the Premier League. Nine goals from six matches is not paltry but greater ruthlessness would transform a promising front six into a potent one. Carrick has to find the right blend from Benjamin Sesko, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba.

Baleba has sparkled in his first two appearances – against Spurs and Atlético – and might have provided the shield from the No 6 berth to ensure a less leaky defence had he not arrived injured.

This has to be the hope for Carrick. Playing Tielemans at No 10 at Atlético suggests the manager may doubt the 29-year-old’s legs, and questions have been raised about whether United are putting in enough of the hard yards. Their 671.4km distance covered in the league is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2km is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).

The trip to an always febrile Elland Road that saves a particular welcome for their cross-Pennines rivals presents a stern challenge. Leeds are ninth and have lost once.

“It’s a great rivalry,” Carrick said, who was full of praise for his Leeds counterpart, Daniel Farke. “There’s big history between the clubs, the areas. That’s what makes these types of games special. You’ve got to embrace the history, what it means.

“I’m sure it will be a fantastic atmosphere on Sunday. It brings an intensity and it’ll be a little bit extra again, on Sunday against us … Of course, we have to be ready, and the boys will be.”

Carrick requires a positive result, though in denying this, he again sounded the right note. “I don’t need results, we all need results,” he said. “It’s not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual, bigger than me, bigger than any player, anyone else who works at this club. It’s not about me, so please …

“I don’t go into every day at work, in this situation, this game, thinking about me. It’s about what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to, and that’s what drives us. So whatever’s best for the club and for the team on Sunday is the most important thing.”
