No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:09:34 GMT

Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package

No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.

Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.

The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.

The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.

The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.

This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.

However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.

Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.

They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”

Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.

EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.

But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.

Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.

According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.

This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.

Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.

Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.

A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.

China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.

While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.

Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.

At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.

Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.

“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.

Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.

The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump.

Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.

“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”

Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.

Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.

Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.

“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”

Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.

Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.

Starlink is produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, but controlled by the US government.

When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.

According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.

The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.

The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.

Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.

“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.

The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.

Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.

Von der Leyen said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions and adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”

Police are carrying out a criminal investigation into a row over the founding of Your Party, which split the leftwing party as it was established last year.

A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan police said they had launched an investigation after they received a report in September 2025 “relating to the alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database”, the Politico website reported.

Your Party was founded in summer 2025 by the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and the former Labour MP Zarah Sultana, both of whom now sit as Your Party MPs in the House of Commons.

But relations between the different factions in the party have been strained since its creation in July last year. That September Sultana revealed a new membership portal on X, and encouraged members to become paying members for £55.

Corbyn described the site as a “false membership system” and told supporters to ignore an email requesting funds. Sultana said her only aim had been to “safeguard the grassroots involvement that is essential to building this party”, and later accused the party of being run by a “sexist boys’ club”.

Officers had now arrested a man on suspicion of an offence under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act, a police spokesperson told Politico. The man was released pending further inquiries and has not been charged.

Officers also previously interviewed a woman in her 30s under caution in connection with the same investigation. The spokesperson added: “The investigation continues.” The police spokesperson did not name any political party in their statement, and the spokesperson did not confirm which political party their investigation was related to.

Sources told the Guardian that the investigation was linked to the long-running dispute connected to the establishment of Your Party. Neither the man arrested nor the woman interviewed by police are MPs and neither have been charged with an offence. Neither Corbyn nor Sultana were accused of wrongdoing, Politico reported.

In January, it emerged that the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) advised the party that while it was taking no further action over the Your Party membership portal launch, it may have involved “serious criminal activity” and should be referred to the police.

A Your Party spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment any further about ongoing police investigations.”

They also said: “We can reassure our members and supporters that our systems are secure and that this was an isolated incident.”

Your Party has struggled to make a widespread national impact since it was founded, while the Green party of England and Wales, rebranded as an eco-socialist party, has seen its membership quadruple.

In February, Corbyn won a comprehensive victory to become the de facto leader of the leftwing startup party. He said Your Party would work with the Green party and others to push for a “coordinated left-flank offensive” against Reform and Labour. Sultana was also voted on to the party’s leadership committee under its collective leadership model.

Corbyn-backed candidates took 14 of the 24 available places on the party’s central executive committee (CEC). Sultana-backed candidates took seven of the seats and three went to independents.

The UK’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, is under pressure to distance himself from a comment made by his wife, the award-winning writer Sarah Helm, in support of Palestine Action.

The post was made in defence of the critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who said she had been forced to pull her books from shelves in the UK after pledging proceeds from their sales to Palestine Action.

Helm, a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent who spent many years covering the Middle East, wrote on X indicating support for the direct action group, which was proscribed last year.

Under terror laws, this could constitute a criminal offence, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison. The ban has so far resulted in more than 3,700 arrests for backing the group, with more than 2,250 people formally charged as terrorists.

In response to comments by the broadcaster Adam Boulton that Rooney’s support for Palestine was “anti-Jewish”, Helm wrote: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action. Sounds like Adam would have all our books swept off the shelves in a jiffy.”

Police said the post was “in the process of being assessed” to determine whether an investigation was required.

Downing Street distanced itself from Helm’s post on Friday, with a spokesperson saying: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”

Helm’s works include a book about the women imprisoned by the Nazis at the Ravensbrück concentration camp, and Loyalty, a play about the Iraq war, inspired by her husband’s decade as the chief of staff to the then prime minister, Tony Blair.

The author, who is writing a book about Gaza, married Powell in 2007. He was appointed in 2024 as a national security adviser under Keir Starmer.

According to government guidance, being married to a suspected or convicted terrorist would normally result in the revocation of security clearance. Under the vetting framework for a job as national security adviser, being married to someone tied to a proscribed terrorist organisation is viewed as creating an automatic, unmitigated national security risk.

Responding to questions about Powell’s position after his wife’s comments, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”

A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries, a free speech group which supports the right for people to protest peacefully, thanked Helm for “defying this absurdly authoritarian ban”.

“How can Andy Burnham’s government possibly defend this ban in the supreme court next month when his own national security adviser’s wife has openly defied it? “We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives. But her defiance further exposes the absurdity of a ban that cannot be enforced against everyone who challenges it. There are simply too many of us who will continue to defy this unjust law until the government is forced to see sense and abandon it.”

However, the Campaign Against Antisemitism called for Helm to “face the full force of the law”.

The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:52:37 GMT

Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbying

John Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian revealed, in the forthcoming budget. It’s about time for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group Positive Money reported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with the Treasury footing the bill.

The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year. This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them hissing. The banks say that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last.

But banks aren’t taxed on their windfall gains, and what levies they face are less than those paid by oil and gas companies. The Bank of England said banks spent £7.7bn on dividends and buying back shares in the first quarter of 2026 without affecting lending. Higher taxes might mean trimming shareholder payouts. There’s nothing to suggest productive lending must take the hit. Over the past five years Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest – which control the majority of UK personal and business accounts – made profits of £200bn. Positive Money says that households lost out on £44bn in deposit interest in 2025. Some of this paid for banking services. But that does not explain why the sum is five times the equivalent average figure for 2009-21.

The chancellor could be more radical. The precedent here is not a socialist one. Margaret Thatcher taxed banks’ windfalls in 1981. A comparable 2.5% levy on today’s interest-free deposits would, a paper by the New Economics Foundation and Positive Money suggests, raise more than £11bn. In August, Positive Money suggested looking at Spain’s success in levying a windfall tax on banks’ net income above €800m. It says that such a windfall tax – levied at the same rate as that paid by fossil fuel companies on a comparable tax base – would bring in £19bn from the UK arms of the big four banks. That would pay for a universal and comprehensive adult social care system.

Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens. Yet the sector is paying the highest bankers’ bonuses since the 2008 global financial crisis. “Most financial sector activity,” concluded a paper published in The Manchester School journal this month, “is simply negative for overall economic performance.” Politicians should stop mistaking finance lobbyists’ demands for a growth strategy. Their job is to curb a finance sector so large that it risks crises and weaker growth. Taxpayers rescued the banks after they helped crash the economy 18 years ago. Public protection carries public obligations. As Sir Philip Augar, the author and former banker, told the BBC: “Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

The Guardian view on Winnie-the-Pooh: now we are 100

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:52:01 GMT

He may have been eclipsed by the more progressive Paddington of late, but AA Milne’s creation is not just a Silly Old Bear

“Pooh, promise you won’t forget about me, ever. Not even when I’m a hundred,” Christopher Robin implores his bear in the final chapter of AA Milne’s The House at Pooh Corner. This week Winnie-the-Pooh himself turned 100, and he certainly hasn’t been forgotten. Birthday celebrations have included a week of special programmes, introduced by the queen, on Radio 4; a collection of Royal Mail stamps; and a Google doodle.

Not bad for “a bear of very little brain” who appeared in four slim books. Winnie-the-Pooh, illustrated by EH Shepard, was published on 14 October 1926 and had sold 150,000 copies in the US by the end of the year.

Despite his success, the honey-loving bear was resented by both Milne and his son Christopher Robin Milne, the first for eclipsing his work as a playwright and comic writer, the latter for stealing his childhood. And he was too sugary for some. “It is that word ‘hummy,’” Dorothy Parker wrote waspishly under her pseudonym Constant Reader, “that makes the first place … at which Tonstant Weader fwowed up”. PG Wodehouse and Evelyn Waugh were equally sniffy. But generations of children disagreed. Winnie-the-Pooh was voted No 7 in the BBC Big Read poll in 2003.

Pooh’s position as Britain’s favourite bear is under threat from a younger ursine model. Separated by 32 years and one day, Michael Bond’s A Bear Called Paddington was published on 13 October 1958. These two polite and accident-prone bears differ in more than a taste for honey or marmalade.

Both stories were created in the aftermath of war: Winnie-the-Pooh was Milne’s escape from the horrors of the Somme; Paddington was inspired by evacuees in the second world war. Pooh was based on a toy from Harrods, Paddington on a solitary teddy that Bond found in a toyshop on Christmas Eve. The Hundred Acre Wood is a sheltered rural idyll; Paddington arrives at a bustling postwar London station. Both are beloved at Buckingham Palace, but it was the bear from Peru who was invited to tea for the platinum jublee of Queen Elizabeth II.

Thanks to three hit films and now an award-winning musical, Paddington has shaken off his slightly fusty image to become an emblem of modern Britain. Where Paddington is progressive, Pooh seems stuck in a posher past.

Aside from being one of the world’s biggest merchandising franchises, Winnie-the-Pooh’s cultural afterlife has been bumpier. Screen adaptations have been mixed, from Disney’s 1966 animation, which EH Shepard declared “a complete travesty”, to the indie slasher horror Winnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey, made after Milne’s US copyright expired in 2022. Pooh has become an unlikely symbol of political dissent in China after President Xi was visually likened to him in 2013, with protesters in Hong Kong picking up the comparison in 2019.

According to a Canadian medical journal, each character represents a form of neurodivergence or mental health disorder: Tigger stands for ADHD, Piglet for anxiety, Eeyore for depression and so on. The article may not have been entirely serious, but the author Matt Haig has described Winnie-the-Pooh as “the ultimate self-help book”. Pooh is not just a “silly old bear”. In our speeded-up age, where children spend more time on screens than outdoors, Milne’s world of freedom and innocence remains deeply comforting, for “in that enchanted place on the top of the forest a little boy and his Bear will always be playing”.

Six-figure payout for senior civil servant sacked over Peter Mandelson vetting

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:44:34 GMT

Former head of Foreign Office Olly Robbins applied for judicial review after Keir Starmer dismissed him in April

Olly Robbins, the former head of the Foreign Office sacked by Keir Starmer over his role in vetting Peter Mandelson, has received a six-figure payout from the government over his dismissal.

Robbins had applied to the high court for a judicial review of the prime minister’s decision to remove him as the top civil servant at the Foreign Office after he was dismissed in April.

He was removed from his post by Starmer after the Guardian’s disclosure that he had overturned a recommendation from UK Security Vetting (UKSV) to deny clearance for Mandelson.

In a statement on Friday, Robbins said he was “grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time”.

He added: “I want to thank the FDA [union] for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life.”

Dave Penman, general secretary of the FDA, which represents senior civil servants, said: “This settlement may bring an end to the judicial review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.

“The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgment of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations – which is quite the feat.

“We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process.”

The government will ultimately have to publish how much it has given Robbins in a settlement, which is believed to be six figures but not as much as the record £860,000 given to former cabinet secretary Chris Wormald after he was forced out by Starmer after just a year in post.

At the time of his dismissal, Downing Street said Robbins had lost the confidence of Starmer and Yvette Cooper, then foreign secretary, due to his handling of the vetting of Mandelson, who was sacked over the extent of his links to the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The Guardian later revealed that Mandelson’s associations with senior figures in China, Russia and Israel had been among the concerns raised by UKSV when it concluded he should be denied clearance. His relationship with Epstein was not among the reasons.

Robbins’ legal submission had made the case that Starmer had no statutory authority to dismiss him as the head of the diplomatic service, and that there had been “no fair procedure” and “no process at all” in the dismissal. It also said Robbins had been given “irrational” reasons for being fired.

There had been strong support for Robbins within Whitehall, with senior civil servants said to believe he had in effect been sacked for doing what No 10 wanted by swiftly passing Mandelson through vetting, and that the focus should instead have been on the prime minister’s initial decision.

The Commons foreign affairs select committee has previously said that Robbins believed he was “delivering the outcome that was wanted” and concluded that his dismissal “seems to have been taken without full due process and the establishment of the facts”.

Questions remain about the defence Robbins mounted, both of his own actions and the system through which the national security establishment vets people, and the lack of mitigation put in place to get around the security concerns.

The Foreign Office refused to hand over a summary of Mandelson’s security vetting to the official tasked with compiling documents detailing his appointment as ambassador to the US, in response to a Commons motion forcing the release of documents linked to the process.

Some criticism has been OTT and a fee rising to £116m heightens demands but, yes, compared with his performances in Germany and for Germany Wirtz has underwhelmed at Liverpool. In the Champions League rout of Lask he was everywhere, exploiting gaps between and behind the Austrian club’s defence and knitting together a dominant display against limited opposition. In the previous game against Manchester City, however, when Andoni Iraola needed big players to step up in the absence of Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai, Wirtz was ineffective, wasteful and withdrawn when his team were chasing the game at 0-1. The physicality and intensity of the Premier League appear to be Wirtz’s biggest issues. He can be swamped, knocked aside, leaving Liverpool’s central midfield exposed. Iraola this week rejected the notion that the playmaker is struggling with English football, although his answer almost veered in support of the argument. “It’s not about whether they are foreign teams or English teams,” the head coach said. “It’s about different kinds of games. It’s not about the competition.” But, as Brentford are likely to demonstrate on Saturday, there is less time to think and little opportunity to get comfortable in the Premier League. Wirtz produced three assists in 11 Champions League games last season, the same amount as he did in 33 Premier League matches. His passing accuracy this season – from an admittedly small sample – is 80% in the Premier League and 91.5% in the Champions League. AH

That is a question that can be levelled at many of Liverpool’s signings since the 2025 title win. The shift towards acquiring expensive “finished products” has left many pining for the hunger and spirit of emerging talent that characterised the club’s re-emergence under Jürgen Klopp. Wirtz does not have an ego to match his price tag. He is a conscientious, dedicated professional who Iraola, like Arne Slot before him, has found to be a good listener willing to put team instructions first. Wirtz was sold on Slot’s vision for him as the central, creative force of a new-look Liverpool attack that would turn the slender wins of the title-winning season into dominant, emphatic victories. Unbelievably so. In his final two seasons in the Bundesliga you could make the case that he was the best player in it. Teams who tried to kick him out of games almost universally failed, making the idea he can’t hack the Premier League physically a flawed explanation for his difficulties. AB

Partly it was, but on a technical and tactical level his success was also partly down to the freedom Xabi Alonso allowed him. As Alonso said in November 2023 (during Leverkusen’s unbeaten double-winning season) every player had responsibility to patrol an allotted zone “but Flo is different” – he was given licence to prod opposing defences as he saw fit. Alonso’s rotation of him made sure he remained fresh and impactful, his hat-trick in the 5-0 win over Werder Bremen that clinched the title in 2024 coming after he was brought on as a half-time substitute. I don’t think we can say that isn’t a factor – but this is something Wirtz himself predicted. He knew it was a risk but was determined to challenge himself. Another point is how different the Bundesliga is tactically; it has a similarly high tempo but is far more chaotic, which is perfect for a player with his sang froid to exploit. AB

British students, like their French peers, have been known to challenge authority

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:32:58 GMT

Pete Crockett says the history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction, while Simon Dawson says Kitty Sayers misses the mark when describing English attitudes. Plus a letter from Kevin Donnelly

Reading Kitty Sayers’ interesting article, I was reminded of the rich, and perhaps too easily forgotten, history of direct action by British schoolchildren (Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why, 10 October). Far from being historically meek or unquestioningly compliant, they have demonstrated a remarkable capacity for challenging authority.

At Marlborough college, troops were once summoned to dislodge rebellious pupils occupying an island in the school grounds. In the late 1700s, Winchester college experienced several rebellions.

Nor was such defiance confined to the more privileged. In 1889, strikes by schoolchildren in the Scottish lowlands spread across Tyneside, London, Bristol and Cardiff. In 1911, a strike beginning at Bigyn school in Llanelli developed into a remarkable wave of protest, reaching some 60 towns across England and Wales.

Schoolchildren and their families also played their part in the extraordinary 1914 Burston school strike, which endured for 25 years and became the longest‑running strike in British history.

Those of us of a certain generation may also recall the National Union of School Students in the 1970s, whose challenges to established educational authority infuriated traditionalists such as the headmaster Rhodes Boyson, who later became a Conservative minister.

The history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction. It also has a rich tradition of collective action and resistance to perceived injustice. Schoolchildren challenging the established order is hardly a peculiarly French phenomenon. There is a substantial, if sometimes overlooked, British history of such action too. Pete Crockett Royal Wootton Bassett, Wiltshire

Kitty Sayers is illuminating on French attitudes to protest, but she misses the mark when describing English attitudes. She says that Britons are subjects rather than citizens; that word deserves more analysis.

In This Land is Our Land, Marion Shoard argues that England is in effect a colonised country, but conquered so long ago that we no longer notice how much it shapes us. Within a generation of 1066, the English landowning class had been almost entirely replaced, and many free peasants were pressed into serfdom. Shoard argues that when, centuries later, the English poor did protest, “as a defeated class, they looked only to improve the terms of their subjection, and … they failed even in that.”

France, by contrast, eventually overturned its feudal order. Edward Carpenter wrote (in Towards Industrial Freedom) that victory at Waterloo had been a misfortune for England, denying us the upheaval that swept such structures away elsewhere. Perhaps that is why a French teenager reaches for the barricade and an English one reaches for a petition.

The British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition is rightly presented as a marvel. As we queue to admire it, we should ask whether we still see the conquest it depicts, and its long shadow over our country, with necessary clarity. Simon Dawson Winterbourne Gunner, Wiltshire

Kitty Sayers identifies the differences between the French and British education systems as a major contributory factor in why French students protest and British students don’t. Another may be in how protests are framed by the mass media in the UK.

Often, the default position is what is known as the “protest paradigm”, which leads journalists to emphasise the methods used by protesters over the message; and in which even legitimate protests then receive delegitimising coverage.

Changing the optics could bring more people out on to the streets, particularly if they feel they have a legitimate reason for doing so, and the media have a major role to play in creating and maintaining that environment for legitimate protest. Kevin Donnelly Sanremo, Italy

Bringing more women out of the shadows and into the Wiki world

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 16:32:52 GMT

We need to work together to build a more inclusive history, writes Mags L Halliday. Plus a letter from Shane Ritchie

Sandi Toksvig is right to highlight the systemic bias in information about women’s lives in history (Pass notes: Is Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rival, 12 October). Her comment about Wikipedia, however, implies that no one is working to correct this bias on the site itself. I belong to several projects whose goals are to reduce the gender gap on Wikipedia.

One, Women in Red, started in October 2014. At that point, only 15.53% of biographies on the encyclopedia were of women. As of October 2026, that has risen to 20.42%, in part thanks to the many volunteers who spend their spare time searching for reliable sources to draw on. The Women in Red project currently publishes an average of 1,500 new biographies every month.

Whenever volunteers are creating a biography, we are hampered by far wider system biases than Wikipedia’s alone. There is the well-established difficulty that earlier historians and archivists did not record the lives of women, making it harder to retrieve them from the shadows.

A quick look in a bookshop shows that this bias towards the Great Man view of history still holds sway, with far more biographies of individual men than of individual women being published. As Wikipedia does not accept primary research by the volunteer editors, there is an urgent need for more secondary sources such as Toksvig’s proposed Mappa Mundi and well-sourced biographies. This is not an either/or situation, but one where people need to work together to build a more inclusive history of the world. Mags L Halliday Exeter

Your article repeats Sandi Toksvig’s claim that the site is edited by “mostly white, middle-aged, European men”, as if it were a closed club. It isn’t. Anyone can edit Wikipedia, with or without an account, from a phone, today. If women’s biographies are missing, the remedy is free and open to Toksvig, to Cambridge and to every reader of this paper. A rival project needs fundraising only if the obstacle were access, and it isn’t.

Most of the gap has a simpler cause. Wikipedia only covers people who have already been written about elsewhere. If newspapers and historians ignored women, Wikipedia has little to work with. That is the record’s fault, not the editors’.

Wikipedia is one of the best things that the internet has produced: free, open, sourced, and fixable by anyone. Its gaps deserve a serious debate. Jokes that hint at an argument without making it are not that. Shane Ritchie Bangor, County Down

I find that the practice has a certain appeal and can fully sympathise with Rachael’s use of her mother’s ashes. Pauline Lowe Bryn Y Maen, Colwyn Bay

‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: reviewers on NAZA documentary

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:42:46 GMT

Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza wins widespread praise around the world

Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.

The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.

In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.

British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.

Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”

The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.

The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an exposé” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.

The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”

The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various organisations, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

Target pensions or welfare, not banks, IMF tells John Healey

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:33:29 GMT

Supporters of planned tax, however, say banks were bailed out by taxpayers during financial crisis and can afford to pay more now

John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget

The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.

Helge Berger, deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue.

Berger replied that given the UK’s current high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.

He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.

He added: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”

As examples, he highlighted the pensions triple lock – which Labour has already said it will reform – and “better targeting [of] social benefits”, adding: “I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”

Berger was speaking in Bangkok, where the IMF has held its annual meetings this week.

City lobbyists have been out in full force, warning the government that higher taxes could force banks to throttle lending, hitting the economy and even forcing some lenders to move jobs and operations abroad.

In a letter sent to Healey and copied to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on 12 October, days before news of the planned tax hike broke, the chief executive of UK Finance, David Postings, shared research commissioned by the lobby group.

It suggested that reversing Tory cuts to the bank surcharge – taking it back to 8% from 3% – would leave annual UK GDP £1.2bn lower in real terms by 2029-30 than it would have otherwise been.

He said it would also see banks issue fewer business loans and mortgages, with lending likely to be £10.4bn lower in 2029-2030 than if the surcharge was held at 3%.

“The UK’s banking sector already makes a vital contribution to the wider economy,” Postings’ letter said. “To sustain this vital contribution, the budget should avoid any increases in bank-specific taxes, as this would risk constraining the sector’s ability to lend and invest.”

However, TUC analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the Treasury has already lost out on £6bn over the three years since the surcharge cut came into force in 2023.

At the same time, banks have been reporting strong profits, largely off the back of high interest rates, with bosses subsequently increasing banker bonus pots and handing billions of pounds to shareholders.

Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buybacks. Over the past five years, those banks have raked in £200bn in pre-tax profits.

Author and former banker Philip Augar said the banks were “enjoying boom conditions”, partly due to good management but partly due to economic conditions “not of their own making”. He said there was room for a “moderate increase in taxation” that would raise about £2bn to £3bn a year.

“The prime minister has said that the burden of taxation has to fall on those with the broader shoulders, and at the moment, it’s hard to think of a sector where the shoulders are much broader than the banking sector,” Augar told the BBC’s Today programme on Friday.

While banks could not expect interest rates benefits to continue forever, Augar said that banks – including those that were bailed out in the 2008 financial crisis – could not have it both ways.

“Banking is cyclical, it’s true. But when it hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out,” Augar said. “When it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment. Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

Some banks have threatened to pull investment, and potentially jobs, from the UK if it hikes taxes, with lobby groups noting smaller overall tax charges in rival financial centres like Frankfurt, Dublin and Amsterdam.

Jamie Dimon, who heads up the largest bank in the US, JP Morgan, said in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks.

But Augar said the government needed to see past the bluster. “There seems to have been a coordinated campaign by the big international banks who have businesses in Britain – JP Morgan, Citigroup, Santander, HSBC and others.

“But they always say this, [and] they rarely move. I think that if the chancellor judges this right, with a moderate increase in taxation or some other form of getting money from the banks, then the business will remain in the UK.”

Of course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayal

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:30:10 GMT

The old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous world

Donald Trump must find it oddly frustrating. He keeps showing the world exactly who he is, and yet the world keeps refusing to believe it. As clearly as he can, he is announcing that he is not the leader of the free world, that he is not even a reliable member of the democratic west, that he is in fact an ally of its enemies – but the west, including Britain, either doesn’t fully get the message or can’t quite bring itself to draw the obvious conclusion.

Trump had another go this week, finding multiple ways to declare that in the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is no mediator or peace broker but a partner of Vladimir Putin. In fairness to him, the US president had loudly issued that declaration within weeks of his return to the White House when, in February 2025, he delivered an on-camera dressing down of Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, seeking to humiliate the Ukrainian leader by telling him “you don’t have the cards”, even as JD Vance demanded their visitor show gratitude. That should have made Trump’s position sufficiently plain, but in the past few days he has all but put it up in lights.

Earlier this week Ukrainian forces found that an essential piece of kit – a version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system used by Kyiv to guide its drones – was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph. That meant not only a sudden shrinking of Ukraine’s ability to strike behind the frontlines, but also the hobbling of an air defence system vital in protecting the capital from Russian jet-propelled drones. This was no technical hitch. Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is owned and controlled by the US government – and, as Reuters reported, the order to limit its use in Ukraine came from the White House. Put simply, Trump actively intervened in the war to weaken Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. “The decision will bring a lot of human losses,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan. “Of course, people will die.”

Trump’s move was hardly a bolt from the blue. This same week, Ukraine endured at least two nights of Russian bombardment without the usual advance warnings from the US of when or where Moscow was about to strike. Trump denied that he had broken off long-established intelligence sharing with Kyiv, but that’s exactly what it looked like.

All this followed the US president’s decision to break the international sanctions regime on Moscow, by agreeing to buy $4bn worth of Russian diesel oil. That volume will barely make a splash in the US market, where high diesel prices are imperilling the Republicans’ midterm chances in several rural states that rely on the stuff, but it will come as a welcome cash infusion for Putin’s war machine. Just as Russia’s military position was looking precarious, Donald Trump has come riding to the rescue. Throw in the US invitation to Putin to attend December’s G20 meeting at one of Trump’s golf clubs in Florida, and you have a US president who might as well be skywriting his support for Russia and his betrayal of Ukraine.

In Trump’s first term, much energy was spent trying to work out what dark secret lay behind this apparent affinity with Moscow. I tend to the view advanced by my expert colleague Luke Harding, who, when asked if Trump is a tool of the Russian intelligence services, answers with a question of his own: if Trump were a Russian asset, in what way would he behave any differently from the way he behaves now?

Whatever the motive, or whether, as Harding suggests, it’s some combination of greed, ideology, dictator envy and kompromat, the facts are unarguable. The most powerful member of the western alliance is, at best, an unreliable partner and, at worst, in league with the alliance’s chief enemy. Why this matters should not need spelling out, least of all in the week when the head of MI5 described Russia as “aggressor number one”. For years now, the Kremlin has demonstrated its willingness to attack Nato member states, usually in the form of hybrid or “grey zone” operations that are not overt acts of war but come instead with a patina of deniability. One study found that there have been than no fewer than “151 confirmed Russian-directed industrial sabotage incidents in Europe between February 2022 and February 2026”, while last weekend brought credible reports of a Russian intention to assassinate executives of key European defence firms.

What should the US’s erstwhile allies do about this new reality? The first task is to keep supporting Ukraine, all the more energetically given that Washington has, in effect, switched sides. The second is to avoid an error that is looming. The midterm elections, which are little more than a fortnight away, are expected to deliver big gains for the Democrats and a big blow to Trump. If Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress, plenty of European leaders will be tempted to exhale deeply, conclude that the orange storm has passed and that normal transatlantic service is about to resume. That would be a grave mistake.

For one thing, while the US president has been unbound by congressional restraint for most of the past two years, it’s not certain that a constrained Trump will be a tamed Trump. On the contrary, one Washington hand warns that he could become a “cornered animal”, even more extreme in the area where a president is freest to act, namely foreign affairs. Of course, Trump will be gone eventually, but there too lies the danger of false comfort. “This shift is permanent,” one former UK cabinet minister tells me. If nothing else, Trump has proved that Trump and Trumpism can happen: now we know that the western alliance is neither guaranteed nor unshakeable, but vulnerable to a change in the US political weather.

All of this means we are living in a newly dangerous world. Witness the richly reported new book War is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman, which lays bare quite how seriously leading policymakers rate the risk of a third world war. It’s an age in which we can no longer rely on others to defend us. The chilling lesson of the Starlink episode for those who depend on US hardware or software is that the US always retains an off switch. In other words, Britain and the rest of Europe have to be able to defend ourselves, with our own armies and our own arms.

after newsletter promotion

The best time for governments to have made this case was the night of that shocking Oval Office scene with Zelenskyy last year. But the second-best time is now. When John Healey delivers his first budget on 28 October, this is the argument he needs to set out. As a former defence secretary, he is especially well placed to do it. The Labour manifesto of 2024 was written before Trump was re-elected, before anyone knew that in the great clash of our time the US was about to align itself with authoritarianism against democracy. Things have changed and that document can no longer be treated as holy writ. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in a changed and perilous world. Trump is telling us that in a crude, loud voice. We must listen.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:28:10 GMT

Kremlin turning to punishment of Ukraine’s population in major cities as frontlines remain frozen

Europe live – latest updates

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.

Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.

The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”

The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.

This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.

Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country.

“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.”

The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections.

The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government.

Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day.

This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it.

The secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.”

To do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more.

Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.”

When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.

Wardley predicts ‘crazy night’ in fight for redemption against Dubois

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:28:01 GMT

After losing his WBO heavyweight title in a brutal first bout in May, the Briton insists he can ‘right those wrongs’ on Saturday night

Five months ago, watching a likely Fight of the Year between Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley in Manchester, a ringside seat offered an initially thrilling insight into the raw brutality of heavyweight boxing. It was easy to be swept up in the drama as Wardley, defending his WBO title, dropped his more seasoned and favoured rival in the first and third rounds. But Dubois, whose courage had been questioned before, got up both times and fought back with admirable resolve.

Dubois soon took control of the contest and administered a punishing beating, round after round, as concern for Wardley intensified. It was a worrying sight as the reeling champion refused to go down amid the damage being done to him by the bludgeoning power by Dubois. A terrible gash opened up across the bridge of Wardley’s nose and his face looked swollen. The end was finally confirmed in the 11th round, after the referee rescued Wardley from his own bravery, but it was the kind of heavy loss which takes years off a fighter’s career.

Wardley is one of the most intelligent and articulate fighters in Britain and it’s surprising that he has insisted on a rematch this Saturday night at the O2 Arena in London. A much longer rest, and then a far less perilous return to the ring, would have been a wise and pragmatic option. But the 31-year-old, whose previously unbeaten record was ruined by Dubois, insisted this week that “the thought of [their first fight] is worse than the reality. You put a bit of blood there, add some water and sweat and a punch that makes it spray everywhere, and all of a sudden it looks like a Quentin Tarantino film. It looks a bit mental.

“But there was no real actual physical damage aside from cosmetically. There was a cut, but my nose wasn’t broken. I could still breathe fine, everything in good working order. I was just leaking a bit [of blood]. But I’ve been hit earlier in my career with harder shots that have rocked me more than anything that happened in the first fight between us.”

He also suggested that fatigue, rather than the concussive force of Dubois’s punches, unravelled him. None of this really matches the sight of the weaving and broken figure Wardley resembled on that compelling but disturbing night in Manchester.

At this week’s press conference Wardley added: “I was unlikely to get through this boxing game unscathed with an undefeated record, because I want to be in there with the best guys. And that puts you in jeopardy. I can right those wrongs. Now is the fun bit.”

Dubois looked unimpressed and, in a typically terse response, dismissed any idea that Wardley would face anything but a night freighted with pain: “I’m feeling stronger, just grounded and ready to go out there and do my job. Do this thing and move on to bigger and better things.”

The 29-year-old Dubois has beaten Anthony Joshua and Filip Hrgovic, who now holds the IBF version of the world title, and he is a prohibitive favourite to beat Wardley again. “I’m a better fighter, an improved fighter,” Dubois said. “I’ll finish it quicker. I’m gonna school him again. That experience, and amateur background that you can’t buy, is what I’ve got on my side. Even without that, I’ve got his number. This time around, it’s going to be more clinical.”

Wardley’s best chance might be to use his own considerable power early in another slugfest and hope that, this time, his punches overwhelm Dubois. “It’s only going one way,” Wardley said. “It’s finishing early one way or another. It’s going to be a crazy night. Everyone, tune in.”

I don’t think he wants to box any more; I think this is a cash-out. Wardley, instead, has insisted that he will use the experience of his two fights against Frazer Clarke to plot an unlikely victory. After he and Clarke fought each to a near standstill in a savage contest which ended as a blood-spattered draw in March 2024, also at the O2, Wardley dismantled the same man and knocked him out shockingly in just over two minutes seven months later. He believes that he can conjure up another startling turnaround against Dubois.

But the cold hard logic of the ring suggests that, this time, Wardley is trading in dangerous fantasy.

Russell Brand was ‘wild-eyed maniac’ when trying to drag woman into toilets, court told

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:21:22 GMT

Woman says she ‘wrenched’ herself free from alleged assault that she says took place when she was working at MTV in 2001

Russell Brand transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag a woman into a men’s toilets for a sexual encounter before she “wrenched” herself free, a court has heard.

The 51-year-old comedian is accused of indecently assaulting the woman, who told Southwark crown court: “I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me.”

The woman, who was working for MTV at the time, said she did not report the incident then because she was “scared” as Brand was famous “and a big asset” to the TV channel.

Brand is facing three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges.

Wearing a dark pinstripe suit, the TV personality sat bolt upright in the dock on Friday as the woman gave evidence from behind a screen.

She said she was working at MTV in 2001 when she met Brand and they had “banter” about an I Am Spartacus T-shirt he was wearing. She later offered to show him the way to the toilets, where he allegedly assaulted her.

The woman said she felt “bewildered and confused”, telling the court: “This person went from someone jovial and friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet.”

Detailing the alleged assault, she added: “His demeanour changed. He grabbed my forearm and he was leaning into the door. It was quite forceful, the grip. It took me unawares, I wasn’t expecting that.”

In response to questions from the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, the woman said Brand began pleading with her to come into the toilets as she tried to get away.

“I said to him: ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go.’ Then he started to plead, almost ‘go on, go on, come in’,” she told the court.

She said he had a “wild” look in his eyes and she had to use her strength to escape his “hard” grip in an interaction that lasted about 20 seconds.

The woman said she told two colleagues what had happened but she did not make a police complaint until she saw a 2023 documentary that accused Brand of sexual misconduct.

“It brought everything back,” she said. “I thought I’d managed to get away. It could’ve been very different … I thought it was the right thing to come forward.”

In cross-examination, the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested the woman had reassessed her memory of the incident after the documentary, but she said it had not changed her mind.

“I don’t think it’s quite as straightforward as that,” she said. “It would have been my word against his, I had a job to consider, I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me. I managed to get myself out of the situation.”

She rejected the barrister’s suggestion that Brand had “invited” her into the toilet for a consensual sexual encounter. She said: “You don’t drag someone by the arm, not in my world anyway. You don’t grip someone to drag them in, that’s not consensual.”

She said he had been “grabbing and pulling” her, telling the court: “That’s not inviting someone in. That’s forcing someone to do something against their will.”

Winter suggested it was “a short-lived, very, very minor incident” and that after the woman declined, Brand “left it there”. The woman responded: “The intent was there. It could have been very different.”

Earlier, the court heard evidence from witnesses relating to the first complainant, who gave evidence on Thursday. She alleges Brand raped her after a fringe cabaret show at the 1999 Labour party conference in Bournemouth.

Andrew Dobson, a former flatmate of Brand’s who composed the music for the show, described his impressions of the comedian, saying he was “a very vibrant character, very egotistical … lively, sort of quite demanding and persuading”.

Dobson told the court: “I think sex was a huge preoccupation for him. I do recall clearly nights where the pursuit of ultimately getting somebody into bed would have been a preoccupation.”

He said there was a “hurried and rushed” tone at their shared guesthouse in Bournemouth on the morning after their final show. “I recall Russell coming in and there suddenly being an urgency to leave,” he said.

John Rogers, who wrote the show, described Brand’s reaction to an “encounter” the actor had had with a woman during the week of the conference, saying it was “a bit odd” and he appeared “flustered”.

The court also heard statements from two women whom the first complainant had told about the alleged rape after the 2023 documentary.

The trial continues.

UK police force pays out after claims it protected officers accused of abusing women

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 15:00:04 GMT

Exclusive: Devon and Cornwall police formally apologise to nine women and settle claim without admitting liability

A police force alleged to have promoted and protected male officers despite knowing they were accused of domestic abuse has formally apologised and paid compensation to nine women, the Guardian has learned.

The women allege they were subjected to a range of abuse including rape, assault, threats, harassment and coercive control while in relationships with male officers from Devon and Cornwall police.

Some of the officers served in positions protecting women from male violence, with one appointed after allegations were made, and another kept in the sensitive position after the force received accusations.

The women allege that the force in south-west England “covered up” the serious crimes, which it denies. The force has vowed to improve how it protects women from police-perpetrated domestic abuse.

Some women suffered for about 15 years, with their tormentors allegedly weaponising the force’s “reputation” for protecting male police abusers to break their victim’s will to seek justice.

The nine women, some of whom served in Devon and Cornwall police, say their claims were mocked or disbelieved and investigations were bungled. Three of the women were arrested after accusations from their alleged abusers. One, a teacher, was cautioned, which was eventually erased from her criminal record.

One senior source who served in the leadership of the force told the Guardian: “At best it was bad investigations, at worst it was collusion with the attackers.”

The women say at least four of the officers who abused them are still serving. The force refused to answer that question. Four of the women served in the force but have now left.

One of the male officers is accused of abusing and threatening his partner, who was then a serving police officer. The woman said: “I had my baby … in my arms. My other child was screaming as he rained punches on any area of my body he could get at. He cornered me in a room and repeatedly kicked me as he stood over me. I was terrified and was begging him to stop.”

It is alleged the male officer was promoted twice after the force received the allegations, and was appointed to a leadership position in the force’s effort to tackle violence against women and girls.

Starting in 2004, the woman complained to police for more than 14 years, and she says nothing was done.

Devon and Cornwall police has agreed to pay compensation to all nine women who sued, and the chief constable, James Vaughan, has personally apologised for the failings, the force said.

Police settled the women’s claim without admitting liability after a two-year legal battle.

Another of the accused male officers was known by colleagues as “Teflon” because nothing stuck to him despite repeated allegations, and known also as “rapey”, and was allegedly promoted.

His former partner Sarah* told the Guardian the officer pursued a prolonged, deliberate and sustained campaign of abusive, controlling and coercive behaviour over 15 years. It included physical abuse, financial abuse, intimidation, manipulation of childcare arrangements and repeated harassment, intended to undermine, distress and exert control.

Another woman, June*, a teacher, said of the officer with whom she had children: “Threats he’d made against me had been routinely dismissed, belittled and ignored. [He said] ‘you’ll lose your house, your job and the kids. Don’t make me angry, I’m about to load a gun.’

“I will never under any circumstances cooperate with the police again. I have lost all faith in their willingness … to protect women from police-perpetrated domestic violence. He knows he has the full protection of the police.”

Another, Freya*, said: “Absolutely it was a cover-up. The police harboured him until his retirement. I got called a liar by officers online.”

Other male and female officers tried to help the women but still the force failed to act, according to the combined testimony from the women.

The scandal comes after repeated promises by policing nationally to prosecute male officers who abuse women. Some of the women who received compensation and an apology say the reality was, and still is, different.

Paula Kressinger, who served in the force for 30 years and has waived her anonymity, criticised the force’s refusal to admit liability. She said: “The police are always trying to cover up their mistakes … trying to protect their reputation. However, I believe we would have more respect and trust in them if they were to … take responsibility for their failings. I know they continue to fail victims of crime.”

Sasha* said: “The police did cover up. Devon and Cornwall promoted my ex-partner … while the abuse continued. This gave a ticket to my abuser to continue his abuse post-separation.”

The inaction by the force spurred on abusers, Sasha said. “During the course of the investigation my ex-partner said everyone in the police laughed at me, and the behaviour by the investigating officers made this seem to be a true statement. The continued disrespect and disregard by Devon and Cornwall police collectively became death by a thousand cuts.

“I cannot express enough how much myself and my children have suffered over a period of 15 years, and to then be totally let down by the police …”

The Devon and Cornwall force was placed into special measures a fortnight ago because of overall poor performance. The force declined to answer a series of questions from the Guardian.

Asked what exactly the apology was for, the force replied that the chief constable met with the women in March 2026 and “apologised for the conduct of Devon and Cornwall police in its investigations of their reports of police-perpetrated domestic abuse”.

Asked whether the nine women were regarded by the force as victims of a crime, it said: “In general terms, any allegations of criminal conduct or misconduct are considered through the appropriate investigative and legal processes. These are recorded and assessed and, where appropriate, subject to criminal and/or misconduct investigation.”

The force also said: “No evidence has been identified to suggest that this was, in whole or in part, the result of a cover-up or misogyny.”

It said none of the accused male officers were any longer in positions to do with protecting women from male violence.

The legal case was brought by the Centre for Women’s Justice, a small charity.

Debaleena Dasgupta, a solicitor for the women, praised their determination and courage and said: “Litigation should never have been necessary. Each of these nine women repeatedly tried to have their reports properly investigated but instead faced errors, indifference and incompetence at every turn. Some even faced contempt.

“The similarities in the failures … indicate a broken system. And none of the safeguards one might expect to pick this up did. There have been endless reviews, inquiries and recommendations, and yet litigation remained my clients’ only option.”

The force said: “Our processes have changed. All police-perpetrated domestic abuse will now be investigated by the force’s professional standards department. We are currently in the process of creating a bespoke advocate role for victims of police-perpetrated domestic abuse and similar offences to ensure their voices are heard and that they are provided with a gold-standard service.”

* Names have been changed.

Not sure where to start with retinoids? Whether you’ve got sensitive, acne-prone or mature skin, here are our beauty expert’s favourite vitamin A creams for everyone

The best LED face masks
