Some studies suggest topical retinol can improve the appearance of fine lines and other signs of skin ageing. I’ve been using it to smooth the look of wrinkles and rejuvenate my complexion for years, and here’s why it’s worthy of a place in your routine, too.

Let me first point out that when I say retinol, I’m really talking about a wider family of retinoids – vitamin A derivatives that include retinol itself. Retinol is just one member of the family, but it’s become well known thanks to its widespread use in over-the-counter skincare.

The benefits of retinoids, from accelerating cell turnover to stimulating collagen production, are well evidenced. Tretinoin was first prescribed in the US in the 1970s as an acne treatment, and retinoids soon revealed their potential beyond breakouts, helping to soften the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, fade pigmentation and smooth skin texture.

However, any changes don’t happen overnight. It can take time to develop a tolerance to retinoids, as side effects such as redness and irritation are common. Over a short period, though, “you can expect to see early improvements in skin texture and brightness within four to six weeks and more significant results around pigmentation, acne or fine lines closer to eight to 12 weeks with consistent use,” says Dr Ahmed El Muntasar, GP and aesthetics doctor. It’s also even more important than usual to use a broad-spectrum face SPF, as retinoids can make skin more sensitive to sunlight.

​​I’m an experienced beauty editor with 17 years as a journalist, so I’ve witnessed the retinoid revolution first-hand – from the early pioneers to today’s more advanced formulas. Pretty much every skincare brand now has at least one retinoid product in its lineup.

Part of my job is to test these products as they launch, so you’d be hard-pressed to find a retinoid I haven’t slathered on my face at some point. And as a fortysomething showing all the natural signs of ageing – fine lines, wrinkles and pigmentation – I’m the ideal test case.

Having carefully considered all the retinol (and retinoid) products I’ve tested over the years, I started by putting together a list of my favourite 15 products. To make the cut, the formula had to be one I’d used until the bottle was empty – or bought again afterwards. For a beauty editor who’s sent skincare to test every day, that’s the real test of a product: whether I’d choose to use it again when I have countless others to try.

I used each product as part of my evening routine for a minimum of eight weeks. As my skin is already accustomed to retinoid use, I could do this without affecting my skin barrier. If you’re new to retinoid use, introduce them into your regime slowly – I really can’t emphasise this enough.

The products were assessed on texture, ease of use, side effects, noticeable skin changes, value and ingredients. Below you’ll find my list of the 10 best performers.

Retinal (short for retinaldehyde) has been fast and furiously coming for retinol’s popularity crown, with an increasing number of beauty brands turning to this advanced retinoid. Medik8 has been using retinal since 2018, and this serum is now among the bestselling retinal serums worldwide.

Why we love it Heavily hyped by experts and consumers alike, I’m here to add to the noise: this vitamin A serum really is excellent. The brand claims it works faster than standard retinol while being gentler on the skin. Medik8 says its crystal encapsulation gradually releases retinal throughout the night, limiting the risk of irritation. And that’s why it’s always my go-to recommendation: I’ve seen such speedy skin rejuvenation and haven’t experienced any of the irritation that can come with integrating retinol into your skincare routine.

I’ve seen this formula banish breakouts, fade pigmentation, plump out lines and wrinkles and firm the skin with continued use. By gradually working my way up the ladder to increase the strength, I’ve seen increasingly impressive results. Add to this its light and easy-to-apply texture, and it really is the best over-the-counter retinoid serum I’ve tried.

It’s a shame that … if you’re new to retinoids, you may still experience breakouts, flaking or dryness.

Product: serum Recyclable packaging: all recyclable except for the pump Size: 30ml Price per ml: from £1.20 Strength and type: 0.01 to 0.24% retinal Vegan? Yes Certified cruelty-free? No

US skincare brand Naturium has been gaining serious momentum in the UK beauty space. That’s because it strikes the sweet spot between science-led skincare – including some top-notch body care – and affordable luxury.

Why we love it Naturium’s formula may not be at the bottom of the price scale, but it comes in a much larger-than-some 50ml tube, so you get a lot of vitamin A for your buck. There are two strengths to choose from here in the UK (in the US, there’s a third, stronger one).

Its lightweight texture absorbs in seconds, making it easy to add into your evening skincare routine. Note that while the serum is bright yellow out of the tube, it massages in clear, so don’t let that put you off.

Just like Medik8, it uses a sustained-release retinal, which the brand says supports skin comfort. I’ve experienced no irritation at all in use, and saw the same rejuvenating results over time. If you’re new to retinoids, I’d still suggest building it into your routine gradually, though.

It’s a shame that … my skin needs a rich moisturiser layered on top to keep dryness at bay.

Product: serum Recyclable packaging: can be recycled at Boots Size: 50ml Price per ml: 64p Strength and type: 0.05% and 0.10% retinal Vegan? Yes Certified cruelty-free? Yes

Clinician-developed skincare is everywhere right now, but Dr Howard Murad was one of the first, in 1989. Now simply known as Murad, the brand is still very much ahead of the curve when it comes to clinical skincare, as this retinal cream shows.

Why we love it It’s a powerhouse formula, combining encapsulated retinal with Murad’s NAD+ Lift Complex, which the brand says boosts production of NAD+, a coenzyme involved in cellular repair that declines with age.

Together, the duo makes an innovative tag team for targeting fine lines and wrinkles. I’ve found it so effective that after just four weeks, my complexion already looks smoother, plumper and firmer, with deeper lines noticeably softened.

But what I love most about this formula is that it feels like a “proper” night cream – its creamy texture is still beautifully lightweight, so you don’t feel like you’re going to bed with a mask on your face. Packed with hydrating ingredients such as squalane, hyaluronic acid and glycerine, to name a few, my dry skin is content, without any need to layer on something else – unlike other retinoid products.

It’s a shame that … it has such a high price, but you get what you pay for with this skincare investment.

Product: cream Recyclable packaging: yes Size: 50ml Price per ml: £1.96 Strength and type: retinal (strength not specified) Vegan? Yes Certified cruelty-free? Yes

Known for its hard-working, ingredient-led formulations at wallet-friendly prices, the Inkey List has done it again with two impressive new retinoid products: an advanced 0.2% retinal serum for experienced users and a beginner-friendly retinol, the latter of which I put to the test.

Why we love it This gentle formula is ideal for first-time vitamin A users, and the brand claims it’s suitable for sensitive and rosacea-prone complexions. It combines 1% Granactive Pro+ and 0.01% retinal alongside hydrating, skin-barrier-supporting and calming ingredients.

In my testing, I experienced no side effects. It’s lightweight, silky and fragrance-free, making it easy to slot into an evening routine, although I did find it could leave my skin feeling dry without a hydrating moisturiser to follow. You may see improvements to skin texture within weeks, but with retinoids, the best results come from playing the long game. Think of this as a stepping stone to a stronger retinoid.

It’s a shame that … it’s a trivial point, but the packaging is basic.

Type: serum Recyclable packaging: yes Size: 30ml Price per ml: from about 32p Strength and type: 1% Granactive Pro+ retinoid and 0.01% retinal Vegan? Yes Certified cruelty-free? Yes

Lancôme has been around for more than 90 years, but it’s still at the top of its beauty game. From mastering mascara to launching cutting-edge skincare – and this product is no exception.

Why we love it In the Renergie CRx serum, Lancôme combines three actives: retinol, vitamin C and X-peptides, in a formula it says is non-irritating. The serum feels luxuriously silky and is a pleasure to use, giving instant hydration without stickiness.

Together, the three actives target the signs of ageing, with vitamin C helping to brighten and peptides intended to soothe the skin. On paper, the serum ticks all the boxes, and I found it equally impressive in use. Having come to the end of the bottle, my skin is smoother, more even-toned and more radiant, with pores and lines less visible.

It’s a shame that … it has such a big price tag. Shop around, though, since it’s sometimes on offer.

Product: serum Recyclable packaging: yes Size: 50ml Price per ml: from £1.92 Strength and type: 0.3% retinol Vegan? No Certified cruelty-free? No

Best for: experienced users

Disrupting the beauty space with its ingredient-led skincare at affordable prices, the Ordinary has proven that beauty innovation can be made accessible to all. A case in point is this 0.2% retinal. The Ordinary recommends it for experienced retinoid users rather than beginners, but the brand says continued use can leave skin looking smoother, firmer and more even-toned.

It’s beautifully lightweight and a little goes a long way, but I have a few niggles. The yellow hue of the retinal can stain clothing – I learned the hard way – so take care when applying. More disappointing is that you get only 15ml for the price, which isn’t quite the excellent value for money I’ve come to expect from the brand.

It didn’t make the final cut … because it may be the cheapest, but it’s also the smallest bottle.

Product: serum; recyclable packaging: yes, through TerraCycle and at Boots; size: 15ml; price per ml: from about £1.01; strength and type: 0.2% retinal; vegan? Yes; certified cruelty-free? Yes

Best for: dry skin

Combine sophisticated formulations, apothecary-style packaging and a heritage dating back to 1851, and it’s easy to see why Kiehl’s has become such a trusted, much-loved brand. And for me, this is one of its standout products: a gentle retinol Kiehl’s says is designed specifically for first-time users and those with sensitive skin.

It contains ceramides, which the brand says help strengthen the skin barrier and improve tolerance of retinol. Having worked my way up the retinoid ladder from beginner formulas to more advanced, I’ve used plenty of bottles of this over the years and have never seen any side effects – not even the dryness that’s so common with retinoid use.

It didn’t make the final cut because … cheaper gentle (although not as luxe) formulas, such as the Inkey List’s Starter retinol serum above, are available.

Type: serum; recyclable packaging: recyclable bottle, non-recyclable pump. Kiehl’s recommends using its own returns scheme; size: 30ml; price per ml: from about £1.28; type and strength: retinol (strength not specified); vegan? No; certified cruelty-free? No

Best for: acne-prone skin

Before retinoids were recognised for their anti-ageing benefits, they were, as mentioned, used to treat acne. This gentle, lightweight retinol serum is great for tackling blemish-prone skin, and it does so with the help of a few other actives. While retinol increases skin cell turnover, niacinamide soothes, and liquorice-root extract helps skin appear brighter.

And, being CeraVe, it’s packed with the brand’s signature ceramides to strengthen and support the skin barrier. In tests, I found it gentle, easy to use, and hydrating, which makes it a great choice for retinol beginners and those with sensitive skin.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it takes time to see results.

Product: serum; recyclable packaging: only through the Boots recycling scheme; size: 30ml; price per ml: about 78p; strength and type: retinol (percentage not disclosed); vegan? No; certified cruelty-free? No

Best for: retinol capsules

RoC says it was the first skincare company to offer stabilised retinol with other ingredients over the counter, and it has several high-quality retinol products in its lineup. My favourites are these biodegradable capsules, which limit exposure to light and air, preserving the retinol’s potency. The pre-measured dose also stops you from using too much.

The formula combines ceramides with retinol, and I didn’t experience any drying or redness in testing, even when used daily. My skin felt soft, healthy and comfortable, while continued use left my complexion looking smoother and brighter and fine lines softer – which is why I regularly go back to using them.

It didn’t make the final cut because … you get only 10.5ml in total, so they can work out quite expensive.

Product: serum; recyclable packaging: only through the Boots recycling scheme; size: 10.5ml; price per ml: from about £3.43; strength and type: retinol (strength not specified); vegan? No; certified cruelty-free? Yes

Best for: sensitive skin

French pharmaceutical brand La Roche-Posay is known for a problem-solving approach to skincare, so it’s no surprise it’s mastered the art of creating a retinol serum for sensitive skin. It’s particularly well suited to those who may have struggled with retinol dryness and irritation in the past.

The reason for this is a gentle formula that includes skin-soothing and skin barrier-strengthening B3 (better known as niacinamide) and glycerine for hydration. I’ve found this cocktail of ingredients ensures it’s well-tolerated by my skin, with none of the irritating side effects of retinol.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s for sensitive skin only – there are better options for other skin types.

Product: serum; recyclable packaging: not entirely; size: 30ml; price per ml: £1.28; strength and type: 0.3% retinol; vegan? No; certified cruelty-free? No

Retinoids, or vitamin A derivatives such as retinol and retinal, are skincare powerhouses backed by scientific evidence that shows they do two clever things.

Firstly, they can speed up the skin’s natural renewal process. “Retinoids help to increase cellular turnover, which naturally slows down as we age,” says El Muntasar. “This means the skin sheds more effectively, revealing newer, fresher skin underneath that looks brighter, more hydrated and even.” They continue to be recommended for those who have acne, as they help unclog pores, reduce inflammation and outbreaks, and fade hyperpigmentation.

Retinoids’ second clever trick is their ability to support collagen and elastin production. As these essential proteins decline, lines, wrinkles and a loss of firmness become more apparent. “They’re not just treating one concern; they’re improving the skin’s underlying structure,” says Dr Sheila Li, founder of Mediject Clinic. “Over time, skin becomes smoother, brighter and more resilient.”

There is no set answer to this. The most effective percentage is the one your skin can tolerate without disrupting the barrier or needing to stop. All the dermatologists I’ve interviewed advise starting with the “go low and go slow” method.

Starting on a low percentage minimises the risk of dryness, irritation, redness and peeling – all common side effects of using retinoids. This gives your skin time to get used to the active and build up tolerance to it.

“Build tolerance gradually,” says Li. “Apply two or three nights a week at first, and increase slowly.”

Retinoids are best used in your evening routine when your skin naturally goes into repair mode, but also because they can increase photosensitivity. This makes a broad-spectrum SPF an even more essential part of your morning routine.

“I recommend pairing a retinoid with a simple, barrier-supporting moisturiser and avoiding too many active ingredients alongside it, especially in the early stages,” says El Muntasar. “Ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, ceramides and niacinamide help support the skin and reduce irritation.”

I like to layer Aestura’s Atobarrier365 cream on top of any retinol product I’m using. It’s a Korean bestseller that’s packed with skin-strengthening ceramides and keeps skin calm and hydrated.

It all comes down to potency. “Prescription-only retinoids, such as tretinoin and adapalene, work faster and treat more severe skin conditions,” says Dr Leah Totton, medical doctor and cosmetic specialist. “But they also carry a higher risk of irritation, redness and peeling and so require medical supervision for safe use.”

For more: The best LED face masks – tested The best cleansers for every skin type The best eye creams to banish bags, puffiness and fine lines The best face moisturisers for every budget

Sabine Wiesel is a freelance beauty editor. Having reviewed skincare products for more than 17 years, she sticks to ingredients like retinol that are backed by science. Her job may sound glamorous, but with so many products constantly on the go, you should see the state of her bathroom

Since my daughter moved out of home, my household has shrunk. A yearly tradition brings us together

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:00:12 GMT

I wait each year for my cumquat tree to fruit. Then I make Mum’s jam

It’s citrus season, and the trees of my streets are heavy with the bright balls of fruit. My son sometimes picks me a lemon or two on his way home from school, and I help myself to the basket of limes that hang from the fence of a nearby house. The potted plant on my balcony fruited early this season, and for weeks I watched as the hundreds of small green cumquats slowly ripened. I finally picked them when they were fattened with juice and seeds and colour, the cat squatting on the ground to watch. When I dropped a cumquat she sniffed at the skin and turned away, as if sensing the sharpness of its flesh.

Since my daughter moved out several years ago, my household has shrunk. It is now only my son and me. And the cat. A scratchy, sullen creature who delights in ignoring us both unless we are sitting in the seat she believes is hers. My son has begun cooking for himself, and so I find my services in the kitchen required less often. Except for the yearly making of cumquat jam.

The jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish. When I was a kid, Mum would scavenge each year in her friends’ gardens for cumquats and then spend close to two days chopping, deseeding, soaking, boiling and jarring the fruit to fill our cupboards with the stained glass orange jam. Years later, when I had children, Mum introduced them to the tart taste, and they were hooked too. When she died, 15 years ago, winter came and went without our usual jars to see us through. We tried eating jam made from other fruits. Seville orange, apricot, rich plum, but there were no memories to the taste, and the jars would sit unfinished in the fridge for months.

Witnessing my grief at losing my mum, some friends bought me a baby cumquat tree in a large yellow ceramic pot that proved itself hardy enough to survive my limited gardening skills. The first year that it flowered with delicate white buds, we watched, delighting in the growth of the cumquats, waiting until they were large enough to pick. My kids helped strip the tree of fruit. It was nothing like the haul Mum used to make jam with, but it filled a bowl. I hacked up the cumquats, not neatly like Mum did, but fast and furious, not bothering to remove the pips because I’d read somewhere they would float up during boiling and you could scoop them from the top with the scum. Impatiently, I didn’t follow the ratio of sugar or simmer for the correct amount of time, and that first batch was overcooked. The jam was too dark in colour, and the texture was all wrong, but we ate it anyway, the taste taking me immediately back to my childhood home, where I’d perch up at the bench each morning before school and work my way through rye toast smeared with jam.

The following year, I channelled Mum’s patience and made two large jars of jam. They were the perfect amber-colour, rich and bright, with chunks of rind and the occasional pip. It wasn’t enough to squirrel away in the cupboard like a true survivalist, but it saw us through a month or two of breakfasts. This year, I managed six jars, enough to spare for giving one to a friend, and another to my daughter when she came for dinner one night. She took half our loaf of fresh sourdough bread with her too so she could replicate the favourite breakfast of her childhood.

My son and I are now down to our last jar of jam, and we have started rationing it without discussion, eating it on toast weekly instead of daily, to make it last as long as we can. I do sometimes buy cumquat jam if I see it at a market, but it never quite tastes the same. There is something treasured in waiting each year for the tree to grow the fruit to make the jam. It is ritual that connects us to the jam that Mum once made.

My cumquat tree still lives in the same yellow pot. It has moved house twice with us, requiring four people to lift it on to a trolley, and it now grows in the strip of sun on our apartment balcony. It is not much to look at it until the flowers come and the fruit arrives, but then it brings with it all the promise of the taste of my childhood.

Nova Weetman is an award-winning author of books for children and young adults

Some Woman review – Anne-Marie Duff is wholly believable but this twisty drama is not

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 13:50:26 GMT

Dorfman theatre, LondonThe far-fetched plot turns and some underdeveloped characters undermine the powerful messages about prejudice in Helen Edmundson’s play

Opposing forces tug against each other in this new drama as Anne-Marie Duff is magnificent amid playwright Helen Edmundson’s implausible plotting. The result is a failed suspension of disbelief yet a convincing central performance.

Duff plays Julie, a mother, ex-wife and working woman whose already over-burdened life is turned upside down by an incident at a tube station when an 11-year-old boy randomly and aggressively insults her. She challenges him, reasonably, and in a series of unconvincing plot turns, winds up facing a legal battle and potential prison sentence.

As a story of an ordinary middle-aged woman being buffeted by patriarchal forces around her, this play is stuffed full of important issues. We hear stories of casual sexual abuse, laughed off by those around Julie. Now we see her life virtually destroyed by the boy’s allegation.

There is mention of CCTV footage and you wonder if an Adolescence-style video reveal is to come. But the plot makes clear that there is no incontrovertible evidence against her, yet she stands to lose everything.

The points about everyday misogyny come through loud and clear, especially that the legal system is rigged to distrust women and believe men (or an 11-year-old boy in this instance). The West End drama Prima Facie, recently adapted for the screen, showed us just that in relation to sexual violence against women. But this is not a courtroom drama and the alleged crimes on which it turns are simply not believable.

Directed by Blanche McIntyre and staged without an interval, there is potential brilliance here, if only the plot were better crafted and so many unfocused issues not thrown at us – from the eating disorder of one daughter (Grace Doherty) to Julie’s difficult relationship with another (Hannah Onslow), both barely explored, as well as Julie’s experience of infidelity and divorce. Each of these issues gets its moment, briefly, with characters around Julie too flimsy to feel true.

The structural failings of the script aside, there are many individually moving and harrowing scenes. They culminate in a confrontation between Julie and the boy’s father (Stephen Wight). Again, this plot-turn challenges the bounds of believability but this time you can brush that aside because the forces of threat, anger and fear feel horribly, sadly real.

Julie seems pushed towards victimhood yet she refuses this foisted powerlessness in a society where toxic masculinity is chillingly in plain sight: men openly express loathing of women, boys spit obscenities at female strangers. Truth is all Julie has and upholds, whatever the legal repercussions. She is not only the everyday victim of misogyny but an everyday female hero too. This message has its own power, however bad the plotting may be.

At the Dorfman theatre, National Theatre, London, until 21 November

Lions lock Hyron Andrews dies at team hotel before Champions Cup game against La Rochelle

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 12:35:54 GMT

SA Rugby said Andrews fell at hotel in tragic accident

Squad will play on Saturday to honour teammate

Tributes have been paid to Johannesburg Lions’ Hyron Andrews after he died in the team hotel on the eve of their Champions Cup game against La Rochelle.

Andrews, 31, who also played for the KZN Sharks and Sale Sharks, could not be revived by emergency services after the alarm was raised at the Atalante-Relais Thalasso hotel on the Île de Ré. A statement from SA Rugby said the lock forward had “passed away tragically” after an accident in which he fell.

“This is terrible and distressing news; our hearts go out to Hyron’s family and the whole Lions rugby community,” said Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union in a statement released after Andrews’ family had been contacted.

“There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maighlin, and for his extended family, friends, teammates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow.

“Hyron was a respected member of the rugby community whose contribution to the game and impact on those around him will be remembered with great fondness.

“His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him.”

The Lions had been preparing to make their debut in the top-tier tournament on Saturday having flown to Europe after a heavy 57-15 defeat by the Bulls, their South African rivals. The squad has chosen to fulfil the fixture in honour of their teammate.

European Professional Club Rugby, the tournament organisers said: “In memory of Hyron, a moment’s silence will be held ahead of every Investec Champions Cup and EPCR Challenge Cup match this weekend.”

Andrews, who was born in Paarl and attended Hoërskool Garsfontein in Pretoria, also represented the Junior Springboks in 2015.

The Lions posted an emotional tribute on Instagram, saying: “It is with broken hearts that we mourn the passing of Hyron Andrews, a valued member of our Lions family. Our deepest condolences are with Maiglin, Hendrix, Emerson and the entire Andrews family during this incredibly difficult time.

“Rest in peace, Hyron. You will always be part of our family.”

Sale reflected on the loss of a “much-loved member” of their squad, who had stayed on past his initial short-term deal through to the end of the 2025-26 campaign, making 45 appearances.

“Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant team-mate. He was so skilled on the field, but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with,” Sharks’ director of rugby Alex Sanderson told the club’s website.

“He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him. It was a big move for Hyron and his wife Maighlin to come to England but he truly made a second home in Manchester and it was incredible to see how he and his family embraced the club and area.”

The tragic incident comes on the 10th anniversary of the death of the Munster coach Anthony Foley in a Paris hotel room in 2016. Foley, who was 42, died in his sleep on the eve of a European tie against Racing 92 after a heart condition caused fluid to build up in his lungs. Tributes are due to be paid to him before this weekend’s game against Racing in Cork, with the Munster players set to wear commemorative presentation jackets featuring the club crest and the number 8, Foley’s position.

An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 12:00:10 GMT

Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation

It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recent Sense and Sensibility movie were also hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it.

After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.

But what makes a good adaptation? Like Odysseus himself, and as every Nancy Meyers fan knows: it’s complicated. I have just written a book about the towering heights and profane depths of adaptation, The Book Was Better, for which I subjected myself to some of the worst viewing experiences possible, including the soft rock opera musical Heathcliff; 1996’s freakishly bad The Island of Dr Moreau; and a horrible three-part version of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. But I also saw plenty of masterpieces that equalled or sometimes surpassed the originals. Here’s what I learned.

The first thing to say is that the quality of the source is irrelevant. I went into my research with some pretty fixed ideas: for instance, that “the brilliant adaptations are nearly always of fiction of the second or third class”, as Anthony Burgess wrote; that some works are “unfilmable”; that classics have more “room to breathe” on TV. Soon I realised none of these were true. Yes, sometimes workmanlike novels, such as the late 60s and early 70s triumvirate Jaws, The Godfather and The Exorcist, can be tuned to a level of genius on screen. But great books can make great films, too: Trainspotting, The Go-Between, The Leopard and Burgess’s own A Clockwork Orange are just a few examples. And sometimes, in the case of The Da Vinci Code and Fifty Shades of Grey, a deeply silly book becomes a deeply silly film.

It is true that certain books lend themselves to the screen more readily. Jane Austen’s immaculate plots of love impeded are templates that can be dressed up in the clothes of any age, like the computer template Cher Horowitz uses to plan her outfits at the start of Clueless – the ne plus ultra of free-handed adaptations. Austen’s novels contain the DNA of all romcoms, just as Robinson Crusoe is found in The Martian, the gothic novel in horror films, or A Christmas Carol in every single Christmas movie. Short stories, with their twisty shocks and rush towards the end point, seem made for cinema; my favourite film, Don’t Look Now, is based on a Daphne du Maurier novella. The murky origins and elasticity of myths and their close cousins, folk and fairytales, make them ceaselessly adaptable, because they leave gaps for a film-maker to fill with their own imaginations.

Being unfaithful is usually helpful. Some of the best adaptations flirt with the source material, taking frightful liberties and then abandoning it like a tabloid love rat. “Steal the parts that you need, and then run as fast as you can,” advised Paul Thomas Anderson; Hitchcock claimed he read The Birds once before making his version, and never thought about it again. (One screenwriter I spoke to told me he was once asked not to read the novel he was adapting as the production company thought it would be a hindrance). Books and films are entirely different beasts, “apples and giraffes”, as author-screenwriter Dennis Lehane once said. Adaptation is an act of translation from the verbal to the visual. A film-maker needs to find their own language.

One of my most beloved unfaithful adaptations is Alfonso Cuarón’s 2006 Children of Men, and not just because it stars Clive Owen at the peak of his physical perfection. It manages to transform a cerebral, theological novel by the Conservative peer PD James into a dystopian thriller about populism, terror and how we treat immigrants, one which – although now two decades old – feels fresher each year. (James was delighted with it.) Cuarón used the novel as a jumping-off point, then left it behind to follow his own adventure. What remained was the central conceit: what if we lived in a world without children? The “what if” high concepts of science fiction and speculative fiction are perfect for playing fast and loose with: a vessel into which a film-maker’s own preoccupations, and the anxieties of their age, can be poured.

When writer-director Sally Potter reinvented Virginia Woolf’s time-travelling fantasia Orlando, she treated it “as if the book never existed”, turning it into a lavish nose-thumb to a UK establishment that had just passed section 28. She was, she said, cruel to the novel to be kind to the film. It’s the destruction-as-creation mantra. In the hands of the right writer and director, a source can, and should, be made to submit to their will: Stanley Kubrick betrayed Stephen King’s vision of The Shining but made a tour de force. Heart of Darkness mutated into a war epic with Apocalypse Now; Red Dragon became, well, a Michael Mann film, the hypnotic Manhunter. An adaptation should never be a hollow greatest hits album. Being too reverential towards a literary source can kill it, which is why I suspect films such as The Hunger Games and The Road, lovingly and stylishly made with few changes, felt slightly bloodless on screen to me.

Can anything really be faithful anyway, and to what? No story is 100 per cent original. (As Alien screenwriter Dan O’Bannon said: “I didn’t steal from anybody. I stole from everybody!”) I don’t even think you can be “true to the spirit” of a text, because the spirit is different for everyone. We all have our own little films running in our heads when we read. Many see The Great Gatsby as a death knell for the US; adapters tend to think: “parties!”. I think Heathcliff is a psychopath who likes to hang little dogs; successive directors clearly didn’t. I loved discovering that Jodie Foster lobbied hard for the part of Clarice Starling in The Silence of the Lambs because, for her, the novel was about a woman saving the life of another woman while “all these fucking men” get in the way. An adaptation may just be a glimpse into another mind’s eye, but their pictures seldom match the ones we had imagined.

Perhaps the most obvious example of this is casting. As sure as night follows day, Hollywood casts a better-looking actor than strictly necessary, although not always reaching “Denise Richards in hotpants as a nuclear physicist in The World is Not Enough” levels. This can be deliberate: in Robert Bloch’s novel Psycho, Norman Bates is physically repellent; Hitchcock wanted the sweet-faced Anthony Perkins for the part to wrongfoot the audience. More often it’s because, as the critic Roger Ebert observed, cinema is a machine for generating empathy, so the thinking goes that leads should be “likable” – which backfired horribly when Bruce Willis was cast as a desiccated English journalist in the notoriously disastrous adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s The Bonfire of the Vanities. But sometimes an actor who is wrong on paper can make a role their own, whether it’s Margaret Rutherford as Miss Marple, Renée Zellweger as Bridget Jones or Michael Caine as Harry Palmer in The Ipcress File (in Len Deighton’s novels he’s a northerner and doesn’t have a name). Charisma goes a long way.

Perhaps in the end, adaptation all comes down to emotions and sensations. “You’ve drunk the drink, and the taste that’s left in your mouth is what you go with,” as Anthony Minghella described adapting The Talented Mr Ripley. Irvine Welsh said you must smell the books. Hossein Amini, who reinvented The Wings of the Dove as “noir in costume”, wanted to recapture that ecstatic moment when “nobody else in the world understood or experienced that book exactly like I did”.

Returning to The Odyssey, I wonder why, even though Nolan did the right things, subordinating it to his worldview and faithlessly reinventing it for our age by turning a wily trickster into a traumatised veteran, the film just made me feel as if I’d been in a war: long periods of boredom and waiting punctuated by violence. Perhaps, ultimately, he overthought it and should have felt it instead? Or maybe, as the late Hilary Mantel said of adaptation, you must “put down the text, and dream it”.

The Book Was Better by Louise Willder (Oneworld, £14.99). To order a copy for £13.49 go to guardianbookshop. com Delivery charges may apply.

I’ve debated with Israel’s most fervent defenders – NAZA debunks their talking points

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 12:00:10 GMT

The film’s testimonies from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers expose years of baseless propaganda. Don’t take my word – take theirs

I watched the extraordinary new Guardian-produced documentary from Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor the other night, and I have struggled to stop thinking about it ever since. The film’s title comes from a Hebrew military term for collateral damage, and it consists of eye-opening interviews with two dozen Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers sitting in darkness, often on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, their voices “digitally altered to disguise their identities”.

At one point, Abraham asks one of the soldiers a remarkably blunt question.

“Do you think it’s a genocide?”

“Yes,” the soldier replies. “Completely.”

He points to what he describes as the “intentional” killing of Palestinian civilians, including children.

“We have to describe things as they really are.” That sentence could serve as the film’s subtitle. Because for the past three years, there have in effect been two wars over Gaza: the war itself, and the war over how we are allowed to describe it.

Has Israel been targeting civilian sites – or is Hamas simply using “human shields”?

Were Palestinian children knowingly killed – or is even making that claim anti-Jewish “blood libel”?

Were hungry Palestinians shot while seeking food – or was Hamas responsible for those killings?

Are many of the Palestinian dead really civilians – or are huge numbers of them “terrorists”?

Does the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza invite comparisons to the Holocaust – or is making such a comparison itself evidence of antisemitism?

NAZA matters because, one after another, Israelis who actually participated in the surveillance and killing infrastructure of the Gaza war weigh in on these issues themselves. And what they say is pretty devastating.

I have spent the past few years debating some of Israel’s most committed defenders – on the live stages of Open to Debate in New York and the Munk Debates in Toronto, on cable news, and on Piers Morgan’s YouTube show.

I wish every one of them would sit down and watch all 80 minutes of NAZA. Not because the film contains another argument from me. Because it contains testimony from precisely the side they think they’re on.

Israel and its supporters have repeatedly claimed that Israel is confronted by the “Hamas human shield strategy” in Gaza, in which “Hamas deliberately embeds its fighters within civilian areas”.

In NAZA, Israeli military and intelligence sources undermine that defense. Listen, for example, to the Israeli source in NAZA who unpacks the AI-led strategy to track and then bomb Hamas commanders at night, in their homes, alongside their families. “Hamas uses human shields in some cases but the human shield claim about private houses is absurd. It’s just not true. We bomb them in houses because that’s how we find them,” he said. “They just come home to sleep. That’s where we catch them.”

The civilians were not shielding the target. The target was followed by Israel to the civilians.

Some have claimed that media coverage of Palestinian children killed in Gaza constitutes “blood libel” and stirs ancient images of “the child-killing Jew”.

“Ask how Israel is able to target innocent children with such deadly accuracy and no one can tell you,” the celebrated British novelist Howard Jacobson wrote. “Ask why they would want to target innocent children … and no one can tell you that either.”

NAZA settles the argument: it is not antisemitic blood libel to point out that Israel knowingly killed children in Gaza. One Israeli intelligence source describes being able to hack the phone of a 12-year-old Palestinian girl in order to figure out when her father – the actual target – might return home. At that point, the house could be bombed.

Abraham asks the obvious question. What happens to the 12-year-old girl?

“You hack her phone and then kill her,” comes the reply.

What is perhaps most chilling is not merely the content of the answer but its delivery: calm, matter-of-fact, almost bureaucratic.

Another Israeli interviewee recalls a boy entering a military-controlled zone. “He didn’t do anything,” the soldier says. “They bombed him.”

Then comes one of the most horrifying details in an already horrifying film: according to the soldier, corpses are left to be eaten by dogs.

So perhaps the question is no longer: why would Israeli forces ever kill children? Perhaps the question instead should be: how much Israeli testimony describing the killing of children are we expected to ignore?

Some military experts are still, after all the slaughter, arguing that Israel achieved a historically low civilian-to-combatant casualty ratio in Gaza, while uncritically parroting Israeli claims that more than 24,000 combatants had been killed.

But NAZA raises a rather fundamental question. Who gets counted as a “combatant”?

Israeli soldiers and intelligence officials describe “annihilation zones” in northern Gaza in which Palestinian civilians who crossed invisible boundaries could be killed.

“Anyone who enters the zone needs to die,” one interviewee says the troops were told.

His unit killed 140 unarmed people in such zones. Yet, he says, they were counted as terrorists anyway. “Whoever you decided to kill was considered a terrorist.”

When reports emerged of Palestinians being shot around food-distribution sites in 2025, supporters of Israel argued that Hamas did the killing.

If they watched NAZA, however, they would hear Israeli soldiers and intelligence officials breezily describe how Israeli military snipers gunned down hungry and desperate Palestinians who had stepped out of line to swarm the food distribution sites like “ants”.

One interviewee tells Abraham how “three separate teams of soldiers would massacre the population” as they tried to reach the food. They did not mention Hamas.

Supporters of Israel have long balked at comparisons between Israel’s government and the Third Reich. In June 2026, Haviv Rettig Gur, Israeli journalist and Middle East analyst at Bari Weiss’s Free Press, published an essay titled: “Why the Gaza war cannot be compared to the Holocaust”. Gur called the comparison an “inversion so callous it’s hard to believe” and argued that its purpose was specifically “to make the Jews into the Nazis”.

In NAZA, an anguished Israeli soldier tells Abraham that he visited Poland as a school kid, studied the Nazis from a very early age, and wondered how such Germans, the embodiment of “pure evil”, could “live with themselves”.

Now, as an adult and as a veteran of Gaza, he says, “I understand it,” revealing how he and his fellow soldiers blew up homes in the strip and then returned to their university degrees. In a haunting line, he says: “I still see those Nazis as evil, but what does that mean I am?”

Understandably, the comparison triggers particularly sensitive reactions among Israelis, and as Abraham himself emphasized in a recent Haaretz podcast, he isn’t interested in a “simplistic and direct comparison”. Rather, he believes the Holocaust holds universal lessons about how individuals contribute to systems of dehumanization.

“He understood something about being a perpetrator,” Abraham said of the soldier. “When we use the words ‘never again’, part of that is about understanding patterns of dehumanization.”

Is this Israeli veteran really engaged in a bigoted propaganda campaign? Or does he have something to teach us about what happens when an entire people are dehumanized?

NAZA has provoked incendiary responses from officials in Israel.

Former Israeli prime minister Naftali Bennett denounced the documentary as a “horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters”. Israel’s military chief, Eyal Zamir, invoked the language of “blood libel” too.

Their rhetoric is beyond parody. We have become numb to Israeli officials smearing and dehumanizing Palestinian eyewitnesses. But are we seriously expected to believe that these Israeli military insiders and eyewitnesses are blood-libeling … themselves?

The inconvenient yet undeniable truth for Israel and its apologists is that over the course of less than 90 minutes, 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence officials have, wittingly or unwittingly, fully exposed 36 months of baseless propaganda, lazy talking points and disgusting lies.

Don’t take my word for it. Take theirs.

Mehdi Hasan is the CEO and editor-in-chief of Zeteo

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian, is currently in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries, including across the UK and the US. It will be available for free on the Guardian’s website from late November

‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 12:00:09 GMT

The comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too far

What could be more disorientating for a comedian than not being able to laugh – for nine hours! – nor elicit laughter from anyone else in the room? I’ll tell you. Try all of the above on a sunny summer weekend while pretending it’s Halloween. Then force the comics to return to the scene of what one of their number, Phil Wang, calls “a cross between a gameshow and a psychological experiment”, and relive the whole ordeal for a man from the Guardian. Is it any wonder Wang, Lou Sanders, Tom Allen and others come across as a little punch-drunk 24 hours after emerging from televised captivity on the smash comedy hit Last One Laughing?

It’s the day after filming, at Elstree Studios, the show’s Halloween special which sees a unique tweak to its winning formula: contestants must not only refrain from laughter but from screaming. “Which I thought might be a non-event,” says Wang, “but it’s actually harder. I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am.” The participating comics – including paranormal obsessive Daisy May Cooper and that maestro of comedy-horror, Reece Shearsmith – seek not only to amuse each other but spook them too. Which makes sense, says host Jimmy Carr. “Laughs and screams come from the same place. There’s surprise in a joke, and there’s surprise in a jump scare. Comedy and horror mess around in the same area. It’s the same bit of your brain.”

Not that Last One Laughing is making serious moves into chiller territory: after all, why tamper with a format that’s given Prime Video such a huge hit? With over 2m people tuning in per episode, series one was the platform’s biggest ever UK launch. The show later won a Bafta for Best Entertainment Programme. “I don’t want to overplay the jump scares,” says Carr – who first persuaded the channel to develop a UK version of what was originally a Japanese hit. “There’s nothing that would trouble anyone. It’s not that kind of show. It’s just fun. It’s ‘event TV’ – especially when it’s tied around something like Halloween – that’s great for bringing people together.”

And for bringing comedians together too – the more so now LOL has joined Taskmaster as the shop window par excellence for standups making the leap from fringe to mainstream. Alongside national-treasure veterans (Bob Mortimer in series one; Mel Giedroyc in series two), Last One Laughing reserves places for up-and-coming acts – see recent Edinburgh comedy award winner Harriet Dyer here. Getting involved, she says, was “a whirlwind, to be honest. But it was a dream come true.” All the participating comics agree, mind you, that you can’t treat LOL like a career opportunity. “You can’t play it like that,” says Tom Allen. “You have to engulf yourself in the moment. And that reveals people’s true character. There’s something very vulnerable about laughing. We feel very open when we do it.”

Few comics are more oversharingly their own self than Lou Sanders, a late casualty (red-carded by Carr in episode six) in series one, now returning for series 2.5. There’s a strict embargo on spoilers today, but when I ask Sanders if previous experience gave her an advantage in the Halloween outing, her response does not suggest a triumphant comeback. “I thought I would be better,” she says. “But I was immediately on the back foot. And Reece got into my head early on.” Then there’s the knowledge that millions are watching. On series one, “Joe Wilkinson said to me ‘no one’s going to watch this,’ and I believed him. And then it did well. This time, you know there’s going to be eyes on it.”

Sanders has been charged with giving me a tour of the LOL house, a bar cum living room cum art deco theatre, like a prefab 1920s ocean liner constructed in a ginormous Elstree hangar. Here is the fruit machine that’s used to prompt new challenges. There the stage on which contestants perform their ‘joker’ party pieces – around which more strictures circulate than you’d expect. (“I thought it would be funny to have a fire on my head,” says Harriet Dyer. “But I was told: no fire. Then I wanted long arms, but I wasn’t allowed them … ”) There are also creepy dolls, just for Halloween. Does it get claustrophobic in here, I ask Sanders? “I wasn’t in here long enough to know” comes her doleful reply.

But if Sanders’ tactics proved inadequate, others enter Last One Laughing with sophisticated strategies all mapped out. “My tactic was to channel Dame Maggie Smith in Downton Abbey,” says Tom Allen. “Very aloof, very lofty. So I channelled everything through my eyebrows, rather than a lot of people, who try not to laugh by biting the inside of their mouth.” Wang had a more attacking approach. “My mantra was: a good defence is a good offence. Get on the front foot, try to get to people. Focus on those you know at first, because you know what makes them tick. And while doing that, watch the people you don’t know, to see what makes them laugh.”

Dyer entered the house with an idea of what not to do. “I think Sam Campbell said on series two that he thought about, like, kids dying to stop himself laughing. So I thought: should I focus on the worst thing that’s ever happened to me? But I’m not sure watching someone be traumatised with what life’s thrown at them makes for very good telly.” Campbell is the maverick Aussie comic who tested the show’s conceit to breaking point last time around, by staying po-faced from start to finish. He eventually lost in a tie-break to David Mitchell. “We nearly broke David,” says Jimmy Carr. “At the end he was going, ‘I don’t think I’ll ever laugh again. I’ve lost that part of myself for ever’.”

Series two’s other breaking point was reached when – great controversy, this – the comic Amy Gledhill was red-carded by Carr for smiling rather than laughing. My own household can’t have been alone in its outrage at this disregard for the show’s core conceit. But Carr is unrepentant. “I mean, we’d got to that stage of the day,” he says: something had to give. “And it’s that water cooler thing: as long as people are arguing about it and having fun, so much the better.”

To Carr, the show is as much sports as entertainment: the key, he thinks, to its success. “There’s a narrative to sports, whereby you’ve got to watch to the end because you don’t know what’s going to happen. And that’s the same thing with this show: it’s competitive, and you want to know who’s going to win.” “And each episode ends on a really effective cliffhanger,” adds Phil Wang, “which is quite hard to achieve with comedy.”

The other clincher, for Carr and the comics, is how rigorously LOL is produced. Says Carr, “the other countries don’t do the set pieces we do”: the guest appearances, the challenges, the props and tricks contestants can bring to the table – much to Lou Sanders’ dismay. “Reece Shearsmith is Mr Halloween, isn’t he? He’s got all that stuff at home! It’s not fair. I haven’t got a severed hand at home, have I?”

According to Wang, “shows that prepare more than they need always prosper. And this show definitely prepares more than it needs.” Every contestant has a camera trained on them throughout, and a dedicated “spotter” hanging on their every smirk. “I presented it in the room yesterday for nine hours,” says Carr. “But I haven’t seen it all yet. When you get in the edit, there’s a whole other show there. There’s all the conversations people have on the screens I’m not watching. I remember on series two discovering all these incredible moments with Diane Morgan we just didn’t know were there.”

The lineup has already been announced for LOL series three, which broadcasts next year. Harry Hill, Katherine Ryan and Lee Mack all feature. What advice – or warnings – would the Halloween participants impart? “You end up in there for so long,” says Wang – lucky for some! – “that your mood goes from giddy and excited to paranoid and nervous. I was doing a lot of pinching, a lot of breathing, a lot of meditation and mindfulness.” It was, says Tom Allen, “an intense experience, trying to withhold two emotions and not let them out of the bag. It’s exhausting.”

But it’s all in the service, says Allen, of something much needed in our not-always-joyful times. “The series speaks to a childlike sense of play, one that reminds us of being in assembly or in class at school and not being allowed to laugh. There’s nothing more exquisite than that burning desire to laugh while having to keep a lid on it, the steam cooker pressure that brings. Last One Laughing returns us to that youthful joy. I think it’s something people really crave.”

Last One Laughing: Halloween is on Prime Video from Friday.

Elon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 11:53:04 GMT

The Tesla Roadster 2 drove up a curved ramp before using SpaceX rocket thrusters to fly, flip and land

Elon Musk has revealed Tesla’s latest model, which he claims will be the world’s first flying car, using technology from his aerospace company SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”.

The billionaire, who hosted a demonstration of the Tesla Roadster 2 at the SpaceX rocket development and testing facility in Texas, said the sports car could go from 0 to 60mph in a record time of less than a second and had thrusters.

A video of the event shows the Roadster, which he said was controlled remotely “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, driving up a curved ramp using suction to grip upside down, before using thrusters to flip, fly and land.

Later in the demonstration the Roadster is seen using the jets to leap over a line of Tesla’s existing models and then accelerate to 60mph in record time.

“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk said in a post on his social media site, X, accompanying a video from the event.

Speaking at the event on Thursday, Musk said: “Flying cars are real. It’s got altitude controls, thrusters and main thrusters in the rear. So it can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics.”

“I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”.

In 2014 Musk expressed his scepticism about a future with flying vehicles.

However, three years later he announced the development of the Roadster 2, which will go into production in 2028 and is priced in excess of $200,000, (£150,000), to create an electric sports car “to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars”.

Sweet nothings, urinal cakes and headless dogs: 10 artworks worth seeing at Frieze

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 11:02:31 GMT

There’s plenty that stands out at Regent’s Park this year, from antidepressant pens and an ibuprofen-dolling robotic arm to Miriam Cahn’s 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture and a 150m-year-old dinosaur skull – still with embedded tooth

Frieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent

The raised platform in the middle of British artist Ella Fleck’s installation vibrates under your feet to the sound of a male voice. He’s whispering sweet nothings, intoning sexual fantasies. It’s all based on third-party agencies that manage OnlyFans accounts, interacting with users, creating fictional relationships that horny guys spend thousands on. It’s a greasy, gross, uncomfortable exploration of sex work on an industrial scale.

Yuli Serfaty’s headless metallic dog sculptures guard this booth, their claws sharp, their heavy teats dragging on the floor. It’s a surreal symbol of femininity pushed to an extreme, a body devalued and exploited. A video shows the creature trying to escape the booth, and succeeding. The whole installation looks like HR Giger meets Wolfenstein 3D, but with a nasty, satirical edge.

Finally, something to help you get through Frieze. Thai artist Rirkrit Tiravanija’s sculpture here is a robotic arm that carefully hands visitors a little red-and-white ibuprofen pill. If you don’t reach out, it just drops it on the floor. The robot does its job, over and over, regardless of if you’re there to receive it. It feels futile, obscene, repetitive, meaningless. Quite the comment on modern life.

It might look like a display of pens, and that’s because it is. But each one is a promotional item from a pharmaceutical company, given out as gifts to American medical professionals. Lazzard bought them in estate sales from real doctors. They become a portrait of selling out, of how healthcare in the US can be bought by corporations. There are pens with branding for antidepressants, ADHD meds, Viagra: corporations are keeping you going, keeping you productive. When it clicks, it’s an incredibly grim conceptual vision of how our bodies are treated as commodities.

The urinal cakes in the Frieze bogs this year aren’t just there to keep whiffs at bay – they’re art. This is urinal cake as sculptural intervention, thanks to artist Gray Wielebinski, who has designed each one with a custom scent and encased them in metal cages. They sort of look like little chastity devices, glistening lumps of odorous chemicals for you to wee on. They’re weird, almost erotic sculptures. You can hear the anguished cry of thousands of artists wishing they’d thought of it first.

There is such an overwhelming amount of (usually very bland) painting at Frieze that it really takes a special painter to stand out. But Swiss artist Miriam Cahn’s installation is a proper diamond among the swill. It’s a whole booth filled with 26 years’ worth of self-portraiture. Each one plumbs new depths of anxious, monstrous introspection. She grins and screams, stands and falls, all in blurred, messy washes of colour. Psychologically intense, overwrought, emotional stuff.

My love for 19th-century French academic painter William-Adolphe Bouguereau verges on a sickness. I mean, I have a Bouguereau tattoo. So finding this little gem among the Dutch flower paintings and Egyptian busts of Frieze Masters was a genuine thrill. It’s a weird, yellowed little thing – based on a Tintoretto – of a man lying prostrate on the ground. The ropes that bind him have been snapped, wood is splintered. Here is the aftermath of violence, the shocking silence after a traumatic event. This is one of the great things about Masters: getting to spot art historical gold hidden away on the back wall of some booth. This gallery also had a gorgeous James Tissot portrait. It’s 19th-century art nerd heaven.

Sign up to Art Weekly

Your weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitions

after newsletter promotion

There are some amazing narratives to discover in the Frieze Masters spotlight section, especially the work of Haitian modernist Luce Turnier, who lived between Paris and Haiti but has largely been forgotten by art history. This small display of stark portraits – like a more sombre Alice Neel – and vitrines is a little glimpse into a lost period of international modernism from an artist who feels ripe for a museum show.

You eventually go antiquities and Flemish art blind walking around Frieze Masters, so finding the fossilised dino skulls that David Aaron Gallery has lugged to the tent is always a bit of Jurassic relief. This year they’ve brought an enormous triceratops skull and an awesome camarasaurus supremus with the tooth of an allosaurus embedded in it. Absolutely brutal, and possibly the only thing my four-year-old would like in either fair.

There’s death and fear written into all of Sohrab Hura’s paintings here. They’re grotesque expressionist scenes of everyday violence: a man kicked to the ground, a crow pecking at a bleeding carcass above a figure staring aghast at a newspaper. It’s like Edvard Munch but with way more blood and guts. The painting of the woman in the dust storm isn’t good, but the rest are great, angry things.

‘I’m bored when I’m not riding’: Billy Loughnane on drive that made him champion jockey at 20

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 11:00:47 GMT

Flat racing’s youngest champion jockey in more than a century on his relentless – and rapid – journey to the top

Billy Loughnane’s mum wanted him to be a vet. “You’d have to ask her why,” he says with a smile that is rarely more than a second or two away. “I’d say money and an easier lifestyle, but I always wanted to be a jockey and made it very clear that was what I wanted to be doing. My parents and family have all been very supportive since.”

It seems fair to say that Loughnane’s career choice was the right one. At Ascot on Saturday, the 20-year-old will be officially installed as Flat racing’s new champion jockey and the youngest in more than a century. Pat Eddery was 22 when he won his first title, Frankie Dettori was 23, while Lester Piggott – who rode his first winner at the age of 12 – was twice that age when he landed his first championship.

Winning the jockeys’ title has been Loughnane’s driving – and oft-stated – ambition since the day of his first ride as a “very nervous” 16-year-old apprentice at Wolverhampton, and it has been clear for several weeks that this was going to be his year. After a slow start in May, he swept past Oisin Murphy, the defending champion, in mid-July and has been extending his lead ever since. What promised to be a close race between the two riders proved to be anything but.

So the pressure was off as a relaxed and sunny champion-elect discussed his achievement at the yard of his main employer, George Boughey, in Newmarket last week, but there was a strong sense too that he would have been equally amiable had he still been locked in a nip-and-tuck title battle. It’s just how he is, and Loughnane has relished every second of the five-and-a-half month journey.

“It’s a full-on season from the moment it kicks off,” he says. “Most days you’re riding out in the morning, so you’re up at 5.30 and on your first horse at 5.45, and riding anywhere from two to eight horses until 9 or 9.30. Then on a typical day it’s an hour in the gym, and if I’m riding at an evening meeting, there’s a bit of time to catch up with things but if not, it’s straight into the car and off you go racing. I’ll ride anywhere from five to nine horses, then it’s back home and do it all again the next day, seven days a week.

“But I’ve really enjoyed it, and I wouldn’t want to be doing anything else. I think when you get to a certain age and level, you don’t want to be riding at Kempton on a Monday night, but I want to go racing every day. I’m bored when I’m not riding.”

Loughnane’s success, as he is quick to point out, is and always has been a team effort. He grew up in a racing yard, son of the trainer Mark Loughnane, who also supplied his earliest rides and winners, and pays great credit too to Boughey and Tony Hind, his agent, whose track record for turning talented riders into champions is unrivalled.

“I’m lucky to have been supported by good people since I started,” he says. “I stepped straight in as a 7lb claimer with George and he’s gone from strength to strength with the horses in his yard, I’m just the lucky one that gets to partner good horses for good people. And Tony is a genius. My life changed as soon as I started working for him.”

When asked to name his most satisfying success of 2026, it is telling that Loughnane does not pick a moment of personal brilliance, where a split-second change of plan paid off, but Bow Echo’s comfortable success in the 2,000 Guineas in May.

“There had been a lot of preparation from all of us here,” he says, “and that was the best buzz I’ve ever had on a racecourse. The way the race went, it couldn’t have gone better. It was just how me and George wanted it to go, and obviously when plans like that come off in Group Ones, it’s fantastic.”

Loughnane has had six days off from racing since the start of August, and while the title race runs from early May to mid-October, there was little letup in his schedule from January to April. He is the only jockey to have reached 150 wins in the championship window, but has more than 220 this year in all, and a week or two off to let his title win sink in is the last thing on his mind.

“Usually at this stage of the year, you’re winding down a bit,” he says, “but Sir Gordon Richards’ record [of 269 Flat winners in a calendar year, set in 1947] is the next goal and I’m just going to keep on blasting through until the end of the year to see how close I can get.”

So, downtime and R&R must wait. “I’ve been with my girlfriend for the last two years and she sorts a lot of stuff outside [racing] and makes my life very easy,” Loughnane says, “and we’ll get a holiday at some stage but probably not until the end of the year.

“There’s the week off in [mid] November [when no UK Flat racing is scheduled, to give riders a guaranteed break], but there’s racing in Bahrain that week, so I imagine I’ll be there.”

It is an ever-turning treadmill but not one that Loughnane is about to abandon just yet. A title defence and “riding as many Group Ones as possible” are top of the list for 2027, as he looks to improve from one campaign to the next.

“It’s relentless, but you have to enjoy it if you want to do it,” he says. “It’s not possible if you don’t.

“And I’m still learning every day. You don’t stop learning and there’s always people around to help and learn off. I’m definitely far from the finished article, but I’m only 20 years old, so I’ll just keep trying to learn off the best.”

Five of the six runners in Saturday’s Champion Stakes at Ascot are in the top 20 of the Longines world rankings, including Calandagan and Ombudsman, the 1-2 in the last year’s race, and Aidan O’Brien’s Constitution River, who bids to give his trainer what would surely be a title-clinching success in the feature event on Champions Day.

Constitution River was an impressive winner of the Eclipse in July but has slipped below his midsummer peak in two subsequent starts and Calandagan could be a better bet at around 2-1 for a repeat success. A light season so far has seen him slip several pounds below Ombudsman in the ratings, but Calandagan did not peak until the autumn last year and was a decisive winner on similar ground 12 months ago, off an identical 84-day break after the King George in late July.

Ascot 12.55: Oisin Murphy has a 40% strike-rate and 42-point level stakes profit for Saeed bin Suroor over the past six seasons and Victory Gold, the winner of a well-run Sandown nursery last time, is an interesting each-way shot at around 16-1, over a trip that should suit his running style.

Ascot 1.30: Three market leaders are closely matched on form and ratings but Highwayman, the St Leger winner, could have more scope for progress than Gregory or Caballo De Mar as he steps up to two miles for the first time.

Ascot 2.05: A race that has seen plenty of shock results in recent years, including a 200-1 winner 12 months ago, and Coppull could spring a minor surprise at around 12-1. Clive Cox’s three-year-old ended up on the wrong side in the Commonwealth Cup here but otherwise has plenty of strong form over track and trip.

Ascot 2.40: A swift return to action for Kalpana after her run in the Arc but she coped with the same turnaround 12 months ago and has several pounds in hand on this field on ratings.

Ascot 3.20 A case can be made for eight of the 11 runners, but Rayif is unbeaten in two starts at a mile and has been kept fresh with this race in mind since his Group One win at Deauville in August.

Ascot 4.35: Track, trip and going should all be ideal for the course-specialist Hickory, whose hold-up running style is particularly suited to Ascot’s straight mile. A high draw is a bonus and he is also reunited with Saffie Osborne, who has been in the saddle for all four of his previous wins here.
