The last thing I did for my mother was illegal

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 11:00:47 GMT

An urn cost more than my rent. So I scattered my mother’s ashes at Yosemite from a Ziploc bag, without the federal permit I couldn’t afford to wait for

My mother is in a Ziploc bag on my lap, wedged between a half-eaten bag of trail mix and my purse.

My stomach is queasy from the switchbacks up to Yosemite, where I’ve come to spread her ashes, and I’m having an existential crisis.

I had imagined this day as a beautiful send-off that would feel profound. Instead, it was all improvisation: a plastic bag, a last-minute decision, and ginger chews to stop me from being carsick.

I thought my 20s would be about kissing the wrong people in Los Angeles bars, not reading paperbacks on a hospital cot while my mom underwent her fifth brain surgery. My friends were off at college, debating sororities and semesters abroad; I was learning an entirely different set of skills.

At 21, I learned my mom had glioblastoma, a deadly brain cancer. Soon I was in the Bakersfield law library, Googling how to become my 16-year-old brother’s legal guardian, and learning that the same charm I used to snag me a table at Nobu could also get my mom a better room at Cedars-Sinai hospital. She ended up in the room Elizabeth Taylor had died in a few weeks earlier, a detail she loved to regale her friends with.

I don’t remember much from that last month of her life. I mostly just remember the goop I wiped from her eyes as she settled into her final nap. The home hospice nurse told my brother and me to give our mother “permission” to let go. Her fragile body was still fighting, and the nurse believed she was holding on for us. So through our snot and tears, we told her to go. But secretly, in every paused breath, I hoped she wouldn’t.

She passed away within eight months of her initial diagnosis. She was 44 years old.

When the paramedics arrived, I left the room. A white sheet over her body would finalize things in a way I wasn’t ready for yet. Eventually, in the middle of everything else, I had to figure out what to do with her body.

Then there was the price tag. A typical funeral with a viewing and burial in the US costs $8,300. Even cremation now costs more than $2,200 – an unthinkable sum for me at the time. I was a senior airman in the US air force, making about $2,200 a month.

When you can’t afford to pay, you end up grieving illegally – as I did.

My mom had asked to be cremated. Because my family and I were “sharing” her remains, we needed a way to divide her across multiple people: me, my brother and my aunt.

The cheapest option the funeral home offered was a maroon plastic box. I bought one, brought her home, and we portioned her into plastic bags.

Later, my aunt took me to a boutique and helped me pick out little wooden boxes for each of us. Small carved wooden things, prettier than what the funeral home had offered – and cheaper. It felt like a repair. It also didn’t quite work. The box had seams, and my mother kept slipping out of the cracks, a thin layer of her showing up on shelves and dressers and inside drawers.

When it came time to drive to Yosemite, I put her back in a plastic bag.

One thing I didn’t know was that scattering human remains in a national park requires a special use permit. That seems obvious now, but when you’re grieving, reading any fine print is a big undertaking.

The industry of dying wasn’t always so onerous. Before the civil war, most Americans died at home and were prepared for burial by their own families. Embalming became widespread only after the war, when battlefield deaths created a mass market for preserving bodies long enough to ship them north.

What followed was tradition making way for a business model: the funeral home, the professional embalmer, the licensed director, the sealed casket, the manicured lawn cemetery.

One factor pushing the industry toward higher prices is consolidation. Over the last two decades, large death-care conglomerates have absorbed independent funeral homes, in some markets amassing enough pricing power to draw federal antitrust action. What used to be a family business is, increasingly, a subsidiary.

None of this happened by accident, and it is not, as the industry sometimes claims, a response to what families want. Justin Crowe, the founder of Parting Stone, a Santa Fe company that turns cremated remains into solidified stones, told me that the shift from burial to cremation went from 5% in 1970 to over 63% today.

“When the customer said, actually, we want cremation,” he said, “I think the industry kind of made a mistake at that moment. It didn’t really nurture that change. It didn’t provide the value to the experience of cremation, like it had to the experience of burial.”

What families were asking for, in other words, was a cheaper, less institutional death – one where the body didn’t disappear into a funeral home and come back as an invoice. But what they got was the same process, marked up, only this time with cremated remains.

And a growing number of families, faced with a version of dignity they could not afford, began improvising.

My friend Danielle Directo-Meston, a fellow journalist in Los Angeles, grew up in a family where death doesn’t happen offstage.

“Filipinos, my family in particular, we go to the cemetery to hang out,” she told me. “We just hang out there for most of the morning and afternoon. And then we’ll go get lunch together.”

They go to sit with relatives who have died, to clean the graves, adorn them with flowers, and spend time as a family; it’s a habit with roots in Undas, the Filipino tradition of spending All Saints’ and All Souls’ Day at the family plot.

Unlike many Americans, Danielle was raised to be comfortable around the dead. She has also had a lot of practice. In the last several years, she has lost a cousin in a motorcycle accident, an uncle after a series of strokes, and both of her grandmothers. She was still not prepared for how the American death-care industry actually operates.

The clearest example came at Rose Hills, a large cemetery in Whittier, California. Rose Hills is owned by Service Corporation International, a conglomerate absorbing independent funeral homes across the country. Danielle’s family was there for a gathering, honoring a passed loved one, when a salesperson approached them.

“When you’re at the cemetery having a family gathering,” she said, “they have salespeople try to sell you on more plots.”

She made it clear this wasn’t one bad day, or one bad salesperson. It was the norm. Anyone attending a service there would encounter it.

After watching her family cycle through this multiple times, Danielle made a different choice for herself. She decided to preplan her own funeral with a Washington-based company that offers natural organic reduction, the process of transforming a human body into soil, legal in a growing number of states.

“It’s around $5,000, which is doable,” she said. “I can pay that when I’m alive, and no one has to worry about it. Compared to $20,000 just for the plot alone at the cemetery, and that’s on top of the mortuary and all of that stuff.”

Danielle will be composted. I scattered my mother by hand in a national park without a permit. Neither of us did what the industry wanted us to do.

Somewhere between the seventh and the eighth bend, I pulled over and slid down an escarpment to an opening with shrubbery and trees. There wasn’t anything particularly special about the space, except for how the light passed through the leaves.

The year before she died, my mother told me she was taking me and my brother to Hawaii. It would have been our first family trip; the furthest we had ever vacationed was Kern River, 90 minutes from home. She had spent years trying to piece together where she came from. Her father was Hawaiian and had left when she was a baby. Her mother had never known her own father either. So my mother spent her life learning who she was the way you learn a language, alone and slowly.

She had already booked the flights for October. But by fall, she was too sick to travel. She died on 26 December after a few months in hospice care, exactly one year after she had told me about the trip.

I looked down at the bag in my hands. I wished I had planned her scattering at night under a full moon, where I could dance naked in front of a fire and chant her blessings. Or that I had carried her to the Redwoods, finding a spot at dawn when the rocks are covered in moss and dew, and the air is crisp. Or even better, smuggled her to Hawaii, and released her over the Pacific at sunset - her favorite time of day.

Instead, I settled on a sunny spot by a newborn tree. It was about 3ft high and eager to grow taller. It would usher in her remains with enthusiasm, and its new life would overcome her old one; a suitable symbolism for the cycle of life.

I opened the bag and shook it around, flinging her into the breeze, watching the particles of a woman who loved me travel toward Half Dome.

I walked back to my car and stretched my arm out the window on the drive down, surfing the wind with my hand. Pieces of my mother flew out from under my fingernails. It is the most loving thing I have ever done for her.

This article was amended on 16 October 2026 to clarify that the author’s mother died after spending a few months in hospice care.

‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 11:00:46 GMT

Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences

For passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist in London after the first UK services started in September.

Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shocked TfL approved it so soon. I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.”

London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demanding Transport for London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations.

Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’s first autonomous cabs for hire.

The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost.

Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides.

The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses at TfL have expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services.

In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers.

The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said.

TfL is understood to see little benefit in the addition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets, even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic.

For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road.

Under current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start of Uber and Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat.

As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets.

That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twice rebuffed in licence renewals as not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene.

City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday.

Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.”

Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.”

Faisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT. We thought, we’re not earning as much driving but we’ll be safe for a while, support the family, pay the bills. But robocabs are a massive concern.

“People might be interested but it will decimate the livelihoods of many people including me – I really wanted some authorities to say no.”

Abdurzak Hadi, an Uber driver and theLondon chair of the ADCU, said Saturday’s protests would follow a similar action held at Waymo’s base in Park Royal in August. He said: “For me as a driver, I’m thinking about competing with a machine that’s not going to get tired, and could work 24 hours a day.

“But as a Londoner with family, I’m thinking about safety. As licensed drivers we’re taught by TfL about safeguarding, looking out for a vulnerable child, or for abuse. Or looking after passengers who can only read your lips. We’re a safety net. But losing my job – that’s also losing a safety net for my family.”

A recent report from the Centre for British Progress thinktank said more than 400,000 UK drivers (121,000 in London) would soon find “much of this work obsolete”, and urged the government to tax autonomous vehicles to help pay for the social consequences and economic losses.

The GMB union has demanded a “just transition” to help drivers reskill and find new work. Speaking at the Labour conference last month, the GMB’s Mark Betteridge said the union was not against change but added: “The people who do these jobs will know the reality far better of what change will look like … Drivers tell us they want some sort of transition plan to get through this.”

The roads minister, Justin Madders, told the meeting that autonomous vehicles could bring “opportunities for well-paid and unionised jobs” and the government wanted Britain to be a “world leader” in the technology. But, he added: “Sometimes government hasn’t worked on the impact on workers … We’re absolutely committed to making sure that doesn’t happen that time.”

An Uber spokesperson said: “Drivers and AVs [automated vehicles], which we believe will also offer considerable benefits to cities, are both expected to grow side by side for quite some time. That said, we shouldn’t hide that autonomous mobility will impact workers, riders, and the communities they live in.

“We are in conversations with the government and local stakeholders to ensure we can realise the promise of AVs while not leaving drivers and communities behind.”

Uber said it had not significantly increased its share of fares in London but VAT changes meant drivers were keeping less of the fares customers paid, and it said it was the only private hire operator in the UK recognising its drivers as workers with employment protections.

Wayve said that with Uber it was taking a “deliberately phased approach”, and had engaged extensively with political leaders, community organisations and accessibility advocates. A spokesperson said its robotaxis could “make a positive contribution to London’s transport system, helping to improve road safety, expand connectivity and give people more ways to travel.

“There is clear excitement in the potential for this technology to support safer, more accessible journeys, provided it is introduced responsibly and in partnership with the city. We have a positive, constructive relationship with TfL and we’re working pragmatically together to ensure any future services meet its expectations.”

A spokesperson for Khan said the mayor was committed to ensuring that Londoners benefitted from the opportunities new technologies could bring but shared “concerns about potential impacts on safety, congestion and jobs”, as any changes needed to “work for our world-leading transport system – including taxi and private hire services, and those who drive them”.

Digested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prize

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 10:34:15 GMT

With his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place

It might have been more, shall we say, diplomatic if Donald Trump had taken some deep breaths after finding out he had been overlooked for the Nobel peace prize for the second year running before virtually declaring war on Norway. But maybe we should just be grateful he refrained from rubbishing the South African human rights activist Navi Pillay, who picked up the award, and shelved his plans to livestream the execution of the Norwegian prize committee. There again, you can understand his frustration. It’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place. Where would we be had not The Donald started a war with Iran which he shows no sign of knowing how to finish and which has forced up the price of global energy? And it was so good to see him intervening so positively in Russia’s war with Ukraine by appearing to side with the aggressor. These are just the things everyone is looking for in a Nobel peace laureate. The president is also put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts; though it would be helpful if he could let us know which ones. Are they ones he has personally started – Trump appears disappointed that Argentina hasn’t invaded the Falklands again – or ones that only he knows about. During a press conference at Chequers in 2025, he claimed to have brought about a lasting peace between Albania and Azerbaijan. Maybe there are other wars going on we just don’t know about. Perhaps Australia and New Zealand have been bombing each other for years with neither side noticing. And perhaps the border between France and Italy has been a no-go zone ever since the fight between Zinedine Zidane and Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final. Still, Trump looks a cert to retain Gianni Infantino’s Fifa peace prize – if only because it seems likely to be scrapped, making him the only winner.

We may be facing higher levels of global threat and energy costs, but the political outlook isn’t all bleak. You’d need to have a major sense of humour failure not to be enjoying Reform sliding in the polls and falling out with one another. Things seemed to start going wrong when the Guardian exposed Nigel Farage’s £5m bung from the Thai-based crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. Nige has still not come up with a convincing explanation of how the money would be spent. Other than maintaining an expensive lifestyle. Then there was the Channel 4 sting when two of Farage’s closest political allies were caught allegedly trying to take an illegal overseas donation. Nige’s excuse? He wasn’t listening to his conversation with the donor. Who hasn’t dozed off when there’s £500,000 at stake? Since then everyone in Reform appears hell-bent on being the worst versions of themselves as the party loses support by tacking ever further to the right. On Monday, Robert Jenrick declared he would personally be happy to give the order for the Royal Navy to blow every small boat crossing the Channel out of the water. This was too much for Zia Yusuf. Zia is widely loathed within the Reform elite but no one has found a way of saying no to his money, so he gets to call himself the bogus title of shadow home secretary. His main objection to Honest Bob’s plan is that he wasn’t the one to think of it first. Meanwhile, Nige just sits back and pockets the money. Seemingly unable to stop his party collapsing around him.

After several years of consultation, the Bank of England has announced the four animals, insects and birds that will appear on the new banknotes. What goes on what denomination has yet to be decided, but the ones chosen are the European hedgehog, the barn owl, the buff-tailed bumblebee and the Atlantic puffin. And while I’d have quite liked to have seen my much-missed dog Herbie, who died last year, on one of the notes, they all seem reasonable choices to me. I guess the last thing the Bank wanted was to start a war between cat and dog lovers. But not everyone is happy. Partly because they are mad but mostly because they don’t apparently understand how the selection process worked. It was the public who got to choose both the theme of the banknotes and the actual creatures. Needless to say, leading the charge against the new notes are Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, who see the hedgehog and the puffin as some kind of woke symbols. A country going to the barn owls and the bumblebees. They have moaned, what was wrong with having Winston Churchill? Are we now ashamed of our past? No, you halfwits. You don’t have to plaster Churchill’s face on everything to prove you are British. Most of us are secure enough in our identity not to need countless flags and symbols as a reminder. It’s just nice to have a change from time to time. And how many people used to see Churchill’s face on a £5 note and feel a well of pride every time you wanted to buy a sandwich? For that matter, how many people even use cash these days? Mind you, once AI has mined all our data from our emails and bank accounts we could be back to a cash and letter-writing society.

In one of his last conversations with a close friend, Jeffrey Archer was asked if he had any regrets. While he admitted to having some flaws, Archer went on to say that there was nothing he would change. I find that remarkable. I’m not expecting him to apologise for having invented so much of his life – a fantasist is going to fantasise – and he had every right to be proud of his book sales. But not to feel a tiny bit of regret about having lied on oath and being sent to prison. Or feel guilty for the lives he ruined as a result of his lies. That feels borderline sociopathic. Isn’t it human to wish you had done some things differently? I’ve been thinking about this now I’ve turned 70. There’s a lot about my life that I love – family, friends, job – but I have a lasting sadness and guilt about my 20s that I find hard to forgive. The waste, the self-destruction, the damage I did to myself and others. Many of those who knew me had doubts I would even live to 30. I had those doubts, too. And sometimes didn’t much care either way. So yes, I have a whole decade I would love to have done differently. The repair job has been a lifetime’s work and it’s still ongoing. It will probably always be thus.

The Celebrity Traitors continues to be addictive television. A class above the civilian version, partly because we all know something about the celebs, but mainly because the game is different. The civilians are playing for money, the celebs are playing for screen time. That’s why Amol Rajan was gutted to be banished inside 24 hours. The one exception was Richard E Grant, who didn’t care one way or the other. Since his wife died he’s become more disinhibited. The worst has already happened to him. Halfway in, Maya Jama and James Acaster are making great traitors. Maya because she’s so hard to read as her face doesn’t move, James because he genuinely believes he’s too nice to be a traitor while stabbing his friends in the back. I’m amazed Jerry Hall is still in. Not because she’s particularly suspicious but more because she’s incredibly annoying. And why has no one asked her what it was like being married to Rupert Murdoch? The faithful who is playing a blinder is Sharon Rooney. So far she has said and done nothing to attract the film crew, which means she’s likely to be around for a while yet. Being boring is not a bad strategy. I’d like to see a version of The Traitors for politicians, and in my forthcoming shows (Birmingham MAC on 31 October, Huntingdon theatre in Worcester on 26 November) I will be inviting the audience to offer suggestions for possible contestants. So please come along and let’s see if we can make it happen.

‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 10:00:02 GMT

Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational rise

When Irish rockers Fontaines DC emerged in 2019, they were a bunch of post-punk poets making abrasive guitar music at a time when Dance Monkey, Drake and The Greatest Showman reigned supreme. But today, as their fifth album Dopamine Chamber is released, the quintet are looking towards a 2027 filled with gigs in UK stadiums, US arenas and headline slots at big European festivals – plus rumours of topping Glastonbury’s Pyramid stage. It’s quite a trajectory.

Their rise has been strangely traditional for a time when social media has culture in a chokehold. Ever more ambitious albums, the support of radio and institutions such as the BBC, and a lot of touring have all played parts. Beyond that, “fact is, they’re one of the best bands in the world,” says fellow countryman Mo Chara, one third of Kneecap.

Fontaines DC formed at the BIMM Music Institute in Dublin in 2014. The school’s dean, Alan Cullivan, describes them as having had “an absolute focus. It was all about writing a better song after a better song after a better song.” They’d apparently play to 30 people in a dive bar one week, then come back three weeks later and half the songs would be new.

That caught the attention of Trevor Dietz, who became their manager and was described by Fontaines as “the sixth member of the band” when he died earlier this year. “He brought this unwavering sense of self-belief, and that was very contagious,” says Jeff Bell, who’d end up signing the band to Partisan Records.

Dietz’s connections brought Fontaines into orbits outside the Dublin gig circuit. By 2017 the band had released the single Liberty Belle and Dietz introduced them to south London band Shame, who were playing their first headline Dublin shows. “We went on this tour together for our first album,” remembers Shame singer Charlie Steen. “It felt like they had their own crowd even with just a few songs out – it’s one thing to have that in Dublin, but it’s another thing to have it in Leicester.” He adds that Fontaines’ frontman Grian Chatten “gave me a Yeats book to read on that tour”: typical of the singer’s unashamed poetic leanings.

BBC Radio 6 Music’s Steve Lamacq was an early champion of the band around the same time. “They sent us the self-released seven-inch of Hurricane Laughter, and we played that a couple of times – it had a power and an atmosphere that a lot of records around at the time didn’t really have,” he recalls.

In March 2018 the band played the Victoria in Dalston, east London, a tiny pub backroom. In the crowd was Lamacq, enthralled by Chatten’s stage presence, and Bell, who flew to Dublin the next week to sign them. “As soon as I met them, it was clear that they were the biggest band in the world,” Bell says. “It just hadn’t happened yet.”

The label developed a clear gameplan with the band. “There were two guiding principles: authenticity and urgency,” Bell says. “If the mixes weren’t right, start again. If an edit didn’t feel right, it didn’t go to radio. If a writer didn’t get it, don’t do the interview. We also made a point of showcasing the lyrics wherever we could; that was a real point of access for a lot of people.” After their 2019 debut album Dogrel went Top 10 in the UK and Ireland, the Covid lockdown could have scuppered them, like it did so many small acts on the rise. But instead of cancelling releases as others did, they pressed ahead with the release of their second album, A Hero’s Death, which was nominated for a Grammy.

The enormous crowds that Fontaines DC now command are not a result of pandering to the TikTok algorithm, though, even mid-lockdown. The band has a presence on social media, but they haven’t done viral video series such as Hot Ones, Chicken Shop Date or Subway Takes. “They are one of those artists that has very quickly become contrarian to the rule, where they’ve taken a less-is-more approach,” says Liam Ward, founder of music-focused social media marketing agency Something Something.

That doesn’t stop Fontaines having hardcore fans who film entire shows for social media and, in Ward’s opinion, this fan activity online is organic (as opposed to manufactured by legions of fake accounts, as deployed by some of their indie peers). “I have not even heard rumours or whispers [of that],” he says. “They put out what they put out, and all of that craziness and noise happens around them.”

Their previous album, 2024’s Romance, which came with DayGlo artwork and rave-adjacent new looks for the members, was derided by some early fans as too pop but became their first platinum seller in the UK and Ireland and earned another couple of Grammy noms. Dopamine Chamber, raved about in a five-star review in the Guardian, is just as strange and arresting. “Arctic Monkeys, in a way, have done a brilliant job setting up a space for Fontaines by being a really interesting rock band who have evolved a lot since the early days,” Lamacq says. “There’s a new, younger audience who are perhaps more lyrically led. They like the vocabulary as well as the music.”

Kneecap’s Mo Chara says Fontaines’ political leanings, citing a homelessness benefit show the band curated, and their stance against the genocide in Palestine, further endeared the group to him and many others. He adds: “If you’re making music as good as they are, the mainstream can’t ignore it, but it feels like they were making music their own way and not to appeal to the masses. The mainstream has come to them rather than the other way round.”

There are plenty of bands making amazing music who don’t reach the upper echelons of commercial success, though. For Abel González, who is on the booking team for Barcelona’s Primavera festival, “it’s all about feelings”. Fontaines first played the festival on a small stage in 2018, but next year they’re among the big-name headliners. “Every time they’ve come back to the festival, they’ve had new things to say, and we’ve wanted to hear them.”

The true reason for Fontaines DC’s dizzying rise likely lies somewhere in the middle of a complex Venn diagram: a once-a-generation confluence of talent, commitment, good people and luck. The consensus seems to be that there’s no limit to how massive they could become. Bell agrees, still rabidly enthusiastic about the band even after they’ve moved from Partisan to current label XL Recordings. “They still haven’t reached the top of their mountain. I’m excited to see where it keeps going.”

Dopamine Chamber is out now on XL Recordings

The WSL so far: goal-shy Arsenal, underrated Brighton and more data pointers

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 09:00:58 GMT

The Gunners’ title hopes look over after five games as draws continue from last season while the Seagulls, actually ninth, are third for expected points

The Women’s Super League table is taking shape for 2026-27. The defending champions, Manchester City, have five wins from five games but more intriguing stories lie elsewhere. Why are Arsenal struggling, who is performing better than results suggest, and in which way are two promoted teams smashing expectations? Here are three key data points.

Opta made Arsenal third favourites to win the WSL before a ball was kicked. Their win at Brighton combined with Chelsea’s draw against Aston Villa in week one meant Renée Slegers’ side rose to narrow favourites. The four games since, from which Arsenal took two points, have torpedoed their title chances.

One reason for their slump is a continuation of a problem from last season. The stats section of our Arsenal pre-season preview highlighted draws in 2025-26 that they deserved to win based on expected goals. That trend has continued this season with positive xG margins of 2.2 and 1.2 in their home games against Crystal Palace (0-0) and Manchester United (1-1) respectively.

Had Smilla Holmberg not scored with her only shot of the campaign in the 95th minute against United, the situation would be even worse. While players inevitably have a small sample of shots at this point, Arsenal’s finishing woes are a collective problem. Only Lisa Baum and Alessia Russo have also scored, with the latter 1.28 goals below her expected goal tally. Scoring three goals in the international break may help Russo’s confidence.

A physical deficiency may also be contributing to Arsenal’s struggles. Gradient Sports award players an athleticism score, a single metric which incorporates stamina, explosiveness and game context. There are 125 WSL players with a score who have played at least 270 minutes this season. Steph Catley is Arsenal’s highest-ranked player, at 31st, and their only representative above 59th. Every other club has at least two players in the top 50, with Chelsea having five. West Ham possessing seven shows this is not a decisive factor in success but Arsenal fans may wonder whether their side need to increase the physical intensity.

Brighton were predicted by Opta to finish seventh. As they are ninth, that forecast looks reasonable enough. Yet the underlying data suggests they deserve to be third, 0.1 expected points behind City. The Seagulls endured a case of wastefulness more extreme than anything Arsenal have offered up when they drew 1-1 with Villa. Despite an expected goal count of 3.17 to 0.03 in Brighton’s favour, Lynn Wilms’s 89th-minute goal robbed them of a victory.

Brighton also drew at Birmingham when leading the expected goals by 1.5 and missed four Opta-defined big chances in their 2-0 defeat at London City Lionesses. If they can make their dominance count, Brighton look capable of at least matching the fifth-place finish they secured in 2024-25.

after newsletter promotion

Productive pressing tends to belong to better teams. Opta’s high turnover metric records when a team win the ball to begin a new sequence of open-play possession within 40m of the opposition goal. If you sort the 2025-26 WSL by the number of high turnovers that led to shots, the five clubs with the fewest were those that finished in the bottom five. The standings were slightly more jumbled if you looked at the percentage of high turnovers that generated shots, to assess effectiveness and efficiency, but the top four teams for this finished in the WSL top five. Promoted London City had the fourth-least productive press by this measure.

Two of their successors are upending these correlations. Palace are third for shot-ending high turnovers, with 12, behind Chelsea (17) and Tottenham (15). The percentage of their possession regains in the final 40m that led to shots is the highest in the division (33.3%), with their fellow promoted side Birmingham (28.6%) next in line.

The West Midlands club are tied with Tottenham for most goals from high turnovers, on three (while Palace have two). Birmingham’s goals were all scored by Océane Hurtré, helping propel her to joint-first in the golden boot race, with five goals.

The 22-year-old French attacker won the ball for two of the three high-turnover goals, including one at Manchester City. Hurtré’s others came in the first and eighth minutes of matches against Palace and Brighton respectively, illustrating the benefit that pressing opponents early can bring.

We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently?

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 09:00:57 GMT

The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator

At last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.

On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour of verbal fluency and practical skills. This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French, into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “global rankings”.

After the second world war, an “academic” secondary education was shaped by the increased demand for a university-educated workforce. Higher education was expanded, but Britain’s technical and vocational schools and colleges were relegated out of sight. Teaching became enslaved to exam quantification and lost contact with the real world.

But the act of excluding communication skills from this academic orthodoxy has come home to roost. Artificial intelligence and mobile phones are progressively distancing young people from adults and each other. I notice gatherings of young people who used to chatter, laugh and banter. They now stand gazing at their screens or they just shout at each other. Conversation – sharing, informing, discussing, sympathising – seems on the way out.

Speaking itself is going out of fashion. Research suggests that in the past two decades the number of words people say each day has shrunk by nearly a third. They prefer texting. A quarter of young people now say they never even answer the phone unless pre-arranged. They fear a phone call means bad news.

Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage. It is about conveying what one means clearly; listening, debating and handling disagreement. Speaking well means using eye contact and appropriately adjusting your tone of voice. It means politeness and tolerance. Above all, it enables young people to present themselves to others effectively, whether in work, play, argument or friendship.

To the Greeks and Romans, oracy was the towering skill of rhetoric. It was central to citizenship. The New Education movement of Steiner and Montessori in early 20th-century Europe stressed building on the qualities of the individual child rather than imposing rote learning from above. It is significant that the movement has seen a revival in the Waldorf schools now favoured by California’s AI executives in Silicon Valley.

That such ideals of progressive education have long been drummed out of the English curriculum is outrageous. The aversion to the spoken word has corresponded with the increasing prominence of maths in the curriculum, its skills beyond foundational arithmetic irrelevant to all but a tiny minority of adults. Children need to master elementary maths in primary school. But after that they only need to know how to use a calculator. I wonder how many readers remember being able to answer this question from last year’s GCSE paper: “The volume of a sphere is 4/3πr³ where r is the radius. Work out the volume of a sphere with diameter 20cm in terms of π.”

It is extraordinary that passing this exam is still required for most apprenticeships. Yet while he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak wanted maths to be compulsory until the age of 18. Small wonder it has long headed the list of “most hated” school subjects.

Quite how the teaching profession will react to Powell is not clear. The hyper-centralisation of British government has meant ever more school time spent on exams. This has led to cutting back on individualised learning and creativity, which typically flourishes in teaching of the arts. Teachers are pressed to “teach to the test”, at peril of damnation from Ofsted. These days, only the private sector dares resist. Winchester college devotes an hour a day to its form of oracy: “div” and “forum” sessions, when pupils discuss contemporary topics not covered by the examination syllabus: scientific ideas, philosophy, politics, music, critical thinking and the acceptance of others’ opinions.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Such speech-centred concepts as group learning and peer tutoring are being pursued in some universities, and the cause was taken forward in the 2024 oracy commission report. But the catch is always resources. The essence of teaching people how to speak must lie in personal contact. It is in the human relationship of tutor and pupil, which was once the essence of teaching as a profession, not a mechanical skill.

One key might lie in killing maths. Leave it to its enthusiasts. For the rest, school should be about the world outside, a world of other human beings. It is about how to go about handling them that young people have most to learn.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answered

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 09:00:56 GMT

With support for far right politics well established across Europe, how might upcoming elections shape its future? Europe correspondents Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam answered Reddit users’ questions about their reporting from the continent

Support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe, with radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.

The Guardian reported this year that nearly a quarter of voters in Europe voted for far-right parties in their most recent national elections, a fivefold increase since 1995.

In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland recently booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Elsewhere, though – in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Sweden, where the Sweden Democrats lost vote share – far-right parties have suffered defeats. But their ideas – and their influence on mainstream politics – are today clearly visible across the continent, notably on policies around immigration and law-and-order.

The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year.

How might these elections shape the political future of Europe? What is the impact of their policies – and what might prevent their continuing rise?

The Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley has reported for the Guardian from 23 of the EU’s 27 member states, while Europe community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam was on the ground in Sweden and Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state to speak with people ahead of the elections.

Jon and Ashifa answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.

One user asked: It’s no secret in Europe that Donald Trump and his allies are funding far-right parties all over the continent. Trump is unpopular enough in Europe that even the majority of people planning to vote for the AfD et al despise him. So how can so many Europeans who hate Trump still vote for the far right?

Jon Henley: You’re absolutely right about the Trump administration’s efforts to promote far right parties in Europe. That was made very plain in the US National Security Strategy policy document last year – I wrote about that here.

But while there may be an ideological affinity between European far right and nationalist voters on issues like anti-immigration, hostility toward the EU, and softer stances on Russia, Trump’s “America First” policies (demands re Greenland, tariff threats, etc.) and constant unpredictability pose major problems for far-right leaders trying to look credible in Europe, because they scare all European voters – including far-right voters.

Leaders including Giorgia Meloni in Italy and Marine Le Pen in France have openly criticised Trump and distanced themselves from his more erratic pronouncements, conspiracy claims and hostility toward European security.

European far-right voters’ support for Trump varies from country to country but is broadly low – clearly peace and security in Europe matter more than anti-immigration sentiment. Ultimately, nation-first means putting your nation first, and Trump has made clear that the US’s interests are not Europe’s interests.

The evidence would seem to suggest that many of Europe’s far-right voters think their own far-right parties will be more responsible as regards (many of) those issues – though whether they actually will be or not is moot, of course.

00000000000000000000 asked: How do you measure when a grassroots movement represents a genuine structural shift versus an isolated vocal minority?

Ashifa Kassam: Our jobs involve covering a wide range of community actions, whether it’s people fighting back against datacentres, protests against tourism, or the vandalisation of mobile phone masts by people who seemingly linked them to the coronavirus pandemic.

Oftentimes the reporting starts small and local. For example, perhaps it’s focused tightly on a protest against tourists in Barcelona or a push to restrict cruise ship dockings in Dubrovnik. From there, myself and the editors often continue to watch these movements and their reach; are politicians responding in any way? Are others joining in? Will the movements lead to policy changes? These are the kinds of questions that I tend to consider when deciding how much to make of the grassroots movements and how much coverage to give them.

At times it’s been incredible to see just where these movements will go, whether it’s the housing protests in Spain that led to snap general elections or the opposition movement that coalesced around Péter Magyar in Hungary in 2024 and which, more than a year later, saw him oust Viktor Orbán from power.

Gramoun-kal asked: Can the EU survive the rise of the extreme right? What if AfD and RN get into power at the same time?

Jon Henley: One of the very few upsides of Brexit is that hardly any European far right parties now want their countries to leave the EU. Instead, they want to “transform it from within”, turning it more into a looser “Europe of nations”.

But that’s not to say the EU would not be considerably weakened by, say, a President Le Pen, who could paralyse decision-making, challenge the supremacy of EU law and push a “France First” agenda undermining the single market and Schengen free-travel zone and opposing EU expansion, climate action, etc.

I’m not sure there’s any imminent risk of the AfD coming to national power in Germany (and if Le Pen wins France’s presidential election, which isn’t certain but looks highly plausible, she is also unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre).

Plus, the AfD is too extreme even for the RN – Le Pen’s outfit (which kicked the AfD out of its European parliament grouping a while ago over various issues including comments to the effect that not all Nazis were bad), has repeatedly made it clear it is not an ally of the German party and does not share its views on eg. “remigration” – the mass deportation of immigrants.

But for sure – if Spain, Italy, France and Poland all see far-right parties in government after elections due over the next 12 months or so, the EU will face some major challenges. I don’t think it will collapse, but it will certainly find it even harder to reach agreement on many major issues than it already does, and so move (even) more slowly. Natalie Tocci wrote a great comment piece about this.

OrangeSpaceMan5 asked: Do you see Nato and the EU disintegrating if we see Far-Right victories across Britain, Germany and France?

Jon Henley: No, I don’t see the EU and Nato disintegrating, just becoming a lot more complicated/difficult to run … The EU could be “eroded from within” above all by far right-led governments using their veto (as Orbán did with Hungary) in major decisions like the EU budget, EU enlargement, the green deal, etc. They may well also simply ignore EU law, as Orbán also did. And for Nato, see previous answer – it would survive but become more paralysed in terms of longer term decision making.

Ashifa Kassam: I think we saw a glimpse of how complicated things can become in the European parliament after an EU vote earlier this year aimed at increasing deportations. The immediate aftermath laid bare just how deeply polarised the EU has already become, as right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” and centre-left and left-wing MEPs shot back with “Shame on you.”

ElendX asked: Why and how have the left and centre parties failed to respond to the concerns of the electorate? How do they now need to respond?

Ashifa Kassam: What comes to mind immediately is the housing crisis in Spain and beyond. It’s been just over two weeks now since the Spanish protests and encampments over the housing crisis burst into public view, laying bare the long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs.

I think it’s an issue that has long been overlooked by many left and centre parties across Europe, even as vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected, and analysts warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. Last year I spoke to Jaume Collboni, the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, who (along with 21 mayors across Europe) are urging the EU to treat the surging housing costs as a “new pandemic” by unleashing billions in funding to boost affordable housing and give mayors a seat at the table to ensure measures capable of tackling housing speculation. Speaking to me, Collboni warned: “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse.”

I also think left and centre parties have done little to address the precariousness of the labour market, ie. the rise of gig jobs and, in many cases, the deterioration of public services. If you keep an eye on the Eurobarometer, the cost of living constantly ranks among the top concerns for people across Europe, hinting at the idea that this could be fertile territory for politicians to focus on. Immigration, in contrast, was in 7th place in the most recent survey.

Jon Henley: I think broadly speaking mainstream parties have failed to adequately address people’s concerns about the cost of living, declining public services (healthcare, education, transport), economic/job security, etc. – as I said above, fear of/anger at some kind of “loss of status” is one of the key drivers of the far right vote. (I’m not suggesting that’s easy – it clearly isn’t, economies are struggling.)

I’d also add that far-right parties are clearly extremely effective at exploiting voters’ concerns politically, including by pointing the finger at the group they think are most to blame and promising to fix things by getting rid of them.

And I’d also note that mainstream parties really have not helped themselves by adopting far-right parties’ framing on several issues in hopes of hanging on to disillusioned voters – electoral evidence shows that almost never works, mainly because, as Marine Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie put it, people tend to prefer the original to the copy.

Dc740 asked: Did you measure any change in online activity for extremist parties like Vox in Spain after the Yandex datacentre was targeted by Ukraine?

Ashifa Kassam: Funny you should ask – earlier this week, I sent out queries on this to several research groups, so it’s something we’re looking into. It’s a really interesting question. Last week, in an interview with news site Eldiario. es, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez was asked whether he was worried about foreign interference in the elections given his high profile opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and the US-Israeli attack on Iran. His answer: “Yes, and not only by nations, but also by non-state actors.”

Capitao_barbosa asked: How much foreign funding, especially from Russia and America, is being funnelled to these parties? And can we value how much indirect support (bots, disinformation by state actors, algorithm meddling on X, etc.) they are receiving?

Jon Henley: Our data team looked at this question a couple of years ago, before the last European parliament elections. They concluded a quarter of all private money donated to political parties in the EU was going to far-right, far-left and populist movements – aided by the fact that only a quarter of EU countries require parties to identify private donors – with €97m (about one in every seven private donation euros across the EU) going to far-right parties.

A European parliament report from 2023 estimated that about $1.18bn in funding towards organisations targeting LGBTQ+ rights and promoting traditional family policies flowed into Europe from 2019 to 2023, and a 2022 declassified US intelligence assessment found the Russian government had covertly funnelled at least $300m to foreign political parties, often in Europe, from 2014.

Ashifa Kassam: We’ve also had some recent reporting on the flow of funds from the US. In July, the Guardian reported that Donald Trump’s state department intended to allocate $12m to organisations in the UK founded by prominent conservatives. Of these funds, $7m was to go to 878, a thinktank that describes itself as being devoted to “the rediscovery of our ancient culture” and “ending mass migration.”

In July, the state department issued a notice of funding, offering grants for organisations and institutions interested in promoting what it described as “civilisational self-confidence in Europe”.

While research out of Europe, such as the Munich-based Ifo Institute, has found “no correlation” between migration and higher crime rates, the US state department notice suggested it was hoping the grants would lead to outcomes including reports on the impact of mass migration on local safety and tools to analyse impact of mass migration on democratic institutions.

One user asked: How serious would you describe the threat these far-right parties pose to democracy? And to what extent do you think there is a collaboration between them and powerful social media personalities or state sponsored online social media propaganda?

Jon Henley: Some far right parties definitely pose more of a threat to democracy than others. Political scientists divide far-right parties into those that essentially operate within basic democratic norms (“radical right” parties), and those that seek to overturn the system, to the extent even of condoning violence (“extreme right” parties).

If we take one example, AfD in Germany could be described as extreme right in some respects (and some local branches are indeed classified as such by German domestic intelligence). Some of its positions are in clear contradiction with liberal democracy: it is openly racist, homophobic, misogynistic. It believes citizens should be ranked by its own warped criteria, including ethnicity, gender and religious belief. It flirts continually with Nazi rhetoric, imagery and symbolism.

On this question I recommend this column by Cas Mudde, a top scholar of populism and the far right, after AfD won in the recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. He argues that mainstream parties have to wake up to the fact that they are not in a battle that’s about vote share and elections, it’s about democracy itself.

Ashifa Kassam: I would add that we’ve seen some fairly high-profile examples of collaboration, from Elon Musk’s repeated endorsements of the AfD on X to his 2025 X talk with the party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel. The Guardian has also regularly explored the interplay between the far right and social media, such as a 2025 investigation that looked at how a network of far-right Facebook groups had become an “engine of radicalisation” by exposing hundreds of thousands of people in Britain to racist and extremist disinformation.

KilmaSelth asked: Do you think the hard right parties tend to moderate as they approach power, or do they maintain their radicalism?

Jon Henley: Based on Meloni and Le Pen, I would for a long time have said yes – Meloni basically struck a bargain to get elected in which she promised to be responsible on the economy, in the EU and as regards foreign policy, as long as she could do her culture-wars stuff domestically. Le Pen has spent years “detoxifying” the National Rally and kicking out over-radical undesirables. But if you look at AfD, they haven’t moderated their language at all – if anything, they’ve hardened it – and it manifestly is not doing them any harm. And as Meloni and Le Pen have moderated their positions, we’ve started to see them being outflanked on their right, by the likes of Roberto Vannacci and his National Future in Italy and Eric Zemmour’s Reconquête in France. So I think we may be heading into a period where the former far right is effectively now part of the political landscape, like “regular” parties that will sometimes win and sometimes lose elections, and will be increasingly challenged on their right by more extreme elements.

Ashifa Kassam: Vox offers another way to look at this question, as the party was founded in 2013 by disgruntled members of the conservative People’s party (PP). Its leader, Santiago Abascal, is a career politician who was among those who saw an opportunity to push further on the right flank of Spanish politics when it came to Catalan separatism, immigration, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. It was a hardline stance that was often (but not always) diluted when Abascal was part of the PP; now as a separate party, they’ve seized on their electoral momentum in some regions to push the party to heed their agenda.

What topic would you like to see a Guardian Conversation on? Email us at conversations@theguardian. com with your suggestions.

Infantino told by top Fifa figures to scrap or depoliticise peace prize after Trump furore

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 08:58:33 GMT

Backlash greeted award of prize to US president

Fifa committee to make recommendations this year

Donald Trump is likely to end up as the only political leader awarded the Fifa peace prize after Gianni Infantino was told at Thursday’s meeting of the Fifa council to make major changes or scrap the controversial award.

The Guardian has learned that several council members demanded the award be abolished and others called for the prize to be depoliticised, with Fifa’s football social responsibility committee to make a recommendation before the next council meeting in Doha on 16 December.

Infantino announced the peace prize had been handed to the social responsibility committee at the start of Thursday’s meeting. Council members returned to the subject later in a series of questions about possible conflict of interests at Fifa.

There is a strong view among council members that the peace prize in its current form is tainted by association with Trump, with some raising concerns that the US president could object and create a diplomatic storm if he does not like the identity of its next recipient.

Fifa’s 22-person social responsibility committee is dominated by representatives from countries loyal to Infantino so abolition may be avoided on the grounds it would represent a humiliation for the Fifa president, although there is a widespread acceptance that change is required.

One council member told the Guardian the most likely outcome discussed is the reinvention of the peace prize as an award for an individual within football who has delivered exceptional work promoting social harmony and responsibility, with a provision stating it cannot be given to a politician.

Article two of Fifa’s statutes prohibits any political or governmental interference in football, one of several reasons why honouring Trump last year triggered such a backlash from many members.

Fifa announced the creation of its peace prize last November with a stipulation that it would “reward individuals who have taken exceptional and extraordinary actions for peace and by doing so have united people across the world”.

AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight back

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 07:49:45 GMT

Tech platforms pillage public-interest journalism for profit. But we have leverage as they sow the seeds of their own downfall

Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet Mediapart

Big tech companies pose an immeasurable threat: socially, politically, militarily and ecologically. They are also causing a profound crisis of information. The tools they design now serve as weapons of mass destruction against democracy. There is so much at stake that an urgent and broad mobilisation is required.

From the harvesting of personal data and the weaponisation of public opinion, to the destruction of jobs, the infringement of civil liberties and environmental damage, ordinary citizens are the main victims of this predatory economy – an economy with an agenda that aligns with the interests of the planet’s most authoritarian and reactionary states.

The threats facing the information landscape affect us all. Journalists of my generation have witnessed four major digital revolutions: the internet, social media, smartphones, and now, artificial intelligence. What fundamentally changes with AI is our relationship with the truth. For big tech companies, the boundary between truth and falsehood has vanished. This makes it essential to reaffirm the role of public-interest journalism. Our mission is to publish information that is in the public interest by seeking the factual truth, standing against “fake news” and propaganda. Our mission is to help create a democratic public sphere that serves citizens.

Yet AI companies are completely reshaping this space to their own advantage; their mission is not the public interest, but generating profits. Their methods include plundering news outlets without authorisation or compensation. By disseminating so-called summaries of our reporting, they siphon off our audiences and revenue, serving the private interests of a select few at the expense of the common good.

The difference between AI-generated content and a real news article is journalism. AI-generated responses are not information. They are merely a logical assembly of words that all too often produces falsehoods, distorts facts and misinterprets information. A real news article is something else entirely. Quality journalism is the product of expertise guided by ethical standards: persuading sources to speak, painstakingly gathering eye-witness testimonies, cross-referencing, verifying and establishing facts. This process relies on reporting or investigative work – in other words, human effort in the field.

Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance; AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator and breeds confusion. Journalism uncovers facts that certain parties – particularly economic and political powers – would prefer to see hidden, ignored, or suppressed. Generative AI uncovers nothing, it merely regurgitates and condenses existing material.

Quality journalism comes at a high price. Some of the costs can’t even be quantified. Journalists who report from war zones for example, risk their lives. Mediapart’s recent investigation into Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party, has resulted in anonymous cyber-harassment and death threats against our editorial team.

Ultimately, media outlets are accountable for the information they publish. They answer to the courts and to their readers. AI companies appear answerable only to their shareholders. They refuse to vouch for the reliability of their conversational agents to evade legal liability. If nothing is done to stop it, this pillaging will result in the destruction of journalism. This is dangerous not just for news publishers, but for all of us, because it signifies the demise of a public sphere defined by free, pluralistic and democratic discourse.

Do we want a public sphere that guarantees access to reliable, independent information, or one governed by algorithms that amplify fake news, deepfakes and propaganda – fuelling fear, anger and division?

Fortunately, the tech companies have sown the seeds of their own downfall. Since they are bleeding dry the very sources of information from which they derive their profits, they are courting their own failure; without quality information, they will produce nothing but AI slop.

This is precisely where we find leverage. OpenAI has admitted that it would be impossible to train today’s leading AI models without using copyrighted material. A Microsoft vice-president acknowledged that training models on quality content significantly improves the quality of output.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

The priority is to act collectively, pressuring these platforms by every available means – including legal action – to uphold the rights of the press and the public. Some newspapers, such as the New York Times, have taken legal action. Its publisher, AG Sulzberger, recently cited a figure of $20m spent on litigation. Legal proceedings are also under way in France – notably through the organisation responsible for collecting press-related neighbouring rights.

Beyond pressuring lawmakers at national and European level, we must broaden our fightback to include the entire research and knowledge community – stakeholders who, like us, are committed to the public interest and factual truth.

It falls to us, as journalists, to convince the public that our work is an essential part of democracy. We have to demonstrate that our reporting – aimed at holding power to account – has real impact and drives change; that it makes sense of a rapidly shifting world and serves as a powerful catalyst for civic action.

Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet Mediapart

Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 07:00:54 GMT

The current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are released

Public services need more investment across the board. Every day, another wretched story. Look at the Institute for Government’s (IFG) Public Services Performance Tracker for a plain assessment of A&E corridor care, councils struggling to meet the demands of social care and the Send system, the courts backlog, GP caseloads or families lost in temporary accommodation. A chancellor approaching a budget is besieged by need. It’s easy for us journalists to pick out shock stories and claim each one is an absolute priority, but how should a chancellor choose?

Today it’s the probation officers, whose conference in Newcastle is launching a ballot for industrial action. Their caseloads overflowed long ago, but now thousands of prisoners released early – 2,000 this month – have been thrust upon them. The responsibility is overwhelming, with officers blamed for crimes their clients commit.

The probation story is told in scores of reports: the National Audit Office found the service running on half the staff needed to cover released prisoners. It also reported failures in electronic tagging, echoed by the IFG reporting only 55% of tags were fitted in time. Napo, the probation officers’ union, blames the problems on awarding contracts to the lowest bidders at prices that mean the job isn’t done properly.

The number of offenders charged with serious further offences while on probation has increased, with the public accounts committee blaming staff shortages. Vacancies leave probation services 25%-30% below target levels. The government is training another 1,300, but that’s not enough, says Napo, considering the high dropout rate once recruits discover the abuse, threats and stress of the work, alongside the fact that the most common cause of staff sickness is mental ill health.

The sheer impossibility of their caseloads caused the government to abandon any attempt to say what their caseload should be, so the “workload measurement tool” was abruptly ditched in September just before the October raft of new prisoner releases. There is no point in stating an official workload standard that can’t be met.

Eleven hostels and seven halfway houses, places that help probation officers supervise released prisoners, have just closed for repairs and because of a lack of staff. Drug addiction and mental health problems untreated in prisons, coupled with cuts to education, training and rehabilitation, make prisoners even less prepared for release.

The probation system was broken by a disastrous privatisation when Chris Grayling (who banned the sending of books to prisoners) split it apart into 21 private companies, with the workforce organisationally divided in two. Private companies only handled offenders judged low to medium risk, while the most serious offenders remained under the control of the state. Companies under-invested, experienced staff left, and none of the innovation promised was delivered. After this ideological privatisation was abandoned in 2021, the probation service never recovered.

The lord chancellor is set to address the probation officer’s conference. “But please,” says Napo chair Ben Cockburn, “no bullshit. Don’t tell us how well we do an exceptionally difficult job. We know that.”. Napo rejected a 5% pay offer on the grounds it falls far behind equivalent offers to workers in local government, police and social work. Under planned industrial action, Cockburn says probation officers will work to contract and refuse unpaid overtime. That, he says, will cause collapse.

What probation officers need immediately is reduced workloads, pruned to the riskiest cases, leaving less serious cases unallocated. “Put the service into special measures,” Cockburn says. He also wants the courts to stop piling on more cases until there are enough staff to cope. “We are firefighting from one emergency to another,” he says – or called away to someone in a police cell, or to a paedophile found dating a woman with a child, or a domestic violence case.

Cutting workloads for probation officers is only a short-term solution, one that avoids the real question. Why is there an ever-rising prison population, despite the sustained, multi-decade fall in crime rates?

“We are addicted to prison,” Cockburn says. In his view, probation works when officers have time for long-term working relationships with offenders. “It’s the best job in the world,” he says, recalling the journey of one prisoner who had committed a terrible crime as a young man. “I saw him in prison, knew him for 15 years, with time for therapeutic work.” But, these days, that’s so rare. “Someone now might see eight different officers, retelling their story over and over, creating no trust.”

Why build more prison cells? An inspection of a brand new private prison, HMP Millsike in East Yorkshire, found it unsafe due to a lack of experienced staff, as well as chronic staff shortages. Even at its opening, it was “chaotic”, lacking basic processes for important things like locking doors and counting prisoners. Hundreds of cells are still empty because of a lack of officers.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Public pressure to lock up more prisoners and supervise them when released will never be matched by a willingness to pay the taxes needed to cover the cost of attracting people to work in this sector. That’s the truth Cockburn wants politicians to be brave enough to tell. This country is not alone in wrongly believing crime is ever-rising when all across Europe it has fallen for decades. But no one believes it. A news and drama fixation on horrific crime stirs primal fears that belie these facts. Politicians everywhere score points with a frightened public by clamouring for more punishment.

When I last visited a hard-pressed prison, I asked the governor what she most needed, and was astonished when she said she wouldn’t invest here, but “right at the start, before the damage is done, in early years”.

Asking where every pound spent does most good is the kind of mega-question budgets don’t answer. But a brave chancellor would cut prison funding down to housing only the most dangerous, and spending better on what works, such as well-funded probation officers.

Keep telling this fact: all crime is horrible – sex crime is at last reported more often – but the overall drop in neighbourhood-level crime in England and Wales has been about 80% since its peak in 1995. Meanwhile, prison numbers have risen significantly. In his upcoming speech at the probation officer’s conference, it would take unprecedented political bravery for the lord chancellor to dare end the pretence that prison works.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist
