The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win

The Guardian Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:52 GMT

The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment

Back in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”.

The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even provided an interactive map (in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”.

This is not just another ugly social policy report from a politically sidelined former minister – it is a gauntlet being thrown down ahead of Britain’s big benefits debate.

Next month, the government is expected to release two major reports into the social safety net: the Timms review on personal independence payments (Pip), which pays for some of the extra costs of disability in England and Wales, and the Milburn review into young people who are out of work.

It wouldn’t be overstating the importance of Westminster reviews to say their recommendations could shape the future of our welfare state for decades to come. With almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) and the disability benefits bill rising in cash terms, Andy Burnham will face immense pressure to use the proposals to launch a once-in-a-generation overhaul of the social security system.

An overhaul in itself is no bad thing. Disabled people applying for benefits face a debilitating mess of bureaucracy and barriers, while too many young people have been abandoned, facing greater obstacles and fewer services. The question is, will the overhaul actually improve conditions for the people who rely on it, or buckle to the anti-benefit sentiment that’s been bubbling up for months?

That the right is not currently in power won’t stop it from wielding significant influence on what’s to come, in large part thanks to its dominance of Britain’s media ecosystem. Legacy media are not even hiding their attempts to shape November’s reforms before they are announced, with the Times this week launching a “welfare inquiry” to investigate the impact of the benefits “crisis” on public finances.

Some of this is made up of concrete policy proposals, such as the Daily Mail’s pitch to radically means-test Pip. But increasingly much of it is just vibes, a vague sense that this disability problem is getting out of control (or having one is becoming “cool”, as the Telegraph recently put it), and that disabled people – particularly the young – are somehow grifting “perks” while everyone else struggles with rising bills.

The changes in how people consume media since the last major benefits reforms in the early 2010s mean the risks of misinformation and outright bigotry are even greater. Last week, Nigel Farage announced plans for a new video studio in Westminster for the launch of Reform TV on YouTube, with the party’s proposed £50bn benefits cuts presumably being lined up as viral content.

Keep an eye out too for a revival of the striver v scrounger rhetoric as energy and housing costs are set to lead to the worst living standards in modern times by 2029-30. There are few easier ways to convince workers that the unemployed should go hungry than when they’re cutting back on their own food shop. It is telling that the CSJ study includes a section directly comparing “economically inactive claimants” with workers: someone on minimum wage would have to work six days a week to match “the security, cash and ease” a disabled person gets from a package of state benefits, it proclaims. About 1.4 million foreign nationals receive working-age benefits, it ominously adds. Divide and conquer never gets old.

A Labour government is no guarantee these divisions – worker v claimants, old v young, migrant v citizen – won’t be espoused from the cabinet table. No recommendations by Timms or Milburn have been confirmed yet, but Whitehall sources say there are potential plans to scrap a key part of universal credit for under-25s and replace it with a multi-billion pound package to get people back into work.

Sure, it’s depressing if ministers are tempted to bow to the prevailing political winds by pulling cash from young people, but it’s not exactly surprising. For decades, the right has set the boundaries for what Britain’s safety net can be, resulting in little more than subsistence-level benefit rates, an ever crueller culture of testing and a sicker population.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The conventional wisdom has always been that change can only go one way: the benefits system can repeatedly become more punitive and error-strewn, but never more compassionate or accurate. For a leader who has defined himself as someone unafraid of large-scale change, Burnham is well placed to challenge that orthodoxy – if he wants. The opportunity to transform the benefits system does not come up often, and it is rarer still for a Conservative prime minister not to be at the helm.

It’s unfashionable to say it out loud but the truth is that Labour has the power to radically improve the disability benefits system: introduce more evidence-based assessments and reduce the need for mass appeals against incorrect decisions; stop using public money to line the pockets of private companies; and end unnecessary reassessments for lifelong disabilities. Similarly, ministers can address why more people need disability benefits in the first place: by investing in threadbare mental health support; addressing NHS waiting times and poor preventive health services; fixing Access to Work; and tackling employer attitudes to disabled candidates.

The right has long believed it has a monopoly on Britain’s benefits system, as if it were still paternalistic Victorians punishing and pitying the lower orders. But check the calendar and it is 2026. There is a Labour government in office and two big wads of research coming that can at last lay the groundwork for remaking our safety net. The millions who rely on it must hold their breath to see whether that chance will be grabbed or thrown away.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

‘You Can See Everything’ Review: The Slippery Mind of Elizabeth Holmes

The New York Times October 15, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

Critic’s Pick

The disgraced tech entrepreneur and the comic Nathan Fielder chat and joust in a dizzying movie about truth, reality and the contours of knowledge.

By Manohla Dargis

When you purchase a ticket for an independently reviewed film through our site, we earn an affiliate commission.

The nominal subject of the trippy “You Can See Everything” is Elizabeth Holmes, the celebrated entrepreneur turned celebrity jailbird. As a portrait, the movie is intimate and analytic, informative and incomplete. It’s also off-the-charts bonkers, which isn’t surprising given the participants. Directed by the comic Nathan Fielder and the filmmaker Lance Oppenheim, the movie is, among other things, a wily, disturbing, self-aware exploration of the relationship between documentarians and their subjects. It’s often funny, even if the questions that it raises about truth, reality and knowledge can make it feel like a tragedy — few movies speak as uncannily to the pathos and destabilizing confusions of the present moment.

At this point, it’s a tossup whether Holmes is better known for her pop-cultural profile or her real-world exploits or if Fielder, the creator of absurdist comedy TV shows like “Nathan for You,” is now the bigger draw. Her fame was relatively brief but sensational. In 2014, Forbes deemed Holmes, the founder of a blood-testing start-up named Theranos, the youngest self-made female billionaire. She claimed, among other things, that her technology would revolutionize health care, which proved untrue. By 2022, Holmes had been found guilty of four charges of fraud for deceiving investors, a turn of events that seemed to baffle even the presiding judge. “What was it that caused Ms. Holmes, regrettably, to make those decisions that she did,” Judge Edward J. Davila asked, before sentencing her to 11 years in prison.

Save to your watch list:

That question hovers over the movie, and is as much a head-scratcher as how Fielder and Oppenheim came to make it. At one point there’s an approving reference to Fielder being someone who looks “at things differently.” It’s a rich line for those familiar with his work; it’s obvious that Holmes and her life partner, Billy Evans, were not. It’s also obvious that they were out to shift public perceptions about her or, at least, the ostensible narrative, and that the filmmakers were aware of the role they were being solicited to play. It’s not for nothing that the documentary opens on a tight shot of Evans’s face. “Nobody knows who she is,” Evans says to someone on the phone, shortly before dropping the words “radical transparency.”

It’s instructive that Holmes isn’t the first person you see in the movie given how she appears in the movie. She was the most famous woman tech entrepreneur to emerge from Silicon Valley, which helped elevate her profile and added frisson of her fall. Her signature look was striking, including long hair that always seemed a smidge messy, as if she were just too busy innovating to comb it. She didn’t seem to blink, which emphasized the whites of her eyes and presumably held others rapt. It’s a neat movie actor trick for creating dominance, which might have been useful in tech-bro land. She blinks in “You Can See Everything” and her distinctive low-pitched voice also seems more natural; it’s about the only thing that does.

Shot over several years, the documentary opens in 2023, 34 days before Holmes entered prison. Throughout it, the filmmakers mix original and extant material, and embrace different documentary approaches (participatory, ethnographic and so on). For the most part, though, “You Can See Everything” — the title refers to a text Holmes sent Fielder — unfolds as a series of intense conversations with Fielder serving as the on-camera interlocutor. Many of these take place in Holmes and Evans’s beachfront place in Del Mar, Calif., where Fielder prods and pushes them in the dining room, on the sofa, wherever, sometimes with the couple’s two young children and her parents in attendance. A number of encounters are shot in such extreme, dermatologic close-up that you become intimately familiar with Fielder’s zits.

Every so often, other members of the small film crew show up on camera, too. These onscreen appearances are reminders of the inherently constructed aspect of the movie and, by extension, the documentary genre, and they dovetail with a movie’s preoccupation with questions of authenticity and artificiality. All the conversations in the movie take place, after all, in front of a small audience that is, in turn, recording these interactions for the far larger movie audience. Whether Holmes’s occasional blinks and tears in these chats are performative is open to question as are her grasp on language, truth, science and reality itself, all of which Fielder seizes on in a series of interactions that grow progressively weirder.

One of Fielder’s superpowers as a performer is his deadpan, which he generally manages to maintain no matter how outlandish the conceit. He’s put it to recurrently unsettling effect on shows in which he — or a version of himself — aggressively toys with the genre of reality television through his interactions with real people. In “Nathan for You,” he offers absurd advice to small-business owners, successfully persuading a frozen-yogurt store manager, for instance, to sell a lab-created fecal-flavored offering, a. k. a. “poo.” The more conceptually ambitious show, “The Rehearsal,” involves him helping people work through assorted personal issues with the use of hired actors and elaborate re-creations of real life.

Both shows are finally less interesting for what they say about their putative subjects than what they say about those of us who watch them and keep on watching in stitches, shock or horror. Fielder likes to test the limits of propriety and (canned) reality, and he’s having some laughs in the process. He’s also creating social psychological experiments that, in their effect, bring to mind Orson Welles’s 1938 broadcast of the H. G. Wells novel “The War of the Worlds,” about an alien invasion. Welles presented part of the drama as breaking news, which panicked listeners, made headlines and irked the Federal Communications Commission. Welles later said that he had underestimated “the extent of our American lunatic fringe.”

That fringe no longer seems marginal, if it ever was. That the world in “You Can See Everything” appears sane is partly because of the legitimacy conferred on Holmes by her fame and the hundreds of millions of dollars that went into Theranos. Serious people took her seriously, which can seem hard to believe given how slippery Holmes and Evans seem here. Indeed, the first image of Fielder in the movie suggests that he and Oppenheim have come to this project with a degree of incredulity. It’s a murky shot of Fielder peering through a window with what looks like comic skepticism. If it’s uncertain what Fielder is thinking at that moment, it is certain that he and Oppenheim have already begun to test your preconceptions.

One of the most gob-smackingly wild things about Holmes is how she was able to scam so many. That’s part of the story here, though the more interesting one concerns what we mean by truth in a world of profound epistemological uncertainty. Again and again, Fielder presses Holmes about her past and her present. He stares into her eyes, and she stares right back, as he interrogates her linguistic elisions and wonders about her grasp on a famous old comedy routine. He also watches her as she watches the 2022 TV drama series “The Dropout,” in which Amanda Seyfried plays Holmes. It’s a dizzying moment, all the more so given that we’re watching, too, swept up in a ricochet of gazes in the mirrored fun house we now live in.

You Can See EverythingRated R for language and male nudity. Running time: 2 hours 54 minutes. In theaters.

Firefighters Race to Control California Blazes as Winds Threaten to Spark More

The New York Times October 16, 2026

West Coast Weather

Power companies shut off tens of thousands of homes and businesses preemptively on Friday.

Power companies shut off tens of thousands of homes and businesses preemptively on Friday.

A firefighting helicopter dropping water as the Bryson Fire, burned in the hills east of Malibu, Calif., on Thursday. Credit... David Swanson/Reuters

Supported by

By Amy Graff and Jill Cowan

Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. Jill Cowan reported from Los Angeles.

Winds howled in the mountains and canyons of Los Angeles County on Friday as emergency officials there and across the state braced for weather conditions that had raised the risk of fires to critical levels.

Several fires have cropped up in the last two days as strong Santa Ana winds combined with dry air and hot temperatures to create especially combustible conditions that were forecast to last into Saturday. Most were quickly contained.

On Friday firefighters began to gain control of one of the most concerning, the Bryson fire, which was burning through dry brush in the Santa Monica Mountains north of Malibu, Calif. The Bryson fire ignited late Thursday afternoon and quickly spread to more than 100 acres and forced evacuations. Late Friday morning, about 12,000 people were under evacuation warnings, according to a New York Times analysis.

Friday was delivering the hottest temperatures and strongest winds of the week, with highs in the 90s and winds up to 50 miles per hour in the valleys and up to 90 m. p. h. in the mountains.

“The winds are still ramping up,” Ryan Kittell, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Oxnard, said Friday morning.

Any new fires that start on Friday could “get really big, really fast,” he said.

Much of Los Angeles County and neighboring Ventura County remained under a red flag warning through Saturday, and mountainous areas of Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo Counties were under warnings through Friday evening. The warnings mean that experts are worried that fires could start more easily and spread quickly if they do.

Southern California Edison preemptively cut power to over 100,000 homes and businesses to try to reduce the risk that power lines knocked over by winds could send sparks flying.

Evacuation order

Evacuation warning

Historical fire perimeter

California

Data as of Oct. 16 at 2:01 p. m.. Historical fire data is shown for the years 2019-2025 and is as of Nov. 13, 2025. Source: Cal Fire. William B. Davis and Joey K. Lee/The New York Times

Leaders in Los Angeles on Friday morning tried to reassure skittish residents of the county’s vast, hilly areas most prone to fires that they are ready for any blazes that might ignite, while also urging residents to stay vigilant.

“We know the uncertainty that comes with these fires, which is why it’s important for us to look out for one another and to stay prepared,” Lindsey Horvath, a Los Angeles County supervisor, said in a news conference on Friday.

“Know your zone, sign up for alerts, have your go bag ready, and if you’re told to evacuate, do so immediately,” she said.

More than 400 firefighters have been sent to battle the Bryson fire, which was about 17 percent contained as of Friday morning.

“Great progress was made by firefighters overnight,” said Anthony Marrone, the Los Angeles County fire chief.

Mr. Marrone said that no structures had been destroyed or damaged so far.

Residents of the remote canyon areas near the fire were ordered to evacuate, while other residents were under warnings. Nearby parks, roads and the Getty Villa, a museum perched above the Pacific Coast Highway in Malibu, were all closed preemptively.

California has had fewer fires this year, with only 300,000 acres burning since Jan. 1, compared with the over one million acres that fires would have typically burned by mid-October.

For Angelenos, Friday’s conditions called to mind the ones that helped lead to the Palisades fire and the Eaton fire last year, which together killed dozens of people and burned thousands of homes. Many residents who were displaced in Malibu and in the nearby Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles still haven’t returned. In the aftermath of those catastrophes, numerous reports found that the county and city were ill-prepared for wildfires of that magnitude.

This week, Los Angeles leaders — including Mayor Karen Bass, whose reputation never fully recovered after she was out of the country when the Palisades fire ignited — have emphasized that firefighters and equipment have already been sent out to high-risk areas, even if there is no active fire.

The Los Angeles County sheriff, Robert Luna, on Friday morning warned would-be burglars that deputies would be on the streets of the evacuated areas and that the department was adding extra patrols.

“If you think you’re going to come in and take advantage of these poor folks who have been asked to evacuate or don’t have power,” he said, they would most likely encounter officers.

Several other fires ignited on Thursday as winds spread across Southern California and up and down the Sierra Nevada Range.

At Camp Pendleton, the Marine Corps base north of San Diego, the Henderson fire started Thursday afternoon and ballooned to more than 1,400 acres. As of Friday morning, it had not been contained.

The winds were strong in San Diego County, too, but the area was not under a red flag warning because rain from the remnants of a far-off tropical storm recently soaked the ground enough to dampen the risk of fires this week. Instead, high wind warnings were in effect there and in the surrounding areas, including Riverside, San Bernardino and Orange Counties.

The windy weather spread east from Southern California into the Southwestern United States, across Arizona, New Mexico and Texas, where high wind warnings and advisories were also in effect. These winds were generated by a cold storm that spread into the Southern Plains and Mexico overnight.

“The front that moved into Mexico helped amplify the winds in Southern California,” said Frank Pereira, a meteorologist with the Weather Prediction Center, an arm of the Weather Service.

Amy Graff is a Times reporter covering weather, wildfires and earthquakes.

Jill Cowan is a Times reporter based in Los Angeles, covering the forces shaping life in Southern California and throughout the state.

‘I’m on a War Footing’: Terry Tao and the Crisis in Math

The New York Times October 16, 2026

The Fields Medalist and celebrated mathematician is on the front lines of a debate about artificial intelligence and the future of his field.

Terence Tao's celebrated status has made him an unofficial spokesman for mathematics, a job that for now is consuming most of his time. Credit... Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times

Supported by

By Elisabeth Bumiller

Reporting from Los Angeles

Terence Tao is typically described as one of the world’s greatest living mathematicians, but right now he is doing very little math.

“I’m on a war footing,” he said while grabbing coffee during a two-day math workshop at the University of California, Los Angeles, that was rife with talk about the existential crisis that artificial intelligence has created in his field.

Days earlier OpenAI had announced that it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven “Millennium Prize problems” that had stymied the greatest minds in math for nearly a century.

“There are no rules any more,” Dr. Tao, 51, said in an interview before the workshop in his modest office on the U. C. L. A. campus, his home since 1996, when he arrived after completing his doctorate at Princeton at the age of 20. “I’m just numb to what would have been jaw-dropping events for me a year ago. At some point, maybe I’ll get hit by a whole wave of PTSD.”

Instead he was hit by a bigger bomb on Oct. 6, when OpenAI released more than 350 findings in nearly every subfield of the profession, including algebra, number theory, theoretical computer science, mathematical logic and topology. Stunned mathematicians, some who were close to solving problems they had worked on for years, found themselves beaten in an instant by A. I.

Dr. Tao, who has been a tenured professor since the age of 24, said senior academics like himself are not as threatened by A. I. as those starting out. But the math world is looking to him for answers. He has accepted that his celebrated status has made him an unofficial spokesman for the field, a job that for now is consuming most of his time.

Until recently his job was as a bridge between the slow-moving world of higher math and the scorching speed of A. I. Dr. Tao, who uses A. I. as an assistant to run calculations, write code, search vast troves of literature and brainstorm ideas, has been experimenting with OpenAI’s models since 2023. He was an enthusiast for a “best of both worlds” future.

OpenAI’s releases have now left him feeling used. “As recently as a year ago, I had a pretty good relationship with many employees at OpenAI,” he said in a recent phone conversation.

“A lot of people I interacted with shared a very common vision of how A. I. should be used — you know, to empower scientists.” But the rush to publish new findings, he said, shows their true purpose. They “used math for what they needed, which was to evaluate their models,” he said. “At this point, I don’t see a way to constructively engage.”

His anger was clear in a post on the widely read math blog Proofs and Prompts after OpenAI’s Oct. 6 release. “I am horrified by the many person-years” of research, particularly by young mathematicians, “being casually disrupted or destroyed,” he wrote.

“Much as one cannot unhear a movie spoiler or a crossword clue, one cannot explore a problem as profitably and richly once one is aware of an existing solution.” He mourned, he added, “the path not taken, and the opportunities lost in the frantic race to develop this technology.”

At the heart of the crisis in the profession is a menacing question. If solving hard problems is a mission of math, what happens when machines can do it faster? So much of higher math — hiring, promotions, graduate training and acclaim — is based on the difficulty, quality and the impact of papers (the written documents explaining proofs) that a mathematician produces.

The consensus is that A. I.-assisted problem solving is the inevitable future, but no one knows exactly what that new world will look like. “Deep uncertainty will persist in these next years,” a draft report by a group of mathematicians meeting at Harvard on Ph. D. education concluded last month.

A. I. does offer “exciting new possibilities” the report reassured. But implicit in its pages was the sense of loss among humans drawn to math for the intellectual adventure of problem solving — often deeply frustrating, sometimes thrilling and euphoric if a personal breakthrough leads to an advance in the field.

“You’ve had epiphanies, right?” Ravi Vakil, a prominent Stanford mathematician and the president of the American Mathematical Society, asked in an interview. “Suddenly everything in the room becomes clear.”

Theoretical, or “pure” math — the math of Dr. Tao — is loved as much for its art as its science. Its primary goal is to add to the understanding of the vastness of math itself. Unlike applied mathematicians, who have generally embraced the power of A. I. to help them solve practical problems in engineering, finance, weather forecasting and other sciences, pure mathematicians study shapes, structures, numbers and abstract concepts.

Still, pure math ultimately has led to, among many other advances, the creation of the internet, microchips, GPS, cybersecurity, encryption, CT scans and other medical procedures. In 2006 Dr. Tao and three partners created the mathematical theory of compressed sensing, which sped up the scan times of MRIs. Today MRIs can produce real-time images of the beating heart, and many children can be scanned without sedation.

He may say he is battle ready, but Dr. Tao hardly projects as a warrior. In his office, he spoke softly in a lilting Australian accent, was self-deprecating, occasionally funny, upset about the relationship he once had with OpenAI and far from the stereotype of a tortured, brooding math genius. He is known for his sunniness in the rarefied realm of pure math, and students remark on his modesty.

He was dressed in faded blue jeans and a loose polo shirt that seemed to hang absent-mindedly from his slight frame. A blackboard that ran nearly the length of the room was covered with computations by one of his three current Ph. D. students, Ben Goldman. Nearby was the bike Dr. Tao had ridden to work, with his lunch from home in a plastic bag strapped onto the rack over the back wheel.

“It’s leftovers from three days ago,” he said.

He spends much of his time in what he calls “community organizing” — pulling together groups of mathematicians, strategizing, responding to the media, delivering lectures on A. I., counseling. “It’s someone screaming for help,” he said. “I can’t help them because I have no bandwidth, but I can identify somebody else they can talk to.”

His own 20-year-old blog has become math’s front page, filled increasingly with guest posts from others but also notes from the graduate class he is teaching and breaking math news. The day he posted a statement he signed along with 24 other winners of the Fields Medal, math’s version of the Nobel Prize, that called OpenAI’s math “detrimental” to the field, his blog shot to 100,000 views.

“My wife says I’m The Huffington Post,” he said.

His lightheartedness faded as he talked about appearing in a promotional video for OpenAI earlier this year. Its roots were in the Trump administration’s suspension last year of $600 million in research grants to U. C. L. A. that threatened the existence of the university’s Institute of Pure and Applied Mathematics, where Dr. Tao is director of special projects.

Dr. Tao reached out to OpenAI as part of an emergency fund-raising drive, and the lab agreed to sponsor a workshop at the institute for what Dr. Tao said was $60,000 to $70,000. It was held in March, when OpenAI conducted an hourlong video interview with him in which he talked about the benefits and risks of A. I.

He expected the entire video to be posted. OpenAI instead cut it to one minute: “I think it’s ready for prime time,” Dr. Tao says of A. I. as he writes rapidly on a blackboard and a soundtrack of joyful music seems to urge him on.

He gave OpenAI permission to use the ad, he acknowledged in his blog. But in retrospect, he wrote, he should have “pushed back harder.”

An OpenAI spokesman, Laurance Fauconnet, said in a statement that “we value our engagement with Terence and the wider mathematics community.” The lab, he said, is “working with the community to turn progress in A. I. into deeper human understanding and new discoveries, and we will continue to act on its feedback.”

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Dr. Tao was not impressed with the writing in OpenAI’s proof of the Navier-Stokes problem. “It is technically readable,” he said. “But no expert I’ve talked to has actually understood the whole argument.” He said the writing is better in the latest release, though he called it a “mixed bag.” Some papers appropriately cited his work, he said, and seemed to have advanced it in a way he thought was plausible. Still, “there is no author that I can have a real conversation with about the results.”

Dr. Tao was aware last month that OpenAI was working on the Oct. 6 release and at the time called the coming results “toxic waste.” Now he calls them “maybe treated waste.”

The first day of the math workshop — the topic was the field of partial differential equations “in the age of A. I.” — got underway in a small auditorium at 9 a. m. The institute’s director, Dimitri Shlyakhtenko, welcomed several dozen academics, including a batch from Harvard, Princeton, the University of Tokyo and Sandia National Laboratories, the home of the nation’s nuclear stockpile testing. The room was expectant, waiting to hear from Dr. Tao on what he thought A. I. might have in store for them.

“Our first speaker does not require introduction,” Dr. Shlyakhtenko said.

Indeed he did not. As Dr. Tao popped up from his seat to take his place at the lectern, it is safe to say that most in the room already knew him as a legend. Born to Chinese immigrant parents in Australia, he taught himself to read at the age of 2, scored 760 on the math portion of the SAT at 8 and won his Fields Medal at 31.

The medal was for his advances in harmonic analysis — the study of breaking down complex waves into simpler ones — but also for work in partial differential equations and the fields of additive number theory and combinatorics. The Fields Medal Committee cited Dr. Tao for his most famous work, with the mathematician Ben Green, on what is known as the Green-Tao theorem, which proved that there are arbitrarily long, evenly spaced sequences of prime numbers — a monumental achievement in the field.

Up at the lectern at U. C. L. A., Dr. Tao began with an apology. His plan, he said, had been to spend the summer developing a “living spreadsheet,” or network, built and maintained by A. I., of academic results about explicit analytic number theory, an unforgiving subfield of math. “But I’ve been a bit distracted in the last few weeks, and I have not actually devoted as much time to this project as I wanted to,” he said.

He finished with another apology. The network was not complete. He had budgeted all of September to get it done, but “some things happened in the meantime.” The crowd chuckled knowingly.

The most intense discussion on A. I. came after lunch. Sometimes it seemed like a group-therapy session.

“As we soul-search about what the role of the human mathematician is, shouldn’t we go back to where mathematics came from?” said Tatiana Toro, the director of the Simons Laufer Mathematical Sciences Institute at the University of California, Berkeley.

Andrea Bertozzi, a U. C. L. A. professor of math and mechanical and aerospace engineering, said that one thing she liked about college math was that “you sat down with your pencil” and coffee and paper, “and you could prove things.” She brought up the cost of solving Navier-Stokes, which OpenAI said took a swarm of 10,000 agents 88 hours to produce a 165-page proof. Was it “something like $6 million?” she asked.

“More like 22,” someone in the audience said.

This led to a round of comments that the cost of A. I. is undemocratic, particularly to mathematicians in developing nations. “Half the world is going to fall behind,” Dr. Toro said.

Dr. Tao, who had the last word, agreed that the field needed to do some soul-searching. But, he mused, given how fast things were moving, maybe he was doing “soul-searching at gunpoint.” At that point, the room laughed.

Mr. Goldman, like Dr. Tao’s two other Ph. D. students, is facing an ambiguous future. He is 25, a graduate of the University of Chicago and now in his fourth year of a five-year program. He doesn’t know what he wants to do after he gets his doctorate, but he said he has long been drawn to the creativity of math research.

“I’m not saying I was necessarily trying to prove the thing that’s going to be in every textbook 30 years from now,” he said. But he would be happy with a proof “that feels like the argument is me somehow, that has my DNA in it and that people will at least for that one result want to know the way I thought about something.”

After the latest OpenAI release, Mr. Goldman said he was plowing ahead with the research for his dissertation, “even if it can be made obsolete by some messy manuscript released by these companies in the next coming months.” He was upset, he said, “to see a field that I love being sort of strip mined.”

Siddharth Mulherkar, a fifth-year Ph. D. student of Dr. Tao, is applying for postdoctoral research jobs for next fall, the next step on the long pursuit of a tenured professorship. Dr. Tao has given him, like the others, the OK to use A. I. in his work. And yet when he discloses on a job application that A. I. helped with the proof he submitted, how will he himself be evaluated?

“Obviously I don’t want to just be pushing buttons and getting answers to problems,” said Mr. Mulherkar, 27, who was born in California but moved to India with his parents and lived there until he arrived at U. C. L. A.

OpenAI’s latest release, he said, has made him even more uncertain. “I’ve spent quite some time training to become a research mathematician in the traditional sense,” he said. He knows he’ll need new skills, but what they are and “what this career is going to look like and what it will value is completely unclear to me.”

Arian Nadjimzadah, 26, another fifth year Ph. D. student of Dr. Tao, said he was shocked by OpenAI’s latest release claiming to have solved the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and other problems related to his own work. “I had to take a couple days from working on math,” he said.

He was particularly frustrated, he said, with the writing in OpenAI’s proof explaining the conjecture. “The result is extremely difficult to read and uses very unfamiliar jargon to us in the field,” he said. “That’s the nice thing when a person posts a result. They’re accountable. They give talks about it, and they help people understand.”

Mr. Nadjimzadah is studying this academic quarter at the Institut Mittag-Leffler outside of Stockholm and is looking for a postdoctoral job. At the advice of Dr. Tao, he is including in his job applications how OpenAI’s Oct. 6 release connects to his current work and future plans.

“He just said it’s important to address the elephant in the room,” Mr. Nadjimzadah said.

To Dr. Tao, the next few years will require the reinvention of math, or at least of math education. The Harvard report recommended, essentially, that math become more human-centric: Doctorate degrees should not be rewarded primarily on the text of a dissertation, as they are now, but more on a rigorous in-person defense. Students should regularly show professors they can speak fluently about their work.

Dr. Tao went further last week when he presented what he sees as the future of math in a lecture at the California Institute of Technology. Despite OpenAI’s releases, he said, most problems at the frontiers of math are unsolved, math remains infinite and the difficulty of problems is therefore boundless. Since A. I. has given mathematicians the ability to collect data on such a vast scale, they will increasingly work in large groups collaborating on once-unimagined projects.

Dr. Tao, who sees each of his three students once a week, said every meeting is “increasingly a therapy session more than technical guidance.” His answer to them is that “if you focus on only the things you could do before, it looks bleak.”

So he has offered hope with advice that amounts to acceptance born of necessity rather than fighting a war. Problem solving is not a destination but a journey, and lessons learned along the way are often more important than the answer itself. Rather than solving a single problem on their own, they can use A. I. to solve 10 problems and find new patterns and more questions to ask.

“They will have to use their imagination,” he said. “This is a time for creativity, and I do hope students rise to the challenge. They didn’t ask for it. But I think many of them will surprise us.”

An earlier version of this article incorrectly described what the Green-Tao theorem proved. It proved that there are arbitrarily long, evenly spaced sequences of prime numbers, not that there are infinitely long, evenly spaced sequences of prime numbers.

Katie Zacharia Is Ousted After 5 Days as White House Press Secretary

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Zacharia was shadowed by questions about how she had presented her legal career and handled her first press briefing.

By Shawn McCreeshTyler Pager and Hamed Aleaziz

President Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was forced out Friday, after less than a week on the job, according to three people familiar with the matter.

The people spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the decision, which was not yet announced. Ms. Zacharia did not respond to requests for comment. But Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday that he had encouraged Ms. Zacharia to “reconsider” the job.

“Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” he told reporters, recounting his conversation with his press secretary. He said he added: “Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this.”

He said Ms. Zacharia might continue to work for him “in some form, but maybe a more pleasant form.”

A few hours later, Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, told The New York Times that Ms. Zacharia will be “transitioning into a new role that will be announced at a later date.”

Ms. Zacharia had gotten off to a bumpy start with her first and final press briefing on Tuesday, in which she largely read off a script and ended questioning after just three queries. That was followed by an onslaught of headlines about whether she had misrepresented herself as a lawyer — the president called her “an attorney” — despite failing her bar exam.

She had just started on Monday, and hadn’t even moved to Washington yet.

It was last Friday that the president offered her the job. A little-known Fox News commentator with whom many in the White House were unfamiliar, she was a surprise pick. While Ms. Zacharia did have the support of Natalie Harp, the powerful West Wing aide who rarely leaves the president’s side, others in the building believed her debut had been a disaster.

She was not a deft communicator.

She had represented herself as a lawyer in the news media, but when asked repeatedly by a reporter on the South Lawn of the White House to say in which state she had passed a bar exam, she twice replied, “When I moved to China.” She later told The New York Times that she had simply misheard the question — even though the president had repeated the reporter’s question to her while standing feet away.

The end was nigh after she appeared on Fox News on Thursday night to be interviewed by the president’s friend Sean Hannity, who asked her a few tough questions and treated her with rare skepticism.

The reception she got on Friday morning on “Fox and Friends” wasn’t exactly friendly, either.

“Do you wish you would have disclosed to the president about the bar and not passing the bar?” one of the hosts, Lawrence Jones, asked her.

“Well, Lawrence,” Ms. Zacharia responded, “those questions weren’t asked.”

The firing of the administration’s top spokeswoman capped off a week of remarkable upheaval inside Trumpworld.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the ambassador to Greece, was fired on television on Tuesday (during Ms. Zacharia’s only briefing). The president spent time in the Oval Office trying to get to the bottom of a vicious fight between two of his loyalists, Richard Grenell and Alina Mildon.

Paolo Zampolli, a longtime Trump confidant who claimed to have introduced the president to his wife, was pushed out at the State Department after one of his internecine feuds spilled into the press. And the daughter of Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, and others in her circle, came under scrutiny for their moneymaking overseas.

Shawn McCreesh is a White House reporter for The Times covering the Trump administration.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

After Roller Coaster Death, Critics Call for Federal Oversight

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Regulation of amusement parks is left to the states, and deaths are rare. But some say stronger rules are needed.

By Jacey Fortin

It was the kind of horrific accident that calls out for an explanation.

Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was thrown from his seat and fell to his death on Monday while riding Goliath, Georgia’s tallest roller coaster and the centerpiece of the sprawling Six Flags theme park just outside Atlanta.

State authorities, as well as the Cobb County Police Department, are investigating, but the question of accountability is complicated: There is no single federal agency that is responsible for enforcing safety standards for rides like Goliath.

Instead, regulations vary from one state to the next, and the amusement park industry has for decades fought against changes to strengthen federal oversight.

In Georgia, annual inspections are overseen by the state’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner. The office has said it “maintains extensive safety requirements” and annual inspections, which “include reviews of required documentation, mechanical conditions, safety equipment and the safe operation of rides.” Goliath passed its most recent inspection on March 16.

The office is now investigating Mr. Kariem’s death, which it says will include a full review of records. Damon Ballard, the deputy chief of police for Cobb County, said at a news conference on Friday that the state’s findings would determine whether criminal charges are filed.

The International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, an industry group, said that many states draw on the same established standards for amusement park safety. In North Carolina, the State Department of Labor oversees amusement park safety. Ohio relies on its Department of Agriculture, and Connecticut uses its Department of Consumer Protection.

Parks themselves have their own stake in keeping patrons safe, since injuries are bad for business.

Despite the tragic accident on Goliath, deaths on amusement park rides are rare. Statistics suggest that a person is far more likely to die of a lightning strike than a roller coaster.

“Guest safety is fundamental to everything our industry does,” the I. A. A. P. A. said in an emailed statement.

But amusement park injuries are not always reported, and the lack of central oversight leaves some researchers and lawmakers uneasy.

“Because this is not nationally regulated, there is no easy way for people outside of the industry, and the parks themselves, to actually get a clear picture of what’s happening,” said Tracy Mehan of the Center for Injury Research and Policy at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Ohio.

“The most recent study that we did was actually published in 2013, if that tells you anything,” she added. That research found that from 1990 to 2010, more than 4,000 children each year, on average, were treated in United States emergency departments for injuries related to amusement park rides.

A 2005 study published in Injury Prevention, a medical journal, found that there were 40 deaths associated with roller coasters in the United States in the decade that ended in 2004, or four per year on average.

Just over a quarter of those who died were park employees, the study found, and most of them had been hit by moving coaster cars. The rest were park patrons. Of those, 18 died of a medical conditions — such as heart attacks or aneurysms — that might have been exacerbated by the ride, and 11 died from falls or collisions.

Another Six Flags coaster, the X2 in Southern California, has been closed since July after three people in multiple lawsuits said they had suffered catastrophic brain injuries from the ride. The lawsuits accused Six Flags of operating a defectively designed ride and of failing to adequately warn passengers about the risks.

In court filings in an earlier case involving X2, Six Flags denied that the roller coaster had caused a rider’s fatal brain injury.

“We do know that there are gaps in amusement park safety policies — I’ve been raising the alarm on these safety concerns for years,” said Representative André Carson of Indiana, a Democrat.

Mr. Carson has been trying to pass a bill that would give the Consumer Product Safety Commission federal oversight over the industry. Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts, another Democrat, has tried many times over the years to pass something similar, but the bills have stalled in Congress.

The International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions has opposed federal oversight laws like the one Mr. Carson has proposed, arguing that state regulators are better positioned than federal ones to keep a close eye on safety.

“We believe the most effective path forward is building on the state programs already in place: strengthening them, ensuring regulators have adequate resources and promoting consistent adoption of proven global safety standards,” the group said.

Martin Lewison, a roller coaster expert who is an associate professor of business at Farmingdale State College and a member of the I. A. A. P. A., said that while any activity comes with risks, riding roller coasters is not inherently dangerous. “In fact,” he said, “it’s probably safer today than it’s ever been.”

Dr. Lewison said that he has ridden on the Goliath roller coaster dozens of times. He said each seat on the ride uses a restraint known as a clamshell, named for its lightly domed shape, that clamps down at a rider’s hips. The seats have no shoulder restraints, which can help hold people in place but may also contribute to head injuries.

The Goliath has an electronic system meant to prevent coaster cars from proceeding down the track unless every passenger’s clamshell is securely in place, Dr. Lewison said. It is unclear whether that system failed on Monday.

Bolliger & Mabillard, the Swiss engineering firm that designed the Goliath, said it was investigating the death and “deeply saddened by this tragic accident.” The company did not respond to questions about the ride’s design.

According to the I. A. A. P. A., which tracks ride injuries in partnership with the National Safety Council, the chance of serious injury for someone who gets on a ride at a fixed-location amusement park in the United States is one in 15.5 million.

It has also found that for every million amusement park rides taken across the country in 2024, there were fewer than two reported injuries, serious or not. “The long-term data continues to demonstrate a gradual decline in injuries per million attendees,” the group said in an email.

After Mr. Kariem’s death on Monday, Six Flags said it had temporarily closed not only the Goliath but also several similar coasters across the country “out of an abundance of caution.”

The closures threaten to worsen financial troubles for Six Flags. The company’s stock price has been falling for years, and a November class-action lawsuit accused Six Flags of misleading investors before a 2024 merger with another amusement park operator, Cedar Park.

The complaint said that for years, Six Flags had “deferred or foregone basic park maintenance, operational improvements, infrastructure repairs, and ride design and development updates.” Six Flags said it could not comment on pending litigation.

Though the Goliath will stay closed while the investigation into Mr. Kariem’s death continues, Six Flags Over Georgia will open its doors on Friday evening.

Jacey Fortin covers a wide range of subjects for The Times, including extreme weather, court cases and state politics across the country.

What Keeps Students Safe in School? Prevention, Not Defenses, Experts Say

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Oregon School Shooting

Advertisement

Supported by

The gunman who killed four in Bend, Ore., entered an elementary school by shooting through a locked door, raising questions about what more schools can do to protect children.

By Shaila Dewan and Dana Goldstein

Alarms, metal detectors and biometrics. Bulletproof chalkboards and ballistic backpacks. Active shooter drills and drones that fire pepper balls. These are just some of the measures schools are using to shield students from an armed attack, fueling what market research firms say is a $4 billion school safety industry.

But critics say such measures turn schools into fortresses to little avail, and may even make children more fearful and less safe.

On Thursday, an armed teenager in Bend, Ore., shot through a locked school door — long considered the simplest and cheapest way to protect against school shootings — to gain entry to Silver Rail Elementary, the authorities said.

He killed three children and a teacher, and was stopped only because he was fatally shot by an armed bystander.

“It is quite normal that there are going to be adults around the country right now saying, ‘What do we need to do to fortify our schools more?’” said Nicole Hockley, the co-founder and chief executive of Sandy Hook Promise, an anti-gun violence group formed after the mass shooting at a Connecticut elementary school where a gunman shot through locked doors and killed 26 people.

“Frankly, I think it’s the wrong question,” she said. “This is not about security. When the threat is at the door, it’s too late.”

School attackers have shot through glass doors, windows and locks, evaded metal detectors or pulled up at dismissal time and opened fire outside.

“A surprise attack by a heavily armed person is almost impossible to prevent. That’s why a military base has big concrete barriers and fences,” said David Riedman, a data scientist who created the K-12 Shooting Database, which tracks shootings around the United States. “A person who wants to cause harm can get into just about any place that they want to.”

Mo Canady, executive director of the National Association of School Resource Officers, said effective doors and locks were important. “Shooting a lock to the point of overcoming its ability to function is very unusual,” he said.

Ms. Hockley said families should also store firearms securely, out of the reach of children: “That is an act that we can all take.”

But experts argued that the first line of defense should be strong relationships between adults and students.

Teachers, counselors and school police officers with close ties to students are often aware of those who could be struggling and considering violence, Mr. Canady said. Ms. Hockley said adults should be thinking about what children need, rather than how to erect barriers that can make students feel like suspects.

“Kids need connection. Kids need trusted adults that they can talk to, and they need systems that are going to respond,” she said. “That’s going to prevent a lot more crisis and tragedy than security measures will.”

Would-be mass shooters often display red flags such as talk of suicide, glorification of notorious school shooters of the past, showing or bragging about weapons, and even declaring their plan to commit violence, a phenomenon experts refer to as “leakage.”

“I’m heartbroken and my heart is with the community in Bend, and I’m also still waiting because I know that we’re going to hear about warning signs that were missed or not acted on,” Ms. Hockley said.

Sandy Hook Promise has trained millions of educators and students to spot warning signs and says that 20 school shootings have been stopped via tips to its Say Something anonymous reporting system. In a study of more than 100 averted school shootings, Dr. Riedman said more than 80 percent were prevented because a community member, relative or classmate came forward to warn authorities.

On Wednesday, the police in a Chicago suburb said they had arrested a teenager who planned to attack a Hindu temple after co-workers reported that he had told them of his plot.

Experts also raised concerns about online radicalization. Dr. Riedman said that a loosening of standards on internet platforms has allowed “influencer extremists” to proliferate unchecked even on mainstream social media sites.

Young mass shooters like the Georgia teen convicted of killing four people in 2024 are obsessed with their status in a loose social media network centered on mass shootings and violence, Dr. Riedman wrote in his Substack newsletter. He wrote that in recordings of phone calls from jail, the Georgia teen asked his mother to search for his name in forums and read the posts aloud.

“The solution is really simple,” Dr. Riedman wrote. Social media companies should resume stricter regulation of content and ban accounts that espouse violence, he said.

School shootings in the United States have declined for the past two years and are on track to decrease again this year, echoing national trends in crime and gun violence, according to Dr. Riedman’s data.

Last year, he recorded 235 school shootings, down from a peak of 352 in 2023, but still far higher than the average of about 80 per year in the five years preceding the Covid-19 pandemic.

According to Everytown for Gun Safety, gunfire on school grounds has resulted in 33 deaths and 63 injuries this year.

Shaila Dewan is a Times reporter covering criminal justice — policing, courts and prisons — across the country.

Dana Goldstein covers education for The Times.

Israeli Settlers Attack Palestinians and Washington Post Journalist in West Bank

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In the latest surge of violence, settlers targeted Palestinians during the olive harvest, a cultural touchstone and economic lifeline in the Israeli-occupied area.

By Azam Ahmed

Azam Ahmed reported from the village of Khirbet Abu Falah where he and a team from The New York Times witnessed the violence.

Dozens of masked Israeli settlers on Friday attacked a group of Palestinians while they were picking olives in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, seriously injuring several people, including a veteran Washington Post photographer covering the harvest.

Shortly after 8 a. m. during the start of the harvest, the settlers, dressed in black, descended on the village of Khirbet Abu Falah, a small hamlet of fewer than 6,000 people northeast of Jerusalem, according to residents and the mayor.

A team of New York Times journalists arrived on the scene around 9:30 a. m. and witnessed the attack. Armed with slingshots and batons, the settlers launched heavy stones at the Palestinians and set trees ablaze, sending dense columns of smoke into the sky and prompting residents to flee. At least one settler carried a firearm.

Panic ensued as the settlers pressed closer and some young residents squared off with them, trying to defend their neighbors.

Videos of the attack, which were verified by The Times, show that the photographer, Heidi Levine, 63, who was wearing body armor with large press tags, was trapped behind the settlers. They began to beat her with bats and sticks, kicking her as she was prostrate on the ground, according to the videos.

We saw Israeli military forces arrive amid the ongoing attacks and begin pressing residents back from the olive fields, which stretch across several acres along the outskirts of the village. They fired dozens of rounds of tear gas. The sound of live fire rang out.

Medics from neighboring communities raced into the swarm to rescue the injured as tear gas filled the area, where dozens of other journalists and activists had gathered.

The Palestinian Red Crescent said three Palestinians were also wounded. Ms. Levine was transported to a hospital in the area of Ramallah, a city in the West Bank. “While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job,” The Post said in a statement.

Doctors have said Ms. Levine has a broken rib and lacerations on her legs, rear end and hip, as well as a serious cut on her left hand, according to Michael Milner, her son.

The Israeli military said soldiers and border police officers were dispatched to the area of Khirbet Abu Falah after receiving a report of a confrontation. It said that a female foreign journalist was injured, adding that all circumstances surrounding the incident would be examined.

“Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts that require a coordinated, multi-agency response,” the military said.

The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said in a statement in English: “The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation.”

Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, settlers have intensified their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank, a campaign of violence that has emptied out entire villages and instilled fear in communities. In recent weeks, their assaults have focused on the olive harvest, a cultural touchstone in the West Bank, with hundreds of villages relying on it as both a communal rite and economic lifeline.

Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group that monitors settler violence, said it has documented 82 violent incidents against harvesters, 135 instances of crop theft, and 39 of damage to or destruction of trees.

The village of Abu Falah has been subjected to several settler attacks in recent weeks, according to the mayor, Nazem Saleh Shuman. In one incident last week, he said, settlers burned three cars.

“This is our land, we were born here, our ancestors come from here, and we’ve lived here all our lives,” he said. “We believe in this place and we take care of it. We have nowhere else to go.”

In the chaos after Friday’s attack began, we saw several men race past a group of Israeli soldiers right near us. The soldiers then chased the men, including a member of a local council, Abed Aljaber Obied, who had a hand-sized red garden tool in his back pocket. Our photographer took a picture of him running away from the soldiers.

We raced after them and heard rounds being fired. Moments later, we saw the man lying wounded on his back, bleeding, the plastic garden tool beneath him.

The mayor identified the man as Mr. Obied, adding that he had been injured by the military.

The military in its statement said it acted to break up the confrontation upon arriving at the scene and “fired warning shots into the air and subsequently toward a suspect who ran toward them carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them.” The military did not identify the subject.

People crowded around to check Mr. Obied’s condition. The soldiers pushed them away, while another placed a tourniquet around his leg. A third soldier screamed at the injured man to present his identification, and warned that he would not let the medics take him if he did not.

The military eventually let him go, and he was in stable condition.

After the ambulance left with Mr. Obied, the soldiers remained on the scene. An armored truck with a multi-barrel tear gas launcher attached to its roof fired dozens of rounds, leaving the crowd heaving.

“This place became unlivable,” the mayor, Mr. Shuman, said after the attacks. “This is a residential place, where the people live next to their fields, next to their land.”

“But it’s become a hell for us,” he added.

Adam Rasgon, Aaron Boxerman, James McManagan and Aric Toler contributed reporting.

Azam Ahmed is international investigative correspondent for The Times. He has reported on Wall Street scandals, the War in Afghanistan and violence and corruption in Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

Is This the Breaking Point for Trump and Zelensky?

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Where the two presidents’ war of words will end is anybody’s guess. But if it continues, it could threaten the crucial operational help that Ukraine still gets from the United States.

By Kim Barker

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

This time, the rupture feels real.

President Trump has long made no secret of his disdain for President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine and his affinity with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. But Mr. Zelensky has always managed to hold on to some form of American support against Russia, going along with fruitless U. S.-led peace talks and heaping thanks and flattery on Mr. Trump for his “strong leadership.”

Now, in the run-up to midterm elections seen as a referendum on Mr. Trump’s presidency, their relationship seems close to a breaking point. The split poses risks to the Trump administration but more critically to Ukraine, whose military still gets crucial operational help from the United States.

For Kyiv, the blows came one after the next in just one very bad week.

Mr. Trump blamed the war launched by Russia against Ukraine almost five years ago for rising diesel prices, instead of what energy experts call the real cause: the war that Mr. Trump launched against Iran. He temporarily lifted U. S. sanctions on Russian diesel sales in what is likely to be a failed attempt to lower those prices. He unilaterally declared an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” in the war that only helped Russia and hurt Ukraine. And he called for a new Ukrainian president.

By midweek, the Ukrainian military was reporting sudden unexplained restrictions on its use of Starshield, a military version of the satellite internet system Starlink that is crucial to Ukraine’s battlefield communications. Elon Musk, the on-again, off-again good friend of Mr. Trump and the chief executive of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, suggested that only the U. S. military and ultimately Mr. Trump could limit Starshield’s usage. Mr. Musk then also called for a new Ukrainian president.

After initially holding back, a visibly angry Mr. Zelensky said he felt betrayed as Mr. Trump openly sided with a Russian leader who is killing Ukrainian civilians by the dozen. Defying Mr. Trump’s cease-fire declaration, Mr. Zelensky said Ukraine would restart its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Asked by the journalist Piers Morgan to clarify whether he believed Ukraine was “losing” the United States, Mr. Zelensky replied simply: “Yes.”

Mr. Trump then told Newsmax that “Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with.”

On Friday in Belgium, Mr. Zelensky seemed to go further. When asked if he was being treated as a scapegoat for Mr. Trump’s problems, Mr. Zelensky, a former comedian with excellent comic timing, gave a sideways smile and paused at length. Everyone laughed. Then he leaned into the microphone and said: “This is my answer.”

Where the war of words will end is anybody’s guess. But if it continues, it will help Russia and hurt the Trump administration, Ukraine and Kyiv’s European allies, according to analysts.

“It is a lose-lose situation,” said Balazs Jarabik, a former European Union diplomat in Kyiv who now works at R. Politik, a political analysis firm. “It’s bad for Trump, I think. It’s bad for Zelensky, obviously. It’s bad for the Europeans.”

The worst case for Ukraine would be if Mr. Trump and his Defense Department were to suspend aid to the Ukrainian military. Kyiv is hoping that such a step would be too politically damaging for Mr. Trump, as he faces criticism from some in his own party over his treatment of Ukraine.

Kyiv relies on the Pentagon-funded Starshield internet network along the front line, as well as on military intelligence that alerts the country to incoming missile strikes and helps it with targeting for its own midrange strikes.

Ukraine also relies on the United States for weapons that it purchases with the help of allies, such as spare F-16 parts, radiation-seeking missiles and Patriot interceptor missiles, the only weapon Ukraine can access that can knock down Russian ballistic missiles.

A loss of this assistance would hurt the Ukrainian military just as it has been performing well against the Russians on the front line. It would also hurt Ukrainian cities that are under constant missile and drone attack and cause more Ukrainian civilians to die, analysts said.

The United States used to be Ukraine’s No. 1 ally in this war. But then Mr. Trump came into office. He said the days of isolating Russia were over, blamed Ukraine for being invaded and upended generations of U. S. foreign policy. Then came a disastrous meeting between Mr. Zelensky and Mr. Trump at the White House, when Mr. Zelensky was berated for not wearing a suit and not being grateful enough for American help.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

While Mr. Zelensky repaired that rift, the United States stopped donating weapons to Ukraine, instead requiring Kyiv and its Western allies to pay for them. Since then, Ukraine has significantly built up its own defense production, softening the blow as the United States has pulled back — and giving Mr. Zelensky more room to speak out.

“The leverage that Trump has with not giving Ukraine things anymore is very limited,” said Nico Lange, a former German Defense Ministry official who is now a senior fellow at the Munich Security Conference. “There is still a public impression, and also the impression maybe with Trump, that Ukraine will lose the war if the U. S. can’t help anymore. But this is not true.”

Still, while European countries provide some intelligence to Ukraine, there’s no substitute for the U. S. intelligence that gives early warnings for cruise missile strikes from ships in the Black Sea or ballistic missile attacks, Mr. Lange said. If Ukraine gets no advance warning of incoming ballistic missiles and has no Patriots to knock them down, Russia will be able to strike with impunity.

“We will die because we won’t receive warnings about ballistic missile attacks,” said Oleh Katkov, a military analyst and the editor in chief of AIN, a Ukrainian media outlet that covers defense and technology. “That means we won’t be able to get to shelters in time. And we won’t have the means to shoot down those missiles ourselves.”

Solomiia Bobrovska, a member of the Ukrainian Parliament’s defense committee and the deputy head of the Ukrainian delegation to NATO, said she worried that the United States would stop providing Patriot interceptors. The worldwide supply of the missiles has been depleted, largely because of the war in Iran, but Ukraine still receives a small number every month.

Ms. Bobrovska also said that Ukraine and its allies needed to find alternatives to U. S. help for the future. She added that Ukraine would not stop fighting, regardless of what happened. “If you want to hear from me the words ‘peace’ and ‘capitulation,’ it’s not an option at all,” she said.

Ukraine got a glimpse this week of what could happen if the United States stopped helping.

Ukrainian officials said that Ukraine received no advance notice from its partners — code language for the United States — for two waves of missile attacks against Kyiv on Tuesday and Wednesday. Those missiles hit just as air-raid alarms came on.

It’s not clear why Ukraine did not get any notice. It might have been because those missiles were S-400s, which travel short distances extremely quickly, which often doesn’t allow for much warning. Ukrainian officials said they received notice of other ballistic attacks.

Then came the Starshield disruptions, which Ukrainian soldiers said interfered with drone launches and a range of other operations. A bipartisan group of U. S. senators has demanded an investigation.

The next couple of weeks could give a sign of what might happen next in the Trump-Zelensky relationship, analysts said.

“We have to see what’s going to happen up to the midterms,” said Harry Nedelcu, a senior director at Rasmussen Global, a European political advisory firm. “We have to see how Trump will play this out. On one hand, he wants to show he’s bringing gas prices down. On the other, he’s facing criticism from his own ranks. Geopolitically, however, of course it’s a stab in the back. A geopolitical betrayal.”

Constant Méheut, Jeanna Smialek, Oleksandra Mykolyshyn and Nataliia Novosolova contributed reporting.

Kim Barker is a Times reporter writing in-depth stories about the war in Ukraine.

Pope Asks Putin for a Cease-Fire for a Ukrainian City Under Siege

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Pope Leo’s Cancer Diagnosis

Advertisement

Supported by

Recovering from lung cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIV spoke with Vladimir V. Putin to make a plea for Oleshky, where mines and drones have trapped some 2,000 people who are at risk of starvation.

By Elisabetta Povoledo and Siobhán O’Grady

Reporting from Vatican City and Kyiv, Ukraine

Just three days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV on Friday spoke by telephone with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, to call for a cease-fire for civilians to evacuate a besieged city in Ukraine, the Vatican and the Kremlin said.

Since his election in May 2025, Leo has called repeatedly for both an immediate halt to the fighting in Ukraine, and for diplomacy leading to a lasting peace. That he would wade into the topic again while still in a Rome hospital, recuperating after having part of a lung removed, highlights his commitment to the issue.

This time, the pope focused on a particular corner of the war, the small city of Oleshky, in the southern Kherson region, where about 2,000 civilians including some 40 children are trapped and hungry, according to Ukrainian officials. Vendors used to regularly bring food to sell in Oleshky’s markets, but those deliveries ended in May, after people attempting to enter and exit the town were killed by mines or drones on the main road in and out.

The Vatican said in a statement that Leo had appealed to Mr. Putin for food and medical assistance to be delivered to the town, and for a safe corridor to be opened to allow people to leave.

The pope “expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation” and “reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace,” it said.

Mr. Putin “thanked the Pope for his willingness to contribute to the resolution of the conflict and his ongoing humanitarian efforts,” according to a statement from the Kremlin. It added that Mr. Putin “supported the Vatican’s intention to facilitate the creation of conditions to ensure the safety of the city’s population and organize vital supplies. Cooperation in this regard was agreed upon.”

But previous statements about commitment to humanitarian aid and evacuation along Ukraine’s front lines have often yielded little.

Oleshky, which had about 24,000 people before the war, sits on the Russian-controlled left bank of the Dnipro River, giving locals few ways out. A mined river bank lies on one side and a mined road on the other. Drones from both sides crowd the skies. Ukrainian troops control the right bank but their efforts to secure footholds on the left bank have been deadly, dangerous and largely unsuccessful.

Ukraine has blamed Russia for the stranglehold on the city and repeatedly called for an evacuation in recent months. Russia has not yet agreed to a safe corridor for evacuation but has acknowledged the humanitarian crisis and blamed Ukraine.

The Kremlin said that in Mr. Putin’s conversation with the pope, “he provided a comprehensive explanation of the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation” in Oleshky, which it described as a Russian city. It lies in the territory Russia seized in its 2022 invasion and has claimed as its own.

Civilians who escaped Oleshky in recent months described severe hunger, and said they were surviving on what little they could harvest from their own gardens. Ukrainian officials have warned that residents are at risk of starvation. Ukrainian troops have delivered some food by drones, but locals said Russian troops stole some of the packages and intimidated people who tried to collect them.

Tetiana Hasanenko, the city’s exiled leader, said she had not heard anything about the pope’s efforts, but that the situation in Oleshky grows steadily more desperate, and she welcomed any efforts to help.

High-ranking Vatican officials have traveled to both Ukraine and Russia since the war began, and a Vatican official said that Leo had spoken with his special envoy for humanitarian issues, Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, after the cardinal returned from Russia late last month.

During that, his third mission to Moscow, Cardinal Zuppi met with Mr. Putin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, and other Russian officials, and spoke about military and civilian prisoners, family reunification, and the repatriation of children.

“We need to strengthen and speed up the checks needed to ensure that families can be reunited,” Cardinal Zuppi said.

The pope caught the world off guard when he announced last Sunday that doctors had found a small growth in his lung and had decided to operate. Two days later, surgeons removed a lower lobe of his right lung and confirmed that the pope had lung cancer.

Information later released by the Vatican suggested the cancer was caught at an early stage. Doctors have not released the results of additional tests to determine what additional treatments, if any, are warranted.

On Friday, the Vatican said that the pope had resumed working and his doctors said he was moving independently.

Leo’s illness has shaken his papacy, casting uncertainty over his long-term plans for the church, which he has so far implemented at a slow pace. When Leo, the first pope born in the United States, was elected at 69, less than 18 months ago, he seemed to have years ahead of him to shape the Roman Catholic Church.

Elisabetta Povoledo is a Times reporter based in Rome, covering Italy, the Vatican and the culture of the region. She has been a journalist for 35 years.

Siobhán O’Grady is a Ukraine correspondent for The Times, based in Kyiv.
