U. S. Budget Deficit Nears $2 Trillion, a Reality Check for Trump’s Cost Cutting

The New York Times October 16, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

Higher interest rates are inflating borrowing costs as the Trump administration spends on the Iran war and tariff refunds.

Note: Data covers fiscal years, which begin in October.

Source: The Treasury Department and the U. S. Office of Management and Budget, via the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

Jacqueline Gu/The New York Times

By Alan Rappeport

Reporting from Washington

The United States budget deficit approached $2 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, its highest level since the pandemic, as spending on the military, safety net programs and interest on the debt dwarfed the Trump administration’s cost cuts, Treasury Department figures showed on Friday.

The widening gap between what the government spends and what it collects in taxes and other revenue comes at a critical moment. Investors are nervous about America’s surging debt load, along with stubborn inflation, and have driven up borrowing costs. Treasury bond yields, which influence interest rates for mortgages, credit cards and auto loans, hit their highest levels in two decades earlier this month before easing.

Those higher borrowing costs come as many Americans, already feeling beleaguered by the cost of living, head to the polls for an election that will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress. While the deficit has been driven up by spending and tax decisions by both political parties, President Trump and Republicans added to the shortfall with an expensive tax cut package in 2025. Mr. Trump, who had promised to curb federal spending, has instead seen it rise on his watch.

The rising deficit, which increased to $1.99 trillion this fiscal year from $1.78 trillion in 2025, is notable because it comes at a time when the economy is growing steadily. The last time the deficit topped $2 trillion was in 2021, when the pandemic prompted Congress to approve a huge stimulus package to help keep the economy afloat. But there is not an immediate crisis that the nation is tackling. Instead, the shortfall stems from increased spending on the military, interest payments on the debt and Social Security benefits, coupled with falling corporate tax receipts as a result of the tax cut package.

The growing deficit could leave the United States in a vulnerable position the next time a national emergency arises.

“When the next crisis strikes, we will almost certainly be more indebted than ever before when entering a crisis, which will limit our capacity to respond and exacerbate the damage we face,” said Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

The fiscal shortfall for the year underscores the difficult battle that the United States is facing as it tries to reduce the national debt, which is a cumulative measure of annual deficits. U. S. debt topped $40 trillion in August. Despite expressions of public concern about deficits, lawmakers have for years continued to cut taxes and allow spending to soar.

“Without real action on these vital fiscal issues, America is careening toward an ominous fiscal crisis that would leave all of us much worse off sooner than anyone in Washington apparently wants to believe,” said Carolyn Bourdeaux, executive director of Concord Action, an advocacy group that promotes deficit reduction.

The problem is a global one with few easy solutions. Deficits have been mounting around the world as nations have increasingly turned to government subsidies to develop advanced technology. Conflicts in the Middle East and in Ukraine have forced countries to spend more on military equipment. Rising interest rates are deepening the fiscal malaise.

“The higher that interest rates move in the government bond market, the less likely it is that governments can finance these interest expenses in a sustainable way, so the stress begets more stress,” said Daleep Singh, chief economist at Prudential Global Investment Management. “It crescendos in the absence of a credible fiscal plan, which is not forthcoming.”

The Congressional Budget Office said last week that spending in the United States has been pushed higher by the growing cost of Social Security benefits and payments to military personnel. Higher long-term interest rates increased the cost of interest on the debt by more than $100 billion from 2025. Overall, spending was up 6 percent to $7.4 trillion.

Tax revenue increased by 3 percent to $5.4 trillion, with individual income tax receipts growing because of higher wages. Corporate tax revenue declined as a result of larger business investment deductions enacted by the 2025 tax legislation.

The biggest setback to the Trump administration was a drop in customs duties as a result of the Supreme Court ruling that the tariffs that Mr. Trump imposed for national security reasons were illegal. The government was required to refund more than $100 billion of tariff revenue this year.

The larger annual deficit deals a blow to the fiscal ambitions of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who upon taking the job said that his goal was to bring the deficit as a share of the economy to 3 percent. After falling from 6.3 percent in 2024 to 5.9 percent in 2025, the measure rose above 6 percent again this year.

Note: Data covers fiscal years, which begin in October.

Source: The Treasury Department and the U. S. Office of Management and Budget, via the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

Jacqueline Gu/The New York Times

Mr. Bessent pledged to produce a fiscal consolidation plan that he has yet to deliver. He has also said that the United States will ultimately have to address its debt problems by accelerating economic growth.

At a news conference in Bangkok this week, Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, suggested that Mr. Bessent was putting too much emphasis on the ability of growth to address America’s fiscal situation.

“We believe that growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustment,” Ms. Georgieva said during the annual meetings of the I. M. F. and the World Bank.

Alan Rappeport is an economic policy reporter for The Times, based in Washington. He covers the Treasury Department and writes about taxes, trade and fiscal matters.

Trump’s Attempt to Deport Ilhan Omar Is Another Leap Toward the Abyss

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Michelle Goldberg

By Michelle Goldberg

Opinion Columnist

In his final speech as president, Ronald Reagan emphasized the essential role of immigration in American greatness. “We lead the world because, unique among nations, we draw our people — our strength — from every country and every corner of the world,” he said. Reagan cited a letter he’d received about how one can’t simply move to France and become a Frenchman or move to Japan and become Japanese. “But anyone, from any corner of the earth, can come to live in America and become an American,” he said.

Donald Trump, who launched his political career with lies about Barack Obama’s birthplace, is devoted to destroying this ideal. For Trump and his movement, real Americans are defined by race and ancestry. The administration’s war on birthright citizenship stems from that belief. It’s the reason Trump, who accused immigrants of “poisoning the blood” of our country, has limited refugee resettlement almost exclusively to white South Africans. JD Vance channeled the same idea last year when, attacking the Jewish Anti-Defamation League, he said, “I think the people whose ancestors fought in the Civil War have a hell of a lot more claim over America than the people who say they don’t belong.”

And now the Trump administration is attempting to strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, who was born in Somalia, of her citizenship so as to deport her. This is more than just another persecution of one of Trump’s political enemies. Rather, his government is tacitly declaring the citizenship of all foreign-born people provisional, their Americanness something that can be revoked. It’s a frontal attack on the idea of constitutional equality. As Hannah Arendt wrote — a quote that the writer John Ganz reminded me of — “One is almost tempted to measure the degree of totalitarian infection by the extent to which the concerned governments use their sovereign right of denationalization.”

This week, as you might have read by now, around 20 Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s home in Washington, seizing her phone and computers, among other things. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that the investigation is aimed at denaturalizing her, a prelude to deporting her. In its attempt to cast out Omar, the administration is looking not just at her own actions but also at those of her father, who applied for citizenship when she was a teenager. Apparently, the case hinges on whether she was 18 rather than 17 at the time.

I have no idea whether Omar or her father (who died in 2020) did anything wrong, but the details of her immigration paperwork are somewhat beside the point. What matters is that Trump targeted Omar for her politics and, even more, her ethnicity. Just months into her first term, he was calling for her expulsion from America, his rally crowds lustily chanting, “Send her back!” In a cabinet meeting last year, he called Omar “garbage” and attacked Somalis more broadly, saying, “I don’t want them in our country.” As his political fortunes have waned, his rhetoric about Somalis has grown increasingly fascistic. On Truth Social last week, he wrote that the “once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants.” As if trying to incite a pogrom, he urged: “Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

Under these circumstances, it would be willfully credulous to assume the administration’s good faith in the Omar investigation. Even if the government ultimately fails to take away her citizenship, as it’s failed in most of its other attempts at political vengeance, it’s sending a message to every foreign-born American. Oppose Trump too loudly, and the government will comb through your paperwork — including paperwork filled out by your parents — for errors that could upend your life.

There is an obvious progression here. This regime has already tried to deport green card holders like Mahmoud Khalil for their political speech. It’s turned hundreds of thousands of Haitians — the group Trump demonized as pet-eating savages — into illegal immigrants overnight by ending their temporary protected status. Now it’s escalated to naturalized citizens. Omar probably won’t be the last. Though Trump has been charmed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, other Republicans have called for his deportation. Representative Andy Ogles, a Tennessee Republican, has asked the Justice Department to review Mamdani’s naturalization documents. In the Trumpian schema, some Americans are here by right, and some only on sufferance.

It’s chastening to think back to 2019, when Trump first tweeted that a group of progressive Democratic congresswomen, presumably including Omar, should go back to the “totally broken and crime infested places from which they came.” At the time, his bigotry was considered shocking. Four Republicans, as well as the Republican-turned-independent Justin Amash, joined Democrats in passing a House resolution condemning his words. Even Representative Elise Stefanik, who’d go on to become one of Trump’s most slavish lackeys, felt the need to denounce him. “While I strongly disagree with the tactics, policies and rhetoric of the far-left socialist ‘Squad,’ the president’s tweets were inappropriate, denigrating and wrong,” she said.

Now that Trump is acting on his gross rhetoric, the response has been more muted; by mass-producing outrages, the administration has numbed America’s ability to recognize their individual gravity. But it’s worth pausing to recognize that, with Trump’s attempt to banish Omar, we’ve crossed yet another once-unthinkable line.

For now, Trump’s power may be waning as his popularity collapses, but if the Republican Party continues on its current course, the next Republican president is likely to begin where he left off. The logic of this brand of politics moves inexorably toward atrocity.

Here’s Arendt again: “Mass cancellation of naturalizations, such as the one introduced by Nazi Germany in 1933 against all naturalized Germans of Jewish origin, usually preceded denationalization of citizens by birth in similar categories.” If there’s one lesson of the last decade, it’s never believe it can’t happen here.

I am the son of an immigrant. This talk of being a "heritage American" is deeply insulting to me and tens of millions of others. I grew up in a household of baseball, hot dogs, root beer and apple pie. I felt no different than any of the other kids I went to school with. We were part of the neighborhood and the neighborhood was part of us. There was no talk of some being more American or others being less. We were all Americans. Ronald Reagan's speech quoted here is my life story. Virtually all of the elders in my family were born overseas. Many started their own businesses. I started my own business. This is the American dream. To do what you want to do. To be independent. To pursue your dreams. And where you were born or where your parents were born had nothing to do with it. No one in this nation has inherently more rights than anyone else based upon ancestry. Reagan understood that. J. D. Vance does not. If we follow Vance's proclamations, we are doomed to decline. The shining city on the hill story will become a fairy tale.

Michelle Goldberg has been an Opinion columnist since 2017. She is the author of several books about politics, religion and women’s rights and was part of a team that won a Pulitzer Prize for public service in 2018 for reporting on workplace sexual harassment.

Russia Appears to Step Up Efforts to Influence U. S. Voters

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

One campaign has created social media posts focusing on U. S. support for Israel to sow discord ahead of the midterm elections.

By Julian E. BarnesDustin Volz and Steven Lee Myers

The reporters have covered foreign efforts to influence American elections for years.

Less than three weeks from elections that could shift the balance of power in Congress, more signs are emerging that Russia and other foreign governments are once again seeking to influence American voters.

An online influence operation backed by the Russian government has been stepping up its attempts to sow division in the United States and inflame tensions around Israel as a political wedge issue, according to a new study by an independent company that tracks digital threats and foreign propaganda campaigns.

The influence operation known as Doppelgänger has created a flood of social media posts pushing themes of how bipartisan support for Israel is collapsing, according to Alethea, the threat intelligence company.

Doppelgänger is run by Russia’s Social Design Agency, a public relations firm. Both the U. S. government and the European Union have imposed punitive sanctions upon it.

On Wednesday, X, the social media platform, announced it had banned 13,000 accounts linked to three separate influence operations connected to Iran, Russia and China. The platform said the fake accounts amplified “content about U. S. politics, targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum.”

U. S. intelligence officials tried to provide a classified briefing to some state officials on midterm election threats on Thursday, according to people familiar with the matter.

That overture hit a snag, however, when the intelligence officials were unable to establish a secure virtual connection to the election personnel, the people said. While such briefings were routine in previous election cycles, Thursday’s would have been the first of its kind in more than two years.

A U. S. official confirmed that a technical issue had postponed the call but said the briefing would hopefully be rescheduled for next week. Election briefings typically include background material and information, rather than intelligence that state and local officials should immediately act on, according to current and former officials.

CNN earlier reported the technical problems with the briefing.

Covert foreign influence campaigns targeting American voters are not new, and their impact on political discourse and voting is unclear. American officials said that they had identified similar influence campaigns in years past, including by Russia, all trying to sow discord over contentious topics.

Lisa Kaplan, the founder of Alethea, said none of the inauthentic posts linked to Doppelgänger had high numbers of views or interactions.

But the volume of posts in the current campaign, and replies under postings that had high engagement, indicated that the messaging was likely getting in front of people.

Propaganda campaigns by the Kremlin and others have evolved over the years to include different platforms, new tactics and, increasingly, the use of artificial intelligence.

In some ways, such operations have grown more difficult to track amid a broad pullback by many social media firms on trust and safety work after years of criticism from conservatives who accused the companies of collaborating with the U. S. government to stifle free expression.

American officials briefed on intelligence reports said they did not know of the precise campaign identified by Alethea. But they said spy agencies have flagged that Doppelgänger and the Social Design Agency have been active ahead of the midterms.

In addition to the influence operations targeting the U. S. midterms, Alethea has tracked posts aimed at Israeli voters, who go to the polls on Oct. 27, and French voters, who will vote next April. U. S. officials confirmed stepped-up Russian campaigns in all three countries.

The New York Times reported in September that classified U. S. intelligence assessments in recent months had concluded that the Kremlin once again had approved a digital influence campaign to peddle covert disinformation across social media in hopes of seeding or amplifying domestic divisions during the election season.

The assessments did not find evidence of any attempts to take aim at voting machinery in a way that could compromise the actual voting process, the officials added.

The new Doppelgänger campaign included more than 50 fake personas — often posing as Israeli women — on X that posted in “synchronized waves” beginning on Oct. 7, the three-year anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel.

Then, a separate network of more than 1,000 accounts deposited those posts into unrelated, high-traffic conversations, yielding an estimated 150,000 posts in total.

“You basically need to conceptualize the Russian influence operations like a dark money political action committee,” Ms. Kaplan said. “If you want to understand their perspective, you have to find out what they are pushing.”

Ms. Kaplan said there are always questions about how effective influence campaigns are, particularly ones built around pushing out thousands and thousands of low-engagement posts. But she said Russia and other adversarial governments would not continue the campaigns if they didn’t think they worked.

“Think about it. It is really hard to hack someone; it is really easy to lie online,” she said. “That is what it boils down to. And if that lie is believed it is just as effective, especially if your goal is to erode trust.”

The posts by the fake personas included links that often directed audiences to fake news articles on clones of legitimate news sites.

Despite the low level of engagement, the Russian propaganda outfit seems determined to amplify perceptions that Democrats have retreated from supporting Israel.

In appearing to target Democrats with negative content, the Doppelgänger push is just the latest effort by Russia to harm the party and support President Trump since his first run for office in 2016.

U. S. intelligence findings and numerous reviews have consistently found that President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia has favored Mr. Trump over Democrats, most of whom are more sympathetic to Ukraine as it battles Russia’s invasion.

In September, a network previously linked to Kremlin trolls posted a series of videos on social media that appeared to rely on A. I. to churn out baseless claims against Democrats running in closely contested Senate races.

Graphika, another threat analysis company, attributed the blitz to a Kremlin-linked operation that experts have called Operation Overload or Matryoshka, which often impersonates real news organizations to spread fabricated content.

New campaigns targeted Senators Cory Booker of New Jersey and John Hickenlooper of Colorado, both Democrats, with fabricated reports of corruption allegations, according to a Graphika analysis.

In October, posts linked to the Matryoshka campaign promoted a conspiracy theory that Democrats in the United States were behind the attempted hijacking of the FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv, the company said, while another Russian influence operation promoted Mr. Trump’s recent deal with Mr. Putin to purchase diesel fuel from Russia.

The campaigns “give us a glimpse of what their objectives are,” said Jean le Roux, a senior researcher at Graphika. “They’re not targeting Republican candidates in the same way.”

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Steven Lee Myers covers misinformation and disinformation from San Francisco. Since joining The Times in 1989, he has reported from around the world, including Moscow, Baghdad, Beijing and Seoul.

Young Voters Say They Are Turning Their Backs on Trump and His Party

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

One of the biggest surprises of 2024 was the swing of young voters, particularly men, away from Democrats to Donald Trump. Now they are swinging back.

By Sabrina Tavernise and Ruth Igielnik

Sabrina and Ruth interviewed more than two dozen young voters for this article.

For Remi Martinez, it’s the deportations. For Michael Johnson, it’s the economy. For Suzanna Bridges, it’s the Epstein files and what she sees as misogyny embedded in the culture of the Trump administration.

All three youthful Americans voted for President Trump two years ago. All three regret it. All say they will vote Democratic this year, or not at all.

“I can’t go red, not this time — no,” said Mr. Johnson, 26, a sales representative for a plastics company in Des Moines.

In 2024, more than half of young men — 55 percent — supported Mr. Trump, according to an analysis of New York Times/Siena University polling, a dramatic departure from past elections when young Americans largely supported Democrats. Young women swung right as well, though not in such striking numbers.

Now, Democrats hold a slim, one-percentage-point advantage with young men, a group that is politically up for grabs. Around 10 percent of young men remain undecided. Among young women, 31 percent of whom supported Mr. Trump in 2024, the analysis found that support for the Republican Party had been cut to just 13 percent.

“Trump’s focus is not good,” said Marcos Jimenez, a 21-year-old studying to be a math teacher in Oakville, Calif. He voted for Mr. Trump on his economic promises, he said, only to get a war and spiraling costs.

“He’s focusing on things outside of the country like wars,” Mr. Jimenez said. “I wish he would focus more here.”

He will be supporting Democrats in the fall, he said: “They’re more for people.”

Young voters — nearly half of whom are people of color — chose Mr. Trump two years ago for many different reasons. Mr. Johnson, an immigrant from Liberia who came to Iowa at 15 and became a citizen soon after, said he had “started seeing the rise in biological males in women’s sports.”

Mr. Johnson was not alone in saying that “threw” him off. In Times/Siena polling, half of young men said they thought the Democratic Party was too far to the left.

And Mr. Johnson was passionate about the election; he said he had persuaded 15 members of his extended family to vote for Mr. Trump, too.

Now he sees bigger problems — the price of gas and housing. Seven of his friends have taken second jobs. So has he, with a day job at the plastics company and a night job at Whole Foods. The rent on his mother’s African goods store is going up, he said, and gas prices are biting.

“Trump’s becoming an old, crazy man,” he said. “He doesn’t care anymore.”

Beyond the youngest voters, the next age group — voters between the ages of 30 and 44 — has also bolted, from a 17-point advantage for Mr. Trump among men of that age to a six-point advantage for Democrats.

“All the woke stuff happening” in the Democratic Party had pushed Remi Martinez, 44, to Mr. Trump, he said. Now Mr. Martinez, a dispatcher for a trucking company in western Kansas, regrets it.

Mr. Martinez is Hispanic and said people should not assume voters like him are opposed to deportations: “I don’t want rapists in my neighborhood either,” he said.

But, he added, Mr. Trump has swept up “hard-working people who have been here for years.”

So many people have been taken from his town of Garden City, a meatpacking area with large Hispanic population, that the town seems “shut down,” he said.

“They were just after everybody,” he said, “pulling over everybody.”

He plans to vote for Adam Hamilton, the Democrat, in the Kansas Senate race and is encouraging his daughter, who’s in her twenties, to support James Talarico in Texas, he said.

“The government needs to have checks and balances,” he said.

Though the movement among young women was smaller, Republicans did get an uptick of support in 2024. Today, Democrats’ lead with the group is vast at nearly 70 percentage points.

Ms. Bridges, 22, grew up in rural central Texas, and as a Catholic, she was put off by Democrats’ positions on transgender youth issues. Two years ago, she cast her first ballot — for Mr. Trump.

Now starting graduate school in international affairs at Texas A&M University, she does not like how Mr. Trump is treating American allies. She was angry when foreign aid was slashed — her faith calls for helping those in need — and when Mr. Trump barred news outlets from the White House.

She said that she found Mr. Trump’s dismissive treatment of the Epstein files appalling, and that his administration was going in reverse on women.

“I’m sure you know who Andrew Tate is,” she said, referring to the online influencer known for his chauvinistic views and who was arrested on charges of rape and sex trafficking. “This administration is pushing for that kind of man right now — hyper, hypermasculine.”

“I’m a Catholic conservative, not a Christian nationalist,” she added. “We have respect for women.”

Ms. Bridges said she did not find the Democratic Party appealing either; she did not trust Mr. Talarico, in part because of his change in position on transgender athletes, and in part because she didn’t like his mixing of faith and politics. She said she did not plan to vote in this election.

That would not be unusual. In 2022 — the last midterm election — only about 30 percent of voters under 30 showed up at the ballot box, compared with close to 70 percent of voters over the age of 65.

Unlike older voters, who tend to be more set in their partisan ways at the ballot box, young voters are still trying ideas on for size.

Liam Howard, 26, grew up in a politically conservative family in New Hampshire that regularly watched Fox News and listened to Glenn Beck, the conservative talk show host. In his early voting years, he said he considered himself a libertarian and voted for Republicans in 2018, his first election.

Then he went to college and “realized that liberals aren’t actually weird,” he said.

Mr. Howard now makes emergency lights for vehicles and lives with his parents because housing in southern New Hampshire has risen out of his reach.

“I can’t even afford a crappy studio apartment working 40 hours a week in a factory,” he said. “Thirty years ago, my job would have bought a house. It’s insane.”

That economic reality has drawn him to politicians like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, and Senator Bernie Sanders, the independent socialist in neighboring Vermont. About 30 percent of younger voters said that they would prefer a democratic socialist, more so than any other age group, according to Times/Siena polling.

Mr. Howard is one of them, and as a democratic socialist, he said he did not vote for president in 2024. Kamala Harris lacked ideas, he said, and he didn’t like her position on Israel. But he is excited by the crop of democratic socialists who have won primaries around the country this season and said he felt motivated to vote.

Despite the broad turn away from the Republican Party, about 44 percent of young men still prefer Republicans in this fall’s elections. Conner Fredrickson, a 28-year-old who owns an I. T. business and lives in Phoenix, said the president was “trying to build America back, make us stronger, make us more independent.”

He added: “Is he doing everything right? No. But nobody does everything right.”

Many younger voters said they were looking for anyone — regardless of party — who could help make life affordable. That has brought a new fluidity to the electorate.

Ryan Gellings, 25, a grocery marketer in Kansas City, Kan., considers himself a Republican. He is Catholic, likes small government and supported Mr. Trump in 2016, though he was too young to vote for him. He still likes what he calls Republican values, but he thinks Republican politicians are mostly yes-men for Mr. Trump. To his regret, he said, he voted for Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for president in 2024.

Now he is drawn to candidates like Mr. Sanders, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York and Representative Thomas Massie, the maverick Republican in Kentucky, because, he said, they seem deeply committed to doing something about the cost of living, no matter which way the political winds are blowing.

“I love that Mamdani is taking care of his people,” he said. “If money is going to be wasted, it may as well be for the people,” Mr. Gellings added.

One-third of voters age 18 to 29 say neither party is focused on the right things, the highest share of any age group.

Mr. Gellings said he was planning to vote for Mr. Hamilton. But mostly, he is frustrated with both parties.

“We’re confused and ready to move — anywhere at this point,” he said. “We are tired of the current conversation.”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed reporting.

Sabrina Tavernise is a writer-at-large for The Times, focused on political life in America and how Americans see the changes in Washington.

Ruth Igielnik is a Times polling editor who conducts polls and analyzes and reports on the results.

$137 Million in A. I.-Generated Ads Flood the Midterms

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Republicans have used A. I.-generated content more often than Democrats, ranging from subtle enhancements to convincing deepfakes.

Note: The “Generated by A. I.” label and red slash were added by The New York Times. Source: AdImpact.

By Stuart A. Thompson

It was an unlikely scene: New York’s mayor and governor appeared to be strolling through a park and gardening together in a sun-drenched suburban yard, promoting a new drug — a “political delusion pill,” they called it — to help voters overcome fears about affordability and crime.

“Side effects may include: chronic wallet shrinkage, higher tax,” a narrator intoned over plucky guitar.

Though the video captured the voices and likenesses of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Gov. Kathy Hochul, the ad was actually an A. I.-generated fabrication. It was produced by the campaign of Bruce Blakeman, the Republican candidate for governor.

Blakeman for New York

Note: The “Generated by A. I.” label and red slash added were by The New York Times. Source: AdImpact.

The ad, which included no disclaimer that it was A. I.-made, was one of more than 220 videos identified by the Wesleyan Media Project, a research group based at Wesleyan University, that used A. I.-generated fakery in ways large and small this midterm season — part of a wave of videos powered by artificial intelligence that have flooded the internet and television screens.

Candidates and political action groups, mostly tied to Republicans, have rushed to adopt the technology, spending more than $137 million to promote such ads this year, the researchers found.

“I think what we’re seeing with A. I. has surprised even us,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a professor at Wesleyan University and the co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “A. I. can be used in so many different ways that it creates new opportunities for advertising. Some of the ways in which A. I. is used, honestly, if there wasn’t a disclaimer on the ad, it would be hard to know that A. I. was there.”

Overall, among 220 ads reviewed, researchers found that …

Swipe for more

Conservative Policy Project

Alabama Conservatives

Committee to Elect Michael Lee

Hilleary for TN CD-06

Swipe for more

Women Speak Out PAC

Senate Leadership Fund PAC

Burt Jones For Georgia, Inc.

Eric Jones For Congress

Note: The “Generated by A. I.” label and red slash were added by The New York Times. Source: AdImpact.

More than 80 percent of the ads were produced by Republican campaigns or Republican-aligned political action committees. Using A. I. has allowed them to make their opponents appear alongside polarizing figures in the Democratic Party, such as Hillary Clinton or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

In one ad from Make Oklahoma Great Again, the Democratic candidate for governor was shown embracing Mrs. Clinton, cheek-to-cheek and hand-in-hand. “Clinton Lover. Trump Hater,” the on-screen text read as President Trump sulked to the side. There was no disclosure that it was A. I.-made. The group spent more than $200,000 promoting the ad on television programming in Oklahoma, according to the media tracker AdImpact.

Make Oklahoma Great Again

Note: The “Generated by A. I.” label and red slash added were by The New York Times. Source: AdImpact.

Yet some ads have gone much further. One ad showed an A. I.-generated version of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, laughing at cards that read “Death to America” and “Celebrate 9/11.” Another showed James Fishback, a Republican primary candidate for Florida governor, hosting a party with Representative Ilhan Omar and Iranian leaders who used scimitars to attack the Star of David.

Researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project suggested that Democrats may be warier of deploying A. I. than Republicans because their supporters are more critical of the technology and eager to see regulation. “Democratic candidates and groups face more reputational risk when using a tool that they are arguing should be regulated,” said Travis N. Ridout, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project and a professor at Washington State University.

One ad from James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, seemed to reflect that dynamic with a title that appeared onscreen reading: “Made by humans, not A. I.”

Ms. Franklin Fowler said there were likely many more A. I. ads than what researchers had found, since some videos were identifiable only because they appeared in one of the 30 states that require some kind of disclosure when deepfakes or other A. I. content is used in political ads. Only 31 percent of the ads the group reviewed disclosed that they used A. I.

“It’s the year of the A. I. election,” said Fred N. Davis III, the founder of Strategic Perception, an advertising firm based in Hollywood, and a 50-year veteran of campaign advertising. “It’s top of mind for everybody in my business and pretty much everybody in the political business.”

Mr. Davis was recently planning to produce a political ad that would have cost nearly $2 million before A. I., requiring hundreds of actors, a wardrobe department, catered meals, and a daylong shoot with tradespeople, cameras, lighting — the works.

Instead, he is planning to use A. I. to create the scene, bringing the ad’s total cost down to about $200,000.

A. I.-generated videos have quickly become an alternative to stock footage that once dominated campaign ads — video, for example, of families furrowing their brows over a stack of bills at a dining table. A. I. can create such scenes instantly and for a fraction of the cost, without viewers even noticing that anything was fabricated.

The campaign for Chip Keaton, a Republican candidate for Oklahoma governor, used A. I. in a similar way. A brief shot at the start of one campaign ad showed a still photograph of Mr. Keaton from his time as an Oklahoma state trooper — but brought to life with his head tilting upward, revealing a broad smile. Mr. Keaton’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Chip Keating For Governor 2026

Note: Only portions of this video were generated by A. I. The label and red slash were added by The New York Times. Source: AdImpact.

“If somebody had a tough childhood growing up, they may not have had any pictures of it, but you can recreate what being alone in a room at Christmastime was like with A. I., and that’s helpful,” Mr. Davis said. “It’s not being deceitful. It really happened.”

Some political operatives have pushed back on requirements to disclose A. I. in such cases because the labels can make the ad seem untrustworthy. “It may just be that it is an editing tool that doesn’t change the nature of the content and is not deceptive,” said Julie Sweet, the director of advocacy and industry relations at the American Association of Political Consultants, a trade group.

“Once you put the disclaimer on, it doesn’t help people distinguish between what is the ‘real stuff’ and which is the A. I.-generated stuff,” she said.

Ms. Sweet’s organization is pushing for federal regulations that would override the patchwork of state laws that require various disclosures, with the goal of labeling A. I.-generated content that is “deceptive” while offering broad protections for political speech.

Bruce Schneier, a security technologist who teaches at Harvard and the University of Toronto, said requiring labeling is just part of the solution. “The problem isn’t A. I.,” he said. “The problem is deception. And it turns out that deception is, you know, a pretty good strategy.”

Mr. Blakeman, the Republican candidate for governor in New York, has been one of the most prolific adopters of A. I.-made media, publishing a flurry of A. I.-generated attack ads this year to his social media feed — at least 22 of them since April. Only a few included a disclosure that A. I. was used or that the video was “manipulated.”

Swipe for more

Note: The “Generated by A. I.” label and red slash added by The New York Times. Source: AdImpact.

The New York State Democratic Party filed a complaint with the state’s Board of Elections in August against Mr. Blakeman’s use of A. I. in advertising, claiming that he had violated a state law requiring political communications that are “materially deceptive” to be labeled A. I.-generated. Mr. Blakeman’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment but told an ABC affiliate in September that the ad was satirical and no disclosure was required.

Misinformation watchdogs had feared that A. I.-generated impersonations of candidates, called deepfakes, and other highly misleading A. I. content would flood the midterms. Instead, researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project found, many ads used A. I. either to make simply innocuous alterations to photographs or videos or to create images too absurd to be believed.

Campaign strategists said voters may object to ads they see as fake or manipulative. Negative attack ads are already unpopular, so adding A. I. on top could create more anger among voters than support.

But Mr. Davis, the ad executive, said that voters are likely to appreciate A. I. ads if they are funny or emotional without being deceptive. He pointed to Spencer Pratt, a former Republican candidate for mayor of Los Angeles, who published reams of A. I.-generated attack ads against opponents, earning plaudits from supporters like Mr. Davis who thought the ads were funny and eye-catching.

Despite the attention, Mr. Pratt failed to build a coalition of supporters and placed third in the primary behind two Democratic candidates.

“You use the entertainment value to get attention, make them listen,” Mr. Davis said. “But then once they’re listening, you better tell them something that makes them vote for you.”

One of the interesting questions that came from this reporting was what to do about labeling A. I. inside ads. I assumed that "label everything that's A. I." would become the status quo. But political operatives made some good points about why that might be unrealistic. A lot of the A. I. fakery was pretty subtle, and honestly pretty innocuous. It reminded me of stock footage that campaigns always buy to populate their videos. (The classic image is the concerned family around a dining table with a stack of bills.) Should you label that kind of clip if that was A. I.-made? And how? And why? When the operatives suggested that only manipulative and deceptive imagery should be labeled, I pressed them to define when something becomes deceptive. Isn't that in the eye of the beholder? It's something we're all going to have to figure out.

Stuart A. Thompson writes for The Times about online influence, including the people, places and institutions that shape the information we all consume.

What Life Is Like in Kyiv as Russia Tries to Make It Unlivable

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

A day in the Ukrainian capital, a new kind of battlefield far from the front, where daily life means assessing — and accepting — deadly risks.

A day in the Ukrainian capital, a new kind of battlefield far from the front, where daily life means assessing — and accepting — deadly risks.

A destroyed garage on Oct. 7 after an attack on an industrial complex that killed two security guards in Kyiv. Credit...

Supported by

By Kim BarkerMaria Varenikova and Oleksandra Mykolyshyn

Photographs by Jędrzej Nowicki

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

The air-raid alarm went off at 3:11 a. m. but offered little warning. Within three minutes, the missiles started to hit, almost 10 teeth-rattling booms that jolted Nikita Horskyi and Alona Horska awake.

The couple launched into what has become a familiar ritual in recent weeks. Mr. Horskyi scooped up their two children. Ms. Horska assembled makeshift beds in the hallway. Their 16-story apartment building has no shelter, and they knew that two walls offered more protection than the exterior wall alone.

Mark, their 10-year-old, thought, “God, help us,” as he said he does after every explosion. He hugged his stuffed goose and curled up in the hallway on a thin mat and a pillow resembling a smiling green monster. Arina, 5, lay down on a blowup bed with sheets of pastel bunnies and hedgehogs.

The family fell back asleep, accustomed to this particular nightmare, until the next missiles hit, two of them nearby, including one that killed a pair of security guards. Mark woke to the sound of glass shattering outside. He fell asleep for a bit longer, then he and his sister got up for school. Soon the jet-powered drones would arrive.

“Of course, it affects my mental state and my nerves,” Mark said. “I have to come up with things to calm myself down.”

This is the story of the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on a recent Wednesday, and how life here has deteriorated. The Russian missiles come more often now, not just at night but all day.

In August, new Russian drones, powered by jet engines and capable of going up to 375 miles an hour, began streaking into cities in exponentially larger numbers. They hit almost without warning. Ukraine has not figured out how to consistently intercept them.

President Trump has recently lifted sanctions on Russian diesel sales, pressured Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries and suggested that Ukraine get a new president. He has said nothing about what Russia is doing to Kyiv. Moscow is killing more civilians in Ukraine than at any time since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.

This Wednesday would be an average day. Not too quiet, not too loud. The air-raid alarm would go on and off seven times, keeping Kyiv under alert a total of about 10½ hours. Parts of the city would lose power and running water. Six people would die.

Source: Kyiv Digital.

Josh Holder/The New York Times

In the fifth year of war, Russia is trying to make the capital unlivable, drive people away and force Ukraine to capitulate. Kyiv, a city shaped like a heart, has become a new kind of battlefield far from the front in eastern Ukraine, where Russian forces have been unable to win the war.

Kyiv has given no indication that it will give up. But it will suffer.

People here once coped with major missile attacks every seven to 10 days and the occasional drone that made it past Kyiv’s defenses. Life was sometimes miserable, like during power cuts last winter. But it was often joyful, with “Blade Runner”-themed raves and pouty influencers parading down hipster streets with camera crews. That Kyiv has been muted. Life has become grayer.

Russia has threatened to knock out power, heat and water in Kyiv this winter. This month Moscow started trying to cut the city in two by hitting bridges over the Dnipro River, which divides the east, where rents are lower, from the west, where most people work.

Every decision, small or big, feels fraught with what-ifs that could be life-changing. People in Kyiv first decide where to sleep. A tent in a subway station. A car in an underground parking garage. A mattress in the hallway. A gamble in bed.

Shopping has turned into a Sisyphean task, because many larger stores make people leave when the sirens start. School is constantly interrupted, because children must go to the schools’ shelters for every alert.

Mark often finds himself in his school’s basement, which is rented out to a gym called the Shogun Fight Club.

There are punching bags, wrestling mats and concrete walls, but no desks or chairs. The children cannot study there. Some follow the paths of drones on apps.

Others play games, like one where a few boys pretend to be Ukrainian recruitment officers and then tackle other boys on the wrestling mats to send them to imaginary front lines. Or the one where the boys throw paper airplanes and paper drones at a burning building drawn on the gym wall in pencil, complete with people waving their hands for help.

Anatoliy Kavunenko, 66, woke before dawn on Wednesday for his early shift. Despite the ongoing alert, he decided to go to his nearby job as a security guard. His wife, Antonina, packed him lunch: eggplant with garlic and buns stuffed with mushrooms. Mr. Kavunenko walked out the door.

About 5:12 a. m., the second round of ballistic missiles hit. Mrs. Kavunenko heard a thundering explosion and tried to call her husband. His phone rang and rang.

Every missile, every drone, changes a neighborhood’s life, a Russian roulette that has damaged thousands of buildings in Kyiv. When the alert ended at 7:05 a. m., people emerged into the acrid, smoky air that has blanketed Kyiv almost every morning for the past two months.

On the east side of the river, a missile set fire to garages over an area the size of a tennis court.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Mrs. Kavunenko, 64, ran there, still wearing her dark-green velvet pajama pants and a light black coat. Firefighters told her that one of the two burned corpses on the ground in front of her was the body of Anatoliy, her husband.

“My brain can’t accept that this black piece of coal is my Tolik,” she said, using his nickname. She held her hand over her heart and took a deep breath.

“Please help me. How can I find out if this is him?”

The Shogun Fight Club shelter doesn’t have room for all students during air-raid alerts, so they attend school in morning and afternoon shifts. Mark’s classes last from 8:30 a. m. until noon. Some days, he never leaves the basement.

Things were better on Wednesday. His fifth-grade class made it through math. In English, the children learned how to pronounce different rooms in a house. At 9:48 a. m., as students practiced the word “bedroom,” an alert went off. Some students cheered. Everyone packed their bags.

The rest of the morning was quiet. Mr. Horskyi, 36, risked driving his motorcycle over the bridge to his office in the frequently battered neighborhood of Lukianivka on the west side.

Mr. Horskyi’s office looks out at two buildings hit by jet-powered drones the week before. Moving trucks had shown up at one building. Mr. Horskyi, who has a business designing motorcycle clothing, had thought about moving, too.

“Sometimes I think that Kyiv is suffering even more than the cities located closer to Russia,” he said. “Right now, it’s like a tricky, tricky question, a tricky choice to leave or to stay. Because actually I love Kyiv.”

About 1 p. m., the air had cleared of smoke, and Oksana Stelmashchuk, 40, who lives a few blocks away, decided to go for a walk with her baby, Sophia. She looked up at an apartment building where pieces of window frames hung from blown-out windows, and stepped back.

Sophia was born into this reality, on Aug. 26, as drones hit a building next to the maternity hospital. Now, her baby was crying, so Ms. Stemaschchuk sat down on a bench in a nearby playground to feed her.

“All the playgrounds in our area are empty now,” she said. At 1:24 p. m., the air-raid alert sounded again. Ms. Stelmashchuk grabbed her phone to check what was flying: only one drone on the outskirts of Kyiv.

“It is still far away, my girl,” she told her baby.

At a nearby McDonald’s, which has been hit at least nine times, the menu was a shadow of its former self. All the attacks in recent months meant it had been stripped to the essentials — burgers and fries. There was no Coca-Cola.

At 3:29 p. m., the air-raid alert went off. Everyone inside the restaurant left for the nearby subway station, the customers hurriedly eating fries. Seventeen minutes later, the alarm ended. The workers filed back up the stairs.

Nearby, people waited for a tram. The air-raid alarm sounded again.

“We’re just so tired of it all,” said Heorhii Vasyliev, 52, who travels all over Kyiv for his construction job.

A drone hit in the distance, a low boom. “Oh,” he said, exhaling. “What can you call normal about any of this? Is this normal? Is war normal?”

On and off, off and on, the alerts continued. A drone on the west side of the river set fire to a Soviet-era, five-story apartment building, where mostly retired people lived. A charred piece of a balcony hung from a nearby tree. Firefighters rushed to put out the flames.

Firefighters hose down a balcony after a drone set fire to a Soviet-era, five-story apartment building.

Inna Sadova, 68, who lives next door, was in her kitchen when the explosion shook her home. Her building has no shelter.

“The neighboring building has a basement, but a basement like that is more of a mass grave than a shelter,” she said.

The jet-powered drones kept coming, and the list of minor atrocities unknown almost anywhere else in the world continued. Two people died on the west side of the river when debris from a drone interception hit a parked car. Two more people would die on the east side after a drone hit a 12-floor apartment building about nine miles north of the Horskyi apartment.

The power went out in much of the city. The water, too, stopped working in parts of Kyiv. So did trams, trolley buses and parts of the subway on the west side. On the east, an entire district of high-rise apartment blocks blinked out, one after the other.

The Horskyi family made the best of it. They lost electricity for three hours, the first time in months, but it came back on, and they had water. In the early evening, they took their French bulldog, Marcy, for a walk, near a building that had been hit 10 days earlier by a drone, where Mark’s history teacher lives. Mark was fascinated that people still lived on the floor above the strike.

The children ate burgers for dinner. They brushed their teeth, put on their pajamas and climbed into their twin beds in their bedroom.

“I didn’t sleep very well last night,” Mark said. “I’ll probably fall asleep really quickly. I’ll just pass out.”

Still, it was a good day, all in all, the children said. Soon they turned off the lights.

Olha Konovalova and Constant Méheut contributed reporting.

I'm one of the reporters on this story about a day in the life of Kyiv. We wanted to be able to show our readers what it's like to be here on the ground since the increase in Russian missile attacks and attacks by new jet-powered drones. Often these attacks by Russia kill one or two people, not enough to merit a headline in the international media. But the constant booms of drones and missiles are relentless now. It's made life much more challenging. People are leaving Kyiv. Ukraine shows no sign of capitulating to Russian demands, but everyone here knows civilians will suffer. Look forward to hearing from readers about what they think.

Kim Barker is a Times reporter writing in-depth stories about the war in Ukraine.

Maria Varenikova covers Ukraine and its war with Russia.

Is Anyone Actually in Charge of the Democratic Party? And Does It Matter?

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Context

This year’s midterm elections are a test of whether a party can be a success and a failure at the same time.

By Charles Homans

It’s hard to think of a worse recent year for the Democratic establishment. It’s also hard to think of a better one.

The Democratic National Committee, ostensibly the nerve center of that establishment, was $2 million in debt as of July, its members in open revolt against their chairman, Ken Martin, a party lifer from Minnesota who was elected last year on a promise to expand the Democrats’ appeal. This year’s primaries played host to a rolling left-wing insurgency, in which progressives and socialists wrestled nominations away from incumbents and favorites of the party’s elected leadership and donor class. Crucial Senate contests in Maine and Michigan became expensive, bruising civil wars. “The establishment Democratic Party is a failed enterprise,” Senator Michael Bennet of Colorado — hardly a bomb thrower — said this month in an interview with the journalist David Sirota.

And yet this same party is, by most polling, the odds-on favorite to retake the House of Representatives next month. It’s also as likely as not to win control of the Senate, a prize that seemed hopelessly out of reach a year ago, when the Democrats faced their lowest approval ratings in a quarter-century of polling. The main super PAC for Senate Democrats is raising more money than it ever has. Republicans are increasingly allocating resources to deep-red states and districts where they have not had to seriously defend seats in years. This is the odd koan hanging over Democratic politics this year: Is it possible for a party to be a failure and a success at the same time?

If the answer is yes — and it is — then it has a lot to do with the vagueness of what we mean when we talk about the Democratic Party and the establishment that in theory runs it. In political rhetoric, the party “establishment” is a noun or, more usually, an epithet that can mean practically anything and anyone — from beleaguered apparatchiks like Martin to elected leaders like Chuck Schumer to talking heads like James Carville, from centrist purple-state senators who enrage liberals to liberal donors in San Francisco and Manhattan who enrage centrists. Are all these people the Democratic establishment? Are any of them?

In their 2024 book, “The Hollow Parties,” the political scientists Daniel Schlozman and Sam Rosenfeld coin a term for the hazy geography of influence that, in very different ways, now constitutes the modern Democratic and Republican establishments: the “party blob.” The formal party structures, they observe, are now overshadowed by advocacy organizations, campaign-consulting firms, donor networks, dark-money super PACs, partisan media and others that have, over time, informally taken on much of the work of selecting candidates and winning elections that once fell to the parties themselves.

These groups share partisan commitments but have no real accountability to voters or official party leaders. Their priorities and incentives are often more complicated than simply winning elections, and they can exist at cross-purposes. But their defining characteristic is their diffuseness. In the party blob, no one is really in charge.

Seventy-five years ago, a cigar-masticating ward boss might have struggled to explain what the Democratic Party — then a kludgy assemblage of Northern liberals, Southern segregationists and blue-collar union workers — stood for. But he could have explained easily enough what it was. The Democratic Party consisted of the state parties, their local affiliates and the national campaign committees. Its leaders appointed delegates who nominated candidates and maintained lists of voters. And they did whatever was necessary to get the latter to cast ballots for the former.

Americans have been conflicted about the role of parties in politics for as long as the country has had them. But the party system mostly withstood challenges to its supremacy until the 1960s, when societal and technological developments like suburban migration, television and public-opinion research began eating into the official Republican and Democratic organs’ monopolies on influence. The most serious blow to the old system came after the Democrats’ cataclysmic 1968 national convention, in which party elites orchestrated the nomination of Vice President Hubert H. Humphrey amid furious street protests. Following Humphrey’s loss in the general election that November, the party, faced with a crisis of legitimacy, agreed to reforms that shifted most of the power to nominate candidates to primary voters.

The new rules stripped influence from big-city mayors and other traditional machers and allowed interest groups — championing constituencies from professional-class feminists to Black and Hispanic voters and politicians, and causes from environmentalism to civil liberties — to step in as power brokers. (Surveying the first post-reform national convention in 1972, one delegate sniffed, “There is too much hair and not enough cigars.”) The reforms didn’t just redistribute power; they also reordered the Democrats’ internal incentives. The newly empowered groups justified their existence less by winning victories for the Democratic Party than within it, claiming turf for their own often-conflicting policy priorities and representational interests.

The modern Democratic party blob was shaped by the post-1968 reforms, but also by a very different erosion of party power that occurred in the G. O. P. over the same period: the rise of a party-conquering conservative movement backed by business-linked philanthropists. Liberal activists first lamented that movement’s network of think tanks, grass-roots organizations and ideologically aligned media, then tried to imitate it, building their own party-outside-of-a-party infrastructure.

Two major external developments have radically accelerated the parties’ blobification in the 21st century. The internet lowered barriers to organizing, fund-raising and communicating outside of party systems, enabling candidacies as disparate as those of Barack Obama, Bernie Sanders and Donald Trump, which shared practically nothing besides an inclination to push at the constraints of the existing party categories. Supreme Court decisions removing nearly all constraints on campaign contributions, meanwhile, have produced an arms race in spending by outside groups, which now eclipses the parties’ and campaigns’ own.

Focused by common purpose in an election season, the constituent elements of the party blob can outwardly resemble a political party. They share partisan loyalties and enmities and agree broadly if not entirely on matters of policy. They pool resources toward the goal of electing some politicians and defeating others and, in 2024, even managed the extraordinary challenge of easing a sitting president out of the race and quickly building consensus around a replacement.

To voters on the receiving end of outside groups’ phone calls, email barrages, TV ads, mailings and door-to-door harangues in the weeks before Election Day, the difference from the parties’ own work is often imperceptible — enough so that a reasonable person might ask what, exactly, is so bad about the blob. The smoke-filled room was never much loved by anyone who wasn’t in it, after all. Is the further decline of the parties in favor of other actors that do many of the same things, often more effectively, really a problem for anyone but Ken Martin?

One answer is that political parties are a little like newspapers: inefficient and anachronistic, maybe, but also delivering intangible benefits that are more clearly visible in retrospect, amid their decline, than they were in their era of hegemony. The Democratic Party’s retreat from red states and rural counties, for instance, clearly hastened its evolution into a party by and for professional-class urban and suburban liberals, confined by that class’s cramped political imagination and language. (“Can I level-set with you?” the subject line of a recent D. N. C. fund-raising email asks.)

Relying on outside organizations and super PACs has also brought a fundamental instability to the work of campaigning. Over the past decade and a half, Democrats have come to depend on grass-roots organizations focused on Black, Latino and young people to register and mobilize voters. But the downsides of that reliance became clear in recent cycles, as those demographics grew less uniformly Democratic and groups like the now-defunct New Georgia Project — a powerful force in Democratic campaigns in that state for a decade — fell victim to chronic nonprofit problems of infighting and fundraising struggles.

Dark money is even more unstable, as the structured donor alliances of two decades ago are supplanted by plutocratically wealthy individual givers. Republican campaigns in the last two elections, for instance, have been heavily funded by a relative handful of Silicon Valley billionaires, some of whom were until recently aligned with Democrats — most significantly Elon Musk, whose $276 million investment in Republican campaign efforts since July dwarfs all donors’ spending combined on the equivalent Democratic effort this year. And the flood of unaccountable outside money has also brought with it a backlash. In this year’s Democratic primary upsets — most dramatically Michigan’s Senate race — left-wing challengers have defeated better-funded opponents in large part by making the funding itself a campaign issue.

This state of affairs, however bleak, is very different from the bleak future that political observers once anticipated would follow the decline of the parties. In the 1980s, a common line of criticism held that the old party organizations had given way to an increasingly empty, image-oriented politics industry: a simulacrum of a participatory process that in reality was tightly controlled by what Joan Didion, surveying the 1988 presidential primaries, described as “a self-created and self-referring class, a new kind of managerial elite.” This was a party blob washed clean of both the corner-bar grit of the machines and the idealism of the reformers who had toppled them, its strategists and media consultants busy re-engineering elections into a post-ideological consumer act like choosing between Coke and Pepsi, building stables of politicians bred mostly for their hair and teeth.

But where, in this picture, would you put the Democratic Socialists of America, which backed the successful challengers in several of this year’s Democratic primaries? The D. S. A.’s rise is at once a story of party-blobification and of a revolt against it. Like the conservatives of the 1970s, the group frankly views the party it occupies as a host for an ideological movement rather than as a partner. It also practices an exaggerated form of the interest-group litmus-test politics that came to dominate Democratic politics in the post-1968 era, measuring its own strength less by general-election victories than by its ability to enforce candidate loyalty to left-maximalist positions.

At the same time, the D. S. A. is an authentically participatory organization, tapping the sort of civic-minded enthusiasm that once fueled party activism — “the least-hollow party in America,” as Schlozman describes it, despite not being a party at all.

Its rapid ascent in Democratic politics, and its candidates’ upset wins, suggests that many Democratic voters have an appetite for the political-participation hack it represents: It is a means of engaging seriously in Democratic Party politics while also casting a vote of no-confidence in the party itself. And the same Democratic consultant class that Didion once supposed would produce an infinite regression of Michael Dukakises has, this cycle, mostly drawn attention for its recruitment of candidates like Graham Platner, the scandal-plagued former Senate nominee in Maine: marketable left-wing insurgents who simultaneously embody an appetite for partisan combat and a skepticism of party.

One obvious factor in this is the extreme negative polarization of American politics — a phenomenon still in its infancy in the ’80s and now advanced enough that Charlie Cook, the veteran political analyst, has suggested thinking of the Democrats’ likely victories next month as a “red undertow” rather than a “blue wave,” in which Republicans are sucked under by Trump’s unpopularity even in the absence of a serious surge of enthusiasm for Democrats. It’s a darkly funny end stage to reach in the country’s long, ambivalent history with parties. If Americans have finally made them irrelevant, it is not by transcending them, but by absorbing what we least liked about them. In a way, we have all become the blob.

Charles Homans is a reporter for The Times and The Times Magazine, covering national politics.

Connections Coach

The comedian may be an unexpected choice for a documentary about the disgraced Theranos founder, but his TV shows suggest why he’s a good fit.

HBO; Showtime; A24Credit...

Supported by

By Kellina Moore

Is the cringe comedian Nathan Fielder cocky or insecure? A conniving prankster or a hapless do-gooder? Sincere or buried under layers of irony? His hard-to-read demeanor is an integral part of his comedy: As his subjects and the audience try to parse that, the nervous giggles ensue.

Fielder is also behind one of the most anticipated documentaries of the year, “You Can See Everything,” which he directed alongside Lance Oppenheim (“Primetime”). The film, out Friday, follows the disgraced founder of Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes, in the days before she is to report to federal prison camp to serve her sentence for her conviction of four counts of fraud. The film’s surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in September stirred up a near-frantic buzz that only intensified after the screening at the New York Film Festival.

To the uninitiated, it might seem odd that a comedian is directing a documentary, but Fielder’s work often employs documentarian practices to humorous effect and blurs the line between reality and fiction. Before you see “Everything” (or after) — here’s a guide to everything else Fielder.

2013–17

Streaming on HBO Max, Hulu and Paramount Plus

What started as “Nathan on Your Side,” a segment on the Canadian news comedy program “This Hour Has 22 Minutes,” grew into Fielder’s first series. In it, the comic, who says he “graduated from one of Canada’s top business schools with really good grades,” comes up with outlandish plans to help out small businesses.

A frozen yogurt shop debuts a new excrement flavor to draw in customers; a bar stages an elaborate play to allow patrons to smoke indoors; an out-of-work mall Santa offers discount photos in July — all harebrained schemes that take typical marketing tactics and turn them on their heads.

“Nathan for You” combines the energy of a prank show (including, arguably, some of the cruelty) with the structure of business-improvement series like “Kitchen Nightmares.” The best known of these stunts may be “Dumb Starbucks,” in which Fielder helped a struggling Los Angeles coffee shop rebrand as the giant chain thanks to laws regarding parodies. The antic made national news, with some even speculating that the artist Banksy was behind it.

The show introduced audiences to Fielder’s awkward persona, proclivity for mixing documentary and comedy and knack for committing wholeheartedly to a ridiculous bit with an utterly straight face.

Save to your watch list:

2022–25

Streaming on HBO Max

Fielder’s critically acclaimed follow-up to “Nathan for You” combined some of the elements from the earlier show — the docu-comedy, the elaborate setups, Fielder’s persona — and an HBO-size budget. Inspired by the unpredictability of life and human behavior, Fielder tries to help himself and others prepare for difficult moments by creating intricate stages for rehearsals.

The first season starts with a man getting ready to confess to his trivia team that he lied about having a college degree. Fielder employs a full-scale replica of the Brooklyn bar where the trivia night is held and fills it with actors. Later, Fielder aims to help a woman decide if she wants to have children or not, using yet another large set along with child actors and even a robot baby.

In the second season, Fielder tackled airplane safety, arguing that a large portion of plane crashes are caused by miscommunication in the cockpit. Cue the full-scale airport replica, a surreal re-creation of the pilot Chesley Sullenberger’s life and Fielder’s successful effort to obtain his own pilot’s license.

Always toying with reality, the show makes viewers question what they are seeing. Frequently, something presented as straightforward truth will be revealed as just another rehearsal led by Fielder as the director with a laptop harnessed to his chest.

Save to your watch list:

2023–24

Streaming on Paramount+

This twisty, uncategorizable puzzle of a show represented Fielder’s first foray into pure fiction. Fielder and Benny Safdie created this drama-thriller-horror-cringe comedy about a newlywed couple (Fielder and Emma Stone) struggling to navigate their tumultuous relationship while filming an HGTV show about eco-friendly homes. Fielder takes his usual awkward, desperate-to-be-loved persona and plays it against a skilled actress. Safdie plays their pushy (and sometimes creepy) producer.

Even in the realm of fiction, Fielder explores questions of truth, the power of framing and the ethics of reality television as the cast and crew try to do good but tie themselves into increasingly complicated knots. The sequences of the show-within-a-show contrasted with what we see behind the scenes reminds us that truth is in the eye of the editor.

Things get increasingly strange, and the 10-episode show ends with a shocking, surreal finale that must be seen to be believed.

Behind a White House Feud That Is Bitter Even by Trump-Era Standards

The New York Times October 16, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

Advertisement

Supported by

Two Trump allies — Alina Habba Mildon and Richard Grenell — are locked in a raging dispute that has its roots in the battle for a share of the spoils in Venezuela.

By Tyler Pager and Anatoly Kurmanaev

The accusations were shocking.

Alina Habba Mildon, who had been one of President Trump’s personal lawyers, stormed into the Oval Office last week intent on taking down another prominent ally of the president. Her target was Richard Grenell, who had earlier served as Mr. Trump’s special envoy to Venezuela and as head of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

Mrs. Mildon had just married a Turkish investor, Turhan Mildon, who has extensive business holdings in Venezuela. He had been in regular contact with Mr. Grenell the previous year both about Venezuela and about supporting the Kennedy Center.

But now Mrs. Mildon was telling Mr. Trump that Mr. Grenell had misallocated millions of dollars that her husband had sent Mr. Grenell in 2025 intended for the Kennedy Center. A lawyer for Mr. Mildon followed up this week by sending the White House documentation intended to back up the accusation, including a text message in which Mr. Grenell was purported to have said he wanted to make Mr. Mildon the “American face down in V,” referring to Venezuela.

Mr. Grenell denied the accusations, calling them absurd.

What actually happened is now at the center of a White House storm that has left Will Scharf, the White House counsel, with the job of discerning who is telling the truth.

The accusations are part of a long-running battle among Mr. Trump’s allies and supporters for a share of the spoils in Venezuela, whose resource riches are now effectively under American control.

This article is based on interviews with more than a dozen people with knowledge of the events, most of whom spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the accusations and the private Oval Office meeting.

Mrs. Mildon went to the White House on Friday after The New York Times sent Mr. Mildon a series of questions about his business interests in Venezuela and his relationships with Trump allies. In the Oval Office, Mrs. Mildon told Mr. Trump that in May 2025, Mr. Mildon transferred $17.6 million to an account at Mr. Grenell’s direction, the people said. Her initial story varied, they said, but she eventually claimed that most of the money was for a business transaction, the details of which remain unclear. Mr. Mildon, she told the president, believed that $5.6 million from the total sum was going to be set aside for the Kennedy Center.

But the money never got to the center, she said.

Mr. Trump, who named himself chairman of the Kennedy Center, called Mr. Scharf into the Oval Office to hear Mrs. Mildon’s accusations.

On Wednesday night, Mr. Mildon’s lawyer sent text messages and a wire transfer receipt to Mr. Scharf to back up Mrs. Mildon’s claims, according to two of the people familiar with the sequence of events. The New York Times has not verified the veracity of Mrs. Mildon’s accusations, which were first reported on Wednesday by Axios.

Mr. Grenell said no financial transaction took place between him and Mr. Mildon or entities related to him.

“I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I’ve never received any payment from him,” Mr. Grenell said.

The dispute centers on a multimillion-dollar wire transfer that Mr. Mildon made to a Texas defense and security equipment company called TX-AT. Mrs. Mildon told the White House that the transfer was made at Mr. Grenell’s direction.

Mr. Grenell said he consulted for TX-AT in 2024 but had no connection to the company at the time that Mr. Mildon says he made the transfer. Mr. Grenell said he had never solicited payments on the firm’s behalf. Representatives at TX-AT did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Mr. and Mrs. Mildon declined to comment, as did Mr. Scharf, who attended the couple’s wedding last month. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesman for the Kennedy Center said the organization is conducting an internal review of relevant pledges and funds and will share its findings with its board.

Last year, as Mr. Mildon worked to build ties to the Trump administration, he became a frequent guest at the Kennedy Center, where he networked with prominent Republicans, and eventually met his future wife, Mrs. Mildon. After one gala concert, he pledged to donate $270,000. He only paid this week, after The Times questioned him on why he had never fulfilled that pledge.

Mr. Mildon and Mr. Grenell shared an interest in Venezuela. Mr. Mildon has extensive business interests there and Mr. Grenell at the time served as Mr. Trump’s special envoy to the country.

Both men had tried to influence Mr. Trump’s policy toward Venezuela for their benefit. And both ended up being sidelined by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who in mid-2025 adopted a more aggressive approach that brought down President Nicolás Maduro and installed Mr. Rubio’s chosen successor in power.

One of the documents that Mr. Mildon’s lawyer sent to the White House includes a text message from May 2025 that purports to show Mr. Grenell saying he wanted to make Mr. Mildon the “American face down in V,” referring to Venezuela. Mr. Grenell said he had never sent that message or anything to that effect.

Mrs. Mildon was once closely allied with Mr. Grenell, but the two have fallen out over the disagreements between him and her current husband.

Mr. Grenell and Mr. Mildon first met around late 2024. Mr. Grenell said he and Mr. Mildon have had some business discussions but that their relationship was primarily social.

The Times reported earlier this week that Mr. Mildon faces the loss of his lucrative cement business in Venezuela, because of his ties to the inner circle of Mr. Maduro, who is in custody in the United States, where he faces drug trafficking charges. In particular, U. S. officials and intelligence officers have scrutinized Mr. Mildon’s relationship to the man who awarded him the cement contract, a Maduro confidant named Alex Saab.

Mr. Mildon says he is 29, but his age is listed as 25 on documents in the United States and corporate records in Britain. He declined to comment on the discrepancy.

Before the United States captured Mr. Maduro, aides to Mr. Trump and some U. S. intelligence officials expressed concern about Mr. Mildon’s work with the Maduro government, according to multiple people briefed on the matter.

Mariana Martínez and Isayen Herrera contributed reporting from Caracas.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Anatoly Kurmanaev covers Venezuela for The Times.
